rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/3p4/3P4/2N5/PPP1PPPP.comment: This is an ultra-rare continuation, yet it is the choice of several very strong Grandmasters. It is somewhat outside the scope of this course, yet we have decided to dedicate a small file to it in order to point you in the right direction. By delaying ...Nf6, Black aims to nip White's central counterplay in the bud.

rn1qkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/3p1b2/3P4/2N5/PPP1PP.comment: It is crucial to get right down to business! White prepares e2-e4, aiming to provoke Black to develop the knight to f6.

rn2kbnr/pp3pp1/1q2p1b1/2pP2B1/4P3/2N5/PP.comment: Markoja-Richter, corr. 2015. White overwhelmingly dominates in the center, and the b2-pawn is clearly untouchable:

rn1qkbnr/ppp2ppp/4p3/5b2/3Pp3/2N2P2/PPP3.comment: An important inclusion, preventing the check on h4 and expanding on the kingside in typical Jobava fashion.

rn1qkbnr/ppp2pp1/4p2p/5b2/3Pp2P/2N2P2/PP.comment: This does not fundamentally change the nature of the game.

rn1qkbnr/pp4p1/2p1pp1p/5b1P/3Pp3/2N1BP2/.comment: The position resembles an improved version of a Fantasy Caro-Kann. White's knight heads to f4, and White will castle queenside after moving the queen either to d2 or even to d3.

rn1qkbnr/ppp2pp1/4p2p/5b2/3Pp1PP/2N2P2/P.comment: An easy move to forget about! Both the knight on f1, as well as the bishop on g6, are trapped! Black cannot save either of them.

rn1qkb1r/pp3ppb/2p1pn1p/7P/3Pp1P1/2NB1P2.comment: Boeven-Mueller, German Senior Championship 2015. White opted for the rather odd Nce2, but simple improving moves yield an excellent position, e.g.

rn2kb1r/ppq2ppb/2p1pn1p/7P/3Pp1P1/2NB1P2.comment: White's aim is to regroup with Bc1, Nhf4, followed by Qd2 and Nd3, controlling key squares in the center. Black is dreadfully cramped.

rn2k2r/ppp2pp1/4pqbp/8/1b1PP3/2NB1N2/PPP.comment: White's central control and prospects along the f-file guarantee us a long-lasting initiative.

rnbqkb1r/pppppppp/5n2/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/R.comment: This is an ultra-rare continuation, yet it is the choice of several very strong Grandmasters. It is somewhat outside the scope of this course, yet we have decided to dedicate a small file to it in order to point you in the right direction. By delaying ...Nf6, Black aims to nip White's central counterplay in the bud. It is crucial to get right down to business! White prepares e2-e4, aiming to provoke Black to develop the knight to f6.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pppp/5n2/3p4/3P4/2N5/PPP1PP.comment: In this chapter, we briefly consider a few rare alternatives to the popular responses. In this chapter, we briefly consider a few rare alternatives to the popular responses.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pppp/5n2/3p4/3P1B2/2N5/PPP1.comment: This move, which maintains developmental symmetry, obviously constitutes one of Black's most popular responses.
A solid continuation, covering the b5-square once and for all.

This is the most concrete and combative response to the Jobava London. Black immediately tries to underscore the awkwardness of the knight on c3. In contrast to the (regular) London System, we do not have the possibility of supporting the pawn with c2-c3. In the dark ages, White automatically responded with 4.e3, and after 4...cxd4 5.exd4, we reach a position that resembles an inferior version of an exchange Caro-Kann. However, the presence of the knight on c3 affords us another exciting possibility that has completely revitalized this variation!

This move does not have too much independent value. Most of the time, Black follows up with 4...Bf5, transposing to a line that we analyze via the 3...Bf5 move order (3...Bf5 4.Nf3 c6). In this file, we give the one legitimate independent variation, in which Black quickly develops their queen to b6 and probes for queenside weaknesses. This move does not have too much independent value. Most of the time, Black follows up with 4...Bf5, transposing to a line that we analyze via the 3...Bf5 move order (3...Bf5 4.Nf3 c6). In this file, we give the one legitimate independent variation, in which Black quickly develops their queen to b6 and probes for queenside weaknesses. However, the presence of the knight on c3 affords us another exciting possibility that has completely revitalized this variation!
This is the most popular move on Lichess, and it is the one you are likely to face at least half the time. Black opens up the dark-squared bishop and establishes a firmer presence in the center.

Most Grunfeld and King's Indian players choose this system. The resulting positions are quite complex, and markedly different from those that arise after 3...Bf5, 3...e6, and 3...a6. We begin by solidifying our center and initiating a furious kingside assault.
Unfortunately for Black, this move virtually loses on the spot. This move loses for a similar reason.

rn1qkb1r/ppp1pppp/5n2/3p1b2/3P1B2/2N5/PP.comment: We answer the symmetrical variation in outwardly modest fashion, opening up our light-squared bishop and setting up the future idea of g2-g4. A few years back, 4.f3 was virtually automatic, but this innocuous-looking move has overtaken 4.f3 in popularity and in hype -- for good reason. Against most of Black's setups, our knight heads directly for e5, as it does in almost every other variation.

rn1qkb1r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/3p1b2/3P1B2/2N1P3/.comment: At this point, Black is at a major crossroads. There are countless ways for Black to develop, starting with the natural developing moves (5...Nbd7, 5...Bd6, and 5...Bb4) and ending with more extravagant moves such as 5...Ne4. We must consider all of them, since White's responses are a bit different in each case.

rn1qkb1r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/3p1b2/3P1B2/2N1PN2.comment: The most popular response by far. Most players do not see the danger awaiting them on the kingside!

This is the most common move on Lichess, with 127,000 or so games at the time of analysis (and, hopefully, many more after the course enters the chess bloodstream :). Believe it or not, this natural developing move is eighth (yes, eighth!) by popularity in the Lichess database. However, at the titled player level, it is the most common move, so it must be treated like a main line. Black immediately contests the e5-square, delaying the development of his dark-squared bishop until we have put our cards on the table. Now, 6.Ne5 makes no sense due to 6...Nxe5; the exchange does not yield any benefit. Instead, we aim for plan B, quickly completing our development and initiating queenside pressure.

r2qkb1r/pppn1ppp/4pn2/3p1b2/3P1B2/2N1PN2.comment: This is still very strong, even though we are no longer trying to trap the bishop. Instead, we are storming the kingside with our pawns. Black has a very hard time stopping g4-g5, which has the potential to be devastating. This leads directly to a scintillating tactical confrontation.

r2qk2r/pppnbppp/4pn2/3p4/3P1B2/2NPPN2/PP.comment: The pawn on h5 is a huge weakness which essentially precludes kingside castling. We can push e4-e5 at our leisure.

r2qkb1r/pppn1ppp/4pn2/3p1b2/3P1BP1/2N1PN.comment: It is important to combine space-grabbing pawn moves on the kingside with simple developing moves. Once the knight leaves f6, g4-g5 no longer comes with tempo, so we hold off on that move for now.

r2qkb1r/pppn1ppp/4pn2/3p4/3P1BP1/2NbPN2/.comment: Do not be fooled by the symmetrical appearance of a position like this. White has a massive kingside space advantage, as well as better-placed pieces. It is not easy for Black to find a suitable home for their bishop, and must constantly reckon with a well-timed g4-g5.

r2qkb1r/pppn1ppp/4p3/3p4/3P1BP1/3bPN2/PP.comment: Here, we recapture on d3 with the queen to preserve the integrity of the queenside. On the next move, we will castle queenside and our minor pieces will dominate in the center and on the kingside. White has a small, but very stable, advantage.

r2qkb1r/pppn1ppp/3Bpnb1/3p4/3P4/2N1PN2/P.comment: Black is entirely paralyzed, and White will have complete dominance over the d-file after the long castle. We can also stick a rook on d6 at our convenience.

r2qkb1r/pppn1ppp/4pn2/3p4/3PbBP1/2N1PN2/.comment: The presence of the pawn on f3 only helps White.

rn1qk2r/ppp2ppp/3bpn2/3p1b2/3P1B2/2N1PN2.comment: Do not be fooled by the appearance of total symmetry: the extra tempo gives us a very pleasant game. It is worth observing that 6.Ne5 - which is our recommended response to 3...a6 4.e3 Nc6 5.Nf3 Bf5 - is less attractive here since Black has already established a pawn on e6.
The customary response (see basic idea #2). White sets up the powerful threat of g2-g4.

A rare and rather dubious move, though it has been the consistent choice of several good players online. The simplest response is to trade knights and quickly push c2-c4, reaching a favorable QGD structure that we have already seen in several other lines.

rn1qk2r/ppp2ppp/3bpn2/3p1b2/3P1B2/2NBPN2.comment: Generally, it is not a great idea to capture on g6 since it hands Black the h-file, but we follow it up with a concrete and powerful idea.

An inexperienced Jobava player would now be tempted to snap off the knight, but we are seldom willing to give up our light-squared bishop for the knight. Given Black's last move, trading the bishop makes very little sense. After recapturing the bishop, Qb3 will come with tempo, leading to a nasty queenside attack and a clear advantage.

rn1qk2r/ppp2ppp/3bpn2/3p4/3P1B2/2NbPN2/P.comment: The point! It transpires that Black has great difficulty defending the pawn, since ...Bd6 drops a pawn (though White must still respond accurately - see analysis below) and ...Rc8 drops the a7 pawn (after which the knight returns to b5). Indeed, there is only one way to defend c7, and it is not all that easy to find.
This is simply bad, as it enables us to ruin Black's pawn structure. Additionally, the bishop on f5 will end up totally out of commission.
Standard Sam! We prepare the typical plan of queenside expansion with b3 and c4, and make the bishop on b4 look rather dumb.

This recapture should be automatic by now! We follow up in traditional fashion by deploying our queen to b3 and building up nasty queenside pressure along the c- and b-files. Now, 8.Ne5 transposes into a position that we reach via the move order 5...Bd6 6.Ne5 h6 7.Bd3 Bxd3 8.cxd3. However, it turns out that we actually have an even better option: we can go straight to work on the queenside.

Trading on our own terms! This clever positional move has a lot more meat on the bone than the meek 8.Bg3. White prepares c2-c4, which underscores the awkwardness of the knight on c6. White's extra tempo means that playing copycat with 8...Ne7 will not end well.

rn1qk2r/ppp2ppp/3bpn2/1N1p4/3P1B2/3bPN2/.comment: Rushing the bishop to a5. This idea constitutes one of Black's main responses to 3...e6 4.Nb5. In this version, the placement of Black's knight on d7 granmts us the ability to engineer nasty queenside pressure. This is actually the most common move, since ...Bb4-a5 is not the easiest maneuver to find for someone who is not experienced in this type of position. Now, it is crucial to refrain from 11.Nb5, which enables Black to seize the initiative with a check on a5 followed by ...Ne4. Instead, we help ourselves to another pawn! We can follow up with Rb1-b7 or Qd4. Black is in serious trouble.

rn1qk2r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/1N1p4/1b1P1B2/3bPN2.comment: Black has no compensation for the pawn. We will follow up by castling kingside; there is nothing to fear along the h-file, since the h2-pawn is very safely protected by the knight. Black will have a hard time finding shelter for their king. As a case in point, 15...Qc4 is met with the powerful 16.Ne5, angling for c6.

rn1qk2r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/bN1p4/3P1B2/2PbPN2/.comment: Deploying the queen with tempo, and preparing c3-c4. In the position after 3...e6 4.Nb5 Bb4+ 5.c3 Ba5, this move is ineffective due to ...Nc6, defending the bishop and cutting off the line of fire toward Black's king. Here, Black has no choice but to meekly withdraw the bishop, since 10...c6 runs into 11.Nd6+ followed by Nxb7.

rn1qk2r/1p3ppp/pbp1pn2/3p4/Q1PP1B2/2NbPN.comment: The queen has done its job on a4, and we now reposition it to the optimal square.

rn1qk2r/1pb2ppp/p1p1pn2/8/2QP1B2/2NbPN2/.comment: White's advantage is indisputable. After buttressing our bishop with h2-h4 and castling short, we will turn our attention toward the center, expanding with e3-e4 and solidifying our center with R(a)d1.

rn1qk2r/ppp2ppp/3bpn2/3p4/3PNB2/3bPN2/PP.comment: Eliminating the knight grants our b5-knight a nice retreating square on c3.
Let the queenside pawn storm begin!

rn1qk2r/ppp2ppp/3bpn2/3p4/3PbB2/4P3/PPPN.comment: Yet again, the knight sally to b5 is very effective.

rn1qk2r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/3p4/1b1PbB2/4P3/PPP.comment: This is a lot better than 10.c4, which would justify the placement of Black's bishop on a5. Now, the bishop is taken out of the game and we follow up with a furious queenside pawn storm.

rn1q1rk1/ppp2ppp/4pn2/3p4/1b1PbB2/2P1P3/.comment: Black is under massive pressure due to the threat of c5 as well as Nc3, when the e4-pawn, in the immortal words of GM Robert Hess, will not be long for this board. Note that ...Nf6 can be savagely met with Bg5.

rn1qk2r/1pp2ppp/p2bpn2/P2p4/3PbB2/4PN2/1.comment: We have built up a massive clamp on the queenside, and things will go from bad to worse once we stick the knight on c5.

rn1qk2r/ppp2ppp/3bpn2/3p4/3P1B2/2NbPN2/P.comment: The power of doubled pawns on full display. The first c4 break served to soften up Black's queenside, and the second instantiation of this pawn advance will cause even more problems. Transitioning to tactics! It transpires that the rook runs out of squares!

rn1qk2r/p1p2ppp/1p1bpn2/3p4/3P1B2/2NbPN2.comment: The rook has breathed its last breath.

rn1qk2r/ppp1bppp/4p3/3p4/3PnB2/2PbPN2/PP.comment: It is always worth including this move to take the sting out of ...g5, which is now duly met with Bh2.

rn1qk2r/pp2bppp/2p1p3/3p4/3PnB2/2PbPN1P/.comment: We are ready to push c4, and we can follow up by smoking the knight out of e4 with Nd2.

rn1qk2r/ppp2ppp/3bpn2/3p4/3P1B2/2NPPN2/P.comment: This leads to immediate material loss:

rn1qk2r/pp3ppp/3bpn2/2pp4/3P1B2/2NPPN2/P.comment: Keeping the tension. Of course, the impulsive 8.Nb5 would have run into 8...Qa5+, sending the knight right back to c3. Now, it appears that Black can cripple our pawn structure by capturing on d4, since Nxd4 runs into a fork. It turns out that Black is in for quite a surprise!

The most sensible option, preparing to castle kingside. Still, by resolving the central tension, we will attain a stable and long-lasting edge. This prevents Nb5, but costs Black another tempo. We pile up on the queenside without any further delay.

rn1qk2r/pp2bppp/4pn2/2pp4/3P1B2/2NPPN2/P.comment: Tabasco! This knight sally is particularly problematic in ...Nbd7 lines. With our king safely tucked away on the kingside, Black doesn't even have the option of hurrying the bishop around to c7. Before invading down the c-file, it makes sense to snap off a pawn and return to b5. Now, we get down to business. The devastating threat of Nc7+ is unstoppable.

This appears to call White's previous move into question: why provoke a move that grabs space and builds a rather imposing wall of pawns? In reality, the dutiful student of this course will know that ...b7-b5 is almost always a dreadfully weakening move, leaving behind massive holes on the light squares (particularly c6) and handing White the keys to a ravaging queenside initiative.

rn1qk2r/p3bppp/4pn2/1ppp4/3P1B2/2NPPN2/P.comment: It may appear that Black is out of the woods after recapturing on c5, but his troubles are only beginning. Note that the rook on c8 lacks a defender - this tactical deficiency is about to become very important, regardless of which piece Black decides to recapture with. Cold-blooded and ridiculously powerful. As in the 10...Qb6 line, Black suffers primarily because the rook on c8 is not sufficiently defended, so the tension down the c-file is always going to favor White. We now combine the threat of b2-b4 with sharp positional play, maneuvering our knight to the optimal d4-square.

rn1qk2r/p3bppp/4pn2/1pPp4/5B2/2NPPN2/PP3.comment: Not fearing ghosts on the c-file: there is absolutely no risk of a discovered attack, since any move by the Black knight can be shut down with Nc6, followed by Nxe7+ and Qxe7 (not to mention that our queen can also simply retreat).

rn1qk2r/p4ppp/4pn2/1pbp4/5B2/2NPPN2/PP3P.comment: Sending the bishop back, and paving the way for a straightforward and devastating tactical blow. This is a lot better than 16.Nxf7+, which only wins a pawn.
We can basically premove Rc7, after which Black will not be able to move a single muscle. Of course, 16...Bxb4 is impossible on account of 17.Rc8+.

rn1qk2r/p3bppp/4pn2/1p1p4/3P1B2/2N1PN2/P.comment: Even better than Nxf6+. The threat of Rc8, which will pick off Black's rook, forces instant resignation. A thematic tactical blow, dealing Black the ultimate punishment for failing to castle in timely fashion. We must remain careful until the end: the sloppy 15.Rxc1 would drop a piece after ...Nxd5, when the check on c8 is parried by ...Bd8 (in contrast to 13...Bb4). Black is a pawn down, and cannot cover both infiltration squares (c7 and c8) at the same time.

rn1qk2r/p4ppp/4pn2/1pbpN3/5B2/2NPP3/PP3P.comment: The rightful culmination of our lightning queenside attack. White wins the bishop.

rnq2rk1/ppB1bppp/4pn2/2Pp4/8/2NPPN2/PP3P.comment: We saw a similar position to this one (with the pawns on d4 and b2) in the 9...Bxc5 10.d4 Bb6 line - this cosmetic difference does not change all that much. Black is still in big trouble due to the threat of Nd6 and the pressure down the c-file.

rn1qk2r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/bN1p4/3P1B2/3PPN2/P.comment: 10.Rc1 is also good, but this is even better, since it essentially leads to a forced queen trade.

rn1qk2r/pp2bppp/2p1pn2/3p4/3P1B2/2NPPN2/.comment: Classic stuff, controlling the center. Black has a very hard time finding useful moves, because we have complete control over the center as well as more active pieces.

rn1qnrk1/pp3ppp/4p3/2bpP3/3P1B2/3P1N1P/P.comment: The doubled d-pawns serve us well, since we can reinforce the center on demand with d4.

rn1qk2r/ppp2ppp/3bp3/3p1b2/3PnB2/2NBPN2/.comment: We do not back down! It transpires that accepting the pawn sacrifice is unwise, owing to Black's lack of queenside development and the vulnerability of whichever minor piece lands on c3.
There is no big hurry to play Qb3; it makes sense to shuttle our king to safety first. Even with the bishop on b4 defended, this move is quite powerful.
Capturing with the bishop leads to much the same consequences as 7...Nxc3, further exacerbated by the fact that Black will have insufficient control over key dark squares in the center.

rn1q1rk1/ppp2ppp/3bp3/3p1b2/3PnB2/2NBPN2.comment: A thematic follow-up, forcibly removing the knights and leaving both of Black's minor pieces hanging. Much better than the greedy 13.Qxb7. The knight on h5 is entirely out of commission, and Black has no good answer to the twin threats of Qxb7 and Qd1,which induces a near-fatal weakening of the dark squares around Black's king.
This does not substantively change the nature of the position, since Black is forced to capture on c3 anyway.
Simple and strong: we threaten to accentuate the queenside pressure with a5, thereby creating even more holes on the queenside.

rn1q1rk1/ppp2ppp/3bp3/3pNb2/3PnB2/2NBP3/.comment: Note that the tempting 14.g4 fails tactically to 14...h6 15.Bh4 g5, when Black retains material equality.

rn1qk2r/ppp2ppp/3bp3/3p1b2/3P1B2/2nBPN2/.comment: This is the ideal square for the queen, where it attacks b7 and prevents castling. Black has no choice but to spend a tempo defending b7, enabling us to bring our knight into the fold. It has already become apparent that the pawn sacrifice is more than justified. Black is saddled with the twin threats of Rxb7 and Bxf5 followed by Qd3, recovering the pawn in both cases. More importantly, the incredible vulnerable placement of Black's bishop grants White a virtually decisive initiative.

rn1qk2r/ppp2ppp/3bp3/3p1b2/3P1B2/2PBPN2/.comment: Taking the b7-pawn with the queen is quite a bit more problematic for Black than 11.Rxb7, which would enable Black to ferry their king to safety.

rn1qk2r/p1p2ppp/1p1bp3/3p1b2/3P1B2/2PBPN.comment: It is crucial to induce ...b6, which further weakens the c6-square and makes it even harder for Black to properly develop his knight.

We now threaten the deadly Bb5+, forcing Black to enter full retreat mode. The most resilient defensive move, preparing to castle kingside by slicing off our control over the f8-square. In order to keep the initiative aflame, we must immediately find greener pastures for the lady.
Opening up the c-file is almost always a good idea in the Jobava London, and this position is no exception.

rn1qk2r/p4ppp/1p1bp3/2Pp1b2/5B2/2PBPN2/P.comment: An important tactical detail. White wins a piece.

rn1qk2r/p1p2ppp/1p1bp3/3pNb2/3P1B2/2PBP3.comment: Black's desire to prepare castling is understandable, but the queen saunters on over to the adjacent square, and Black's problems are multiplied hundredfold!

r2qk2r/p1pn1ppp/1p1bp3/3pNb2/3P1B2/2PBP3.comment: A picturesque final position! Black drops the queen due to the threat of checkmate on e7.

rn1qk2r/p4ppp/1p1bp3/2ppNb2/3P1B2/2PBP3/.comment: Black is tied hand and foot!

rn1q1k1r/p1p2ppp/1p1bp3/3pNb2/3P1B2/2PBP.comment: A magnificent prophylactic move, taking away the c8-square from Black's queen (once again, Black pays a very steep price for weakening the light squares on the queenside). The point of this becomes clear if Black plays 13...f6: The queen is trapped!
It is obviously not enough to force Black's king onto a compromised square. We now turn our attention back to the queenside, prying open the c-file and adding fuel to the fire.

rn1q1k1r/p1p3pp/1p1bpp2/3p1B2/3P1B2/2PNP.comment: The attempt to generate kingside counterplay (which resembles our own g4-h4 idea) falls short on account of a lovely counterblow.

rn1q1k1r/p1p4p/1p1bpp2/3p1Bp1/3P1B2/2PNP.comment: Counter-attacking the knight and summarily halting Black's kingside pawn play. Needless to say, we are more than willing to part ways with the g4-pawn in order to win an additional tempo. An important insertion, using the weakness of the e6-pawn to open up the c-file. The bishop is poisoned, since Black will get massacred on the e6-square and in the center.

rn1q1k1r/p1p4p/1p1bpp2/3p1B2/3P1NP1/2P1P.comment: We are happy to trade queens, but only on our terms! Taking on d7 enables Black to develop the knight and open up escape squares for the a8-rook.

rn5r/p1pqk2p/1p1bNp2/3p1B2/3P2P1/2P1P3/P.comment: White's central pawn phalanx is totally decisive. We will follow up by infiltrating down the c-file with Rac1, doubling rooks if necessary. It is instructive to observe how Black's knights are utterly dominated by our pawns - in particular, the d4 and g4-pawns take away the crucial e5 and f5 squares, condeming the horsies to a passive existence.

rn1q1k1r/p6p/1ppbpp2/3p1Bp1/3P1BP1/2PNP3.comment: The pawn cannot be defended, and our bloodthirsty heavy pieces will tear Black's pitiful army to shreds.

rn1qk2r/p1p2ppp/1p1bp3/5b2/2pP1B2/3BPN2/.comment: An important nuance, forcing the bishop away from its protection of the c3-pawn. In order to keep the bishop on a5, Black must seriously weaken seventh rank.

rn1qk2r/p1p2ppp/1p1bp3/5b2/2pP1B2/2PBPN2.comment: Only now, after Black has opened up a direct line of fire to the knight, do we infiltrate with the rook! Black is under assault from all sides. The two pieces are incomparably more powerful than the rook, and the c3-pawn is condemned. Victory is a matter of rather straightforward technique.

rn1qk2r/p1p2ppp/1p1b4/3p1p2/3P1B2/2P1PN2.comment: Fork city! We have recovered the pawn, and Black's position is in shambles.

rn1q1rk1/p1p2ppp/1p1b4/3p1p2/3P1B2/2PQPN.comment: Just when it seems like Black has gotten his king to relative safety, we gang up on the monarch with our queen and minor pieces. The following sequence - 15 moves long - is hardly forced, but it clearly illuminates the extent of White's dominance, and culminates with one of the most beautiful mating combinations that we have ever come across!

rn1q1rk1/p1p2p1p/1p1b2p1/3p1pN1/3P1B2/2P.comment: A thematic attacking idea, shattering Black's kingside.

rn1q1rk1/p1p2p1p/1p1b2p1/3p1pN1/3P1BP1/2.comment: Transforming our advantage. With the g-file wide open, White's attack will not stop with the queens off the board; the rooks are more than happy to pick up the slack!

rn3rk1/p1pq1p1p/1p1b2p1/3p1pN1/3P1BP1/2P.comment: Much stronger than the penny-pinching 18.Bxc7. We have far greater fish to fry! Setting up the threat of Ne6+, and driving Black's king further into the abyss. Clearing g5 for a more deserving piece. Black's king has been rudely shuttled all the way from the kingside to the queenside. Now, 25.Rxd5 obviously keeps a decisive advantage, but we came across a far more beautiful crusher that we cannot help but include: Simply divine! The rook is sacrificed in order to establish control of the b-file. Note that the rook on b1, which thus far has patiently awaited its turn, finally has its moment in the sun! Together with the knight and bishop, it is the architect of the mating construction. A crucial detail!

rn1qk2r/ppp2ppp/3bpn2/1N1p1b2/3P1B2/4PN2.comment: In contrast to the 3...e6 line, there is no other way to parry the threat of Nc7+.

r2qk2r/ppp2ppp/n2bpn2/1N1p1b2/3P1B2/2P1P.comment: An important and profound positional idea (typical idea #6). Trading away our pawn on d4 seems anti-positional at first blush, but concrete considerations always transcend general reasoning! The point of this move is, of course, to clear the d4-square for our knight. Once it moves back to d4, Black will suddenly be confronted with a host of incredibly nasty positional threats, and his poor coordination will not permit him to address all of them at once. This is obviously forced, since the knight must remain on a6 to guard c7. The point! White has no less than three serious positional threats: 1) Nxf5, gaining the bishop pair (although temporarily) and leaving the d-pawn isolated and weak; 2) Bxa6, crippling the queenside pawn structure; 3) Qa4+, forcing the king to f8. This is unquestionably the lesser evil, but it leaves Black with a pawn structure that is worse than George Washington's teeth!

r2qk2r/pppnbppp/n3p3/1N1p1b2/Q2P1B2/2P1P.comment: White has a raging initiative, and Black has no way to relieve the pressure whatsoever. The knight from e5 cannot be kicked out (...f6 runs into Nxe6 and ...Bd6 drops a minor piece to Nxg6), and we can add even more heat with h2-h4 and/or c2-c4. In the worst case scenario, White can always snatch the pawn on a6 and castle kingside, when Black will have no compensation whatsoever. But there will likely be no need to cash in your chips in this way.

rn1qk2r/ppp2ppp/3bpn2/3pNb2/3P1B2/2N1P3/.comment: This is probably Black's best move from an objective standpoint, but it leads to a familiar type of position in which White is definitely having all the fun. Most knowledgeable players make this move automatically. By opening up an escape square on h7, Black removes the danger from the advance of the g-pawn. As in the case of 6...Nbd7, this is a sign that we should switch our approach to methodical positional play. As usual, ignoring the brewing storm on the kingside leads to trouble.
A masochistic move! Now, White's kingside pawn storm will be even more devastating.

rn1qk2r/ppp2pp1/3bpn1p/3pN3/3P1B2/2NbP3/.comment: As always, we recapture with the pawn to increase our central control, open the c-file, and carve out a path to b3 for our queen. This position is quite similar to the one that arises after 5...Bd6 6.Ne5 h6 7.Bd3 Bxd3 8.cxd3; the addition of the move ...h6 does not substantively alter the nature of the ensuing struggle. If anything, ...Bd6 is a significantly more useful move, so we would argue that this is a somewhat improved version of an already-pleasant position. As usual, we recapture with the pawn, leading to the classical central pawn formation. Our powerful knight on e5, coupled with our total control over key central squares, promises White a very pleasant game.

r2qk2r/pppn1pp1/3bpn1p/3pN3/3P1B2/2NPP3/.comment: This is the only way for Black to justify delaying the development of their DSB; remember that this move is not possible when the bishop is on d6 due to dxe5, winning a piece. Now, recapturing with the pawn makes little positional sense.

r2qk2r/ppp2pp1/3bpn1p/3pn3/3P1B2/2NPP3/P.comment: Black has gotten rid of the knight, but the other pieces are more than happy to pick up the slack. Given the relatively docile nature of the position, we have the luxury to spend a tempo creating luft for our king and preventing a knight sortie on g4, which will become important once our queen leaves its initial square.

r2q1rk1/ppp2pp1/3bpn1p/3pB3/3P4/2NPP3/PP.comment: Black has no good answer to the threat of f4-f5, with tremendous play on the kingside.

r2q1rk1/ppp2pp1/3bpn1p/3pB3/3P4/1QNPP3/P.comment: As usual, the impulsive 12...b5 would be met with 13.Ne2 followed by Rac1, accentuating the weakness of the c6-square.

1r1q1rk1/ppp2pp1/3bpn1p/3pB3/3P4/1QNPP3/.comment: There is no question that Black can keep the balance with computer-like precision, but our vast experience in such positions convinces us that Black has a very unenviable task ahead of him.

1r1q1rk1/pp1n1pp1/3pp2p/3p4/3P4/1QNPP3/P.comment: Preparing to double rooks and assert our dominance on the queenside.

1r3rk1/pp1n1pp1/1q1pp2p/3p4/3P4/1QNPP3/P.comment: Obviously, the queen trade would play right into Black's hands.

1r3rk1/pp3pp1/1q1ppn1p/3p4/Q2P4/2NPP3/PP.comment: Our next step is to involve the pawns with b2-b4, increasing our control over key squares on the queenside. Furthermore, Black has quite a few tactical minefields to sidestep; the most natural move walks right into a vicious tactical shot.

1rr3k1/pp3pp1/1q1ppn1p/3p4/Q2P4/2NPP3/PP.comment: Bang! This is why we went through the trouble of doubling rooks!

1r4k1/pp3pp1/1q1ppn1p/3N4/Q2P4/3PP3/PPr2.comment: Capturing the queen is a lot less clear after ...Rxc1+.

1r4k1/pp3p2/1q1ppp1p/8/Q2P4/3PP3/PPr2PPP.comment: Black is down a pawn, and his kingside is in shambles. We will follow up with Qc7, when our opponent's position will collapse like a house of cards.

r2qk2r/pppn1ppp/3bpn2/3pNb2/3P1B2/2N1P3/.comment: See 4...c6 5.Nf3 e6 6.Ne5 Nbd7 7.g4. At this point in your Jobava journey, this move should be second nature (with the exception of those who have decided to start with this line). Black is already in deep yogurt.

r2qk2r/pppn1ppp/3bpn2/3pNb2/3P1BP1/2N1P3.comment: As usual, this is clearly superior to 7...Bg6, although it occurs quite a bit more rarely in online play.

r2qk2r/ppp2ppp/3bpn2/3pnb2/3P1BP1/2N1P3/.comment: A situation that you should be intimately familiar with by now! To prevent the loss of a minor piece, Black has to accept a decisive weakening of his kingside.
Amazingly, we have transposed to 3...a6 4.e3 Nc6 5.Nf3 Bf5 6.Ne5 e6 7.g4 Nxe5 8.gxf5, so we advise you to head on over to the 3...a6 file and refresh your memory on the subsequent moves.

r2qk2r/ppp2pp1/3bp3/4nbPp/3PpB1P/4P3/PPP.comment: Bortnyk-Ajay, Chess.com (blitz) 2021. This position hardly needs elaboration!

rn1qk2r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/3pbb2/3P1B2/2N1P3/P.comment: An important position that has occurred frequently in the blitz practice of the authors of this course. It is vital to avoid the tempting 9.Rg1, due to 9...g5. We have both lost countless games in precisely this fashion, especially to Minh Le and Firouzja. Instead, we must target the knight on g4 straightaway. Chasing the knight away. We saw a very similar idea (and position) in the 5...Bd6 6.Ne5 0-0 line; here, Black's king is still in the center, but that does not change any of White's ideas. As always, ...Qh4+ is coolly rebuffed by Bg3. Incredibly tempting, but wrong!

rn1qk2r/ppp2pp1/4pn2/3pbb1p/3P1B1P/2N1P3.comment: As is the custom, we immediately drag Black's king into the open. There is no good answer to the devastating threat of Qg6+, since 12...Ng4 runs into 13.Bg5 followed by either f2-f3 or Bh3.

rn1qk2r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/3pPb2/5B2/2N1P3/PPP.comment: A very difficult move to find, since this involves a minor piece sacrifice (note that this is Black's best move in the 5...Bd6 6.Ne5 0-0 version as well). The alternative, however, leads to a position that can only be described as hellish.

rn1qk2r/ppp2p1p/4pn2/3pPbp1/5B2/2N1P3/PP.comment: In contrast to the ...0-0 line, here this move is incredibly effective, since the capture on e4 enables us to favorably trade queens and draw Black's king onto a vulnerable square.
Delaying the capture of the bishop to take away the h4-square from Black's queen. The immediate 11.gxf5 leads to a total mess after 11...Qh4+.

rn1qk2r/ppp2p1p/4pn2/3pPbp1/8/2N1P1B1/PP.comment: White loses the e5-pawn and the game.

rn1qk2r/ppp2p1p/4pn2/4Pbp1/4pB2/2N5/PPP2.comment: Ignoring the forbidden fruit! Capturing on h3 would have led nowhere good after ...Qh4+. Surgical chess. With this intermediate move, we put a permanent stop to ...Qh4-related shenanigans and exert our complete dominance over the kingside.
Black is in deep trouble, since 12...exd5 loses immediately to 13.Bg5 Qd7 14.Bh3, with total devastation to follow.

rn2k2r/pppq1p1p/4pn2/4Pbp1/4pB2/8/PPPQNP.comment: Black has no good way to defend against the twin threats of Nxg7+ and Bxh6 followed by Nf6.

rn1k3r/ppp2p1p/4pn2/4Pbp1/4pB2/2N5/PPP2P.comment: The customary move, threatening h4-h5 and forcing Black's bishop to leave the g-file. In turn, this will enable us to gang up on the tender g7-pawn.

rn1k3r/ppp2p1p/4pn2/4Pbp1/4pB1P/2N5/PPP2.comment: Obviously, ...Rg8 would have dropped the knight on h6. Black's objectively best option was to simply abandon the g7 pawn, but we trust that you can handle the resulting position on your own!

rn1k3r/ppp2p1p/4pnb1/4P1p1/4pB1P/2N5/PPP.comment: Quiet and deadly. There is no defense to h5, which will pick up the bishop.

rn1qk2r/ppp2p1p/4pnb1/3pP1p1/5B1P/2N1P3/.comment: Hitting where it hurts! Taking on f5 results in immediate disaster after Nxd5, so Black has no choice but to allow the partial dissolution of his center and the creation of a powerful protected passer on the kingside. Needless to say, this is vastly superior to the listless 13.Ne2. The resulting endgame is utterly miserable for Black.

rn1qk2r/ppp2p1p/4pn2/3pPbpP/5B2/2N1P3/PP.comment: The monster pawn on g5 affords us the clearly better game. Note that the pawn on e5, though isolated, is quite easy to defend. More precisely, Black does not have the time to attack it, since we threaten Bxf5 and the trade on d3 enables us to stick our queen on g6. Even if it were to be captured, the open e-file would probably favor us anyway.

r2qk2r/ppp2p1p/2n1pnb1/3pP1pP/5B2/2N1P3/.comment: Black is under fire from all sides, e.g.

rn1qk2r/ppp2ppp/3Bpn2/3p4/3P4/2NbPN2/PPP.comment: Mr. Copycat is in for a rather nasty surprise in this position: Stunning and immediately decisive. Black's queenside collapses faster than the Stock Market in 1929. This is the only way to avoid losing a minor piece, though it leads to a dead lost endgame nonetheless.
Fighting fire with fire! This forces Black to give up the e-pawn on our terms.

rn1qk2r/ppp2ppp/3B1n2/3pp3/3P4/2NbPN2/PP.comment: Black loses the e-pawn, and with it the game. We have a great position, with prospects on both sides of the board. The stock plan in such positions is Kh1 followed by Rg1, but we shouldn't forget about Russian schoolboy-type moves such as Rad1 and (eventually) e3-e4.

r2q3r/pppn1kp1/3bpnp1/3p2Pp/3P1B1P/2N1P3.comment: Black cannot keep e6 protected and answer the threat of a discovered check at the same time.

1r1qk2r/ppp2ppp/3bp3/3pP2P/4bBP1/2n1P3/P.comment: Despite the chaotic appearance of the position, Black is in big trouble. Both of his bishops are vulnerable, and f2-f3 is threatened.

r2qk2r/ppp2ppp/3bp3/3pP2P/4bBP1/2P1P3/P1.comment: Black's bishop has run out of squares! An empty check.

r2qk2r/ppp2p1p/3bp3/3pP1pP/4bBP1/2P1PP2/.comment: Black has run out of ways to stave off the inevitable. He will have some compensation for the pawn due to the somewhat flimsy placement of our monarch, but a few careful consolidating moves, such as Bg2 and Rf1, should render this compensation meaningless.

rn1qk2r/ppp2ppp/3bp3/3p3n/3P1B2/2NPPN2/P.comment: We are happy to give up the bishop, but only on our terms!

rn1qk2r/ppp2ppp/3bp3/3pB2n/3P4/2NPPN2/PP.comment: This horrific move loses on the spot.

r2qk2r/pppn1ppp/3bp3/3pB2n/3P4/2NPPN2/PP.comment: No more analysis is required! Black will drop h5 with check, with further material losses to follow.

r2qk2r/ppp2ppp/3bp3/1N1pn2n/3P4/3PPN2/PP.comment: The threat of g2-g4 forces Black to introduce serious kingside weaknesses with 10...g6. We can follow up by castling and reinforcing our central control with d3-d4. Once the knight drops back to c3, it can prepare further central expansion with e3-e4.

rn1qk2r/p4ppp/1p1ppn2/3p4/3P4/2NPPN2/PP3.comment: Now, Black is best advised to castle, though his position remains quite thankless after 11.Rc1 Ne8 12.e4. it is far more natural to try to chase the knight away from b5, but that leads to immediate calamity:

rn1qk2r/p4ppp/1p1ppn2/1N1p4/3P4/3PPN2/PP.comment: Pow! Indirectly defending the knight and hitting d6, which Black can only defend with his king.

rn1qk2r/5ppp/pp1ppn2/1N1p4/3P4/3PPN2/PP3.comment: Moving to the open file and shutting down the b8-knight's development prospects. Black is in terrible shape.

rn1qk2r/ppp2ppp/3bpn2/3p1b2/3PNB2/4PN2/P.comment: Interestingly, we have transposed to a known theoretical position that occurs in the Trompowsky Opening (1.d4 Nf6 2.Bg5). There is only one difference: here, it is White to move! We put our extra tempo to immediate use, knocking the bishop off of e4.

rn1qk2r/pp3ppp/2pbp1b1/3p4/2PPnB2/4P3/PP.comment: It is worth flicking in this move to grab some space on the kingside and soften up the bishop on g6.

rn2k2r/pp3pp1/1qpbp1bp/3p4/2PPnB1P/1Q2P3.comment: A classic idea in the Semi-Slav and many other openings. Black has no choice but to acquiesce to the queen trade, opening up the a-file and handing us a queenside attack on a golden platter.

r3k2r/pp1n1pp1/2pbp1bp/2Pp4/3PnB1P/1P2P3.comment: We are playing squarely for two results. We will follow up either with b4-b5, shattering Black's pawn chain and opening up avenues of infiltration, or with Nb3-a5, when Black will have a very hard time defending the b7-pawn, since we (permanently) control the b8-square.

rn1qk2r/ppp2pp1/3bpn1p/3pNb2/3P1BP1/2N1P.comment: This is unquestionably the lesser evil, but Black's position will remain utterly miserable.

rn1qk2r/ppp2pp1/4pn1p/3pbb2/3P1BPP/2N1P3.comment: The normal response is to capture the bishop on g6, crippling Black's pawn structure. However, since Black has already castled, it is worth starting with gxh5, in order to pop open the g-file and facilitate the ensuing attack.
This is far more effective than the stereotypical Nxg6.

rn1qk2r/ppp2pp1/4p3/3pbb1n/3P1B1P/2N1P3/.comment: Black is utterly screwed on the kingside: we will castle queenside, stick a rook on g1, and rush the h-pawn up the board. The smoke has cleared, and the next step is to target Black's incredibly weak kingside pawns.

rn2k2r/ppp2pp1/4pq2/3pbb1n/3P1BQP/2N1P3/.comment: Cold-blooded and powerful, taking the sting out of ...Qxf2 (which will now be met by Qxe6+).

r3k2r/ppp2pp1/2n1pq2/3pbb1n/3P1BQP/2N1P3.comment: Turning up the pressure dial on the e6-pawn. A vital positional resource, ending Black's counterplay along the f-file.

r2qk2r/ppp2pp1/2n1p3/3pbb1n/3P1BQP/2N1P2.comment: Black's defenses are stretched to the limit, and a gorgeous maneuver seals the deal.
The pressure on g6, coupled with the deadly threat of Qxh5+, is decisive.

rn1qk2r/ppp2p2/4pn1p/3pbbp1/3P1BPP/2N1P3.comment: Attacking g6 and paving the way for a timely queenside castle. Further analysis is hardly needed! Black's position is in shambles. We can follow up by castling queenside, or by taking direct action on the kingside with gxh6, Bxh5, and Qh7+. In either case, Black's position is virtually resignable.

rn1qk2r/ppp2pp1/4p2p/3pPb2/5Bn1/2N1P3/PP.comment: Not fearing the check on h4, which is parried with Bg3. Black's knight is sent into exile on h6, when our kingside attack, coupled with our superior piece placement and the total safety of our own king (after we castle), ensures overwhelming compensation for the pawn.

rn1qk2r/ppp2pp1/4p2p/3pPb2/5Bn1/2N1PP2/P.comment: An ingenious defensive move, attempting to pry the bishop away from its protection of the e3-pawn.

rn1qk2r/ppp2p2/4p2p/3pPP2/5p2/2N1P3/PPP4.comment: This check appears intimidating, but White's king calmly sidesteps the trouble by remaining in the center.

rn2k2r/ppp2p2/4p2p/3pPP2/7q/2N1p3/PPP1K2.comment: Protecting the f2-square. We are obviously in no rush to capture the e3 pawn.

rn2k2r/ppp2p2/4p2p/3pPP2/6q1/2N1p3/PPP1K.comment: An important nuance: the immediate 14.Kxe3 runs into ...d4+, so we have to wait for Black's queen to leave the fourth rank to capture the pawn.

rn2k2r/ppp2p2/4p2p/4Pq2/3p4/2N1K3/PPP4P/.comment: To our knowledge, this is the only position in the entire course in which White's king sits on d4 - and the queens are still on the board! Upon closer inspection, it becomes clear that the king is unassailable: it will quickly evacuate back to e3, and Black's initiative fizzles out within a few moves.

3rk2r/ppp2p2/2n1p2p/6q1/8/2NB4/PPPK3P/R3.comment: Phew! Our king has finally reached a safe square, where it is surrounded by friendly forces. Black has nothing better than to acquiesce to the queen trade, when victory will be a matter of straightforward technique.

r2qk2r/ppp2pp1/2n1p2p/3pPb2/8/2N1BP2/PPP.comment: A superb defensive move that nips Black's initiative in the bud. We prepare to meet ...d4 with Rd1, when Black's play in the center will be instantly disarmed.

r2qk2r/ppp2pp1/2n1p2p/4Pb2/3p4/2N1BP2/PP.comment: It may seem more intuitive to castle queenside, but 12.0-0-0 would be a grave error on account of 12...Qh4, when White has no way to save both minor pieces. The issue is that 13.Bf2 runs into Qf4+. In this version, after 12...Qh4+ 13.Bf2 Black's queen is unable to move away with check. One of the few situations in which remaining in the center is more desirable!

r3k2r/ppp1qpp1/2n1p2p/4Pb2/3p4/2N1BP2/PP.comment: Black's compensation for the piece is virtually nonexistant.

r2qk2r/ppp2pp1/2n1p2p/3pPb2/5Bn1/2N1PP2/.comment: Meeting fire with fire! Opening up the center will enable us to more effectively take advantage of Black's incredibly weak pawns.

The queen is better placed on e2 than on d2, since ...d4 can now be met with 0-0-0. Furthermore, after we castle, e3-e4 will come with far greater effect due to the x-ray that our rook will exert against Black's queen.

3rk2r/ppp2pp1/2n1p2p/4Pb2/4pBn1/2N2P2/PP.comment: Just because the queens are off the board doesn't mean that White's attack is over! Au contraire, we are just getting started!

3rk2r/ppp2pp1/2n1p1bp/4P3/4PBn1/2N5/PPP4.comment: The twin threats of exf6 and Bxh6 spell immediate doom.

r2qk2r/ppp3p1/2n1pp1p/3pPb2/5Bn1/2N1PP2/.comment: Setting up the devastating threat of e3-e4.

r2qk2r/ppp5/2n3bp/3pp3/6n1/2N2P2/PPP1Q2P.comment: Black's center has been fully shattered, and we now turn our attention to the kingside. Among other things, White threatens h4-h5 and Qxh6, as well as the prosaic Nb6.

rn1q1rk1/1pp2pp1/p2bpn1p/3pN3/3P1B2/2NPP.comment: Amazingly, this lovely tactical shot is even more effective than 10.Nxf7.

rn1q1rk1/1p3pp1/p1pbpn1p/3pN3/3P1B2/2NPP.comment: Now that our queen has left d1, it is important to take the sting out of the move ...Nh5, which can now be met by the prosaic Bh2. In fact, our next step is to drop the bishop down to h2 (or g3) on our volition, in order to reinforce the knight with f2-f4. The computer assigns White a very modest plus, but our experience leads us to believe that Black's cramped position and lack of a clear plan affords White excellent prospects in the middlegame.

rn1q1rk1/2p2pp1/p1pbpn1p/3p4/3P1B2/2NPP3.comment: Amazingly, this position has occurred once over the board - in a game played by none other than Shakhriyar Mamedyarov, in the year 2000! Black suffers decisive material losses.

rn3rk1/1pp1qpp1/p2bpn1p/3pN3/3P1B2/2NPP3.comment: Black's last move was a terrible positional mistake, and we exploit it immediately by reinforcing our control over the newly-weakened c6-square. Before planting our knight on c6, it is worth piling up on the c-file with Qc2.

A typical positional move, aiming to situate the knight on c5 when the moment is right. Notice, once again, the indispensable role played by White's central pawn mass: all of the crucial squares in the center, particularly e5 and e4, are under White's control. It is incredibly difficult for Black to find helpful improving moves. White's campaign is one of slow, but steady, queenside expansion. The queen will make way for the other rook, and once we are doubled on the c-file, the queenside pressure will reach a peak.

rn3rk1/1p2qpp1/p1pbpn1p/3pN3/N2P1B2/3PP3.comment: We continue to improve our position in countless ways. The knight will hop into c5, and Black will ultimately be forced into a nasty positional concession.

r2qk2r/pppn1pp1/3bpn1p/3pN3/3P1B2/2NPP3/.comment: In contrast to the position that arises after 6...Nbd7, the presence of the pawn on h6 affords us an exciting additional possibility.

r2q1rk1/pppn1pp1/3bpn1p/3pN3/3P1B2/2NPP3.comment: The experienced Jobava player will not bat an eye at this move, which sets up the potentially devastating advance of the g-pawn to g5. Black is best advised to immediately remove the knight from the pawn's line of fire.

r2qnrk1/pppn1pp1/3bp2p/3pN3/3P1B1P/2NPP3.comment: The threat of g4-g5 is instantly crushing, e.g.
Playing on both sides of the board! We deploy our queen to an optimal square and increase the queenside pressure.

r2qnrk1/pp1n1pp1/3bp2p/2ppN3/3P1BPP/2NPP.comment: Obviously, opening up the h-file with ...hxg5 merely hastens Black's defeat!

r2qnrk1/pp1n1p2/3bp1pp/2ppN1P1/3P1B1P/2N.comment: White has opened up a raging attack on Black's king. We threaten both the prosaic h4-h5 and the lovely Nxg6, and Black's impotent army is powerless to stop the avalanche.

1r1qnrk1/pppn1pp1/3bp2p/3pN3/3P1B1P/1QNP.comment: An important positional detail, buttressing the bishop on f4 and taking the venom out of ...f7-f6.

1r1qnrk1/pp1n1pp1/2pbp2p/3pN3/3P1B1P/1Q1.comment: Black's incredibly passive situation means that we are in absolutely no hurry to make any committal moves. Defending the b4-square is always a good idea.

1r1qn1k1/pp1n1rp1/2pbppNp/3p4/3P1B1P/PQ1.comment: We will follow up by gradually intensifying the kingside pressure with f3 and g4, while the king can be tucked away to safety on d2. White's robust central pawn phalanx means that our king will almost always remain completely safe in the center.

rnbqkb1r/1pp1pppp/p4n2/3p4/3P1B2/2N1P3/P.comment: This is, without question, one of Black's best lines from an objective standpoint. There is no doubt that Black equalizes, but we stress that the position remains complex and difficult to handle from a practical standpoint. From this position, Black has two main setups: the first involves striking at the center right away with ...c7-c5. In response, we will trade on c5 and quickly prepare the typical central breakthrough e3-e4, granting us a nice space advantage and easy piece play. The second plan, more seldom seen at the club player level, involves grabbing as much queenside space as possible with ...b7-b5, and following up with ...Bb7 to prevent e4. We are quite proud of our recommendation against this second plan, which involves quickly closing up the queenside and transitioning our focus to a lightning kingside attack. This is extremely popular online, with over a hundred thousand games! Although developing the knight to c6 is natural, it blocks the c-pawn, handing White immediate supremacy in the center. Of course, we have also committed the same transgression, but we have the benefit of the extra tempo! We harness our development advantage by quickly shepharding the knight to e5, and following up with g2-g4 in the event that Black develops the bishop to f5.

rnbqkb1r/1pp2ppp/p3pn2/3p4/3P1B2/2N1P3/P.comment: The typical shot works to perfection here. This is necessary in order to maintain an objectively acceptable position, but from a practical standpoint, White has a major initiative. This is far more common than 7...Nxe5, but sends Black even further into deep trouble. The only way to extricate the bishop is to introduce near-fatal weaknesses on the kingside. As usual, the threat of h5 induces a decisive kingside weakness.

We ain't gonna give that pawn up easy! It turns out that Black has no way to win back the pawn without yielding the bishop pair, which turns out to be incredibly valuable in this particular structure. It is essential to avoid this move, after which our queenside will collapse like a house of cards. This has been the choice of many strong GMs; in particular, Belarussian GM Sergei Zhigalko has played this line regularly against the authors of this course. Black aims to rapidly deploy the bishop to b7, making it virtually impossible for White to break in the center with e3-e4. We spent a long time on this move, and are proud to recommend a rare idea that confronts Black with serious practical problems.

Preparing to reinforce the pawn with b4, and essentially forcing Black's hand. Preventing the further progress of Black's b-pawn, and setting up the main idea of the line. This is a rare, but extremely dangerous idea. We freeze Black's queenside play entirely, preventing ...c7-c5. Without this idea, Black is essentially stalemated. We, on the other, have clear ways to improve our position: the knight will be centralized on e5, the bishop developed to d3, and once Black castles kingside, our queen is immediately transported to h3, creating long-lasting and potentially fatal threats on the kingside. Do not be fooled by the engine's assessment: our practice and analysis reveals that Black's position is very hard to play due to the conspicuous absence of a clear active plan. An important inclusion. By preventing ...Bb4, we are making it difficult for Black to find active prospects for the dark-squared bishop. More importantly, we are preparing to take control of the queenside with a well-timed b2-b4, which will make it exceedingly difficult for Black to attain much-needed activity on the queenside.

rnbqkb1r/1pp2ppp/p3pn2/3p4/3P1B2/2N1PN2/.comment: Here, it is important not to capture on d5, as that enables Black to develop quickly and dangerously with 8...e6.

rnbqkb1r/1pp2pp1/p3pn1p/3p4/3P1B2/2N1PN2.comment: Adding insult to injury! After we castle, the threat of g4-g5 will spell immediate doom to the Black king.

This is the only way to muddy the waters, although White still emerges from the complications with a nearly winning position. Now, the intuitive 12.Nxd5 gives Black a nagging initiative, so the silicon fiend unearths a delightful idea that defies belief: Simply leaving the f4-bishop en prise! Upon closer investigation, the idea of this move should become clear: after Black takes the bishop, we will capture the pawn on f7, when the threat of h4-h5, coupled with the prospect of a nasty check on c6, spells immediate doom for a totally uncoordinated and underdeveloped Black army. Ideas like these are why we love the Jobava.
Black's position is in ruins. Note that ...Nb4 is not scary, as our queen simply drops down to e2.

rnbqkb1r/1pp2ppp/p3p3/3p4/3PnB2/2N1PN2/P.comment: This move should be automatic as well!

rnbqkb1r/1pp2ppp/p3p3/3p4/3PNB2/4PN2/PPP.comment: A staggering number of games concluded in this fashion. Black loses the bishop.
Shattering Black's center and carving out a dominant outpost on e5. We see the exact same idea in the 3...c5 line.

r1bqkb1r/1pp2ppp/p1n1pn2/3p4/3P1B2/2N1PN.comment: Black has zero compensation for the pawn, and ...Ne4 always runs into the devastating Qh5+.
Here, it is important to preserve the bishop pair rather than to greedily capture on e6, which leads to the complete dissolution of White's center after the trade on f4.
The rook on c1 and pawn on a3 change nothing: this shot is as strong as ever.

r1bqkb1r/2p2ppp/p1n1pn2/1p1p4/3P1B2/2N1P.comment: This move prevents the easy development of the bishop. Black's king has nowhere safe to go, and his structure is in shambles.

r1b1k2r/1ppq1ppp/p1nbpn2/3p4/3P4/P1N1PN2.comment: White has the bishop pair (for now) and a pleasant bishop. Next, we will castle queenside and can play either in the center (e3-e4) or expand on the kingside with f2-f4.

r1b1kb1r/1pp1qppp/p1nBpn2/3p4/3P4/2N1PN2.comment: This is the best practical try. The computer gives equality (as usual), but Black's position is remarkably hard to play and traps exist by the basinful.

r1b1kb1r/1pp1qppp/p1nBpn2/8/3Pp3/2N2N2/P.comment: Only 14...Kb8 preserves a double-edged position; the natural moves all fail to the same trap, which wins immediately:

r1b1kb1r/1pp1qpp1/p1nBpn1p/8/3PN3/5N2/PP.comment: Black struggles with the weak pawn on e6, and the bishop has great potential once it returns to g2. Black can maintain the balance with computer-like play (starting with 19...Qh4), but there is no question that any normal human would prefer White.

rnb1kb1r/1ppq1ppp/p3p3/4B3/3Pp3/4PN2/PPP.comment: Grabbing space and inducing even more kingside weaknesses.

rnb1kb1r/1ppq1pp1/p3p3/4B2p/3Pp2P/4PN2/P.comment: Total domination in the center and an unstoppable attack on the queenside. Our next move is to b2-b4, and after the pawn appears on b5, Black will probably be best advised to resign in order to avoid a total massacre. Also do not forget about the possibility of a rook lift to c3, particularly if Black's queen appears on c6.

rnbqkb1r/1pp2ppp/p3p3/8/3PpB2/2P1PN2/PP3.comment: An astute positional move, preparing to recapture on d4 with the bishop. It may seem more intuitive to recapture with the pawn, but that would grant Black active prospects for his dark-squared bishop, and subject us to long-term pressure down the d-file. On d4, the bishop lords over the entire position, preventing the active development of Black's DSB and keeping the d-file closed for business. Our next step is to complete our development and get our king to e3, when Black experiences long-term problems with the e4-pawn.

rnbqkb1r/1p3ppp/p3p3/2p5/3PpB2/2P1PN2/PP.comment: White will combine kingside and queenside expansion. Next up is g4 followed by h4, and we can expand on the queenside with a4-a5 as well - that is why we left the rook on a1! Finally, after g4 is played, remember that you can transfer your light-squared bishop via f1 to g2, when Black will likely lose the e4-pawn.

rnbqkb1r/1pp2pp1/p3pn1p/3p4/3PNB2/4PN2/P.comment: As tempting as it is, this move meets with an incredible refutation that gives Black attacking chances.

rnbqk2r/1pp1bpp1/p3pn1p/3p4/3PNB2/4PN2/P.comment: The weakness of the d4-pawn grants Black sufficient counterplay. Black's attack fizzles out, and White's material advantage will be decisive. Note that the g2-square is controlled by our bishop! As in the 13...Bb4 line, taking the bishop leads to unnecessary complications. Instead, we sidestep the bishop and act with surgical precision. Who cares about the bishop? Black is unable to save the rook and the knight at the same time. The queen trade is inevitable, after which Black loses even more material.

rnbqk2r/1pp2ppp/p3pn2/3p4/1b1P1B2/2N1PN2.comment: Initiating kingside pressure. It is rather painful to part ways with the bishop pair, but there was nothing we could have done: 9.Bg5 would be futile on account of 9...h6 followed by ...g5. See 8...Bd6 9.g4. Here, the only difference is in the placement of the knight; we believe that it is even better on e2, since ...Bxf4 will always be met with Nxf4.
An annoying little move, aiming to fully destroy Black's kingside pawn structure with Bxf6. The bishop pair is meant to be given away!
This sacrifice deserves serious merit, although it leads to a rather chaotic tactical battle that requires intense study.

rnbqk2r/1pp2ppp/p2Bpn2/3p4/1b1P4/2N1PN2/.comment: An ingenious positional move, opening up the f-file. Our long-term pressure along the f-file will guarantee White a stable advantage. Also, do not forget about c2-c4, which would come at the least convenient moment for Black.

rnb1k2r/1pp2ppp/p2qpn2/3p4/1b1P4/2N1PN2/.comment: Black has no good answer to the straightforward idea of dropping the queen to h3 or g2 and following up with h5, blasting open the h-file. Having induced the dreadfully weakening ...b6, we initiate queenside operations without further delay. It may seem rather brazen to push the c-pawn once we have castled queenside, but Black's pieces are too passive and uncoordinated to present a serious dangerous to our king. Worst comes to worse, the king can always find shelter on b1 or a1. Black's king, on the other hand, has nowhere safe to run. This natural move loses quickly: Black has no obvious continuation: the pawn on d5 is hanging, and his position is on the verge of collapse. Picking up the knight with interest. Even with the queens off the board, we are able to generate a massive initiative in the center with a series of accurate moves:

rnb1k2r/1pp2ppp/p2qpn2/3p4/1b1PP3/2N2N2/.comment: Now, the meek 14.Nxe4 would enable Black to repair his center with 14...d5. Instead, our intentions are far more violent.

rnb1k2r/1pp2ppp/p2qpn2/3P4/1b2p3/2N2N2/P.comment: Black is in trouble: he will lose either d6 or e4, or both. Whichever pawn we capture first, we will bring out the rest of our pieces and surround the other one, likely with Bg2 and Re1 or Rhd1.

rnbqk2r/1pp2p2/p3pp1p/3p4/1b1P4/2N1PN2/P.comment: White has a stable plus in the endgame. We will plant the knight on h5, tying Black down to f6, and follow by preparing c2-c4 or even (after Bg2 and Rhf1) f4-f5, accentuating the weakness of the f6-pawn. Bringing the knight into position. We now threaten to freeze the f6 pawn with g2-g4, when Black will have no good answer to the threat of Nh5. This move is just as powerful here as with the pawn on f6. By opening the h-file, we shift our focus from the f-pawn to the h-pawn. Anatoly Karpov would kill for such a position with White! Our next step is to develop the bishop and stack the rooks. Black's ability to defend h6 is limited by the poor coordination of his pieces and by the fact that the knight on c6 has no access to any central squares.

rnbqk2r/1pp2ppp/p3p3/3p4/1b1PnBP1/2N1PN2.comment: This is also good, and perhaps even more straightforward than 11.Ng3.

It appears that we have blundered a piece, but this is all part of the plan. In return for the minor piece, we will receive two pawns and, most importantly, fantastic chances to checkmate Black on the kingside. From a practical perspective, Black's position is untenable. The h-file is about to open up, and Black will have no answer to the massive amount of material that we will pile up on the h7-pawn, which will include the bishop and the other rook.

rnbqk2r/1pp2ppp/p3p3/3p4/1b1PnBPP/2N1PN2.comment: A scary-looking tactic, but it is easy to parry.

rnb1k2r/1pp1qppp/p3pn2/3pB3/1b1P4/2N1PN2.comment: Using the g-pawn as a "hook" to open the h-file, a typical motif worth remembering!

rnb1k2r/1pp1qppp/p3pn2/2bpB3/3P3P/2N1PN2.comment: Black has a permanent weakness on h7. We will accumulate the pressure with Rdh1, when the pawn's days are likely numbered.

r1bqkb1r/1ppn1ppp/p3pn2/3p4/N2P1B2/4P3/P.comment: In human terms, Black is already in massive trouble.

r1bqkb1r/2pn1ppp/pp2pn2/3p4/NP1P1B2/4P3/.comment: This move signals the key difference between 7.b4 and 6.b4: the knight in d7 is now under fire, and after 8...Bxb4+ 9.c3 we attack two minor pieces at the same time. Amazingly, Black can make this line work using an insane sequence of computer moves, but White still maintains an objective advantage at the end. Most people who stumble into this line will have done so unintentionally!
It transpires that Black has serious compensation for the pawn, in the form of pressure on the c3-pawn and the constant possibility of ...Bxa4. We have to proceed with the utmost precision.

r1bqkb1r/2pn1ppp/pp2p3/3p4/NP1PnB2/2P1P3.comment: Not fearing the check on h4, which is cooly rebuffed by g2-g3. Practically speaking, Black is already in very serious trouble. The engine finds ways to keep Black's initiative going, but it is safe to say that a human will not be able to demonstrate anything resembling sufficient compensation for the piece.

r1bqkb1r/2pn2pp/pp2pp2/3p4/NP1PnB2/2P1PP.comment: Poking and prodding at the b6-pawn. Now, ...b5 yields the c5-square, so Black must defend obediently.

Preventing ...e5, and preparing to develop our knight. We aim to complete our development with Bd3 and 0-0, when Black's compensation will simply evaporate. The engine finds a way to keep the spark of Black's initiative going, but we will bet a silver dollar that this position will never occur in your tournament or online practice :)

r1bqkb1r/1pp2ppp/p1n1pn2/3p4/N2P1B2/3BP3.comment: A rather devious move, threatening to win a piece with ...e5 followed by ...e4. As in most Jobava positions, this knight sally is incredibly effective. In particular, it underscores the extent to which Black misses his dark-squared bishop in these sorts of positions; it is remarkably difficult to kick our minor pieces away from e5; Black can only do so at the cost of seriously compromising the activity of his own minor pieces.

r1b1kb1r/1pp1qppp/p1n2n2/3pp3/N2P4/3BP1B.comment: Turning up the pressure dial on d5. We have a litany of improving moves that we can follow up with, such as a4-a5 (to grab space on the queenside) and Qd3 (to threaten the h7 pawn and coordinate the rooks). If we can induce ...e5-e4, then we will use the d4-square as an outpost for the queen.

r1b1kb1r/1pp1qp2/p1n1pnp1/3p3p/N2P4/3BP1.comment: We are more than happy to enter an opposite-colored bishop middlegame, where our vise-like grip on the dark squares, coupled with the prospect of opening the center at our leisure with e3-e4, guarantees White a pleasant edge. Black, on the other hand, will have a very hard time deploying his light-squared bishop to a reasonably active square.

r1bqkb1r/2p2ppp/p1n1pn2/1p1p4/N2P1B2/3BP.comment: Using tactics to halt the progress of Black's pawn. Of course, c3 is untouchable due to Rc1.

r1bqkb1r/2p2ppp/p1n1pn2/1p1p4/NP1P1B2/3B.comment: Prying open the queenside, and creating a serious long-term weakness on a6. Note that in response to 13...bxa4, we first have to withdraw the dark-squared bishop to g3 in order to take the sting out of ...e5. Then, we will recapture on a4 and turn up the queenside pressure.

rnbqkb1r/1pp2ppp/p3pn2/3p4/3P1B2/2N1P3/P.comment: Securing the bishop pair and reopening the possibility of e3-e4.

r1bqkb1r/1pp2ppp/p1n1pn2/3p4/3P1B2/2N1P3.comment: We now transition to a plan of kingside expansion, preparing to underscore the vulnerability of the f5-bishop with f2-f3 followed by g2-g4. Even without the pawn on d4, our knight is perfectly safe on e5, and the bishop that will take its place in the event of ...Nxe5 will pose the serious threat of Bxf6, crippling Black's kingside pawn structure.

We have seen this typical move many times in these variations (such as in the 7...Bf5 line, 14...h5 sub-variation). The queen is chased away to a far less desirable square, making it easier for us to exploit the countless weaknesses in Black's position. In particular, we put our knight in position to infiltrate the dreadfully weak b6-square, which spells immediate doom for Black.

r1bqk2r/1pp2ppp/p1nbpn2/3p4/3P1B2/2N1PP2.comment: Transitioning to a furious kingside attack! Even without a knight on e5 to guide them forward, the kingside pawns constitute a formidable force. As a result of Black's compromised queenside pawn structure, the Black king has no safe place to hide.

r1bqk2r/1pp2ppp/p1nbpn2/3p4/3P1BP1/2N1PP.comment: Black's king has nowhere to run! This move halts the progress of White's pawns on the kingside...or so it seems. We take the opportunity before Black has castled to smash open the e-file, giving us a dangerous and enduring initiative.

r1bqk2r/1pp2pp1/p1nbpn1p/3p4/3P1BP1/2N1P.comment: Forcing the queen away from c5 and preparing to entrench the knight on b6. It may seem that the knight is anything but stable here, but we will use some fascinating tactics to justify its placement!
The attack is already quite devastating.

1rbqk2r/1pp2pp1/p1nbpn1p/3p4/N2P1BP1/4PP.comment: The point is revealed: the knight is untouchable due to the fork on e3!

1rbqk2r/1pp2pp1/p1nbpn1p/3p2P1/N2P1B2/4P.comment: Just when it seems that our attack has fizzled out, a lovely tactical shot comes to the rescue. Gorgeous! The queen is taboo due to Nxd7+, and Black is forced to part ways with his extra pawn. We have recovered our material investment, and stand clearly better. Our pawn structure is superior, and we can continue stoking the coals of attack by bringing our bishop out to h3. Of course, ...Qb7 is not dangerous on account of b3, and Black's "attack" comes to an end.

r1bqk2r/1pp1bppp/p1n1pn2/3p4/N2P1B2/4P3/.comment: Black loses a ton of material.

rnbqkb1r/1pp2ppp/p3pn2/3p4/3P1B2/P1N1P3/.comment: I have faced this move several times in blitz (DN), and it makes a good deal of sense: 7.b4 is now quite a bit less desirable, since the bishop on g7 will exert rather nasty pressure on our knight. Instead, we defend the pawn in an altogether different way:

rnbqkb1r/1pp2ppp/p4n2/3pp3/3P1B2/P1N1P3/.comment: This removes the knight from the line of fire of Black's bishop, and threatens Nb6. Note that ...Qa5+ is never dangerous in such positions due to c3 (followed by b4, chasing the queen right back to its initial square). Refraining from the greedy Qxd5, which causes unnecessary complications. With the knight on a safe square, there is nothing to fear from the deployment of Black's bishop to the long diagonal. An astute positional move. The rook will support the c2-c4 breakthrough.
Here, and only here! The lackluster 7.Bg3 enables Black to recover the pawn without consequences.

rnbqkb1r/1pp2ppp/p4n2/3pp3/N2P1B2/P3P3/1.comment: Black has no compensation for the pawn. Moreover, he can barely move, since ...Nde5 will always run into Nb6. We will follow up by completing our kingside development, when our extra pawn and superior piece placement gives us a near-decisive advantage.

rnbqkb1r/2p2ppp/p4n2/1p1pp3/N2P1B2/P3P3/.comment: This is why we put the rook on c1!

rnbqkb1r/1pp2ppp/p4n2/3pp1B1/3P4/P1N1P3/.comment: This combative move does not solve Black's problems, but it leads to a good deal of tactical complexity, so it is worth looking over the following moves very carefully.

rn1qkb1r/1pp2ppp/p3bn2/3pp1B1/3P4/P1N1P3.comment: We refrain from capturing on d4, which enables Black to entrench his knight on a powerful central square. As always, this move is innocuous and merely hastens Black's demise.
Of course, this is the point of deploying the bishop to g5. Black loses the d5-pawn without compensation.

rn1qkb1r/1pp2ppp/p3bn2/3pp1B1/N2P4/P3P3/.comment: This nondescript developing move accomplishes nothing, and enables us to attain an ideal setup on the queenside.

rn1qkb1r/1pp2ppp/p3b3/3pp1B1/N2Pn3/P3P3/.comment: A crucial detail that justifies the entire line! We shut down Black's queenside counterplay, and prepare to recapture the pawn on c3 with a dominant position. The piece sac on b4 leads nowhere: Simple and cold-blooded, preventing Black's only idea. The c3-pawn is not going anywhere! First, we will complete our kingside development, and then capture the pawn at our leisure. Black's position is resignable. Fearless and incredibly powerful. The piece sacrifice is temporary; we will use our control over the b6-square and the dreadful placement of Black's queen to gain the material back with interest.
First, the knight is placed on b6 to slice off the queen's only evacuation route. We now threaten b2-b4, which will trap Black's queen.

rn2kb1r/1pp2pp1/pN3q1p/3ppb2/3P4/P3PN2/1.comment: Shutting down Black's counterplay on the d-file.

rn2kb1r/1pp2pp1/pN3q1p/3p1b2/3Pp3/P3PN2/.comment: Black is borderline lost due to our immense control over key light squares, including e4 and c4. Black also struggles with a total lack of coordination and an inability to find a suitable square for the dark-squared bishop.

rn3rk1/1pp1bpp1/p4q1p/3p1b2/2NPp3/P2BPN2.comment: f3-f4 is coming sooner rather than later.

rn2kb1r/1pp2ppp/p3bq2/3pp3/3P4/P1N1P3/1P.comment: Withdrawing the queen from the center and offering a queen trade. Black has absolutely nothing in return for the pawn.

rn1qk2r/1pp1bp1p/p3bp2/3pp3/1P1P4/P1N1P3.comment: Standard fare, deploying the knight to the beautiful b6-square. Halting the progress of Black's d-pawn. Despite the somewhat chaotic apperance of the position, Black has no active plan and no compensation for the pawn.

rn1qk2r/1pp1bp1p/p3b3/3ppp2/NP1P4/P2BP3/.comment: Taking the sting out of ...e4, which will no longer come with tempo.

rn1qk2r/1pp1bp1p/p3b3/3pp3/NP1P1p2/P2BP1.comment: Keeping things tight in the center! A devastating final resource, underscoring the potency of the knight. Trading on e5 hands over a decisive pawn phalanx in the center, while 19...Qc8 enables us to recapture the c3-pawn with the other knight, when its colleague on d5 will be unassailable. Black is objectively lost.

rn1q1rk1/1pp1bppp/p3bn2/3pp1B1/1P1P4/P1N.comment: White is now up a pawn for no compensation, but there is one more detail worth mentioning.

A devious resource that was employed against DN in a recent speedrun game. Now, 11.0-0 (as played in the game) runs into 11...Ne4, and Black wins material. As usual, our top priority is to lead our c3-knight to the promised land.

rn2qrk1/1pp1bppp/p3bn2/3pp1B1/1P1P4/P1N1.comment: Cold-blooded and powerful. Black is out of active ideas, and we can improve our position in a litany of ways, ranging from Nb6 to c2-c3 to Rf1-d1.

r1bqk2r/1ppn1ppp/p2bpn2/3p4/3P1B2/P1NBP3.comment: This rare move presents a serious challenge to White's setup. There is no question that Black equalizes, but we can definitely pose some serious problems with accurate play. An inventive way to prevent Qf3, but this enables us to change the pawn structure in our favor.

A classic maneuver: the queen is ferried over to h3, where it exerts long-term pressure against the h7-pawn. Without the possibility of ...c7-c5, Black is consigned to total passivity and must defend very precisely merely to avoid getting checkmated in the next few moves.

r1bqk2r/1ppn1ppp/p2bpn2/8/3PpB2/P2BP3/1P.comment: Asking Black a rather nasty question. Castling fails tactically, while ...g6 creates long-term weaknesses on the kingside. Black can maintain objective equality with a host of computer moves, but no one in their right mind would prefer Black's position here! Trying to force pieces off the board fails tactically.

r1bq1rk1/1ppn1ppp/p2bpn2/8/3PpBQ1/P2BP3/.comment: Black loses the exchange, since 12...Qf6 drops the knight (and then the rook).

r1bq1k1r/1ppn1ppp/p2bpn2/8/3PpBQ1/P2BP3/.comment: A great example of a position where the computer evaluation is utterly useless. The computer gives 0.00, but we strongly believe that White's position is incomparably preferable. We will expand on the kingside with h4-h5, and can follow up by dropping the queen to h3 and advancing the g-pawn. Black has no active plan.

r1bqk2r/1pp2ppp/pn1bpn2/3p4/3P1B2/P1NBPQ.comment: The ideal setup is now complete. We are exerting massive pressure on h7, and intend to follow up with the prosaic g4-g5.

r1bqk2r/1pp2ppp/pn1bpn2/3p4/3P1B2/P1NBP2.comment: This creates massive holes on the kingside, which we can exploit by repositioning our bishop to a more active square.

r1bqk2r/1pp2ppp/pn1bp3/3p4/3PnBP1/P1NBP2.comment: Ignoring the hanging knight on c3, which is non-essential to our attack. Unsurprisingly, given the superiority of our pieces, the tactics work out perfectly for White. It is important to appreciate the value of these types of moves. Even though White is down a piece, we are in no big hurry, and it is worth bringing in the big boys to ensure that the attack is decisive.

r1bqk2r/1pp2p1p/pn1bp3/3p2p1/3PNBP1/P2BP.comment: Smashing through Black's pitiful pawn shell.

r1bqk2r/1pp2p1p/pn1bp3/6p1/3PpBP1/P2BP2Q.comment: Another important quiet move, setting up the threat of a discovered check. The simplest threat is Nxf8+ followed by h8=Q. Black's king is forced back into the ring of fire. And now the coup d'grace, skewering the queen! Nominally, Black has a lot of material for the queen, but the minor pieces can only spectate as we get our rook to g1 and follow up with Qg4/g5/g6, setting up unstoppable threats along the g-file.

r1b1k2r/1pp2p1p/pn1bp3/3p2q1/3Pn1P1/P1NB.comment: Forcing the queen off of the g-file and lending further support to the knight, taking the sting out of ...Bxe5.

r1b1k2r/1pp1qp1p/pn1bp3/3p4/3PnPP1/P1NBP.comment: The point of this move is not to shuttle the king to safety; it was perfectly safe in the center. Rather, by connecting the rooks, we are setting up the unstoppable threat of a sacrifice on g7!
Now, a beautiful sequence decides the game:

r1b1k2r/1pp1qp1p/1n1bp3/p2p4/3PnPP1/P1NB.comment: This line demonstrates the incredibly potency of White's construction.

r1bqk2r/1pp1bp1p/pn2pnpQ/3p2B1/3P4/P1NBP.comment: The rook lift to h3 will lead to immediate checkmate. The extent of Black's queenside paralysis is rather picturesque.

rnbqkb1r/1p3ppp/p3pn2/2pp4/3P1B2/P1N1P3/.comment: This very likely transposes to 4...b5 5.a3 Bb7 6.b4 e6. Of course, Black can also play this line without fianchettoing the light-squared bishop, but that hardly changes the general tenor of the game. White's plan will remain the same: to entrench a knight on e5, develop the light-squared bishop to d3, and light the kingside on fire by maneuvering the queen to h3.
For now, we keep the tension, awaiting a more opportune moment to trade on c5.

r1bq1rk1/1p2bp1p/pn2p1pB/2ppP3/1P6/P1NBP.comment: In these types of positions, you almost never want to capture the rook on f8 because the bishop is such a valuable attacker. White is dominating on the kingside, but we do not even have to rush with h4-h5: an even more powerful continuation in response to 14...Kh8 would be to shuttle the knight around to d4 via e2.

rnbqkb1r/1p3ppp/p3pn2/2pp4/3P1B2/P1N1PN2.comment: Black continues to expand on the queenside.

rnbqkb1r/5ppp/p3pn2/1ppp4/3P1B2/P1N1PN2/.comment: It is important to throw this move in to discourage ...Nh5.

rnbqk2r/5ppp/p2bpn2/1ppp4/3P1B2/P1N1PN1P.comment: We cannot hold off on this move any longer, since Black was ready to play ...c4 or ...b4. We now proceed to quickly prepare the e4 pawn break. This forces Black to make another move with his dark-squared bishop, thereby losing a tempo.

rnbqk2r/5ppp/p2bpn2/1pPp4/5B2/P1N1PN1P/1.comment: This is a very common response, but Black will be unable to easily recover the pawn.

rnbqk2r/5ppp/p3pn2/1pbp4/5B2/P1N1PN1P/1P.comment: Importantly, the knight on c6 hinders the development of Black's bishop, and makes it impossible for him to stop e4.
There is no way to win the c5-pawn, which can be supported with b2-b4 as necessary. Our queen can also park itself on e3.

rn1qk2r/1b3ppp/p3pn2/1pbp4/5B2/P1NBPN1P/.comment: Before pushing the e-pawn, we complete our deverlopment.

rn1q1rk1/1b3ppp/p3pn2/1pbp4/5B2/P1NBPN1P.comment: The time has come! Our pieces are perfectly placed to deal with the consequences of this breakthrough.

rn1q1rk1/1b3ppp/p3pn2/1pbp4/4PB2/P1NB1N1.comment: The most common response, resolving the central tension straightaway.

rn1q1rk1/1b3ppp/p3pn2/1pb5/4pB2/P1NB1N1P.comment: A very important idea; this is almost always the desirable response to ...d4. The knight is re-routed to d2, and it can later find a home on b3.
Moving the rook to a better spot and setting up the positional threat of Be4, which will dislodge Black's queen from its active post. This move looks scary, but it simply loses a piece:

rn1q1rk1/1b3ppp/p3pn2/1pb5/4pB2/P2B1N1P/.comment: Staking a claim in the center and popping open the b1-h7 diagonal.

rn1q1rk1/1b3pp1/p3pn1p/1pb5/4pB2/P2B1N1P.comment: White is better for several reasons: 1) The pawn on d4 is a long-term weakness that cannot be easily eradicated; 2) We will proceed with Qe2-e4, a nasty idea that will induce a serious kingside weakness; 3) We have many auxiliary ways to improve our position, such as Rfd1 (after Qe2), Nb3-d2-e4-d6, and a timely a3-a4 can also be employed to underscore the hidden vulnerability of Black's queenside structure. In contrast, Black has no clear way to improve his position or cause problems on either side of the board.

rn1q1rk1/1b3ppp/p3pn2/1pb5/4pB2/P1NB1N1P.comment: This position occurred in Bortnyk-Baryshpolets, Nabokov Memorial 2015. This is best, leading to a small edge. White controls the crucial d4-square.

rn1qr1k1/1b3ppp/p3pn2/1pb5/4p3/P1NBBN1P/.comment: Our dark-square control, coupled with the nasty threat of Qb6, secures a very pleasant game for White. Black's queen on h5 is also somewhat out of commission.

rnbq1rk1/5ppp/p3pn2/1pbp4/5B2/P1NBPN1P/1.comment: We see a virtually identical position in the 7...b5 line; the placement of the pawn on b7 does not change the nature of the position. We are ready to push e3-e4, posing Black with serious positional problems.

rnbq1rk1/5ppp/p2b1n2/1p2p3/3pP3/P2B1N1P/.comment: An innovative alternative, although this is quite unnecessary, since 13.Ne2 transposes into a line that leads to a very dangerous position for Black.

rn1q1rk1/5pp1/p2bbn1p/1p2p3/3pP3/P2B1NNP.comment: This position epitomizes the power of the Jobava London, especially with respect to its ability to puzzle even the strongest engines. Stockfish 15, upon reflection, gives equality with a very small preference to Black. But if you look at White's online results, they are staggering (I myself have won almost all my games, including a crushing win over Nepomniatchtchi - O.B.). This is because White has a very clear plan: to maneuver the f3-knight to h4 (and later to f5) and to blast open the f-file with f2-f4. Black, on the other hand, does not have any clear plan of action on the queenside, since the b4-square is guarded and the c2-pawn is well-defended. If this explanation doesn't convince you, perhaps the subsequent analysis will!

rnb2rk1/4qpp1/p3p2p/1pbnP3/3p1B2/P2B1N1P.comment: Black is in a vise-like grip. The bishop can be maneuvered to h4, and White can follow up by amputating the d5-knight with Qd2 and Nf4.

r1bq1rk1/5ppp/p1nbpn2/1ppp4/3P4/P1NBPN2/.comment: White has a small but stable advantage, much akin to the Exchange Caro where Black has closed in his bishop with a premature ...e6. We will inevitably ensconce on our knight on e5 and follow up by building up the kingside pressure.

rnbqkb1r/5ppp/p3pn2/1ppp2B1/3P4/P1N1PN2/.comment: With the dark-squared bishop gone, it is a perfect opportunity to resolve the tension in the center and launch a furious kingside offensive.

rnbqk2r/3nbppp/p3p3/1pPp2B1/8/P1N1PN2/1P.comment: Blasting open the center, after which our knight will sink its teeth into the juicy d6-square!

rnbqk2r/5ppp/p3pn2/1pbp4/5B2/P1N1PN2/1PP.comment: We follow up with the typical developing move to d3, preparing e3-e4.
