rnbqk2r/5ppp/p3pn2/1pbp4/5B2/P1NBPN2/1PP.comment: Without question, Black's setup constitues one of the more problematic lines of play against the Jobava London. Black makes it very difficult for us to open up the center with e3-e4 (in contrast to lines with an early ...Nc6, when it is quite a bit easier to carry out this break) while developing his minor pieces to very active posts. In order to avoid getting squeezed, we must insist on pushing e4 as quickly as possible.

rn1qk2r/1b3ppp/p3pn2/1pbp4/5B2/P1NBPN2/1.comment: This move somewhat contradicts the purpose of Black's overall setup, which is to discourage e3-e4. Still, it is a natural developing move and must be taken seriously.

r2qk2r/1b1n1ppp/p3pn2/1pbp4/5B2/P1NBPN2/.comment: Now, the top computer move is 10...e5, which we refuse to take seriously because no one in their right mind would ever chance upon such a move. Barring that, the position is equal objectively, but definitely easier to play for White.

Despite Black's best efforts, we have succeeded in pushing e4, leading virtually by force to a series of piece exchanges in the center. The resulting position may appear rather lifeless, but upon closer inspection, it turns out that White certainly has the easier practical game.

r2q1rk1/1b1n1ppp/p3pn2/1pb5/3pPB2/P2B1N2.comment: This is tempting, and it works on certain occasions (usually with the queen on d1), but here it fails due to the unfortunate placement of White's queen:

r2q1rk1/1b1n2pp/p3pp2/1pb3Bn/3pP3/P2B1N2.comment: It appears that our pieces are all moving backwards, but we have in fact provoked serious, potentially decisive, weaknesses on both sides of the board. We currently threaten to trap the knight with g2-g4, forcing Black to overextend himself even further.

r2q1rk1/1b1n2pp/p4p2/1pb1p2n/3pP3/P2B1N2.comment: Poking at the weak b5-pawn, and opening up the c4-square for our bishop.

r2q1rk1/1b1n2pp/p7/2b1p1pQ/Pp1pP3/3B4/1P.comment: It turns out that this ultra-natural move is a mistake, but find us a human player who will refrain from this move!

r2qk2r/1b1n1ppp/p3pn2/1pb5/3p1B2/P1NBPN2.comment: Now, 12.0-0 transposes into a position that we reach via 9...Nc6 10.0-0 0-0 11.e4 d4 12.Nb1, but we have a superior move:

r2qk2r/1b1n1ppp/p4n2/1pb1p3/3p1B2/P2BPN2.comment: with excellent kingside prospects connected to the idea of opening the h-file with h2-h4.

r2qk2r/1b1n1ppp/p4n2/1pbpB3/8/P1NBPN2/1P.comment: Black doesn't recover the pawn easily, and must continue to make computer moves.

r2qk2r/3n1ppp/p3p3/1pb5/4bB2/P4N2/1PP1QP.comment: The position has simplified considerably, and the symmetrical material may lead you to believe that the position is devoid of serious winning chances. That could not be further from the truth! Black's queenside is rather weak, and the pawn on b5 is more of a liability than an asset. White's play is ultra straightforward: we will castle and quickly position our rooks on d1 and e1, when White's superior pieces grant us easy practical play.

3r1rk1/3n1pp1/p3p2p/1pbqB3/8/P4N1P/1PP1Q.comment: White has an indisputable initiative, with control over the center and a better-placed bishop. Black must continue to make precise moves to keep equality.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/5n2/2pp4/3P1B2/2N5/PPP1.comment: This scintillating counterstrike, which gained notoriety a few short years ago, is incomparably more exciting and challenging than the meek 4.e3. Our idea is straightforward: we aim to exploit our lead in development by blasting open the center. In a way, this move can be thought of as a massively improved Albin Countergambit (1.d4 d5 2.c4 e5). Black is now at a crossroads: three different captures are possible, and all of them must be considered carefully. The resulting positions are complex and full of exciting tactical possibilities.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/5n2/2pp4/3PPB2/2N5/PPP2.comment: By far the most popular recapture at the highest levels. Black captures the pawn and forces a knight trade, opening up an annoying queen check on a5 and eliminating the future possibility of Nc3-b5. Incidentally, it is the least popular of the three captures online, but due to its objective potency, we have decided to promote it as the main line. Along with 4...cxd4, this is the most popular capture online (with approximately 5,000+ games on Lichess at the time of analysis).

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/8/2pp4/3PnB2/2N5/PPP2PP.comment: We recapture the pawn on c5, posing Black with an unenviable dilemma. Trading queens hands over control of the d-file, while refraining from the trade with 5...Qa5 gives White a dangerous middlegame initiative. It is only move 5, yet we are already asking Black a serious question!

This is our main recommendation, bringing out the bishop and pinning the knight. It is worth spending some time on the alternative 6.Qa4, which is an incredibly dangerous (if objectively dubious) line that will bring you rapid victory if Black is not prepared. Objectively, this is a terrible move, but in our experience, even Grandmasters don't know how to react. A single mistake can change the evaluation to White's favor, so it is more than reasonable to keep this move in your back pocket. The idea is twofold: the queen on a4 supports a rapid queenside attack with Nb5, and the d-file is cleared so that the rook will exert more influence when it reaches d1. In order to prove an advantage (and avoid losing the game), Black must generate a string of computer moves that have proven too difficult to find even for top GMs. A very difficult move to play, as this sends the knight to b5. This is as good as 6...d4 objectively, but from a practical perspective, the ensuing position is virtually unplayable for Black. Justifying the placement of the queen! The most straightforward response, calling White's bluff. This is the most popular move, but it immediately digs Black into a deep hole. Covering the check and attacking the bishop. White is winning due to the unstoppable threat of Nd6+, e.g.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/8/2Pp4/4nB2/2N5/PPP2PPP.comment: This is by far the most popular move online (with 2,000 or so games), but it gives us full control over the d-file and leads to a rather dubious endgame. It is important to realize that the trade of queens hardly diminishes White's attacking potential; our initiative does not vanish simply because the ladies are off the board! A few general pointers to help you understand this position better: 1) The pawn on e4 can be either attacked with Nge2-g3, or traded off directly with f2-f3. Both options are on the table depending on Black's setup. 2) After the recapture, White has the immediate threat of situating a knight on b5, forcing Black to contort themselves with the immensely awkward ...Na6. 3) The pawn on c5 is a strength rather than a weakness: it significantly restricts the mobility of Black's dark-squared bishop, and it can be easily supported both with pawns (b4) and with pieces (Be3). Black must stop the knight sortie to b5, but this move comes at the great cost of weakening the b6-square. We target that square without further delay. Black pays a steep price for ignoring the threat! A cute desperado sacrifice, winning even more material. The knight is easily evacuated through c7, when White's material advantage will prove decisive.

rnb1kb1r/pp2pppp/8/q1Pp4/4nB2/2N5/PPP2PP.comment: Using tactics to defend the c5-pawn.

This more restrained move is a sensible alternative. We prepare to construct the typical a3-b4-c5 pawn chain, which will make it rather difficult for Black to operate on the queenside in any meaningful way. Of course, the idea of Na4-b6 is still very much in the cards.

Threatening c5-c6. This is the only way to keep Black's position afloat, although it fails to solve all of Black's problems: The queen trade suits us just fine, since Black will be saddled with the long-term weakness of the e4-pawn.
Preparing to castle queenside! Of course, we could not care less about the c5-pawn: our only allegiance in this line is to rapid development.

rnb1kb1r/pp2pppp/8/q1Pp4/1P2nB2/2N5/P1P2.comment: Although it comes with tempo, this move is almost never scary. The bishop calmly retreats, and Black is left with further weaknesess in the center.

rnb1k2r/pp2ppbp/6p1/q1Pp4/1P2nB2/P1N5/2P.comment: Black is completely paralyzed. Even castling kingside is not possible due to Bxf6, while castling queenside - well, we will leave the analysis of that move to the reader!

rnb1kb1r/pp3ppp/4p3/q1Pp4/1P2nB2/2N5/P1P.comment: It may seem more natural to drop the bishop back to e3, but it is important to reinforce the b4-pawn due to the possibility of ...a6-a5, when a2-a3 fails due to the hanging knight on a4. Therefore, we have to find alternate arrangements for the b4-pawn. Perfectly exploiting the drawback of Black's previous move. Most importantly, this move secures the knight on a4, taking the sting out of the capture on b4.
Solidifying White's queenside pawn chain, and taking the sting out of ...a5.

rnb1kb1r/pp3ppp/4p3/q1Pp4/1P2nB2/P1N5/2P.comment: A sad necessity. Otherwise, we send away the knight with c2-c4. Black cannot makle a single effective move: leaving d7 enables us to jump into b6. Black is simply lost!

rnb1kb1r/pp2pppp/8/q1Pp4/4nB2/2N5/PPP1NP.comment: An interesting move, trading the e-pawn for the c-pawn, although it does not fully solve Black's problems.

r1b1kb1r/pp2pppp/2n5/q1Pp4/4nB2/2N5/PPP1.comment: Pinning the knight and indirectly defending the e4-pawn. This is the classic response to ...Qa5, reinforcing the threat of Nxe4.

r1b1kb1r/pp2pppp/2nB4/q1Pp4/4n3/2N5/PPP1.comment: Now, it is the queen's turn to sink her teeth into the weak d6 square! In reality, this is just a fancy of way of inducing a queen trade.

r1b1kb1r/pp2pppp/2nB4/q1np4/8/2N5/PPP1NP.comment: The computer assigns a modest advantage to White, but in reality, Black's position is very difficult. The e4-pawn is a long-term weakness, and Black is also saddled with problems related to the placement of his king. On e7, it is constantly subject to pressure down the e-file, and Black must also keep a close eye on the knight sorties to d5 and f5. Our next step is to castle queenside, after which the capture on e4 immediately becomes a threat!

r1b1kb1r/pp3ppp/2n5/q1Ppp3/4n3/2N1B1N1/P.comment: Black attempts to stir things up on the queenside, but we use the d6-square to gracefully get out of danger.

r1b1k2r/pp3ppp/2n5/2qpp3/4n3/2N3N1/PPP2P.comment: Yet again, the d6-square costs Black and arm and a leg.

r1b1k2r/pp2qppp/2nN4/3pp3/8/2N5/PPP2PPP/.comment: Rather than greedily capturing on b7, it is better to focus on active development:

r1b2k1r/pp2qppp/2nN4/3pp3/8/2N5/PPP2PPP/.comment: with a powerful and long-lasting attack. Note that ...Rd8 is not scary in the least, as Black has no way to reinforce the pressure on the knight. We can follow up by developing the bishop to e2 and placing a rook on f1.

r1b1kb1r/pp4pp/2n5/q1Pppp2/4n3/2N1B1N1/P.comment: Black has no effective discovery against the queen, since 14...Be8 runs into 15.Be6+. Our next step is to castle queenside.

rnb1kb1r/pp2pppp/8/q1Pp4/4nB2/2N5/PPPQ1P.comment: This is automatic at most levels, although after this capture White's initiative becomes virtually decisive. This is Black's best move, but his problems are only just beginning!

rnb1kb1r/pp2pppp/8/2qp4/4nB2/2N5/PPPQ1PP.comment: A sensible move, preventing Bb5. Of course, we have a second square that we can develop the bishop to!
As usual, this loses on the spot:

rnb1kb1r/pp3ppp/8/2qpp3/4nB2/2N5/PPPQ1PP.comment: It is worth spending an hour or so mastering the ensuing complications. White is better, but the position remains very sharp and it is important to be precise on every move. Black opens up a pathway for his dark-squared bishop, but this move comes at the serious cost of (a) weakening the d5-square, and (b) enabling our bishop to seek greener pastures on g5, where it will incessantly pressure Black's knight.
Forcing a favorable queen trade due to the threat of Nc7.

rnb1kb1r/pp3ppp/8/2qpp3/2B1nB2/2N5/PPPQ1.comment: White threatens to capture on c6 and deliver mate on d8, forcing Black's hand.
Black's position collapses due to the twin threats of Nxe4 and Qxf6.

rn2kb1r/pp3ppp/8/2qppb2/2B1nB2/2N5/PPPQ1.comment: Initiating a favorable queen trade. The bishop on d5 is an absolute menace, so Black's hand is forced:

rn2kb1r/pp3ppp/8/2qNpb2/2B1nB2/8/PPPQ1PP.comment: with a stable edge in the endgame. We will, as usual, follow up with Ne2-g3, putting significant pressure on the e4-pawn. The rook on h1 will be deployed to d1, lending further support to the d6-bishop.

rn2kb1r/pp3ppp/8/2qpp3/2B1nBb1/2N5/PPPQ1.comment: A cute little intermezzo, forcing Black's queen onto a more awkward square.

Yet again, we use the e4-pawn to supercharge the development of our kingside. And now, we stick the knight on d5 in order to force a transition into a favorable endgame, in which our initiative rages on.

rn2kb1r/pp3ppp/3q4/3pp3/2B1n1b1/2N1B3/PP.comment: Here, it is important to realize that we are not in the business of winning the e4-pawn: we have much bigger fish to fry! As such, we use the e4-pawn as fuel to accelerate our development. From a practical standpoint, White's initiative is decisive, e.g. Black has to stay pegged to the d7-square, so the bishop is lost.

rn2kb1r/pp3ppp/8/2qppb2/2B1nB2/2N2P2/PPP.comment: Black has insufficient compensation for the pawn, practically speaking. White has many ways to improve the position and ultimately smoke the rook out of g2. For instance, we could follow up with Kc1-d1, Be5-g3, and Bc4-b3, when we will threaten to simply trap the rook with Nf4.

rnb1kb1r/pp3ppp/8/1Nqpp3/4nB2/8/PPPQ1PPP.comment: Here, the main thing is not to take the rook, because Black will take the bishop and we will have a very hard time retrieving our knight. Instead, we calmly move the bishop to a more active spot:

rnb2b1r/pp2kppp/8/1Nqpp1B1/4n3/8/PPPQ1PP.comment: Black has clearly insufficient compensation for the exchange.

rn2kb1r/pp1bpppp/8/2qp4/4nB2/2N5/PPPQ1PP.comment: Black is already in serious trouble, and must play like an engine to avoid losing on the spot. We will give you a few sample lines to illustrate the potency of White's attack.

rn2kb1r/pp1bpppp/8/2qp4/4nB2/2N5/PPPQNPP.comment: This automatic developing move loses immediately, although Black's position is already quite dire. Yet again, this move creates far too many weaknesses in the center, and sends our bishop to where it wants to go anyway!

r3kb1r/pp1bpppp/2n5/2qp4/4nB2/2N5/PPPQNP.comment: No trade! The knight on b3 is a major asset, since it can hop into c5 at a moment's notice. Posing the twin threats of Nc5 and Nb5. Cold-blooded prophylaxis! By covering the g4-square, we prevent any shenanigans related to ...Bg4 and ensure that our rook will stay attached to the d1-square. We also prepare a devious idea:
The knight on e4 is untouchable due to checkmate on d7! Time to dig Black a grave! The queen is tossed around like a small boat in the raging ocean.

r3kb1r/pp1bpppp/1qn5/1N1p2B1/4n3/8/PPPQN.comment: The other knight joins in the party. White now has the utterly unstoppable threat of Bxf6 followed by Nd5, when one of the horsies will infiltrate c7 or f6. For instance:

r3kb1r/pp1b1ppp/2n1p3/2qp4/3NnB2/2N5/PPP.comment: The second point of our 12th move! The queen is banished to g6, where she will merely passively spectate the affairs in the center. The threat of Nc7 is simply unstoppable.

r3kb1r/pp1bpppp/8/2qpn3/4NB2/8/PPPQNPPP/.comment: We could fill an entire separate course listing all of White's threats in this position.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/8/1Bpp4/3PnB2/2N5/PPP2P.comment: An important intermezzo, moving the bishop onto a defended square with tempo. This is moving more human White is up a piece, but our lack of development makes it difficult for us to untangle. It is crucial to follow up with several accurate moves: Exploiting the fact that b5 is untouchable due to Qxa8. This cold-blooded developing move is incredibly hard to play, yet it is the only move that keeps Black in the game. The queen is trapped, but we are not out of tricks! Sacrificing the bishop in order to generate an escape square for our queen! White has an overwhelming amount of material for the queen, as well as massive pressure along the eighth rank. The queen has escaped, and Black has clearly insufficient compensation for the exchange. We will follow up by chasing the bishop away with h3, and trying to get our knight out and castle as quickly as possible. This is the only way to prove an advantage! Black ignores the threat of Nc7, instead focusing on setting up a sacrifice on f2. If your opponent uncorks this move, then it is time to take off your hat! Another insane only move, deflecting the bishop from its protection of the knight on c7. This is what we are talking about when we say that Qa4 is a good move from a practical standpoint! This is a far more human move, and it hands over a massive initiative:

White's lead in development and the nasty possibility of a discovered attack against Black's rooks gives White a long-lasting initiative. Unfortunately, this fails to a string of wild tactical shots:   Unfortunately, our tricks have come to an end, and White does not have sufficient compensation for the pawn. Still, the compromised position of Black's king means that White has excellent practical chances after 12.0-0-0. We grab the rook and we WILL live to tell the tale! The queen rushes to the support of the knight. We will neutralize the check on b4 with a series of checks aimed at forcing the queens off the board. Forcing the king onto a more vulnerable square. The smoke has cleared, and Black has insufficient compensation for the exchange. This leads directly to a position in which White has overwhelming practical compensation for the pawn. It is rather hard to believe that a human can find this move, although it is one of the only ways that Black can stay alive! with a long-lasting edge in the endgame. The c2-pawn is untouchable due to an inventive tactical idea: Cashing in our chips! Black has definite compensation due to the bishop pair, but I definitely prefer White. Note that Black does not threaten to capture on f4, so we can proceed with calm development. This is almost automatic at all levels, although 6...a6 is a serious alternative that must be studied carefully.

r1bqkb1r/pp2pppp/2n5/2pp4/3PnB2/2NB4/PPP.comment: Another blow, forcing Black to give up the exchange or lose his knight.

rn1qkb1r/pp1bpppp/8/1Bpp4/3PnB2/2N5/PPP2.comment: The main thing to understand about this position is that the prospect of ...c6-c5 is not scary at all: our queen has plenty of spots to choose from, and ...c5 will seriously weaken Black's control over the d5-pawn. In fact, our next move will show that we actually want to induce ...c5!
Black has recovered the knight, but is still dead lost. We are threaten to run Black over in the center with e4-e5.

rn1qkb1r/pp1bpppp/8/1Bpp4/3PnB2/2N2N2/PP.comment: Preparing c2-c4. We will follow up by advancing the pawn to c5, and supporting further queenside expansion with b2-b4.
A shrewd move, setting a vicious trap: taking the pawn leads to the loss of a minor piece after ...e5. Instead, we ferry the queen over to b3.
Here, there are three interesting alternatives, all of which promise extremely good practical play.

rn1qkb1r/pp1b1ppp/4p3/1Bpp4/3PnB2/2N2N2/.comment: Grabbing the pawn hands over a massive initiative to White: We will recover the pawn on the next move. Black's position is in shambles.

Forcing Black's pawn forward. Black's pawns look imposing, but they are no match for White's well-developed army. With our next move, we force liquidation into a favorable endgame. Switching gears, from tactical to positional! By controlling c5, we are preventing the annoying prospect of ...c6-c5 and setting up a long-lasting blockade on the dark squares. Our space advantage and more active pieces give us a pleasant game.

rn1qkb1r/pp1b1ppp/4p3/1BppN3/3PnB2/2N5/P.comment: The most reasonable move, reinforcing the threat of ...c5. Once again, we do not fear this move, but rather encourage it! Things go from bad to worse, since Black's knight has nowhere good to go! Increasing the blockade on the c5-square.

Of course, the knight on a4 is a great asset, since it threatens to jump to b6, targeting Black's center and Black's rook simultaneously. For this reason, Black has no choice but to recapture on d5 with the knight, permanently crippling his queenside and giving White a long-lasting advantage. winning a ton of material.

rn2kb1r/pp1b1ppp/4p3/qBppN3/3PnB2/2N5/PP.comment: In this position, we uncork a series of absolutely stunning tactical blows, one after the other.

rn2kb1r/pp1b1ppp/4p3/qB1pN3/2pPnB2/2N5/P.comment: We start with a counterblow against Black's queen, drawing Black's bishop out of its initial square.

rn2kb1r/pp1b1ppp/4p3/qB1pN3/1PpPnB2/2N5/.comment: This is the only way for Black to stay in the game, although the situation remains extremely critical. Note the tertiary use of the pawn on c5: in the first place it is a decoy, in the second place...also a decoy, but in the third place, it offers the knight a temporary support!

rn2k2r/pp1b1ppp/4p3/qB1pN3/1bpPnB2/2N5/P.comment: Now, the second knight jumps into the game!
We start by undermining the g7-pawn in stylish fashion. You can now see the hidden role that the bishop was playing on f8: it was defending the g7-pawn!

rn2k2r/pp1b1ppp/4p3/qB1NN3/1bpPnB2/8/P1P.comment: White has now amassed three pawns for the piece!

rn2k2r/pp1b1ppp/8/qB1pN3/1bpPnB2/8/P1P2P.comment: with a raging attack down the e-file. A single mistake loses the game for Black, e.g. Even better than 21.Rxe6.

rn2k2r/pp1b1ppp/2B5/q2pN3/1bpPnB2/8/P1P2.comment: A rather sad product for Black, keeping in mind that he has made it this far! White threatens Qg6, and after the correct 22...Bd6 (the only move), we have a draw in our pocket with Qg6-h7. But we can certainly keep things going, e.g. White picks up both the bishop and the rook!

rn2kr2/pp1b1ppp/2B5/q2pN3/1bpPnB2/8/P1P2.comment: Deflecting the queen onto a more vulnerable spot.

rn2kr2/pp1b1ppp/2B5/2qpN3/1bpPnB2/P7/2P2.comment: White has recovered one of the minor pieces, and the attack rages on. We can follow up by capturing on c4, when we will have four pawns for the piece and long-term chances against Black's king.

rn2k2r/pp1b1p1p/4p2p/qB1pN3/1bpPn3/2N5/P.comment: And now it is time for part II, highlighting the undefended rook in the corner. Black's position collapses. This move is infinitely better than the limp 16.Qxf6.

rn2k2r/pp1b1p1p/4p2p/qB1NN3/1bpPn3/8/P1P.comment: White emerges from the complications an exchange ahead.

rn1qkb1r/pp1b1ppp/4p3/1B1pN3/2pPnB2/2N5/.comment: Black suffers from a bad pawn structure. White's play is very straightforward: we will bring the rook on e1 and exert tremendous pressure on Black's center.

rn2kb1r/pp1bpppp/8/qBpN4/3PnB2/8/PPP2PPP.comment: An important resource, covering the check with the knight. Note that 10...e5 is ineffective, since the square is defended twice and only attacked once.

rn2kb1r/pp1bpppp/8/qBp5/3PnB2/2N5/PPP2PP.comment: Black has no effective discovery, since we can simply take on d8 wherever Black's bishop goes.

rn2kb1r/pp1b1ppp/4p3/qBp5/3PnB2/2N5/PPP2.comment: We saw a similar move in the 6...a6 line. The point of this move is to undermine the g7-pawn, creating the massive threat of Bxg7 Kxg7 Qg5+. Black's only defense is to move the bishop away from c5, leading to a queen trade and an endgame in which Black's compensation for the pawn is nonexistant.

rn1qkb1r/pp1bpppp/8/1Bpp4/3PNB2/8/PPP2PP.comment: We will explain this move in greater depth in the main line (8...Ne4). Here, the idea is much the same: we permanently disfigure Black's pawn structure and open up a direct pathway to e5 for one of our pieces.

rn2kb1r/pp1b1ppp/1q2p3/1Bpp4/3PNB2/8/PPP.comment: Black's pawns are tripled, and he has no easy way to develop the f8-bishop. Black's pawn structure says it all!

rn2kb1r/pp1bpppp/1q6/1Bpp4/3PnB2/2N2N2/P.comment: This is the most dangerous of the three options, leaving the queens on the board and forcing Black to find a series of accurate moves in order to stay alive. We will give the other two alternatives (11.Be5 and 11.Be3) without commentary, but they are definitely worth looking into in greater depth.

This is likelier to be chosen by someone unfamiliar with this line. Black rushes to complete his kingside development. Deploying the knight to the best square on the board and forcing Black's rook out of a8.
Another difficult move to find. Black counterattacks our vulnerable pieces in the center, but enables us to reestablish material equality.

rn2kb1r/pp1bpp1p/1q4p1/1Bpp4/3PnB2/2N2N2.comment: In the ...c5 line, we almost always castle queenside! With Black's pieces as passive as they are, there is little to no threat to White's monarch on the queenside.
An important move, restricting the mobility of the rook and preparing to optimize White's queenside structure with a2-a4.

rn2k2r/pp1bppbp/1q4p1/1Bpp4/3PnB2/2N2N2/.comment: Ignoring the threat on e6 by going the other way does not serve Black well:

rn3rk1/pp1bppbp/1q4p1/1Bpp4/3PnB2/2N2N2/.comment: Reinforcing the threat on e7. It is important to chase the queen away from b4: the tempting 16.Nxd5?? blunders mate on b2. The queen cannot keep d5 and e7 protected at the same time. Hitting the rook. There is nothing to fear along the d-file, e.g. and Black loses absolutely everything. Exchanging off Black's strongest piece, leaving the rest of his army unable to protect the d5-pawn and the incredibly vulnerable king at the same time. We are in no rush to take on f6. First, it is important to centralize the knight. Transforming our advantage: the powerful knight is given away in order to cripple Black's queenside pawn structure and initiate a decisive attack. Forcing the queen to relinquish its control of the d4-square.

rn3rk1/pp1bppbp/1q4p1/1Bpp2B1/3Pn3/2N2N2.comment: Black has managed to reestablish material equality, but strategically, White is still entirely dominating. We consolidate our advantage by establishing the knight on d4.
White is winning both positionally and tactically: e7, a7, and c6 are all under fire, and White can follow up by establishing the knight on c5 and prying Black's queen away with a timely a2-a4.

rn2r1k1/pp1bppbp/1q4p1/1Bpp2B1/3Pn3/2N2N.comment: Using tactics to pick off the pawn. Of course, the bishop is untouchable due to the discovered check on b6.

rn3rk1/pp1bppbp/1q4pB/1Bpp4/3Pn3/2N2N2/P.comment: White has a huge initiative. Our next move is Qd4, when we will threaten to capture on e6. In the event that Black doubles on the f-file, we can always solidify the f4-pawn with the calm g2-g3.

rn2kb1r/pp1b1ppp/1q6/1Bppp3/3PnB2/2N2N2/.comment: Black has kept his extra pawn, but at great cost. We are threatening Nxd5 followed by Ne6, when Black will have no choice but to part ways with the d5-pawn.

The position is equal, but I still prefer White - by a smidge. After the exchange of knights, Black will have a hard time deploying his bishop, and we have an easy path toward improving the rest of our pieces with Ke2 and Rd1 (or Rg1). There is no question that if Black has made it this far, he probably deserves the draw!

rn2k2r/pp1bppbp/1q4p1/1Bpp4/3PnB2/1PN2N2.comment: a2 is untouchable since the knight hangs. It is far more important to improve our queenside structure than it is to defend the measly f3-pawn!

rn2k2r/pp1b1pbp/1q4p1/1BppN3/3PnB2/1PN5/.comment: Black is saddled with weaknesses all across the board, and we will continue to improve and prepare infiltration by doubling rooks on the d-file.

rn2k2r/pp1b1pbp/1q4p1/1Bpp4/3Bn3/1PN2N2/.comment: with excellent winning chances due to Black's incredibly weak b-pawns.

rn2kb1r/pp1bpp1p/1q4p1/1Bpp4/3Pn3/2N1BN2.comment: The endgame is unclear and probably dynamically equal, but we have a clear plan of improvement: Ke2, a2-a3 (if necessary) followed by Rad1. Also worthwhile is the idea of probing for kingside weaknesses with h4-h5.

rn2k1r1/pp1bpp1p/1q4pb/1BppB3/3PN3/5N2/P.comment: Objectively, the position is equal, but we believe that White's play is quite a bit easier. We can improve our position with Ke2 followed by Rad1, and a well-timed h4-h5 threatens to shut down Black's bishop and will provoke more weaknesses on the kingside.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/8/2p5/3PpB2/8/PPP2PPP/R.comment: Black is at a crossroads. The queen trade hands over control of the d-file, leading to a very pleasant endgame for White. Most players prefer to go directly for the c-pawn, an extra option afforded by the absence of the knight on c3.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/8/2P5/4pB2/8/PPP2PPP/R2.comment: In contrast to the endgame arising after 4...dxe5 5.dxc5 Qxd1+ 6.Rxd1, this is an improved version for Black since Nb5 is no longer a threat. However, Black still faces a host of positional problems: the c5-pawn still majorly restricts Black's development and coordination, and White's control over the d-file gives us great play in the center. Objectively, the position is equal, but we have unearthed several ways to confront Black with serious practical problems. We will see this prophylactic move again in the main line (7...Nc6). The idea is to reinforce the c5-pawn, taking the sting out of ...e5. Turning our focus to development. It is, of course, very important to stop ...f5-f4, which would loosen our grip on the c5-pawn. We now continue our development. The knight is heading not for b5 but for d5, where it will lord over the entire position. We can follow up by exerting our influence on the queenside with b4-b5.

rnb1kb1r/pp2pppp/8/q1P5/4pB2/8/PPP2PPP/R.comment: You attack, we defend! As usual, this move is seldom to be feared in Jobava London endgames. We have plenty of resources with which to maintain the integrity of our queenside pawn structure.

It may seem counterproductive to rid Black of his doubled pawns, but we must generate active prospects for our minor pieces. Once the f-file is opened, Black will also have to deal with long-term pressure against the f7-pawn. A worthy alternative, although this move enables Black to build up a rather imposing kingside pawn mass. We will leave a deeper analysis of this move to you, but here is a sample line illustrating White's potential: This prevents Bc4, but the bishop is immediately targeted by our bloodthirsty knight. The trade of bishops is in our favor, since Black is left with a lame dark-squared bishop (that darn c5 pawn again!) Yet again, the knight has made its way to d5. As usual, we will increase the pressure dial on the queenside with b2-b4. We now aim to develop our bishop to c4 and apply serious pressure on Black's f7-pawn. Blocking the check and opening up a pathway for our own queen.

r1b1kb1r/pp2pppp/2n5/q1P5/1P2pB2/8/P1P2P.comment: This is better than the meek 11.c3, since we simultaneously complete our development and fully immobilize Black's knight.

r3kb1r/pp1bpppp/2n5/qBP5/1P2pB2/8/P1P2PP.comment: The b4-pawn is still untouchable. We will continue to improve our position by castling, and ferrying the knight over to c3. Once the weakening ...f5 is induced, we can rip open the center with the typical idea f2-f3, or double on the d-file and put significant pressure on the d7-bishop. Finally, our knight from c3 can seek greener pastures on b6.

rn2kb1r/pp2pppp/4b3/q1P5/4pB2/2P5/PP3PPP.comment: with massive pressure on the kingside. Note that in response to 15...h6, we will simply drop our knight back to f3, putting pressure on the e5-pawn. We will then have the ability to play on all three sides: b2-b4 is the classic idea on the queenside, h4-h5 is one way to expand on the kingside, and the weak pawn on e5 will provide ample fodder for play in the center. A clever retreating move. Of course, it is a retreating move in name only, since our intentions are extremely aggressive. We aim to root out Black's only active piece (the knight on c6 being fully restricted by the pawn on c3) with Bc4, when Black will be left with two minor pieces that will not be quite as capable of holding his position together. Castling and threatening Rxf5+!

rn2kb1r/pp2pp1p/4b1p1/q1P5/2B1pB2/2P5/PP.comment: Reinforcing the pawn on c5, and untying our hands for direct action on the kingside. The point of 9.f3 is on full display. White has full-scale pressure on the kingside, and the tempting 16...f4 creates a massive hole on e4 that we will use as an outpost for the knight.

rnb1kb1r/pp2pppp/8/2q5/4pB2/2P5/PP3PPP/R.comment: Picking up the pawn on e4.

rnb1kb1r/pp2pppp/8/2q5/Q3pB2/2P5/PP3PPP/.comment: This move is exceedingly rare, but it has been the choice of several strong players in recent months.

r1b1kb1r/pp2pppp/2n5/2q5/Q3pB2/2P5/PP3PP.comment: The queen is tucked away on an excellent square, from where it lords over both sides of the board while remaining fully impervious to attack. An important position has been reached. Black has two main ways of continuing: there is 9...Bf5, forcing White's queen to decide straightaway, and the more methodical 9...g6, preparing to fianchetto the bishop (which will pose a rather evil threat indeed). Both moves must be examined through the looking-glass, although 9...g6 has been the almost automatic choice of most top players in recent months.
This move has occurred quite a few times online!

r1b1kb1r/pp3ppp/2n5/q3p3/4Q3/2P1B3/PP3PP.comment: Of course, we do not fear the capture on f3, which will hand us full control of all the light squares in the center. Deploying the bishop to an extremely active post.

r1b1k2r/pp2bppp/2n5/q3p3/4Q3/2P1BN2/PP3P.comment: In order to parry the mate threat, Black must either swing his knight to f6, leaving its vis-a-vis fully entrenched on g5, or hand over the bishop pair, giving White a clear advantage in both cases.

r1b1kb1r/pp2pp1p/2n3p1/2q5/4QB2/2P5/PP3P.comment: On a4, the queen is mostly impervious to attack and discourages Black from castling queenside.
For now, we proceed with our development.

r1b1kb1r/pp3p1p/2n3p1/2q1p3/Q4B2/2P5/PP3.comment: This brazen move creates a lot more problems than it solves!

r1b1kb1r/pp3p1p/6p1/n3p3/5B2/2P5/PP2BPPP.comment: A lovely pawn sac to open up the c-file and engineer massive pressure on Black's king.

r1b1kb1r/pp3p1p/2n3p1/3qp3/Q4B2/2P5/PP3P.comment: Black's queen gets tossed around, and the worst is yet to come.

r1b1kb1r/pp3p1p/2n3p1/3qp3/Q1B2B2/2P5/PP.comment: Several of our blitz games reached this position. The queen has to move, and we will capture f7, with a decisive fork.

r1b1kb1r/pp3p1p/6p1/n3p3/8/2P1B3/PP3PPP/.comment: White holds a small but significant edge in the endgame for several reasons: 1) We have already castled, and staked our claim on the d-file. Black will not only have a hard time castling, but will experience difficulties in deploying the a8-rook, since the a7-pawn will hang. 2) Our subsequent development is clear. The f1-bishop belongs on b5, while the knight will be deployed to f3. 3) As the subsequent lines reveal, the e5-pawn is also a target that we can chip away at with our f-pawn.
Reinforcing the e5-pawn appears sensible, but merely throws more oil into the fire.

r1b1kb1r/pp5p/5pp1/n7/5p2/2P1B3/PP4PP/2K.comment: The e-file has been blasted open, and our pieces come out with furious vigor.

r4b1r/pp3k1p/4bpp1/nB6/5B2/2P5/PP4PP/2KR.comment: Black is in deep trouble, both strategically and tactically. Our rook will come to f1, creating long-term tactical threats along the f-file (such as Ng5+, followed by a discovered check with the bishop). Furthermore, our control over the d-file is particularly problematic, since Black's bishop cannot leave e6 (due to Rd7+). Finally, we can centralize our knight with Nd4, and if the bishop, the knight will move on to f5.

r1b1kb1r/pp2pp1p/2n3p1/2q5/4QB2/2P2N2/PP.comment: This way of developing has given quite a few Jobava London players grief, since Black generates the hidden threat of ...Bxc3+. Hans Niemann himself blundered in this position at the most recent World Blitz!

r1b1k2r/pp2ppbp/2n3p1/2q5/4QB2/2P2N2/PP3.comment: This is much more exciting (and far more rare) than the more standard 11.Qe3. White keeps the queens on the board and prepares a rapid kingside attack by means of Bf4-e3, Qh4, and ultimately Bh6. Black faces very serious practical problems in the center and on the kingside.
This rare move is a very reasonable way to sidestep the complications arising after 11...0-0. Black's queen retreats to a somewhat safer square, and threatens the b2-pawn.

r1b2rk1/pp2ppbp/2n3p1/2q5/4QB2/2P2N2/PP3.comment: Forcing the queen onto an inferior square, and paving the way for the development of our other bishop.

r4rk1/pp2ppbp/2n3p1/2q2b2/4QB2/2P2N2/PP1.comment: With the Black queen on a5, we go the other way (to h4), but here, it makes more sense to exert queenside pressure with our queen, since we are given the opportunity to do so.

r2R2k1/pp2ppbp/2n3p1/2q2b2/Q4B2/2P2N2/PP.comment: The position is equal according to the engine, but it is definitely easier to play White. We can proceed by creating a luft square with h2-h3, and then gradually roll our queenside pawns up the board. It is worth starting with a2-a4, since that is the least committal of the queenside pawn moves. Later on, we will follow up with b2-b4-b5. Black, on the other hand, has quite a hard time making something concrete of his pawn majority.

r4rk1/pp2pp1p/2n2bp1/q4b2/2B4Q/2P1BN2/PP.comment: Keeping a pair of rooks on the board is crucial if we want to maintain a long-lasting initiative. With every trade, the power of White's kingside pressure diminishes considerably. Note that control over the d-file is hardly important, since all of the potential infiltration squares (d1, d2, d3, etc.) are fully covered by our rook and minor pieces.
Defending while attacking! This move provokes a serious weakness on the kingside, but more importantly, it buys us a tempo that we can use to light the fire of our initiative!
Taking the sting out of the threat of Ng5.

r4rk1/pp2pp2/2n2bp1/q4b1p/2B4Q/2P1BN2/PP.comment: We have faced this type of move countless times in blitz.

r4rk1/pp2pp2/5bp1/q3nb1p/2B4Q/2P1B3/PP3P.comment: An interesting alternative that sidesteps ideas related to the weak back rank.

r4rk1/pp2pp2/5bp1/q3nb1p/2B4Q/2P5/PP1B1P.comment: and 22...Bd3 no longer works due to a crucial tactical detail:

r4rk1/pp2pp2/5bp1/q3n2p/2B4Q/2Pb4/PP1B1P.comment: It is important to refrain from h2-h3, which would enable Black to capture the rook on e5 with check (after ...Rxf1+ Kh2). Instead, g2 is the ideal escape square for the king, since it will also maintain contact with the rook on f1, straining the bishop on d3.

r4r2/pp2ppk1/5bp1/q3n2p/7Q/2PB4/PP1B1PPP.comment: Simple and decisive - this disarms all of Black's play on the first rank.

r4rk1/pp2pp2/5bp1/q3n2p/2B3PQ/2Pb4/PP1B1.comment: Another difficult only move, preparing to parry a check on the eighth rank with ...Bf8.

r4rk1/pp2ppb1/6p1/q3n2p/2B3PQ/2Pb4/PP1B1.comment: It turns out that block drops a piece: there is no way to stop the simultaneous threats of Qxe5 and Qd8+-xd3. A lovely display of the queen's power in an open board!
This is obviously a draw with best play, but White retains serious practical chances. We will bring our king up to the center and create a passed pawn on the queenside.

r4rk1/pp2pp2/5bp1/4qb1p/2B4Q/2P1B2P/PP3P.comment: Opening up a direct attack against the e7-pawn.

r4rk1/pp2pp2/6p1/4qb1p/2B4b/2P4P/PP1B1PP.comment: Black has succeeded in getting the heavy pieces off the board, but he has gone from the frying pan into the fire. White threatens to massacre Black's vulnerable queenside pawns with Bb8.

r4rk1/pp2pp1p/5bp1/q3nbQ1/2B5/2P1B3/PP3P.comment: White holds a small but very stable edge in the endgame. We will have a much easier job creating a passed pawn on the queenside, and we have many easy ways to improve our position: queenside expansion with a4-a5, as well as straightforward improving moves such as Rfe1 and Bd5 come to mind.

r4rk1/pp2pp1p/2n2bp1/q4bN1/2B4Q/2P1B3/PP.comment: Objectively position is even, but our bishop pair and more active light-squared bishop gives us a practical plus. Indeed, Black has to find the somewhat inhuman 16...Qa4 to keep the balance; a few inaccurate moves will hand White a stable plus, e.g.

r4rk1/pp2pp2/2n2bp1/q4bNp/2B4Q/2P1B3/PP3.comment: Another scintillating blow, hitting the queen and the bishop at the same time!

r4rk1/pp2pp2/2n2bp1/q5Np/7Q/2P1B3/PPb1BP.comment: We are unquestionably better in the endgame. As usual, our plan is to gradually advance the queenside pawns, with the dual aims of creating a passed pawn and restricting the mobility of Black's knight, which is already greatly restricted by the c3-pawn.

r4rk1/pp2pp2/2n2bp1/q2R1bNp/2B4Q/2P1B3/P.comment: This only move is virtually impossible to find! It leads to a wild tactical battle that ultimately peters out into a draw, but 10 more computer moves stand between Black and the peaceful result! This is the human move, and it loses on the spot: All of White's previous moves come together beautifully. Black must recapture the rook, opening up the pathway for White's queen. This is why we induced ...h7-h5! The only way to stave off mate, though Black's days are obviously numbered. Prying open either the g-file or the b1-h7 diagonal. In both cases, White's attack becomes decisive.

r4rk1/pp2pp2/2n3p1/3R1bNp/2B4Q/2q1B3/P4P.comment: Covering the check, and sending the queen on a journey to h1.

r4rk1/pp2pp2/2n3p1/3R1bNp/2B4Q/8/P2BKPPP.comment: White has exactly one tempo before the checks resume, and we put this tempo to very good use:

Black solidifies his center and prepares an eventual queen sally to b6. As usual, we initiate kingside operations and pose Black with an early dilemma. Analogously to the position after 4...Bg7 5.h4, Black has two main ways to meet Harry's march: Black can continue developing with 5...Bg7 (transposing to a position that we analyze via the 4...Bg7 5.h4 c6 move order), or meet White at the top with 5...h5. We answer the symmetrical variation in outwardly modest fashion, opening up our light-squared bishop and setting up the future idea of g2-g4. A few years back, 4.f3 was virtually automatic, but this innocuous-looking move has overtaken 4.f3 in popularity and in hype -- for good reason. Against most of Black's setups, our knight heads directly for e5, as it does in almost every other variation.

This scintillating counterstrike, which gained notoriety a few short years ago, is incomparably more exciting and challenging than the meek 4.e3. Our idea is straightforward: we aim to exploit our lead in development by blasting open the center. In a way, this move can be thought of as a massively improved Albin Countergambit (1.d4 d5 2.c4 e5). Black is now at a crossroads: three different captures are possible, and all of them must be considered carefully. The resulting positions are complex and full of exciting tactical possibilities.

This is a very important move that forces Black to make a positional concession. Black must either give away the bishop pair and damage his pawn structure with 4...Bd6, or permanently misplace his knight with 4...Na6. In the latter case, Black will push away the knight with ...c6, but the knight from a6 will still have a very hard time rejoining the game. There is no question that this is the worst of Black's three main lines, but it is the most popular by a country mile. Black has no way to defend c7 without giving up additional material. You will undoubtedly win more than a handful of games in this way!

There is no doubt that Black equalizes, but we stress that the position remains complex and difficult to handle from a practical standpoint. From this position, Black has two main setups: the first involves striking at the center right away with ...c7-c5. In response, we will trade on c5 and quickly prepare the typical central breakthrough e3-e4, granting us a nice space advantage and easy piece play. The second plan, more seldom seen at the club player level, involves grabbing as much queenside space as possible with ...b7-b5, and following up with ...Bb7 to prevent e4. We are quite proud of our recommendation against this second plan, which involves quickly closing up the queenside and transitioning our focus to a lightning kingside attack. This is extremely popular online, with over a hundred thousand games! Although developing the knight to c6 is natural, it blocks the c-pawn, handing White immediate supremacy in the center. Of course, we have also committed the same transgression, but we have the benefit of the extra tempo! We harness our development advantage by quickly shepharding the knight to e5, and following up with g2-g4 in the event that Black develops the bishop to f5.

This is the most common response online, by quite a wide margin. Our next steps are to develop the knight and ready ourselves for queenside castling. Ignoring White's plan leads to a quick and decisive kingside attack. Amazingly, 5...0-0 is the second most common move online, with around 37,000 games at the time of analysis. A welcome statistic indeed! Black takes the plunge. This is second in popularity behind 6...Nxh5, but objectively it is clearly Black's best try. Still, the resulting positions - with a wide open h-file granting us exciting attacking opportunities at every turn - are virtually impossible for a human to handle accurately. This keeps the h-file closed, but creates a host of weaknesses in the center and on the kingside.
