In this line, the strategic potency of Nb5 is on full display: the knight on a6 will have a very difficult time rejoining society: the shortest path involves ferrying the knight around to d6 via c7 and e8, which already takes a staggering number of moves. Our general approach is to quickly complete our kingside development. After we do that...okay, how about we cross that bridge when we get there!

rnbqk2r/ppp2ppp/3bpn2/1N1p4/3P1B2/8/PPP1.comment: Black is at a further crossroads. He can chase the knight away immediately with 5...c6, focus on kingside development with 5...Be7, or strike at the center straightaway with 5...c5. All of these eventualities must be carefully considered - each leads to a fundamentally different type of battle.

The first step is obvious: we block the check with our pawn, sending the bishop back to a5. A clever, dastardly resource! Rather than putting our cards on the table with the immediate 6.b4, we set up the threat of b2-b4 and a4-a5, which will trap the bishop on b6. Black must respond by attempting to chase away our knight.
Thank you for the bishop pair!

rnbqk2r/ppp2ppp/3bpn2/1N1p4/3P1B2/4P3/PP.comment: The main move at a high level. Black retains maximum flexibility, developing his kingside and reserving the possibility to chase away White's knight at a more convenient moment.

rnbqk2r/ppp1bppp/4pn2/1N1p4/3P1B2/4P3/PP.comment: It is quite clear that our journey to b5 has been anything but a waste of time. Not only is Black's knight awkwardly placed, but it is outright vulnerable: Black must now reckon with the positional threat of Bxa6, permanently ruining Black's queenside structure and creating a massive hole on c5 that we can easily access with our knight.
It is always a good idea to reinforce the knight, taking the sting out of ...Bd7.

rnbqk2r/ppp1bppp/4pn2/3p4/3P1B2/2N1P3/PP.comment: We certainly don't miss the opportunity to create massive, long-term weaknesses on the queenside.

rnbqk2r/ppp2ppp/3bpn2/3p4/3P1B2/2N1P3/PP.comment: Calmly continuing our development. It is important to remember that the combination of ...Bb4 and ...Ne4 is almost never scary in the Jobava: we almost always respond by castling, giving up the c3-pawn but attaining a massive initiative in return. In this case, we will also attain total positional domination on the queenside.

rnbqk2r/ppp2ppp/3bpn2/3p4/3P1B2/2N1PN2/P.comment: As with 8...Ne4, we are more than happy to give up a pawn in exchange for full control over the dark squares.

Pushing the pawn may eradicate the weakness on c6, but it does not rid us of the outpost on c5. We are almost always happy to achieve the d4-f4 pawn bind, which resembles a Maroczy Bind shifted one file to the right.

rnbq1rk1/ppp2ppp/3bpn2/3p4/3P1B2/2N1PN2/.comment: Seizing the b-file and preventing Black from deploying the bishop to b7. Striking while the iron is hot!

In contrast to the 8...Qa5 line, here Black keeps the dark-squared bishop, but it is unable to move back to the a3-f8 diagonal. As such, White still holds complete domination over the dark squares, and the imminent prospect of Ne5 will push Black over the edge. Preventing Ne5 does more harm than good: Preventing Black from castling, and reinforcing our control over key dark squares along the a3-f8 diagonal. We saw a similar move in the 8...Qa5 line (see White's 15th move). If the pawn is captured, Black's entire queenside will be in tatters; if it isn't, the pawn will deliver a further blow to Black's defensive capacity once it reaches c5.
The queen has been forced onto a more vulnerable square, enabling our knight to jump into the action.

rnbqr1k1/ppp2ppp/3bpn2/3p4/3P1B2/2N1PN2/.comment: Now, another pawn is temporarily sacrificed in order to tear open the queenside and increase the power of our initiative.

rnbqr1k1/ppp2ppp/4pn2/2bpN3/3P1B2/2N1P3/.comment: Black is absolutely screwed: he can barely move, his queenside is collapsing, and our pieces are on optimal squares. This line really showcases the multi-faceted nature of the Jobava London: it is an opening that promises its adherents not just tactical victories, but strategic masterpieces as well!

rnbq1rk1/ppp2ppp/3bpn2/3p4/3PNB2/4PN2/PP.comment: Defending the pawn with the queen prevents Rb7, but opens Black up to a devastating attack on the kingside. It is worth flicking in this move, which forces Black's bishop on an even more awkward square. Suddenly, we transition from the queenside to the kingside! It turns out that our previous move had a hidden aim: White now intends the gorgeous e3-e4, opening up a pathway from the queenside to the kingside for our rook! In addition, we threaten the banal Bh6, forcing Black to burn a crucial tempo.

rnbq1rk1/pp3ppp/3bpn2/2pp4/3PNB2/4PN2/PP.comment: And now, we entrench the bishop on the sexiest outpost on the board!

rnbq1rk1/pp3ppp/3Bpn2/2pp4/3PN3/4PN2/PPP.comment: A lovely positional sacrifice, giving up the center pawn in order to carve out a devastating path for our knight.

rnbqr1k1/pp3ppp/3Bpn2/2pp4/3PN3/4PN2/PPP.comment: It took us a while, but we finally got our knight on a perfect square! c6 is hanging, and Black has no choice but to allow the infiltration of our rook.

rnbqr1k1/pp3ppp/3Bpn2/2ppN3/3PN3/4P3/PPP.comment: This line is worth reviewing several times. Note that White sacrifices three pawns, and all three sacrifices are entirely positional in nature. First, the c3-pawn is sacrificed to spark the flames of the initiative. Then, after the queen is ferried to a3, we open up the queenside with c2-c4. Once Black declines the pawn, it is driven to c5, and we finish with a sacrifice that enables us to carve out a devastating pathway for our knight. A certified Jobava Classic!

rn1q1rk1/pppb1ppp/3bpn2/3p4/3PNB2/4PN2/P.comment: There it is! We saw this same move in the 11...f6 sub-variation, although it was played for an entirely different reason (to get the knight to e5). Here, the knight is already on e5, and this move is played in order to lift the rook over to the kingside.
Note that total dominance of our knight over Black's entire army! The king is now boxed in, and a beautiful mating pattern seals the deal:

rnbq1rk1/ppp2ppp/B2bpn2/3p4/3P1B2/2N1PN2.comment: Naroditsky-Makhnyov, Chess.com (blitz) 2023. Now, the natural response is 12.Ne5, but it is beat out by a scintillating positional sacrifice: As usual, this move is futile, but this time for a more tactical reason:
A sad necessity, but this creates long-term weaknesses on the kingside.

rnbq1rk1/ppp2ppp/B2bp3/3p4/3PnB2/2N1PN2/.comment: Exploiting the uncastled nature of Black's king!

rnbq1rk1/pp3ppp/3bpn2/2ppN3/3P1B2/2N1P3/.comment: We saw a very similar idea in the 8...a5 variation, with the minor difference that Black's rook was on a8 and the pawn was still on c6. These cosmetic differences change very little: White still threatens Bxf6 followed by Nd7, and White is still very much incapable of dealing with the problems that await him on both sides of the board.

rnbq1rk1/pp3ppp/B2bpn2/3pN3/3p1B2/2N1P3/.comment: A pretty in-betweener, driving the queen away from d8 and setting up Bxf6.

rnb2rk1/pp1q1ppp/B1Nbpn2/3p4/3p1B2/2N1P3.comment: White is better on both sides of the board!

rnbq1rk1/pp3ppp/B2bpn2/3pN3/3P1B2/2N5/PP.comment: Instead of the regular 14.Na4, here we have a tactic that leads to immediate victory:

rnbqk2r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/3p4/1b1P1B2/2N1PN2/.comment: See typical idea #1: the knight is once again placed between the two bishops!

rnbqk2r/ppp2ppp/3Bpn2/3p4/1b1P4/2N1PN2/P.comment: Yet another textbook move, preparing to lift the queen up to h3 in the event that Black castles. If Black tries to root out the knight on e5 straightaway, a secondary point of this move is revealed: Boom shaka-laka! The queen on f3 renders ...Kxf7 impossible, and Black has no choice but to part ways with a very important pawn. An important detail: the myopic 11.Nxh8 led to a far more double-edged position, since we would run the risk of losing the knight. Defending the pawn and preventing ...e5! We have completed our minor piece development, and are fully ready to initiate aggressive action on the kingside. We will do so by flying our queen to h3, and, if necessary, supplementing with g4-g5. Black's main issue is that he has nothing going on the queenside, giving us a free hand on the other side of the board. The power of the knight on e5 can hardly be overstated: it lords over the entire position, making it virtually impossible for Black to get anything going in the way of counterplay.

The most logical move: Black initiates counterplay in the center and aims to undermine our knight. As it turns out, we are more than happy to go along! A sensible attempt to prepare ...Nd7 by protecting the bishop. However, it is much to slow, and the knight on e5 is so well-defended that Black will not possibly be able to get it to move! Here, Black puts more immediate pressure on the knight, so it is worth amending the queen's path to lend the knight further support:

rnbqk2r/pp3ppp/3Bpn2/2pp4/1b1P4/2N1PN2/P.comment: The knight on e5 no longer requires the support of the d4-pawn, since the bishop does the job perfectly well.

rnbqk2r/pp3ppp/3Bpn2/2Pp4/1b6/2N1PN2/PPP.comment: Now, it is time for typical idea #5: the queen is ferried over to h3 before initiating a furious kingside storm.

rnbqk2r/pp3ppp/3Bpn2/2bp4/8/2N1PN2/PPP2P.comment: Having induced serious weaknesses on the kingside, we move on to the pawn storm phase. Our next step is to shift the queen to g3 in order to leave open the path for the h-pawn.

rnbqk2r/pp3ppp/3Bpn2/2bp4/6P1/2N1PN2/PPP.comment: It is always important to be patient in the Jobava London, and this line is no exception. Before rolling up our sleeves on the kingside, we ensure the safety of our king (and threaten Nb5).

rnb1k2r/ppq2ppp/3bpn2/3p4/6PP/2N1PN2/PPP.comment: While the computer will likely hold off the attack, we believe that the position is totally untenable from a human perspective. We will either open the h-file with hxg6 or, in the event of ...g5, smash open the kingside with f2-f4.

rnbqk2r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/3p4/1b1P1B2/2NBPN2/.comment: As always, we are more than willing to part ways with a pawn in order to achieve a harmonious setup and gain control of key queenside squares (typical idea #8).

rnbq1rk1/ppp2ppp/4pn2/3p4/1b1P1B2/2NBPN2.comment: A familiar idea, establishing a very nasty pin against Black's knight.

White's compensation is absolutely massive: Black has no good way to end the pin, since ...g5 creates fatal weaknesses on the kingside and ...Qc7 allows us to capture on f6. We can follow up by intensifying the pressure with Ne5 and f2-f4, followed by a rook or queen lift to the kingside. On the queenside, Black has no active prospects and no good way to activate the light-squared bishop.

r1bqk2r/pp3ppp/4pn2/2np4/1b3B2/2NBPN2/PP.comment: Black has spent endless tempi to get the knight to an active square, only to be sent back to a6!

rnbqk2r/pp3ppp/3bpn2/2pp4/N2P1B2/4PN2/PP.comment: The knight on e4 appears imposing, but it can be kicked away at our convenience with f2-f3.

rnbqk2r/pp4pp/3bpp2/2ppN3/N2PnB2/4P3/PPP.comment: The knight has been ferried over to an ideal square. Now, both knights control c5, and we threaten to win the knight with f2-f3. The position plays itself: Nac5 can be followed by Re1, when Black is sinking under the weight of his endless weaknesses.

rn1q1rk1/pppbbppp/4p3/1N1pB2n/3P4/2PBPN2.comment: Now, rather than the meek 11.g3, we can exploit the vulnerability of Black's knight with a lovely tactic:

rn1q1rk1/pppbb2p/4ppp1/1N1pB1Nn/3P4/2PBP.comment: Now, 12...Kxh7 leads to rapid checkmate after 13.Qxh5, so Black must part ways with a lot of material and give up the final pawn which provides shelter to the king.

rn2bqk1/ppp1b1n1/4p1B1/1N1pp3/3P2Q1/2P1P.comment: with three pawns and a rook for two pieces, as well as domination on tthe queenside and the straightforward idea of pushing the h-pawn all the way to h6.

rn1q1rk1/pp1bbppp/4pn2/1N1p4/2pP1B2/2PBP.comment: We have achieved our ideal minor piece setup, and can improve our position in a litany of ways.

rn3rk1/pp1bbppp/1q2pn2/1N1p4/2pP1B2/2P1P.comment: Needless to say, we could not care less about giving up a measly pawn on the queenside. With this move, we set up a queen-bishop battery, which will likely lead to a swift and decisive attack against Black's king.

rn3rk1/pp2bp1p/1q2pnp1/1b1p2N1/2pP1B2/2P.comment: Typical idea #3: we rush the h-pawn up the board, and Black has too many weaknesses and not enough defenders on the kingside to do anything about it. Obviously, we do not even think about trading queens!

rn3r2/pp2bpk1/1q2pn1p/1b1p2pP/2pP1B2/2P1.comment: A thematic piece sacrifice, smashing open the kingside. With the queen entirely out of commission on b3, Black cannot lend nearly enough reinforcement to the kingside and the attack will end the game in a matter of a few moves.

rn3r1k/pp2bp2/1q2pn1P/1b1p2p1/2pP1B2/2P1.comment: Rebuilding the battery! This time, Black has no pawn to put on g6, and the bishop blocks the f-pawn. Checkmate is coming on the next move.

rnbq1rk1/ppp1bppp/4pn2/1N1p4/3P1B2/4PN2/.comment: A very interesting move favored by GM Arjun Erigaisi, one of the leading specialists of this line. White's idea could not possibly be more straightforward: we want to checkmate Black on the kingside! As a bonus, this move opens up an escape square for the bishop on h2, which takes the sting out of a knight jump to h5. The engine is slow to approve of this move, but careful analysis shows that Black's position is incredibly difficult to handle.

rn1q1rk1/pp1bbppp/2p1pn2/1N1p4/3P1B1P/2P.comment: As always, this kind of position favors White, since the knight on b5 cannot be easily driven away.

rn1q1rk1/pp1bbppp/2p1pn2/1N1p4/P2P1B1P/2.comment: Hoping to meet bxc4 with ...Bxb5 followed by ...Qxc3+. But we have a lovely positional move up our sleeve:

rn3rk1/pp1bbppp/2p1pn2/qN1p4/P2P1B1P/2P1.comment: Gorgeous. By covering the e1-a5 diagonal, we ensure that ...Qxc3 does not come with check, so 11...Bxb5 no longer works. After the trade on b3 (which is forced, since we threaten to take on c4), the queen will be driven back to b6 and we will finally be able to deploy our light-squared bishop to d3.

rn3rk1/pp1bbppp/1qp1pn2/1N1p4/P2P1B1P/2P.comment: It is a good idea to shuttle our knight back to d2 in order to reinforce the e4-square and open up the b-file. It appears that Black has gotten the better of us tactically, but yet another scintillating retreating knight move proves otherwise. Simply divine! The knight moves back to its initial square, establishing contact between the queen and bishop, and facing Black with two threats at the same time. Black has nothing better than to give up the exchange, when his compensation will be woefully insufficient.

rnr3k1/pp1bbppp/1qp1pn2/1N1p4/P2P1B1P/2P.comment: Our king has been ferried to safety, and Black has nothing going on on the queenside.

rnbq1rk1/pp2bppp/2p1pn2/1N1p4/3P1B1P/3BP.comment: Should we meekly shift the rook to b1? Absolutely not! With the knight no longer on f6, the correct idea should be second nature to a seasoned tactician. Greek gift time! Yes, seemingly every idea has its moment in the sun in the Jobava London. This move decides the game instantly. A classic concept, removing the pawn from f7 before returning to h5 and delivering check on h7. Black is mated by force.

rnbq1rk1/pp2bppp/4pn2/2pp4/3P1B1P/2N1PN2.comment: Driving the pawn down to h5 and creating the rather nasty threat of h5-h6, which will provoke long-term weaknesses on the kingside.

rnbq1rk1/pp2bppp/4p3/2pp4/3P1B1P/2n1PN2/.comment: Yet again, we are happy to part ways with a pawn (typical idea #8).

rnbq1rk1/pp2bpp1/4p3/2pp3p/3P1B1P/2P1PN2.comment: We dominate on both sides of the board, and can follow up with Ne5.

rnbq1rk1/pp4pp/5p2/2bppB1n/5BPP/2N1PN2/P.comment: It appears that our queen is trapped, but we have a nice way to trade it off for its counterpart. We have two pawns for the exchange, and Black's incredibly weak kingside pawns will give us plenty of targets. Furthermore, the h4-pawn - once an attacker - has now become a fearsome passed pawn which will keep Black's rooks at bay.

rnbq1r2/pp2bpp1/4p1k1/2pp2Nn/3P1B1P/2N1P.comment: Black's king is caught in the crossfire of a lovely attack that quickly results in mate.

rnbq1rk1/pp2bpp1/4pn1p/2pp3P/3P1B2/2N1PN.comment: Time to rip open the g-file! White's attack proceeds at a furious pace, while Black has very little going on the other side of the board.

rnbq1rk1/pp2bpp1/4pn1p/3p2BP/8/2N1PN2/PP.comment: Dark-square domination! Black is utterly paralyzed.

rnbq1rk1/pp2b1p1/4p2p/2pp1p1P/3P1Bn1/2N1.comment: The g4-knight is the last obstacle standing between White and Black's monarch. Note that we are not just playing on the kingside: the long-term threat of a well-timed capture on a6 is yet another headache that Black must manage.

rnbq1rk1/pp4p1/4pB1p/2pp1p1P/3P4/2N1P3/P.comment: It is the perfect opportunity to capture on a6, since we will follow up by capturing on c5 and opening up the d4-square for our queen.

rn3rk1/pp4p1/4pq1p/2Pp1p2/3Q1Nb1/4P3/PPP.comment: Despite the loss of a pawn, White maintains complete dominance of the key e5-square, which will be used as an outpost for the knight. This, coupled with the passed pawn on c5, gives White overwhelming compensation for the pawn.

rnbqk2r/ppp2ppp/3bpn2/1N1p4/3P1B2/2P5/PP.comment: A critical position. It may appear that White's queenside play has ground to a complete halt, but the party is only beginning. This is a more desirable way to chase away the knight from a strategic point of view, but it contains a fatal tactical flaw: Black grants us access to the d6-square!

rnbqk2r/1pp2ppp/p2bpn2/1N1p4/3P1B2/2P5/P.comment: Counterattacking the bishop! This is the first of many fantastic tactical moves that pose serious problems for Black on the queenside.

rnbqk2r/1pp2ppp/3bpn2/1p1p4/1P1P1B2/2P5/.comment: The first step is always to open the diagonal for our bishop and buttress the b-pawn. It is crucial not to rush with taking the bishop, as it is pinned to the rook on a8. We still do not take the bishop!

Using the compromised position of Black's knight to stake a claim in the center. Clearly, Black has insufficient compensation for the exchange. Our next step is to calmly develop our kingside and ferry the king to safety.
An incredibly deep move. While 9.Bd2 is far more natural, the bishop is better placed in the following variation:
With the rook gone, Black instantly loses the pawn.

rnbqk2r/1pp2ppp/3bpn2/1p1p4/1P1P1B2/2P1P.comment: The only way to maintain a feasible position, although this move is not at all easy to find.

Now that White's bishop cannot return to d2 to block the check on c3, this is a far more serious idea. However, White's king is able to dodge the checks by journeying to f3! Hunting for the c-pawn is almost never effective, as Black loses a ton of tempi in the process and we are able to attain an ideal setup.

rnbqk2r/1p3ppp/2pbpn2/1p1p4/1P1P1B2/2P1P.comment: White has overwhelming compensation for the pawn.

rnbq1rk1/1pp2ppp/3bpn2/1p1p4/1P1P4/2P3B1.comment: White's position is preferrable:we have quite a bit more space, long-term pressure down the h-file, as well as total domination over key queenside squares and the eventual possibility of pressure down the c-file.

rn1qk2r/1ppb1ppp/3bpn2/1p1p4/1P1P1B2/2P1.comment: An inventive alternative to the more conventional 11.Nf3, pinning the knight on f6 and inducing a major kingside weakening with ...h6-g5. If Black does not chase the bishop away, White will maintain lasting pressure on the kingside.
It is vital to keep the bishop pair.
Cool, calm, and collected! All alone on our territory, the Black queen is fighting a lost cause.

rn1qk2r/1ppb1pp1/3bpn1p/1p1p2B1/1P1P4/2P.comment: Now that Black has castled kingside, ...g7-g5 comes with a far steeper price tag. In the finest traditions of the Jobava London! With the dark squared bishop gone, Black will have a very hard time insulating the kingside against the litany of threats that our bloodthirsty queen-bishop tandem will pose.

We readily sacrifice the pawn on b5 in order to complete our development. The idea is to properly time the trade on a8 and to follow up with Bxf6, permanently ruining Black's kingside pawn structure and offering White a lasting initiative. Putting the bishop on g5 to work! Black instantly pays the price for the sloppy capture on a1. The queen must babysit the a8-square, forcing Black to recapture with the pawn.
The queen is terribly overextended, paralyzing the knight on a5. Setting up the vicious threat of Bxf6+ and Qh4+, picking off Black's queen.

rn1qk2r/1ppb1pp1/3bpn2/1p1p2p1/1P1P4/2P1.comment: Quiet and powerful. By completing our development, we ensure that our kingside attack will never fizzle out.

rn1qk3/1ppb1pp1/3bpn2/1p1p2pr/1P1P4/2PBP.comment: Black has nothing better than to give back the material with 19...Ne4.

rn1qk2r/1ppb1pp1/3bpn1p/1p1p2B1/1P1P4/2P.comment: White has fantastic compensation for the pawn, as defined by several factors: 1) The bishop on b5 has no active prospects, while the knight has countless ways to join the game, ranging from Nf4-Nh5 to the more creative d5 followed by Nd4. 2) Black's pawn structure on both sides of the board, but particularly the kingside, is horrific. 3) We control the center and the only open file on the board; 4) There is no shelter anywhere on the board for Black's king. The subsequent lines are obviously not forced, but they nicely illustrate the way in which these factors translate to a monster initiative.

rn1q1r2/1ppb1ppk/3bpn1p/1p1p2B1/1P1P4/2P.comment: Incredible geometry. After provoking ...Kh7 (which may seem counterproductive), the queen returns to b1, attacking the bishop and creating an x-ray against the King. But White does not follow up with e5+, which would be futile. The correct continuation is far more explosive! There is the rub! The bishop is forced away from c6, leading to the destruction of Black's entire queenside. What a variation! The zigzag pattern adopted by our queen leaves quite the lasting impression.
From a practical perspective, White's compensation for the two pawns is absolutely overwhelming. Black is facing a litany of threats in the center and on the kingside, the most immediate being Nf5.

rn1q2r1/1ppb1ppk/3bpn1p/1p1p2B1/1P1P4/2P.comment: The queen shuttles back to b1, forcing Black's king to relinquish its control over the h6-pawn.

rn3qrk/1ppb1pp1/3bpn1p/1p1p1NB1/1P1P4/2P.comment: Back to c1 we go! The pressure has reached a zenith, and in order to emerge unscathed, Black must uncork a series of jaw-dropping computer moves. A lovely deflection sacrifice that would be decisive if not for an even crazier counter-combination. Luring the king to g2, upon which Black can intercept the c1-h6 diagonal with ...e3+ and pick up the rook on d8. Of course, we refuse to cooperate!

rn1qk2r/1ppb1pp1/3bpn1p/1p1p4/1P1P3B/2P1.comment: It is far from easy to make these moves, which permanently weaken Black's kingside. The resulting position - while objectively balanced - remains very difficult for Black to accurately navigate.

rn1qk2r/1ppb1p2/3bp2p/1p1p2p1/1P1Pn3/2P1.comment: A typical prophylactic move, dealing a blow to the knight's prospects. Wonderfully inventive chess! The king embraces its new role as an integral part of the kingside mosaic. Its role on f2 will be revealed on the next move. Despite our outward lack of piece coordination, we are able to hold Black's knight at bay on the strenghth of some badass tactics.
This weakens the e5 square and enables us to maintain the bishop pair.

rn1qk2r/1ppb1p2/3bp2p/1p1p2p1/1P1P4/2P1P.comment: The king feels perfectly at home on g3, and the time has finally come to complete our development.

rn1qk2r/1ppb1p2/3b3p/1p1pp1p1/1P1P4/2PBP.comment: Having done its job on g3, the indefatigable monarch ducks back to safety on f2.

rn1qk2r/1ppb1p2/3b3p/1p1pP1p1/1P6/2PBPPn.comment: While the position remains level, White's practical play is quite a bit easier. Our knight will find a lovely home on d4, while the rook on h1 keeps Black's queen tied down to the h4-pawn.

rn1qk2r/1ppb1p2/3bp2p/1p1p2p1/1P1P4/2n1P.comment: The knights are pinned, and Black loses a minor piece:

rnbqk2r/1pp2ppp/3bpn2/1p1p4/1P1P4/2P5/P2.comment: It turns out that Black's bishop is most certainly not out of the woods! The smoke has finally cleared, and it is obvious that we are the one calling the shots. We can follow up by solidifying our central control with f2-f4. Black suffers from a lack of space and the permanent weakness of the b5-pawn.

rnbqk2r/1p3ppp/2pbpn2/1p1p4/1P1P4/2P5/P2.comment: Underscoring the counterproductive nature of Black's seventh move. This move now comes with tempo, enabling us to recapture Black's bishop while keeping our queenside pawn structure fully intact. Black's knight sally to h5 has been an abject failure: we are ready to recapture the bishop on a5, and Black has no way to recover the pawn.

rnbqk2r/1p3ppp/2pb1n2/1p1pp3/1P1PP3/2P5/.comment: Had the bishop been on d2, Black could have captured it with their knight! As it stands, White is simply winning, since we will recapture the bishop and chase away or even trap the knight with f2-f3.

r1bqk2r/1pp2ppp/1n1bpn2/1p1p4/1P1P4/2P1P.comment: This is the best square for White's queen. On b1, it is far away from the predations of Black's knights, and will link up with bishop (after Bd3) to exert nagging pressure on the e4-knight. Note that ...Nc3 is nothing but an empty threat, in response to which we can simply bring our queen up to b3.

r2q1rk1/1ppb1ppp/1n1bpn2/1p1p4/1P1P4/2P1.comment: We have successfully completed our kingsid development and kept Black's queenside counterplay at bay. We will follow up by castling and deploying the rook to c1. White's total control over all of the key queenside squares renders Black's compensation for the exchange virtually nonexistant.

r2qk2r/1ppb1ppp/2nbpn2/1B1p4/1P1P1B2/2P1.comment: We have successfully navigated the queenside chaos, and it is clear that White will have all the fun in the middlegame. After castling, we can intensify the pressure with Ne5 and Bg5.

rn1q1rk1/1ppb1ppp/3bpn2/1p1p4/1P1P1B2/2P.comment: The extra pawn is meaningless: our excellent piece coordination, bishop pair, and firm control over all key dark squares in the center grant us excellent prospects in the middlegame.
This move underscores the importance of dark-square control in this variation. The bishop has a few questions to ask of the Black queen!

rn1qr1k1/1ppb1ppp/3Bpn2/1p1p4/1P1P4/2P1P.comment: A lovely sequence indeed. Black loses an exchange for no compensation. Note the path taken by White's bishop, which started on f4 and ends all the way on the other side of the board!

r1bqk2r/1ppn1ppp/3bpn2/1p1p4/QP1P1B2/2P5.comment: Note that we do not even have to rush to take the pawn - it is going nowhere!

rnbq1rk1/1pp2ppp/3bpn2/1p1p4/1P1P1B2/2P1.comment: This move almost never works tactically, since our bishop is trained at the knight on b8.

r1bq1rk1/1ppn1ppp/3bpn2/1p1p4/QP1P1B2/2P.comment: Black has no way to win back the pawn.

r1bq1rk1/1ppn1ppp/3bpn2/1p1p4/1P1P1B2/2P.comment: Oftentimes, this move is not as advisable with Black's knight on d7 and no bishop on d6, since Black can now simply capture our knight. In this specific position, however, we can effectively recapture on e5 with the pawn, driving away Black's knight and leading to an incredibly strong kingside attack.

r1bq1rk1/1ppn1ppp/3bp3/1p1pN3/1P1P1B2/2P.comment: The threat of f2-f3 renders Black's knight an utterly ineffective defender.

r1bq1rk1/1ppn2pp/3bp3/1p1pNp1Q/1P1P1B2/2.comment: Picking up the pawn with interest.
Black is dominated on the dark squares, and cannot defend e6 and c7 simultaneously.

r1b2rk1/1ppnqp1p/3bp1pQ/1p1pN3/1P1P1B2/2.comment: The march of the h-pawns spells big trouble for Black. Note that we can push h4-h5 against virtually any move, including ...f6. The attack is decisive.

rnbqk2r/1pp2ppp/4pn2/1p1p4/1b1P1B2/2P1P3.comment: Intrepid play is a prerequisite if you want to consider yourself a real Jobava player! As scary as this appears, Black simply does not have the firepower to exploit the king's compromised position. He has no choice but to spend time on castling and on activating his knight with ...Ne4; we will use this time to carve out shelter for our king on g2.

rnbq1rk1/1pp2ppp/4pn2/1p1p4/1b1P1B2/2PBP.comment: Forming a queen-bishop battery, and preparing to meet 12...c6 with the devastating 13.b6.

rnbq1rk1/1pp2ppp/4p3/1p1p4/1b1PnB1P/2P1P.comment: It appears that Black has trapped our bishop, since opening the f-file is unthinkable. But we have one more trick up our sleeve.

rnbq1rk1/1pp3pp/4pp2/1p1p4/1b1PnB1P/2P1P.comment: Counterattacking Black's knight, and forcing Black to relinquish his control over the c3-bishop. The tactics work out in White's favor.

Another counterblow, this time hitting the bishop! If the bishop retreats to a5, we can finally save our bishop by taking twice on e5. Gorgeous tactics. The threat of Ne6+ forces Black to leave the knight on f3. Our king will journey back to the promised land to pick it up! This time, under the able protection of the knight, it will be quite a bit safer on that square. Note that 23...Qe7 should be met with 24.Qxd5, covering the e4-square.

rnbqk2r/ppp2ppp/3Npn2/3p4/3P1B2/8/PPP1PP.comment: This is one of the only lines where Black attains the pawn structure that we are used to having after Bd3 Bxd3 cxd3 (see typical idea #2). However, Black lacks a dark-squared bishop, which renders this pawn structure quite a bit less effective. The other bishop does not have active prospects, and preparing the ...e6-e5 pawn push - while opening up a diagonal for the bishop - will create even more targets in the center.

rnbqk2r/pp3ppp/3ppn2/3p4/3P1B2/8/PPP1PPP.comment: White's advantage is defined by two factors: (1) the bishop pair and (2) the long-term pressure that we will exert against the d6-pawn.

rnbqk2r/pp3ppp/3ppn2/3p4/3P1B2/4P3/PPP2P.comment: This is best according to the computer, but it is virtually never played and does not really change the tenor of the position.

r1bqk2r/pp3ppp/2nppn2/3p4/3P1B2/4P3/PPP2.comment: Transposes to 6...Nc6 7.Nf3 0-0 8.c3 Re8 9.h3. This is surprisingly common, but it simply drops a pawn for no compensation.

r1b1k2r/pp3pp1/2nppn1p/q2p4/3P1B2/2P1P3/.comment: It is quite important to throw this move in in response to ...h6, since Nf3 allows Black to pick up the bishop with ...Nh5.

r3k2r/pp1b1pp1/2npp2p/q2p4/3Pn3/2P1P2P/P.comment: (Niemann) After the trade, Black will have a very hard time keeping d6 protected.

r1b1k2r/pp3ppp/2nppn2/3p4/3P1B2/2P1P3/qP.comment: Recovering the pawn and preventing Black from castling. Things are already quite bad for Black:

r1b1k2r/pp3ppp/2nBp3/3p4/3Pn3/2P1P3/qP3P.comment: A strange-looking move, but it prevents the queen from escaping via a5 and - much like Nb5 (see typical idea #7) - lures Black's knight to an incredible passive square.

r1b1k2r/pp3p2/2n1p3/3p2pp/3Pn3/2P1P1B1/q.comment: Preparing to meet ...h4 with Be5 f6 Bxe4, when Black can only take one bishop at a time! White's advantage is not up for debate.

r1bq1rk1/pp3ppp/2nppn2/3p4/3P1B2/4PN2/PP.comment: It is always a good idea to buttress the d4-pawn, rendering ...e6-e5 even less effective.

r1bq1rk1/pp3ppp/2nppn2/3p4/3P1B2/2P1PN2/.comment: Activating the knight and reinforcing the d6-pawn.

r1bq1rk1/pp3ppp/2npp3/3p4/3PnB2/2P1PN1P/.comment: This move is the opposite of scary. The x-ray against White's king my appear concerning, but with the d4-pawn as secured as it is, Black has absolutely no way to convert his temporary development advantage into anything tangible. After we complete our kingside development, Black will experience long-lasting problems with his center.

r2q1rk1/pp3ppp/2np4/3ppb2/3Pn3/2P1PN1P/P.comment: Under different circumstances, this type of pawn structure can favor Black, but with no dark-squared bishop, it makes a lot less sense. We have active ideas on both sides of the board.
Since ...e4 is never scary, we simply continue our development.

r2q1rk1/pp3ppp/2np4/3ppb2/3Pn3/1QP1PN1P/.comment: Recovering the knight and leading to a miserable endgame for Black. His pawn structure says it all!

r4rk1/1p1q1ppp/p1np4/3ppb2/3Pn3/1QP1P2P/.comment: The pawn advances to g5, where it will either trap the knight or force the horsey to lose contact with the crucial d5-pawn.

2rq1rk1/pp3pp1/2np3p/3ppb2/3Pn3/2P1PN1P/.comment: This is a great square for the queen, from where it pressures two pawns and stays out of the way of the rest of our pieces.

2r2rk1/pp1q1pp1/2np3p/3ppb2/3Pn3/1QP1PN1.comment: Continuing to improve our position by reinforcing the bishop, which will prove useful in the event that Black takes on d4.

2r2rk1/pp1q1pp1/2np2bp/3p4/P2pn3/1QP1PN1.comment: We can continue to improve with Rad1 and Qa2, paving the way for a potential pawn storm on the kingside. Black is saddled with tons of weaknesses in the center, and has no easy way to improve.

2r2rk1/pp1q1pp1/3p3p/3p1b2/3nn3/1QP1P2P/.comment: It is also possible to take with the e-pawn, but we prefer this recapture, which opens up the queenside. This may seem to favor Black, but his control of the c-file is temporary - Black must burn a tempo to prevent Bb5, which we will use to contest the c-file with Rac1.

r1bq1rk1/pp3ppp/2npp3/3p4/3PnB2/2P1PN2/P.comment: This is not particularly scary. It is rather painful to part with our dark-squared bishop, but almost all of Black's problems will remain in the resulting position.

r3r1k1/pp1b1ppp/2nppq2/3p4/3PnB2/2P1PN2/.comment: We have a nice space advantage and excellent prospects on the queenside.

r2qr1k1/pp3ppp/2np4/3ppb2/3Pn3/2P1PN1P/P.comment: Hitting where it hurts! The only (tactical) way to defend both pawns is ...Qb6, but the queen trade further damages Black's pawn structure and makes it harder for them to defend d5.

r1bq1rk1/pp4pp/2npp3/3p1p2/3PnB2/2PBPN2/.comment: This move recurs constantly in the 4...Bd6 line. In this case, we take the sting out of ...g7-g5.

r1b2rk1/pp4pp/2nppq2/3p1p2/3PnB2/2PBPN1P.comment: Tucking the bishop away and ensuring its permanent safety.

r4rk1/pp1b2pp/2nppq2/3p1p2/3Pn3/2PBPN1P/.comment: This move succumbs to a lovely tactical refutation that underscores how nicely our pieces are coordinated.

r3brk1/pp4pp/2nppq2/3p1p2/3Pn3/2PBPN1P/P.comment: An inventive idea, preparing to kick away the knight with f2-f3. Black has no choice but to add another defender to d6.

r3brk1/pp4pp/2nppq2/3p1p2/3PB3/2P1PN1P/P.comment: Picking up the bishop on d7 and emerging a pawn ahead.

r3brk1/pp2q1pp/2nppn2/3p1p2/3P4/2PBPP1P/.comment: More excellent maneuvering. The bishop politely steps away to make room for the knight.

r4rk1/pp2q1pp/2np1nb1/3ppp2/3P4/2PNPP1P/.comment: The bishop has its moment in the sun! On a4, it hits the knight on c6, threatening to win a pawn and forcing Black to create serious dark-square weaknesses by advancing the pawn to e4.

r4rk1/pp2q1pp/2np1nb1/5p2/B2Pp3/2PNP2P/P.comment: An incredibly deep move, keeping contact with the f5-pawn so that Black's bishop cannot retreat to f7. White's control over the dark squares ensures total domination.

r4rk1/pp2qbpp/2np1n2/5p2/B2PpN2/2P1P2P/P.comment: The queen is ferried over to g3. We have the bishop pair, the superior pawn structure, and excellent prospects on the f-file.

r4rk1/pp2q1pp/2B2nb1/3p1p2/3Pp3/2P1P2P/P.comment: It may seem that Black has fully rectified his pawn structure and has solved his positional problems, but they are in fact only beginning! Note that we have complete and permanent dominance over the dark-squares: the bishop on h2 is the hidden engine of our position. We can assert our advantage by activating our queen and knight, creating a situation in which Black is devoid of pawn breaks and of any active opportunities on either side of the board.

r4rk1/p5pp/2p1q1b1/2np1p2/Q2Pp3/2P1P2P/P.comment: The knight trade opens up the d4-square, which we can use as an outpost for our queen. Our bishop controls b8 and prevents Black from engineering the ...f4 pawn break. After we reposition our queen to b4, we can accumulate the queenside pressure with b2-b4 and a2-a4 (preparing b5), or blast open the center by preparing c3-c4. Even after an endless series of accurate moves, there is no end in sight to Black's suffering.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pp1p/5np1/3p4/3P1B2/2N5/PPP.comment: Black is at an early crossroads: the most popular move by a country mile is 4...Bg7, but Black has a few serious alternatives that must be studied carefully.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pp1p/5np1/3p4/3P1B2/2N1P3/P.comment: By far the most common response, completing the fianchetto. Although much less popular than 4...Bg7, this alternative must be taken seriously. Black solidifies his center and prepares an eventual queen sally to b6.

rnbqk2r/ppp1ppbp/5np1/3p4/3P1B2/2N1P3/PP.comment: As usual, we initiate kingside operations and pose Black with an early dilemma. Analogously to the position after 4...Bg7 5.h4, Black has two main ways to meet Harry's march: Black can continue developing with 5...Bg7 (transposing to a position that we analyze via the 4...Bg7 5.h4 c6 move order), or meet White at the top with 5...h5. This is not just a "bullet move," but a very dangerous system that confronts Black with serious problems. White's idea is to shove the pawn down to h5, when the resulting exchange sacrifice (i.e. ...Nxh5 Rxh5 gxh5 Qxh5) offers White a massive initiative, which can turn decisive if Black fails to reinforce the d5-pawn or unwisely decides to castle kingside. At a high level, Black almost always responds by pushing their own h-pawn one or two squares, but both of these options create long-term weaknesses on the kingside that we will use to spark the flames of an eventual kingside attack.

rnbqk2r/ppp1ppbp/5np1/3p4/3P1B1P/2N1P3/P.comment: Here, the exchange sacrifice is fully justified, since the d5-pawn will be undefended in the resulting position, costing Black a crucial tempo. This is the most common response online, by quite a wide margin. Our next steps are to develop the knight and ready ourselves for queenside castling. Ignoring White's plan leads to a quick and decisive kingside attack. Amazingly, 5...0-0 is the second most common move online, with around 37,000 games at the time of analysis. A welcome statistic indeed! Black takes the plunge. This is second in popularity behind 6...Nxh5, but objectively it is clearly Black's best try. Still, the resulting positions - with a wide open h-file granting us exciting attacking opportunities at every turn - are virtually impossible for a human to handle accurately. This keeps the h-file closed, but creates a host of weaknesses in the center and on the kingside.

rnbqk2r/ppp1ppb1/5np1/3p3p/3P1B1P/2N1P3/.comment: Proceeding with development. See 4...Bg7 5.h4 c6 6.Be2 h5 7.Nf3.

Highlighting the ineffectiveness of Black's fourth move. Black must now waste another tempo to defend the d5-pawn, giving us the window of opportunity that we need to develop long-lasting kingside pressure. This is the best possible version of the exchange sac, since Black's king has found itself on the worst possible square. Our next step is to complete our development while leveling threat after threat against Black's hapless king.

Rome was not built in a day! Before launching our kingside attack, we must do the bare minimum to complete our queenside development and shuttle our king to relative safety. With this move, we also take the sting out of ...cxd4, which will greatly increase the potency of the bishop sortie to h6. The typical exchange sac works to perfection here, since the d5-pawn is undefended and the newly-castled king will get absolutely terrorized.
It transpires that the pawn on h5 is untouchable due to g2-g4, trapping the bishop! Black has no choice but to retreat in shame.

Now, h5 obviously becomes a serious threat. Black's response is virtually forced. This is an interesting move that both of us have played, and it offers decent practical compensation for the exchange. However, objectively, there is no question that Black is significantly better with only a few accurate moves. The exchange sacrifice is far less effective here, since Black does not need to spend an additional tempo guarding the c6-pawn (compared to the same position in the 4...a6 line). Black uses this tempo to maneuver the knight to f6, dousing the flames of White's initiative. There is no question that White has good practical chances here, but we decided against reccommending this line, since White's compensation is objectively insufficient.

rnbqk2r/ppp1ppb1/5np1/3p3p/3P1B1P/2N1PN2.comment: The early bishop sortie to g4 is very common, but the bishop will be tossed around by our pawns. We respond by unpinning our queen and reinforcing the idea of Ne5.
Our response to this move is one and the same!

rn1qk2r/ppp1ppb1/5np1/3p3p/3P1BbP/2N1PN2.comment: A nifty little resource, shuttling the knight to b3 and prying the queen away from the d5-pawn.
This exchange is squarely in White's favor: the resulting pawn structure offers White fantastic play in the center and on the kingside, as well as the bishop pair.

r2qk2r/pppnppb1/5np1/3p3p/3P1BbP/2N1PN2/.comment: Striking at the center without delay.

This creative night sally underscores the awkwardness of the bishop on g4, which will provide fuel for a furious pawn storm in the center. f2-f3 and e3-e4 is coming, and Black can do absolutely nothing about it.

r2qk2r/pppn1pb1/4pnp1/3p3p/3PPBbP/2N2N2/.comment: It is almost always worth investing a tempo to improve the safety of our king.

r2qk2r/1ppn1pb1/p3pnp1/3p3p/3PPBbP/2N2N2.comment: Deploying the rook, and applying pressure on g6.
An ingenious move, opening up a line of fire to the h4-pawn. Since our lead in development is quite vast, we can afford to leave the h-pawn en prise!

r2qk1nr/1ppn1pb1/p3p1p1/3p3p/3PPBbP/2N2N.comment: This pin is quite nasty, since Black cannot afford to play ...f6 for obvious reasons.

A cold-blooded response, sending the queen back where it belongs! It is now time to smash open the center at all costs! At this point in your Jobava journey, moves like these should not elicit any surprise.

r2qk1nr/1ppn1pb1/p3p1p1/3p2Bp/3PP1bP/2N2.comment: Black is paying a steep price for advancing his h-pawn and opening the g-file: we threaten the devastating Nxh5 gxh5 Bf6, while Black's "attack" hasn't even gotten off the ground. The knight is hanging, and Nxh5-Bf6 is imminent.

r2qk2r/1ppnnpb1/p3p1p1/3p3p/3PPBbP/2N2N2.comment: Another blow, removing the final defender from the e-file. Obviously, taking with the queen loses to Re1, so Black's king has no choice but to go on a walk. A surgical follow-up check, preventing ...Kf8.

r2qk2r/pppnppb1/5np1/3p1bNp/3P1B1P/2N1P3.comment: In order to generate a suitable escape square for the bishop, Black must cede total control of the center.

r1bqk2r/pppnppb1/5np1/3p3p/3P1B1P/2N1PN2.comment: This is the strongest move, but it is very infrequently played. Objectively, the position is dynamically equal, but there is no question that it is quite a bit easier to play White. An important resource, indirectly defending the b2-pawn.

r1bqk2r/pppnppb1/5np1/3p3p/3P1B1P/2NBPN2.comment: Building up the kingside pressure. and White will send away the bishop on the next move.

r1bq1rk1/pppnppb1/5np1/3p3p/3P1B1P/2NBPN.comment: Lovely tactics! Black is posed with an ultimatum: take the knight and run the risk of losing their queen, or transition into a rather unpleasant endgame in which White's space advantage and better-placed pieces offers the better practical chances.

Our knight is ferried to f4, when the pressure against g6 will become seriously alarming. Black has nothing going on the other side of the board. The tactical battle has subsided, and it is time to switch gears to methodical positional play. The first step is to optimize our queenside pawn structure.

r1bq1rk1/pppnppb1/6p1/3p3p/N2PnB1P/3BPN2.comment: Do not be afraid to castle kingside even with the pawn on h4, since Black lacks the machinery and activity to exploit this cosmetic damage. The pawn on e5 is incredibly nasty, since it controls important squares and severs the coordination between Black's pieces.

r1bq1rk1/pppnppb1/6p1/3p3p/N2PBB1P/4PN2/.comment: Sacrificing the e5-pawn for a furious initiative on both sides of the board.

r1bq1rk1/1ppnppb1/5np1/p2p3p/P2P1B1P/2NB.comment: Step one has been achieved, and now it is time for step two: maneuvering the knight to f4, and opening up the queenside with c2-c4. White has a small but stable edge in the endgame. Following that, we will place our rook on b1 and exert nasty pressure on Black's b7-pawn. There is no question that White stands better, and we are playing essentially for two results.

rnbq1rk1/ppp1ppb1/5np1/3p3p/3P1B1P/2N1PN.comment: Straightforward and powerful: we threaten to smash open the kingside with g2-g4, which will likely lead to the summary execution of Black's monarch.

This is the only way to "justify" the bishop's development to g4, but the resulting pawn structure works squarely in our favor. White's pawn structure may be visually unappealing, but the pawn on f3 will help prepare e4, and the semi-open g-file works in our favor as well. Preparing to castle kingside.
Now, 9.g4 is hasty due to ...Nxe5 and ...Nxg4, so one more patient preparatory move is required.

r1bq1rk1/pppnppb1/5np1/3p3p/3P1B1P/2N1PN.comment: 11.g4 was possible, but there is no hurry: we are in charge in the center, and Black is too passive and poorly coordinated to generate serious prospects on the queenside.

r1bq1rk1/p1pnppb1/5np1/1p1p3p/3P1B1P/2N1.comment: Our next move will Rdg1, when everything will finally be ready for g2-g4! Of course, 12...b4 merely exacerbates the issue due to 13.Na4, when Black will be saddled with additional queenside weaknesses.

rnbqk2r/ppp1ppb1/5np1/3p3Q/3P1B1P/2N1P3/.comment: A crucial resource, aiming our queen-bishop battery at the c7 pawn. Black has no way to defend it without decisively compromising his king safety.

rnbqk2r/pp2ppb1/2p2np1/3p3Q/3P1B1P/2N1P3.comment: Had Black saved a tempo on ...c6, he would have been able to ferry his knight over to f6, forcing our queen out of h5 and essentially consolidating his material advantage. In this line, we beat him to the punch - with totally devastating effect. This and the next moves truly emphasize how deadly the queen + knight tandem can be in the right circumstances. This defensive approach is quite common online. Now, 10.Qh2 obviously maintains a decisive advantage, but we have a much simpler approach, cashing in our chips and attaining a decisive material advantage in the endgame. The pawn on c7 cannot be defended!

Surgically precise. We saw this exact idea in the 4...a6 5.h4 Bg7 variation. The pawn on c7 represents Black's last hope to generate counterplay; without it, Black will be left without even an iota of play. Bringing the knight to f6 does not change the nature of the position in any way; the knight is a good defender, but it will be horribly outmatched.

rnbqk2r/p3ppb1/1pp2np1/3p3Q/N2P1B1P/4P3/.comment: An old friend comes knocking! We are more familiar with the c2-c4 idea in a positional context, but it is just as powerful here. Opening up the c-file enables us to deploy our rook, when the pressure against c7 quickly becomes decisive.

rnbqk2r/p3ppb1/1pp2np1/7Q/N1pP1B1P/4P3/P.comment: Now, ...b5 runs into the deadly Nc5+, so Black must part ways with the c4-pawn.

rn1qk2r/pb2ppb1/1pp2np1/7Q/N1pP1B1P/4P3/.comment: It should be clear even to an untrained eye that White's attack is utterly crushing.

rn1qk2r/pp1bppb1/2p2npQ/3p4/3P1B1P/2N1P2.comment: The knight on h5 is unassailable, and it controls the key f6 and g7-squares, restricting Black's already ultra-cramped position even further. We can continue by castling queenside, completing our development with Be2, and even finding appropriate digs for the other knight with Na4-b6.

rn1qk2r/ppp1ppb1/5np1/3p3p/3P1BbP/2N1P3/.comment: Black has recovered the pawn, and the ensuing check on c3 may appear rather disconcerting, but Black's position remains virtually untenable due to the semi-open h-file, the lack of active prospects for the LSB, and the permanent weakness of the e6-pawn.

rn1qk2r/ppp2pb1/4bnp1/3pp2p/3P1B1P/1NN1P.comment: We will follow up by castling queenside, landing the d5 pawn in serious trouble. Obviously, Black cannot even dream of any compensation for the pawn!

rn1qk2r/ppp2pb1/4pnp1/3p3p/3P1BbP/2N1P3/.comment: Unpinning the knight and preparing to trade on our own terms.

rn1qk2r/ppp2pb1/4pnp1/3p3p/3P1BbP/2NBP3/.comment: The bishop pair and our incredibly active rook guarantee us excellent winning chances in the endgame.

r2qk2r/ppp1ppb1/2n2np1/3p1b1p/3P1B1P/2N1.comment: The standard response to Black's last move, underscoring the awkwardness of Black's bishop and preparing g2-g4, which will pave the way for our queen to land on the h-file.

2rqk2r/ppp1ppb1/2n1bnp1/3p3p/3P1BPP/2N1P.comment: Once the queen lands on h2, Black is totally doomed. This patient move highlights the extent of our dominance. There is no need at all to hurry with Bh6; Black has absolutely nothing going on the queenside. Now, we are ready to thrust the bishop into h6 and follow up with Nf4, with utterly decisive consequences.

Beautiful!! This position occurred in "Boknoy2019" - "Mustang6000", Lichess (blitz) 2021. White committed a small inaccuracy with Rg7, enabling Black to prolong the game with ...Ke8. Believe it or not, Black actually went on to win the game! Instead, immediate victory is yielded by a move on the other side of the board:

2rqk2r/ppp1pp2/2n1bnpb/3p3p/3P1BPP/2N1PP.comment: The point of getting the knight to c5 was not to win a pawn, but to close off the king's only escape hatch!

r1bqk2r/p1p1ppb1/2n2np1/1p1p3p/3P1B1P/2N.comment: Gorgeous maneuvering. We prepare f2-f3 and Qh4, when the attack will finally begin in earnest!
Black's queen is but a paper tiger, since 14...Qb1+ is cooly met with 15.Kd2 (followed by f2-f3, to eliminate the possibility of ...Ne4+).

r1bqk2r/p1p1ppb1/2n2np1/3p3p/1p1P1B1P/2N.comment: Cold-blooded and ridiculously powerful. Black's queenside activity has come to a shuddering halt, and now it is our time to shine!

Removing the final obstacle. Without its last faithful defender, the Black king will be left entirely to its own devices. To use a phrase that both of us promised not to use in this course, the position plays itself!

r1bqk2r/p1p1pp2/2n2npb/3p3p/1p1P1B1P/2N1.comment: A simple but lovely tactic to top it all off. Rh1 is unstoppable, and mate follows in a few moves.

r1bqk2r/p3ppb1/p1p2np1/3p3Q/3P1B1P/2N1P3.comment: Having mangled Black's queenside, it turns out that we do not even need to waste any time capturing the pawn on c7! Instead, we can turn directly to the most important task at hand: getting the rook to h1 as quickly as possible.

r1bqk2r/p3ppb1/p4np1/2pp3Q/3P1B1P/2N1P3/.comment: Rh1 is coming, and Black's king is doomed.

rnbqk2r/pp2ppb1/5np1/2pp3Q/3P1B1P/2NBP3/.comment: The point of this move is not so much to snag a pawn (we will give it right back) but to prevent ...c4, ensuring that our bishop remains singularly trained on the h7-pawn.

rnb1k2r/1p2ppb1/p4np1/2qp3Q/5B1P/2NBP3/P.comment: Black will lose the h-pawn, and with it, any hopes of not getting checkmated before move 20!

rnbqk2r/pp2ppb1/2p2np1/3p3p/3P1B1P/2N1PN.comment: Our approach is identical to the one we adopt in the main line (5...h5), quickly entrenching our knight on e5 and preparing to ferry our king to safety at a moment's notice.

r1bq1rk1/pp2ppb1/2p2np1/3pn2p/3P1B1P/2NB.comment: Black's position is cramped and unpleasant, and is powerless against the ensuing series of kingside pawn breaks.

r1bq1r2/pp1nppk1/2p3p1/3p3p/3P3P/2NBP3/P.comment: Continuing to batter away at Black's kingside!

r1bq1r2/pp1nppk1/2p3p1/3p3p/3P1P1P/2NBP3.comment: Screwing in the pawn, leaving Black's bishop with no active prospects and the g4-pawn without a key defender.

r1bq1r2/p2np1k1/2p3p1/3pPp1p/3P1P1P/2pB4.comment: Black's position is riddled with holes. We can follow up with Rdf1 and Rh4, picking up the g4-pawn and proceeding to destroy Black on the kingside.

rnbqk2r/ppp1ppb1/5np1/3p3p/3P1B1P/2N1P3/.comment: Obviously, we are only willing to trade on our own terms. It is almost always worth throwing in this prophylactic move, which ensures that ...Ne4 will never cause us headaches. The fate that awaits Black after this careless move shows that Black cannot keep his king in the center forever.

rn1qk2r/ppp1ppb1/5np1/3p3p/3P1BbP/2N1P3/.comment: The Black monarch's days of restful solitude are over. The moment he escapes to the kingside, we will pry open that side of the board with g2-g4. Threatening exd5, and virtually forcing Black to permanently weaken the dark squares in the center. White is more active and better coordinated. Our likeliest follow-up is g4, which is rather problematic for Black even though the king is on the other side of the board. Without any support, the pawn storm is anything but scary.

You should not bat an eye at this move by now, which simultaneously prepares g2-g4 and e2-e4. Taking the sting out of ...b4, which will now create a complex of weak squares on the queenside that we are in perfect position to exploit. An instructive move, showing that our play is not only limited to the center and kingside in this line. We use the attack on c6 to force Black's queen back to his side of the board, which in turn allows our queen to find an ideal perch on a3.

rn1qk2r/ppp1ppb1/5np1/3p3p/3PPBbP/2N5/PP.comment: Having induced these weaknesses, we now switch gears and force the queens off the board.

rn1qk2r/ppp2pb1/4pnp1/3p3p/3PPBbP/2N5/PP.comment: It transpires that Black is facing a rather problematic double-attack: there is no way to guard d6 and a7 at the same time! Black has no choice but to part ways with the corner pawn.

rn1q3r/pppk1pb1/4pnp1/3P3p/3P1BbP/2N5/PP.comment: Black's drawing chances are significant, but we are obviously playing for two results. Note that Black has no way to cut off the knight's evacuation route, since ...Rb4 will always run into a3.

rn1qk2r/ppp1ppb1/5np1/3p3p/3P1BbP/2N1PP2.comment: Black's "attack" has fizzled out before it began.

rn1q1rk1/ppp1ppb1/5np1/3p3p/3P1BbP/2N1PP.comment: As is so customary in the Jobava London, we combine play on both sides of the board. Having taken the c5-square under firm control, we now turn our attention to the kingside, carrying out a typical sacrifical operation aimed at opening the h-file. The queen joins the party, hitting Black where it hurts.

rn1q1rk1/ppp1ppb1/5np1/3p3p/N2P1BbP/4PP2.comment: Who needs the queen anyway? We can finally see the importance of placing the knight on a4. Having done our job on the kingside, we will once again switch our attention to the other side of the board, deploying our rook to the a-file (it is especially good on a3, where it lends additional support to the e3-pawn) and entrenching the knight on c5 when the time is right.

r1bq1rk1/ppp1ppb1/n4np1/1N1p3p/3P1B1P/2P.comment: Developing the bishop and preparing h5.
Black's queenside counterplay has ground to a halt, while we are just getting started on the other flank. We will follow up by trading on g6 and maneuvering the knight to e5.

r1bq1rk1/ppp1ppb1/n4np1/1N1p3p/3P1B1P/4P.comment: In contrast to 5...h5, we will have a harder time engineering a kingside attack, but from a strategic perspective, our advantage is indisputable.

r2q1rk1/ppp1ppb1/n4np1/1N1p3p/3P1BbP/2P1.comment: Supporting the knight and taking the sting out of ...Bxf3. Black can barely move a muscle, e.g.

rnbq1rk1/ppp1ppb1/5np1/3p3p/3P1B1P/2N1PN.comment: The only reasonable attempt to muddy the waters, though it falls woefully short.

rnbq1rk1/pp2ppb1/5np1/2pp3p/3P1B1P/2N1PN.comment: With the light-squared bishop gone, Black is unable to sustain his center without creating additional weaknesses.
This centralizing move is far more accurate than the immediate 8.0-0-0, which would enable Black to generate troublesome queenside counterplay with ...Qa5.

rnbq1rk1/pp3pb1/4pnp1/2pp3p/3PPB1P/2N2N2.comment: Our last two moves underscore the strategic error inherent in the trade on f3.

r1bq1rk1/pp1n1pbn/4p1p1/2ppP2p/3P1B1P/2N.comment: Everything is now in place for the decisive breakthrough.

r1bq1r1k/pp1n1pbn/4p1p1/2ppP2p/3P1B1P/2N.comment: White's knight joins in from the other side. Once it reaches d6, Black will be unable to deal with the countless threats coming from every side.

r1b2r1k/pp1n1pbn/4p1p1/1NppP2p/3P1B1q/3B.comment: Calm, cool, and collected! It is important to shoo Black's queen away from the kingside before reopening the g-file.

r1b2r1k/pp1nqpbn/4p1p1/1NppP2p/3P4/3B1NB.comment: Imprisoning Black's rook and reopening the g-file.

rnbq1rk1/pp3pb1/4pnp1/2Pp3p/5B1P/2N1PN2/.comment: Intrepid and powerful! This move is almost never as scary as it looks; we disarm it by vacating an escape route for our king.

rnbq1r2/pp3pbk/4pnp1/2PN3p/5B1P/4PN2/PPP.comment: The check on a1 is innocuous, and we can always bring our bishop to d3 to clog up the d-file.

rnbqr1k1/pp3pb1/3Bpnp1/2Pp3p/7P/2N1PN2/P.comment: In the words of my coach, White has compensation for his extra pawn :)

rnbq1rk1/pp2ppb1/5np1/2ppN2p/3P1B1P/2N1P.comment: This position has occurred countless times in high-level tournament practice. Our first step is to control the e4-square and restrict the mobility of the f6-knight.

r1bq1rk1/pp2ppb1/2n2np1/2ppN2p/3P1B1P/2N.comment: A crucial follow-up, controlling the e4-square and preparing g2-g4.

r1bq1rk1/pp2ppb1/5np1/1B1pN2p/1n1p1B1P/2.comment: We are used to this idea with colors reversed (i.e. ...Bb4-Ba5 in response to Nb5). Black's superficial queenside play has been fully disarmed, and we proceed to push the knight back to c6.

r1bq1rk1/p3ppb1/2p2np1/3pN2p/3p1B1P/2N1P.comment: As usual, we assert our dominance on both sides of the board. By controlling c5, we permanently halt Black's queenside play. The stage is now set for a lightning kingside offensive.

r1bqnrk1/p3ppb1/2p3p1/3pN3/N2p1BpP/4PP2/.comment: The computer assigns White a relatively modest plus, but from a human perspective, Black's position is nearly hopeless. Black has no good answer to the manifold threats on the kingside, e.g.

r1bq1rkb/p3pp1n/2p3p1/3pN3/N2p1Bp1/4PP2/.comment: A final flourish, connecting the rooks; we only need one of the towers to checkmate black on the h-file.

r1bq1rk1/p3ppb1/2p2np1/3pN3/N2p1BP1/4P3/.comment: with the unstoppable threat of Ned7, which will remove the only defender of the h7-square and lead to quick checkmate. This line is worth reviewing several times, for it clearly illustrates our ability to dominate on both sides of the board. It is worth thinking of the queenside as the "positional side," to be used primarily for the sake of optimizing the placement of the "Jobava knight." The h-file, on the other hand, is used to do the checkmating!

r1bq1rk1/pp2ppb1/2n2np1/3pN2p/3P1B1P/2N2.comment: This tempting move plays right into our hands.

r2q1rk1/pp2ppb1/2n2np1/3pNb1p/3P1B1P/2N2.comment: Shepherding the king to safety and protecting b2 and d4. Black has no good answer to the typical plan of g2-g4 and h4-h5, which will tear open the kingside and quickly lead to a decisive attack. It is also possible for White to play it slow.

A very interesting and unusual idea that poses serious practical problems. As is the custom all throughout the 3...g6 variation, White combines positional and tactical play on the two flanks: on the queenside, we wish to trade on c6 and control the c5-square with Na4. On the kingside, we are awaiting the perfect opportunity to blast open the landscape with g2-g4 and h4-h5. Black can maintain the balance with perfect computer play, but from a practical standpoint, the position is virtually unplayable.

Asserting dominance over the c5-square. Note that Black has absolutely no potential to develop a queenside attack, since the b8-square is permanently under our control and our last move renders ...c6-c5 impossible. While the engine finds a way to prolong the game, all human moves lead to Black's rapid demise.
Clinical precision! Trading off the light-squared bishop decisively loosens Black's control over h7.
Prying open the h-file in thematic fashion. 15...Kg7 merely hastens Black's demise after 16.Bh6+, so he has no choice but to partake of the forbidden fruit.

r2q1rk1/pp2ppb1/2n2np1/3pN2p/3P1B1P/2Nb1.comment: This recapture makes a lot of sense when you keep in mind that the queen's optimal square is on h2.

r2q1rk1/pp2ppb1/2n2np1/3pN2p/3P1B1P/2NB1.comment: We will follow up with Rdg1 and Nxg4. Black's days are numbered!

r2q1rkb/pp2pp2/2n2n2/3NNbpp/3P1B1P/5P2/P.comment: Just as in the 13...gxh5 line, this move is an integral part of White's attacking strategy. Eliminating the final defender of the h7-square spells immediate doom.

r2q1rk1/pp2ppb1/5np1/3pnb1p/3P1B1P/2N2P2.comment: This is Black's most resilient continuation from an objective point of view, but it leads to a position that we can only refer to as indefensible. Pow! In contrast to the other lines within the 10...Qb6 sub-variation, the decisive invasion will occur along the g-file.
Black has succeeded in staving off checkmate for the time being, but his position remains untenable from a practical standpoint. The following line demonstrates the truth of this statement:

r2q1rk1/pp2ppb1/5np1/3pBb1p/3P3P/2N2P2/P.comment: It may seem that White's attack has ground to a halt, but we are actually just one short step away from setting up a mating net.

r2q1r2/pp2ppbk/5np1/3pBb1p/3P3P/2N2P2/PP.comment: Calm developing moves like this one should no longer come as a surprise to you. This sets up the virtually unstoppable threat of Nf5+, when ...Kg8 is met with Qxg6+ (that is why we need the services of the bishop!).

r2q1r2/pp2ppbk/5np1/3pBb1p/2BP3P/2N2P2/P.comment: Black is checkmated seven ways to sunday, e.g. The computer's top suggestion here is 22...Qg1+, which tells us all that we need to know about the position!

2rq1rk1/pp2ppb1/5np1/3pnb1p/3P1B1P/2N2P2.comment: Given the total lack of counterplay on the queenside, we are well within our rights to optimize the safety of our king before rolling up our sleeves on the other side of the board.
It may seem counterintuitive to trade off the queens, but we have plenty of pieces with which to finish Black off on the kingside. Black loses the h5-knight, and with it, the game.

r2q1rk1/pp2ppb1/2n2np1/1B1pNb1p/3P1B1P/2.comment: This move is no better than it was on the previous move. In fact, it merely encourages us to do what we wanted to do anyway: assert our dominance over the c5-square.

r2q1rk1/pp2ppb1/5np1/1B1pnb1p/3P1B1P/2N2.comment: A familiar situation: Black has run out of active ideas on the queenside, and the stage is set for decisive kingside action. The tempting 17.g4 is possible, but we have at our disposal a far more powerful - and much more beautiful - idea. A picturesque position that is worth examining for more than a few seconds! Yes, your suspicion is correct - Black's queen is trapped in the middle of the queenside, and he has absolutely no good answer to the threat of a2-a4. At this point, you should be ready to execute the last two moves automatically. With the c5-square under complete control, the stage is set for decisive action on the kingside.

r2q1rk1/1p2ppb1/5np1/pB1pnb1p/N2P1B1P/5P.comment: It is rather amazing that we win the game without making a single attacking move on the kingside. Such is the unique power of the Jobava London!

r2q1rk1/pp1nppb1/6p1/1B1pPb1p/5B1P/2N2P2.comment: It may seem brazen to give up the e5-pawn, but our development is our top priority. Furthermore, once Black takes a bite of the forbidden apple, we swiftly transition our initiative to the center.

r2q1rk1/pp2ppb1/6p1/1B1pnb1p/5B1P/2N2P2/.comment: Here, do not walk into 16.Nc7?? Qxa2 17.Qxd7 Rad8 and White loses instantly!

A critical position has been reached. The natural move is, of course, 15.Nxd5, but that allows Black to force the queens off the board with 15...e6. Instead, we seize the opportunity to force the dark-squared bishops off the board, rendering Black's monarch even more susceptible to all sorts of shenanigans.

r2q1rk1/p3pp2/2p3pb/3p1b2/6pP/2N2P2/PPPQ.comment: The point of White's entire strategy is on full display in the event of 19...Bxg4, which runs into 20.Qd4+ - that is why it was so important to trade the bishops. Black has no choice but to accept a miserable endgame.

r2q1rk1/p3pp2/2p3pb/8/4p1PP/8/PPPQ4/2KRR.comment: Clamping down on the kingside and forcing the queen trade on our terms. We will recover the e4-pawn on the next move, when Black's deficient queenside pawn structure, coupled with the superior activity of our rooks, will grant us excellent winning chances.

r2q1rk1/pp3p2/2n1p1pQ/1B1p1b1p/7P/2N2P2/.comment: Boom shaka-laka! The point of this move, believe it or not, is not to follow up with h5, but rather to open up the knight's access to e4 and g5.

r2q1rk1/pp3p2/2n1p1pQ/1B1p4/6bP/2N5/PPP5.comment: The point! The threat of Ng5 is absolutely devastating.

rnbqkb1r/pppp1ppp/4pn2/3P4/8/8/PPP1PPPP/.comment: An important inclusion, preventing the check on h4 and expanding on the kingside in typical Jobava fashion.

rnbqkb1r/pppp1p1p/4pn2/3P2p1/6P1/8/PPP1P.comment: Refraining from the greedy 6.Nxd5, which enables Black to light the center on fire with 6...e5. Instead, we focus on central and kingside expansion.
An incredible idea! White simultaneously threatens f4-f5 and Be2. In order to keep the minor piece alive and preserve the balance, Black must reproduce several impossible computer moves.

rnbqkb1r/pp1p1p2/4pn1p/2pP2p1/4P1PP/8/PP.comment: Markoja-Richter, corr. 2015. White overwhelmingly dominates in the center, and the b2-pawn is clearly untouchable:

rnbqkb1r/pppp1p1p/5n2/3Pp1p1/4P1P1/8/PPP.comment: Law-Sen, corr. 2005. It is important for White to immediately evacuate the queen from h5. A few accurate moves douse the flames of Black's initiative and secure the extra piece:
The endgame is miserable for Black, who suffers from a total lack of coordination and a permanently weak pawn on d4.

rnbqkb1r/pppp1ppp/4pn2/3P4/4P3/8/PPP2PPP.comment: This does not fundamentally change the nature of the game.
Jobava London-1...d5 2.Nc3 Bf5  2023 White's central control and prospects along the f-file guarantee us a long-lasting initiative.

rnbqkb1r/pp1p1pp1/2p1pn1p/3P2B1/4P3/8/PP.comment: The position resembles an improved version of a Fantasy Caro-Kann. White's knight heads to f4, and White will castle queenside after moving the queen either to d2 or even to d3.

rnbqkb1r/pppp1pp1/4p2p/3PP2n/6P1/8/PPP2P.comment: An easy move to forget about! Both the knight on f1, as well as the bishop on g6, are trapped! Black cannot save either of them.

rnbqk2r/pp1p1pp1/2pbpn1p/3P4/4P1P1/3B4/P.comment: Boeven-Mueller, German Senior Championship 2015. White opted for the rather odd Nce2, but simple improving moves yield an excellent position, e.g.

rnb1k2r/ppqp1pp1/2pbpn1p/3P4/4P1P1/3B4/P.comment: White's aim is to regroup with Bc1, Nhf4, followed by Qd2 and Nd3, controlling key squares in the center. Black is dreadfully cramped.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/2p2n2/3p4/3PPB2/2N5/PPP.comment: By far the most popular recapture at the highest levels. Black captures the pawn and forces a knight trade, opening up an annoying queen check on a5 and eliminating the future possibility of Nc3-b5. Incidentally, it is the least popular of the three captures online, but due to its objective potency, we have decided to promote it as the main line. Along with 4...cxd4, this is the most popular capture online (with approximately 5,000+ games on Lichess at the time of analysis). We recapture the pawn on c5, posing Black with an unenviable dilemma. Trading queens hands over control of the d-file, while refraining from the trade with 5...Qa5 gives White a dangerous middlegame initiative. It is only move 5, yet we are already asking Black a serious question! This is by far the most popular move online (with 2,000 or so games), but it gives us full control over the d-file and leads to a rather dubious endgame. It is important to realize that the trade of queens hardly diminishes White's attacking potential; our initiative does not vanish simply because the ladies are off the board! A few general pointers to help you understand this position better: 1) The pawn on e4 can be either attacked with Nge2-g3, or traded off directly with f2-f3. Both options are on the table depending on Black's setup. 2) After the recapture, White has the immediate threat of situating a knight on b5, forcing Black to contort themselves with the immensely awkward ...Na6. 3) The pawn on c5 is a strength rather than a weakness: it significantly restricts the mobility of Black's dark-squared bishop, and it can be easily supported both with pawns (b4) and with pieces (Be3). Black must stop the knight sortie to b5, but this move comes at the great cost of weakening the b6-square. We target that square without further delay.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/2p5/3p4/3PnB2/2N5/PPP2P.comment: Black pays a steep price for ignoring the threat!

Aiming for b6! This more restrained move is a sensible alternative. We prepare to construct the typical a3-b4-c5 pawn chain, which will make it rather difficult for Black to operate on the queenside in any meaningful way. Of course, the idea of Na4-b6 is still very much in the cards.

Threatening c5-c6. This is our main recommendation, bringing out the bishop and pinning the knight. It is worth spending some time on the alternative 6.Qa4, which is an incredibly dangerous (if objectively dubious) line that will bring you rapid victory if Black is not prepared. Objectively, this is a terrible move, but in our experience, even Grandmasters don't know how to react. A single mistake can change the evaluation to White's favor, so it is more than reasonable to keep this move in your back pocket. The idea is twofold: the queen on a4 supports a rapid queenside attack with Nb5, and the d-file is cleared so that the rook will exert more influence when it reaches d1. In order to prove an advantage (and avoid losing the game), Black must generate a string of computer moves that have proven too difficult to find even for top GMs. A very difficult move to play, as this sends the knight to b5. This is as good as 6...d4 objectively, but from a practical perspective, the ensuing position is virtually unplayable for Black.

Preparing to castle queenside! Of course, we could not care less about the c5-pawn: our only allegiance in this line is to rapid development. This is automatic at most levels, although after this capture White's initiative becomes virtually decisive. This is Black's best move, but his problems are only just beginning!

rnbq1b1r/ppN1kppp/2p5/3pp3/3PnB2/8/PPP2P.comment: A cute desperado sacrifice, winning even more material. The knight is easily evacuated through c7, when White's material advantage will prove decisive.

r1bqkb1r/pp2pppp/n1p5/1N1p4/3PnB2/8/PPP2.comment: Using tactics to defend the c5-pawn.

r1bqk2r/pp2ppbp/n1p3p1/1N1p4/1P1PnB2/P7/.comment: Black is completely paralyzed. Even castling kingside is not possible due to Bxf6, while castling queenside - well, we will leave the analysis of that move to the reader!

r1bqkb1r/pp1npppp/2p5/3p4/NP1PnB2/8/P1P2.comment: Although it comes with tempo, this move is almost never scary. The bishop calmly retreats, and Black is left with further weaknesess in the center.

r1bqkb1r/pp1n1ppp/2p1p3/3p4/NP1PnB2/8/P1.comment: It may seem more natural to drop the bishop back to e3, but it is important to reinforce the b4-pawn due to the possibility of ...a6-a5, when a2-a3 fails due to the hanging knight on a4. Therefore, we have to find alternate arrangements for the b4-pawn.
Solidifying White's queenside pawn chain, and taking the sting out of ...a5.

r1bqkb1r/1p1n1ppp/2p1p3/p2p4/NP1Pn3/8/P1.comment: Perfectly exploiting the drawback of Black's previous move. Most importantly, this move secures the knight on a4, taking the sting out of the capture on b4.

1rbqk2r/1p1nbppp/1Np1p3/1B1p4/1B1Pn3/8/P.comment: Total and complete paralysis! The computer's top suggestion is 13...0-0, which tells you all you need to know about this position!

r1bqkb1r/pp1n1ppp/2p1p3/3p4/NP1PnB2/P7/2.comment: A sad necessity. Otherwise, we send away the knight with c2-c4.

r1bqkb1r/p2n1ppp/2p1p3/1p1p4/NP1PnB2/P7/.comment: White's well-protected passer on c5 guarantees us a long-lasting advantage in the endgame.

r1bqkb1r/p2n1ppp/2p1p3/1p1p4/NPPPnB2/P7/.comment: Black cannot makle a single effective move: leaving d7 enables us to jump into b6. Black is simply lost!

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/2p5/3p4/3PnB2/2N5/PPP1N.comment: An interesting move, trading the e-pawn for the c-pawn, although it does not fully solve Black's problems.
Pinning the knight and indirectly defending the e4-pawn.

rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/2p5/3pB3/3Pn3/2N5/PPP1NP.comment: Immediately targetting Black's strongest piece. Now, it is the queen's turn to sink her teeth into the weak d6 square! In reality, this is just a fancy of way of inducing a queen trade.

rnbqk2r/pp3ppp/2pb4/3pB3/3Pn3/2N5/PPP1NP.comment: The computer assigns a modest advantage to White, but in reality, Black's position is very difficult. The e4-pawn is a long-term weakness, and Black is also saddled with problems related to the placement of his king. On e7, it is constantly subject to pressure down the e-file, and Black must also keep a close eye on the knight sorties to d5 and f5. rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/2p5/3p4/3P1B2/2N3n1/PPP.comment: This is the classic response to ...Qa5, reinforcing the threat of Nxe4.

rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/2p5/3pp3/3P4/2N1B1n1/PPP.comment: Yet again, the d6-square costs Black and arm and a leg. Black attempts to stir things up on the queenside, but we use the d6-square to gracefully get out of danger.

rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/2p5/3pp3/3Pn3/2N1B3/PPPQ.comment: Black has no effective discovery against the queen, since 14...Be8 runs into 15.Be6+. Our next step is to castle queenside.

rnb1kb1r/pp2qppp/2p5/3pp3/3PN3/4B3/PPPQN.comment: Rather than greedily capturing on b7, it is better to focus on active development: with a powerful and long-lasting attack. Note that ...Rd8 is not scary in the least, as Black has no way to reinforce the pressure on the knight. We can follow up by developing the bishop to e2 and placing a rook on f1.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/2p5/1B1p4/3PnB2/2N5/PPP.comment: This is the only way to keep Black's position afloat, although it fails to solve all of Black's problems:
It is rather hard to believe that a human can find this move, although it is one of the only ways that Black can stay alive!
This is almost automatic at all levels, although 6...a6 is a serious alternative that must be studied carefully.

rnb1kb1r/1p2pppp/pqpB4/1B1p4/3Pn3/2N5/PP.comment: The queen trade suits us just fine, since Black will be saddled with the long-term weakness of the e4-pawn.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/2p5/3p4/3PnB2/2N5/PPPQ1.comment: A sensible move, preventing Bb5. Of course, we have a second square that we can develop the bishop to!
As usual, this loses on the spot:

rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/2p5/3pp3/3PnB2/2N5/PPPQ1.comment: It is worth spending an hour or so mastering the ensuing complications. Black opens up a pathway for his dark-squared bishop, but this move comes at the serious cost of (a) weakening the d5-square, and (b) enabling our bishop to seek greener pastures on g5, where it will incessantly pressure Black's knight.
Forcing a favorable queen trade due to the threat of Nc7.

rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/2p5/3pp3/2BPnB2/2N5/PPPQ.comment: Black's position collapses due to the twin threats of Nxe4 and Qxf6.

rn1qkb1r/pp3ppp/2p5/3ppb2/2BPnB2/2N5/PPP.comment: Initiating a favorable queen trade. The bishop on d5 is an absolute menace, so Black's hand is forced:

rn1qkb1r/pp3ppp/2p5/3Npb2/2BPnB2/8/PPPQ1.comment: with a stable edge in the endgame. We will, as usual, follow up with Ne2-g3, putting significant pressure on the e4-pawn. The rook on h1 will be deployed to d1, lending further support to the d6-bishop.

rn1qkb1r/pp3ppp/2p5/3pp3/2BPnBb1/2N5/PPP.comment: A cute little intermezzo, forcing Black's queen onto a more awkward square.

rn2kb1r/pp3ppp/2pq4/3pp3/2BPn1b1/2N1B3/P.comment: Here, it is important to realize that we are not in the business of winning the e4-pawn: we have much bigger fish to fry! As such, we use the e4-pawn as fuel to accelerate our development. From a practical standpoint, White's initiative is decisive, e.g. Black has to stay pegged to the d7-square, so the bishop is lost.

rn1qkb1r/pp3ppp/2p5/3ppb2/2BPnB2/2N2P2/P.comment: Black has insufficient compensation for the pawn, practically speaking. White has many ways to improve the position and ultimately smoke the rook out of g2. For instance, we could follow up with Kc1-d1, Be5-g3, and Bc4-b3, when we will threaten to simply trap the rook with Nf4.

rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/2p5/1N1pp3/3PnB2/8/PPPQ1.comment: Here, the main thing is not to take the rook, because Black will take the bishop and we will have a very hard time retrieving our knight. Instead, we calmly move the bishop to a more active spot:

rnbq1b1r/pp2kppp/2p5/1N1pp1B1/3Pn3/8/PPP.comment: Black has clearly insufficient compensation for the exchange.

rn1qkb1r/pp1bpppp/2p5/3p4/3PnB2/2N5/PPPQ.comment: Black is already in serious trouble, and must play like an engine to avoid losing on the spot.
