Yet again, this move creates far too many weaknesses in the center, and sends our bishop to where it wants to go anyway!

This difficult move is the only way to maintain practical chances. We now shuffle our knight around to b3, opening up the diagonal for our light-squared bishop and cementing our advantage. No trade! The knight on b3 is a major asset, since it can hop into c5 at a moment's notice.
Time to dig Black a grave! The queen is tossed around like a small boat in the raging ocean.

rn2k2r/pp1bbppp/1qp5/1N1pp1B1/3Pn3/8/PPP.comment: The other knight joins in the party. White now has the utterly unstoppable threat of Bxf6 followed by Nd5, when one of the horsies will infiltrate c7 or f6. For instance:

rn2k2r/ppqbbppp/2p5/3pp1B1/3PN3/8/PPPQNP.comment: Black is busted: the knight heads to d5, and we can follow up with Bc4. Black cannot move a muscle.

rn2kb1r/pp1bpppp/2p5/q2p4/3PnB2/2N5/PPPQ.comment: Posing the twin threats of Nc5 and Nb5. Cold-blooded prophylaxis! By covering the g4-square, we prevent any shenanigans related to ...Bg4 and ensure that our rook will stay attached to the d1-square. We also prepare a devious idea:

rn2kb1r/pp1b1ppp/2p1p3/q2p4/3Pn3/2N1B3/P.comment: The second point of our 12th move! The queen is banished to g6, where she will merely passively spectate the affairs in the center. The threat of Nc7 is simply unstoppable.

rn1qkb1r/pp1bpppp/2p5/3p4/3P1B2/2N3n1/PP.comment: We could fill an entire separate course listing all of White's threats in this position.

rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/2p5/1B1pp3/3PnB2/2N5/PPP.comment: Justifying the placement of the queen! The most straightforward response, calling White's bluff. The crux of White's idea. The knight cannot leave c6 due to the discovered double check on c7, which will pick up the rook on a8.

rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/2p5/1B1pB3/3Pn3/2N5/PPP2.comment: This is the most popular move, but it immediately digs Black into a deep hole. Covering the check and attacking the bishop. White is winning due to the unstoppable threat of Nd6+, e.g.

This is the only way to prove an advantage! Black ignores the threat of Nc7, instead focusing on setting up a sacrifice on f2. If your opponent uncorks this move, then it is time to take off your hat!

We grab the rook and we WILL live to tell the tale! The queen rushes to the support of the knight. We will neutralize the check on b4 with a series of checks aimed at forcing the queens off the board. Forcing the king onto a more vulnerable square. The smoke has cleared, and Black has insufficient compensation for the exchange.

Another insane tactical blow, opening up a pathway for the queen to h4. Hopefully, you are beginning to see the practical appeal of 6.Qa4!

rnbqk2r/ppB2ppp/2p5/1B1p4/1b1Pn3/2N5/PPP.comment: White is up a piece, but our lack of development makes it difficult for us to untangle. It is crucial to follow up with several accurate moves:

rnbqk2r/1pB2ppp/p1p5/1B1p4/1b1Pn3/2N5/PP.comment: Exploiting the fact that b5 is untouchable due to Qxa8.

rnbqk2r/1p3ppp/p1pB4/1B1p4/1b1Pn3/2N5/PP.comment: This cold-blooded developing move is incredibly hard to play, yet it is the only move that keeps Black in the game.

rn1qk2r/1p3ppp/p1p5/1BBp4/1b1Pn1b1/2N5/P.comment: The queen is trapped, but we are not out of tricks! Sacrificing the bishop in order to generate an escape square for our queen!

rn1qk2r/1p3ppp/2p3b1/1pBp4/1b1Pn1P1/2N4P.comment: White has an overwhelming amount of material for the queen, as well as massive pressure along the eighth rank.

rnbqk2r/pp3ppp/2p5/1BbpB3/3Pn3/2N5/PPP2P.comment: Another insane only move, deflecting the bishop from its protection of the knight on c7. This is what we are talking about when we say that Qa4 is a good move from a practical standpoint! This is a far more human move, and it hands over a massive initiative:

rnbqk2r/pp3ppp/2p5/1Bbp4/3Pn3/2N3B1/PPP2.comment: White's lead in development and the nasty possibility of a discovered attack against Black's rooks gives White a long-lasting initiative. Unfortunately, this fails to a string of wild tactical shots:

rnb1kb1r/ppq1p1pp/2p2p2/1B1p4/3PN3/4B3/P.comment: with a long-lasting edge in the endgame. The c2-pawn is untouchable due to an inventive tactical idea:

rnbqkb1r/pp2p1pp/2B2p2/3p4/3PnB2/2N5/PPP.comment: Cashing in our chips! Black has definite compensation due to the bishop pair, but I definitely prefer White. Note that Black does not threaten to capture on f4, so we can proceed with calm development.

rn1q1b1r/p3pkpp/2p1bp2/3p4/3PnB2/2N2N2/P.comment: Preparing c2-c4. We will follow up by advancing the pawn to c5, and supporting further queenside expansion with b2-b4.

rnb1k2r/pp3ppp/2p5/1B1pB3/1b1P3q/2N2PP1/.comment: The computer indicates that Black is somewhat better, although I would be rather terrified to handle the Black pieces here! White intends to castle kingside, when the straightforward threat of Nc7 will cause major problems.

rn1qkb1r/pp1bpppp/2B5/3p4/3PnB2/2N5/PPP2.comment: Taking with the pawn is rather senseless, as it loses a pawn for virtually no compensation and enables White to open up the entire center.

rn1qkb1r/p2bpppp/2p5/3p4/3PnB2/2N5/PPP2P.comment: The main thing to understand about this position is that the prospect of ...c6-c5 is not scary at all: our queen has plenty of spots to choose from, and ...c5 will seriously weaken Black's control over the d5-pawn. rn1qkb1r/p2b1ppp/2p1p3/3p4/3PnB2/2N2N2/P.comment: We will recover the pawn on the next move. Black's position is in shambles.

rn1qk2r/p2bbppp/2p5/3p4/3PnB2/5N2/PPP2PP.comment: Chipping away at Black's pawn chain. Our pieces are far more active, and Black faces a host of practical problems, e.g.

rn1qkb1r/p2b1ppp/2p1p3/3pN3/3PnB2/2N5/PP.comment: Black's pawns look imposing, but they are no match for White's well-developed army. With our next move, we force liquidation into a favorable endgame.

rn1qkb1r/p2b1ppp/4p3/2ppN3/3PnB2/2N5/PPP.comment: Switching gears, from tactical to positional! By controlling c5, we are preventing the annoying prospect of ...c6-c5 and setting up a long-lasting blockade on the dark squares. Our space advantage and more active pieces give us a pleasant game.

rn1qkb1r/p2b1ppp/4p3/2pp4/3PnB2/2NN4/PPP.comment: The most reasonable move, reinforcing the threat of ...c5. Once again, we do not fear this move, but rather encourage it! Things go from bad to worse, since Black's knight has nowhere good to go! Increasing the blockade on the c5-square.

rn2kb1r/p2b1ppp/4p3/q1pp4/3PnB2/2NN4/PPP.comment: In this position, we uncork a series of absolutely stunning tactical blows, one after the other.

rn2kb1r/p2b1ppp/4p3/q2p4/2pPnB2/2NN4/PPP.comment: We start with a counterblow against Black's queen, drawing Black's bishop out of its initial square.

rn2kb1r/p2b1ppp/4p3/q2p4/1PpPnB2/2NN4/P1.comment: This is the only way for Black to stay in the game, although the situation remains extremely critical.

rn2k2r/p2b1ppp/4p3/q2p4/1bpPnB2/2NN4/P1P.comment: Note the tertiary use of the pawn on c5: in the first place it is a decoy, in the second place...also a decoy, but in the third place, it offers the knight a temporary support! Now, the second knight jumps into the game!

rn2k2r/p2b1ppp/4p3/q1Np4/1bpPnB2/2N5/P1P.comment: An incredible move, desperado-sacrificing the knight in order to shatter Black's center. The resulting position is virtually unplayable from a practical point of view. Obviously, 16...Bxe6 17.exd5 drops the bishop, so this is a sad necessity.

rn3r2/p2bkppp/4p3/q1Np4/1bpPnB2/2N3P1/P1.comment: Deflecting the queen onto a more vulnerable spot.

rn2k2r/p2b1ppp/4p3/q2p4/1NpPnB2/2N5/P1P2.comment: It may appear that Black has finally doused the flames of White's initiative, but the party is only begining. rn2k2r/p2b1ppp/4p3/3p4/1qpPnB2/2N5/P1P2P.comment: We start by undermining the g7-pawn in stylish fashion. You can now see the hidden role that the bishop was playing on f8: it was defending the g7-pawn!

rn2k2r/p2b1p1p/4p2p/3p4/1qpPn3/2N5/P1P2P.comment: And now it is time for part II, highlighting the undefended rook in the corner. Black's position collapses. This move is infinitely better than the limp 16.Qxf6.

rn2k2r/p2b1p1p/4p2p/3N4/1qpPn3/8/P1P2PPP.comment: White emerges from the complications an exchange ahead.

rn1qkb1r/p2N1ppp/4p3/2pp4/3PnB2/2N5/PPP2.comment: Black is forced to acquiesce to the endgame, since recapturing with the knight drops the pawn on d5. Trading on our own terms. The immediate queen trade lets Black off the hook. Black's center collapses, e.g.

rn2kb1r/p2q1ppp/4p3/2pp4/3PnB2/2N5/PPP2P.comment: Of course, the knight on a4 is a great asset, since it threatens to jump to b6, targeting Black's center and Black's rook simultaneously. rn2kb1r/p2q1ppp/4p3/3N4/2pPnB2/8/PPP2PPP.comment: Black suffers from a bad pawn structure. White's play is very straightforward: we will bring the rook on e1 and exert tremendous pressure on Black's center.

rn2kb1r/pp2pppp/2b5/q7/3PnB2/2N5/PPP2PPP.comment: Black has no effective discovery, since we can simply take on d8 wherever Black's bishop goes.

rn3rk1/pp2ppbp/2b3p1/2qp2B1/3Pn3/P1N2N2/.comment: There is nothing to fear along the d-file, e.g. and Black loses absolutely everything.

rn3rk1/pp2ppbp/2b3p1/2qp2B1/3Pn3/2N2N2/P.comment: Forcing the queen to relinquish its control of the d4-square.

rn3rk1/pp2ppbp/2b3p1/2qp2B1/N2Pn3/5N2/PP.comment: White is winning both positionally and tactically: e7, a7, and c6 are all under fire, and White can follow up by establishing the knight on c5 and prying Black's queen away with a timely a2-a4.

rn3rk1/pp2ppbp/1qb3pB/3p4/3Pn3/2N2N2/PPP.comment: White has a huge initiative. Our next move is Qd4, when we will threaten to capture on e6. In the event that Black doubles on the f-file, we can always solidify the f4-pawn with the calm g2-g3.

rn2kb1r/pp2pppp/2b5/3p4/3QnB2/2N2N2/PPP2.comment: Another difficult move to find. Black counterattacks our vulnerable pieces in the center, but enables us to reestablish material equality.

rn2kb1r/pp3ppp/2b5/3pp3/3QnB2/2N2N2/PPP2.comment: Black has kept his extra pawn, but at great cost. We are threatening Nxd5 followed by Ne6, when Black will have no choice but to part ways with the d5-pawn.

After the exchange of knights, Black will have a hard time deploying his bishop, and we have an easy path toward improving the rest of our pieces with Ke2 and Rd1 (or Rg1). There is no question that if Black has made it this far, he probably deserves the draw!

rn2kb1r/pp3ppp/2b5/1N1pp3/3qnB2/5N2/PPPQ.comment: Black is saddled with weaknesses all across the board, and we will continue to improve and prepare infiltration by doubling rooks on the d-file.
with excellent winning chances due to Black's incredibly weak b-pawns.

rn2kbr1/pp2pppp/2b5/3pB3/3qn3/2N2N2/PPPQ.comment: Objectively, the position is equal, but we believe that White's play is quite a bit easier. We can improve our position with Ke2 followed by Rad1, and a well-timed h4-h5 threatens to shut down Black's bishop and will provoke more weaknesses on the kingside.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/2p5/3p4/3PNB2/8/PPP2PPP.comment: Black is at a crossroads. The queen trade hands over control of the d-file, leading to a very pleasant endgame for White. Most players prefer to go directly for the c-pawn, an extra option afforded by the absence of the knight on c3. In contrast to the endgame arising after 4...dxe5 5.dxc5 Qxd1+ 6.Rxd1, this is an improved version for Black since Nb5 is no longer a threat. However, Black still faces a host of positional problems: the c5-pawn still majorly restricts Black's development and coordination, and White's control over the d-file gives us great play in the center. Objectively, the position is equal, but we have unearthed several ways to confront Black with serious practical problems.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/2p5/8/3PpB2/8/PPP2PPP/R.comment: We will see this prophylactic move again in the main line (7...Nc6). The idea is to reinforce the c5-pawn, taking the sting out of ...e5. A clever prophylactic move, taking the sting out of ...e5.
Blocking the check and opening up a pathway for our own queen. Picking up the pawn on e4.

rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/2p5/4p3/3Pp3/4B3/PPP2PPP.comment: It may seem counterproductive to rid Black of his doubled pawns, but we must generate active prospects for our minor pieces. Once the f-file is opened, Black will also have to deal with long-term pressure against the f7-pawn. A worthy alternative, although this move enables Black to build up a rather imposing kingside pawn mass. We will leave a deeper analysis of this move to you, but here is a sample line illustrating White's potential:

rnbqkb1r/pp4pp/2p5/4pp2/2BPp3/4B3/PPP2PP.comment: It is, of course, very important to stop ...f5-f4, which would loosen our grip on the c5-pawn.

rnbqk2r/pp2b1pp/2p5/4pp2/2BPp3/4B1P1/PPP.comment: We now continue our development. The knight is heading not for b5 but for d5, where it will lord over the entire position. We can follow up by exerting our influence on the queenside with b4-b5.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/2p5/8/1P1PpB2/8/P1P2PPP.comment: As usual, this move is seldom to be feared in Jobava London endgames. We have plenty of resources with which to maintain the integrity of our queenside pawn structure.

rnbqkb1r/1p2pppp/2p5/8/1p1PpB2/P7/2P2PPP.comment: This is better than the meek 11.c3, since we simultaneously complete our development and fully immobilize Black's knight.

rn1qkb1r/1p1bpppp/2p5/8/1P1PpB2/8/2P2PPP.comment: The b4-pawn is still untouchable. We will continue to improve our position by castling, and ferrying the knight over to c3. Once the weakening ...f5 is induced, we can rip open the center with the typical idea f2-f3, or double on the d-file and put significant pressure on the d7-bishop. Finally, our knight from c3 can seek greener pastures on b6.

rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/2p5/4p3/3P4/4BN2/PPP3PP/.comment: This prevents Bc4, but the bishop is immediately targeted by our bloodthirsty knight.

rn1qkb1r/pp3ppp/2p5/4pb2/3P4/4BN2/PPP3PP.comment: We now aim to develop our bishop to c4 and apply serious pressure on Black's f7-pawn.

rn1qkb1r/pp3ppp/2p5/4p1N1/3P4/4B3/PPP1b1.comment: The trade of bishops is in our favor, since Black is left with a lame dark-squared bishop (that darn c5 pawn again!)

rn1qkb1r/pp4p1/2p4p/4pp2/3PN3/4B3/PPP1K1.comment: Yet again, the knight has made its way to d5. As usual, we will increase the pressure dial on the queenside with b2-b4.

rn1qkb1r/pp3ppp/2p1b3/4p3/3P4/2P1BN2/PP4.comment: A clever retreating move. Of course, it is a retreating move in name only, since our intentions are extremely aggressive. We aim to root out Black's only active piece (the knight on c6 being fully restricted by the pawn on c3) with Bc4, when Black will be left with two minor pieces that will not be quite as capable of holding his position together.

rn1qkb1r/pp3ppp/2p5/4p1N1/2bP4/2P1B3/PP4.comment: with massive pressure on the kingside. Note that in response to 15...h6, we will simply drop our knight back to f3, putting pressure on the e5-pawn. We will then have the ability to play on all three sides: b2-b4 is the classic idea on the queenside, h4-h5 is one way to expand on the kingside, and the weak pawn on e5 will provide ample fodder for play in the center.

rn1q1b1r/pp3k1p/2p1b1p1/4pp2/2BP4/2P1B3/.comment: Reinforcing the pawn on c5, and untying our hands for direct action on the kingside.

rn1q3r/pp2bk1p/2p1b1p1/4pp2/1PBP4/2P1B3/.comment: The point of 9.f3 is on full display. White has full-scale pressure on the kingside, and the tempting 16...f4 creates a massive hole on e4 that we will use as an outpost for the knight.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/2p5/8/3PpB2/2P5/PP3PPP/.comment: This move is exceedingly rare, but it has been the choice of several strong players in recent months.

rn1qkb1r/pp1bpppp/2p5/8/3PpB2/2P5/PP3PPP.comment: The queen is tucked away on an excellent square, from where it lords over both sides of the board while remaining fully impervious to attack.

rn2kb1r/pp1b1ppp/2p5/q3p3/3Pp3/2P1B3/PPQ.comment: Of course, we do not fear the capture on f3, which will hand us full control of all the light squares in the center. Deploying the bishop to an extremely active post.

rn2k2r/pp1bbppp/2p5/q3p3/3Pp3/2P1BN2/PPQ.comment: In order to parry the mate threat, Black must either swing his knight to f6, leaving its vis-a-vis fully entrenched on g5, or hand over the bishop pair, giving White a clear advantage in both cases.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pp1p/2p3p1/8/3PpB2/2P5/PP3PP.comment: On a4, the queen is mostly impervious to attack and discourages Black from castling queenside.
For now, we proceed with our development.

rnbqkb1r/pp3p1p/2p3p1/4p3/Q2PpB2/2P5/PP3.comment: This brazen move creates a lot more problems than it solves!

rnb1kb1r/pp3p1p/2p3p1/q3p3/Q2PpB2/2P5/PP.comment: A lovely pawn sac to open up the c-file and engineer massive pressure on Black's king.

rnb1kb1r/pp3p1p/2p3p1/3qp3/Q2PpB2/2P5/PP.comment: Black's queen gets tossed around, and the worst is yet to come.

rnb1kb1r/pp3p1p/2p3p1/3qp3/Q1BPpB2/2P5/P.comment: Several of our blitz games reached this position. The queen has to move, and we will capture f7, with a decisive fork.

rnb1kb1r/pp3p1p/2p3p1/q3p3/Q2Pp3/2P1B3/P.comment: White holds a small but significant edge in the endgame for several reasons: 1) We have already castled, and staked our claim on the d-file. Black will not only have a hard time castling, but will experience difficulties in deploying the a8-rook, since the a7-pawn will hang. 2) Our subsequent development is clear. The f1-bishop belongs on b5, while the knight will be deployed to f3. 3) As the subsequent lines reveal, the e5-pawn is also a target that we can chip away at with our f-pawn.

rnb1kb1r/pp3p1p/2p3p1/Q3p3/3Pp3/2P1B3/PP.comment: Reinforcing the e5-pawn appears sensible, but merely throws more oil into the fire.

rnb1kb1r/pp5p/2p2pp1/Q7/3Ppp2/2P1B3/PP4P.comment: The e-file has been blasted open, and our pieces come out with furious vigor.

rn3b1r/pp3k1p/2p1bpp1/QB6/3PpB2/2P5/PP4P.comment: Black is in deep trouble, both strategically and tactically. Our rook will come to f1, creating long-term tactical threats along the f-file (such as Ng5+, followed by a discovered check with the bishop). Furthermore, our control over the d-file is particularly problematic, since Black's bishop cannot leave e6 (due to Rd7+). Finally, we can centralize our knight with Nd4, and if the bishop, the knight will move on to f5.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pp1p/2p3p1/8/3PpB2/2P2N2/PP3.comment: This way of developing has given quite a few Jobava London players grief, since Black generates the hidden threat of ...Bxc3+. Hans Niemann himself blundered in this position at the most recent World Blitz! This is much more exciting (and far more rare) than the more standard 11.Qe3. White keeps the queens on the board and prepares a rapid kingside attack by means of Bf4-e3, Qh4, and ultimately Bh6. Black faces very serious practical problems in the center and on the kingside. This rare move is a very reasonable way to sidestep the complications arising after 11...0-0. Black's queen retreats to a somewhat safer square, and threatens the b2-pawn.

rnbqk2r/pp2ppbp/2p3p1/8/3PpB2/2P2N2/PP3P.comment: Forcing the queen onto an inferior square, and paving the way for the development of our other bishop.

rnb1k2r/ppq1ppbp/2p3p1/8/3Pp3/2P1BN2/PP3.comment: This is more modest than 14.Bc4, but it keeps the fourth rank open for our queen.

rn2k2r/ppq1ppbp/2p3p1/5b2/3Pp3/2P1BN2/PP.comment: With the Black queen on a5, we go the other way (to h4), but here, it makes more sense to exert queenside pressure with our queen, since we are given the opportunity to do so.

rn3rk1/ppq1ppbp/2p3p1/5b2/Q2Pp3/2P1BN2/P.comment: The position is equal according to the engine, but it is definitely easier to play White. We can proceed by creating a luft square with h2-h3, and then gradually roll our queenside pawns up the board. It is worth starting with a2-a4, since that is the least committal of the queenside pawn moves. Later on, we will follow up with b2-b4-b5. Black, on the other hand, has quite a hard time making something concrete of his pawn majority.

rn2k2r/pp2ppbp/2p3p1/q4b2/2BPp3/2P1BN2/P.comment: Keeping a pair of rooks on the board is crucial if we want to maintain a long-lasting initiative. With every trade, the power of White's kingside pressure diminishes considerably. Note that control over the d-file is hardly important, since all of the potential infiltration squares (d1, d2, d3, etc.) are fully covered by our rook and minor pieces.
Defending while attacking! This move provokes a serious weakness on the kingside, but more importantly, it buys us a tempo that we can use to light the fire of our initiative!
Taking the sting out of the threat of Ng5.

rn2k2r/pp2ppb1/2p3p1/q4b1p/2BPp3/2P1BN2/.comment: We have faced this type of move countless times in blitz.
Opening up a direct attack against the e7-pawn.

rn2k2r/pp2ppb1/2p3p1/4qb1p/2BPp3/2P1B3/P.comment: An interesting alternative that sidesteps ideas related to the weak back rank.

rn2k2r/pp2ppb1/2p3p1/4qb1p/2BPp3/2P5/PP1.comment: This is obviously a draw with best play, but White retains serious practical chances. We will bring our king up to the center and create a passed pawn on the queenside.

rn2k2r/pp2p1b1/2p2pp1/4qb1p/2BPp3/2P5/PP.comment: Simple and decisive - this disarms all of Black's play on the first rank.

rn2k2r/pp2pp2/2p2bp1/q4b1p/2BPp3/2P1BN1P.comment: Black has succeeded in getting the heavy pieces off the board, but he has gone from the frying pan into the fire. White threatens to massacre Black's vulnerable queenside pawns with Bb8.

rn2k2r/pp2pp1p/2p2bp1/4qb2/2BPp3/2P1B3/P.comment: White holds a small but very stable edge in the endgame. We will have a much easier job creating a passed pawn on the queenside, and we have many easy ways to improve our position: queenside expansion with a4-a5, as well as straightforward improving moves such as Rfe1 and Bd5 come to mind.

rn2k2r/pp2ppbp/2p3p1/q4bN1/2BPp3/2P1B3/P.comment: Objectively position is even, but our bishop pair and more active light-squared bishop gives us a practical plus. Indeed, Black has to find the somewhat inhuman 16...Qa4 to keep the balance; a few inaccurate moves will hand White a stable plus, e.g.

rn2k2r/pp2ppb1/2p3p1/q4bNp/2BPp3/2P1B3/P.comment: We are unquestionably better in the endgame. As usual, our plan is to gradually advance the queenside pawns, with the dual aims of creating a passed pawn and restricting the mobility of Black's knight, which is already greatly restricted by the c3-pawn. Another scintillating blow, hitting the queen and the bishop at the same time! This only move is virtually impossible to find! It leads to a wild tactical battle that ultimately peters out into a draw, but 10 more computer moves stand between Black and the peaceful result! This is the human move, and it loses on the spot: All of White's previous moves come together beautifully. Black must recapture the rook, opening up the pathway for White's queen. This is why we induced ...h7-h5!
The only way to stave off mate, though Black's days are obviously numbered. Prying open either the g-file or the b1-h7 diagonal. In both cases, White's attack becomes decisive.

Covering the check, and sending the queen on a journey to h1. White has exactly one tempo before the checks resume, and we put this tempo to very good use: Black has made it quite far, but his most difficult challenge is still ahead! Another impossible only move! Black sets up the threat of ...Nd4+, which will grant him just enough counterplay against our king to eke out a draw. It is time for the king to go on an incredible journey:

rn2k2r/pp2ppb1/2p3p1/q4bNp/2BPp3/2P5/PP1.comment: A gorgeous way to sidestep the checks! The center is often the best place to run, since the king has so many avenues of escape. Black has run out of meaningful checks, and has no choice but to return dishonorably back to g7. Now, it is our turn to start attacking! It appears that there is plenty of fight left, but we use our optimally-placed minor pieces to quash Black's resistance with a lovely mating pattern:

Jobava London-3...c5  2023 If Black was able to find all 27 moves of these moves, then it is time to tip your hat and offer a draw, because you are most likely facing Magnus Carlsen, Stockfish 800, or a combination of the two!

rn2k2r/pp3pb1/2p3p1/q3pbNp/2BPp3/2P5/PP1.comment: Remember, pinned pieces protect (PPP), so ...Kxh8 is illegal!

rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/2p1pn2/3p4/3P1B2/2N1P3/P.comment: The typical shot works to perfection here. This is necessary in order to maintain an objectively acceptable position, but from a practical standpoint, White has a major initiative. This is far more common than 7...Nxe5, but sends Black even further into deep trouble. The only way to extricate the bishop is to introduce near-fatal weaknesses on the kingside. As usual, the threat of h5 induces a decisive kingside weakness. At this point, Black is at a major crossroads. There are countless ways for Black to develop, starting with the natural developing moves (5...Nbd7, 5...Bd6, and 5...Bb4) and ending with more extravagant moves such as 5...Ne4. We must consider all of them, since White's responses are a bit different in each case.

We ain't gonna give that pawn up easy! It turns out that Black has no way to win back the pawn without yielding the bishop pair, which turns out to be incredibly valuable in this particular structure. It is essential to avoid this move, after which our queenside will collapse like a house of cards. This has been the choice of many strong GMs; in particular, Belarussian GM Sergei Zhigalko has played this line regularly against the authors of this course. Black aims to rapidly deploy the bishop to b7, making it virtually impossible for White to break in the center with e3-e4. We spent a long time on this move, and are proud to recommend a rare idea that confronts Black with serious practical problems.

Preparing to reinforce the pawn with b4, and essentially forcing Black's hand. Preventing the further progress of Black's b-pawn, and setting up the main idea of the line. This is a rare, but extremely dangerous idea. We freeze Black's queenside play entirely, preventing ...c7-c5. Without this idea, Black is essentially stalemated. We, on the other, have clear ways to improve our position: the knight will be centralized on e5, the bishop developed to d3, and once Black castles kingside, our queen is immediately transported to h3, creating long-lasting and potentially fatal threats on the kingside. Do not be fooled by the engine's assessment: our practice and analysis reveals that Black's position is very hard to play due to the conspicuous absence of a clear active plan. See 4...b5 5.a3 Bb7 6.b4 e6 7.Nf3. An important inclusion. By preventing ...Bb4, we are making it difficult for Black to find active prospects for the dark-squared bishop. More importantly, we are preparing to take control of the queenside with a well-timed b2-b4, which will make it exceedingly difficult for Black to attain much-needed activity on the queenside.
Securing the bishop pair, or forcing the knight to a6.

rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/2p1pn2/3p4/3P1B2/2N1PN2/.comment: Here, it is important not to capture on d5, as that enables Black to develop quickly and dangerously with 8...e6.

Here, it is important to preserve the bishop pair rather than to greedily capture on e6, which leads to the complete dissolution of White's center after the trade on f4. This is the most common move on Lichess, with 127,000 or so games at the time of analysis (and, hopefully, many more after the course enters the chess bloodstream :). Believe it or not, this natural developing move is eighth (yes, eighth!) by popularity in the Lichess database. However, at the titled player level, it is the most common move, so it must be treated like a main line. Black immediately contests the e5-square, delaying the development of his dark-squared bishop until we have put our cards on the table. Now, 6.Ne5 makes no sense due to 6...Nxe5; the exchange does not yield any benefit. Instead, we aim for plan B, quickly completing our development and initiating queenside pressure.
The most popular response by far. Most players do not see the danger awaiting them on the kingside!

rnbqkb1r/pp3pp1/2p1pn1p/3p4/3P1B2/2N1PN2.comment: Adding insult to injury! After we castle, the threat of g4-g5 will spell immediate doom to the Black king.

This is the only way to muddy the waters, although White still emerges from the complications with a nearly winning position. Now, the intuitive 12.Nxd5 gives Black a nagging initiative, so the silicon fiend unearths a delightful idea that defies belief: Simply leaving the f4-bishop en prise! Upon closer investigation, the idea of this move should become clear: after Black takes the bishop, we will capture the pawn on f7, when the threat of h4-h5, coupled with the prospect of a nasty check on c6, spells immediate doom for a totally uncoordinated and underdeveloped Black army. Ideas like these are why we love the Jobava.
Black's position is in ruins. Note that ...Nb4 is not scary, as our queen simply drops down to e2.

rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/2p1p3/3p4/3PnB2/2N1PN2/P.comment: This move should be automatic as well!

rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/2p1p3/3p4/3PNB2/4PN2/PPP.comment: A staggering number of games concluded in this fashion. Black loses the bishop.
Shattering Black's center and carving out a dominant outpost on e5. We see the exact same idea in the 3...c5 line.

rnbqkb1r/p4ppp/2p1pn2/1p1p4/3P1B2/2N1PN2.comment: This move prevents the easy development of the bishop. Black's king has nowhere safe to go, and his structure is in shambles.

rnbqk2r/pp3ppp/2p1pn2/3p4/1b1P1B2/2N1PN2.comment: Black has zero compensation for the pawn, and ...Ne4 always runs into the devastating Qh5+.

Initiating kingside pressure. It is rather painful to part ways with the bishop pair, but there was nothing we could have done: 9.Bg5 would be futile on account of 9...h6 followed by ...g5. See 8...Bd6 9.g4. Here, the only difference is in the placement of the knight; we believe that it is even better on e2, since ...Bxf4 will always be met with Nxf4.
An annoying little move, aiming to fully destroy Black's kingside pawn structure with Bxf6. The bishop pair is meant to be given away!
This sacrifice deserves serious merit, although it leads to a rather chaotic tactical battle that requires intense study.

rnbqk2r/pp3ppp/2pbpn2/3p4/3P1B2/2N1PN2/P.comment: White has the bishop pair (for now) and a pleasant bishop. Next, we will castle queenside and can play either in the center (e3-e4) or expand on the kingside with f2-f4.

Generally, it is not a great idea to capture on g6 since it hands Black the h-file, but we follow it up with a concrete and powerful idea. The point! It transpires that Black has great difficulty defending the pawn, since ...Bd6 drops a pawn (though White must still respond accurately - see analysis below) and ...Rc8 drops the a7 pawn (after which the knight returns to b5). Indeed, there is only one way to defend c7, and it is not all that easy to find. Do not be fooled by the appearance of total symmetry: the extra tempo gives us a very pleasant game. It is worth observing that 6.Ne5 - which is our recommended response to 3...a6 4.e3 Nc6 5.Nf3 Bf5 - is less attractive here since Black has already established a pawn on e6. Now, 8.Ne5 transposes into a position that we reach via the move order 5...Bd6 6.Ne5 h6 7.Bd3 Bxd3 8.cxd3. However, it turns out that we actually have an even better option: we can go straight to work on the queenside.
The customary response (see basic idea #2). White sets up the powerful threat of g2-g4.

A rare and rather dubious move, though it has been the consistent choice of several good players online. The simplest response is to trade knights and quickly push c2-c4, reaching a favorable QGD structure that we have already seen in several other lines.

rnb1k2r/pp2qppp/2pbpn2/3p2B1/3P4/2N1PN2/.comment: This is the best practical try. The computer gives equality (as usual), but Black's position is remarkably hard to play and traps exist by the basinful.

rnb1k2r/pp2qppp/2pbpn2/6B1/3Pp3/2N2N2/PP.comment: Only 14...Kb8 preserves a double-edged position; the natural moves all fail to the same trap, which wins immediately:

rnb1k2r/pp2qp2/2pbpp1p/8/3PN3/5N2/PPP2PP.comment: Black struggles with the weak pawn on e6, and the bishop has great potential once it returns to g2. Black can maintain the balance with computer-like play (starting with 19...Qh4), but there is no question that any normal human would prefer White.

rnb1kb1r/pp1q1ppp/2p1p3/4B3/3Pp3/4PN2/PP.comment: Grabbing space and inducing even more kingside weaknesses.

rnb1kb1r/pp1q1pp1/2p1p3/4B2p/3Pp2P/4PN2/.comment: Total domination in the center and an unstoppable attack on the queenside. Our next move is to b2-b4, and after the pawn appears on b5, Black will probably be best advised to resign in order to avoid a total massacre. Also do not forget about the possibility of a rook lift to c3, particularly if Black's queen appears on c6.

rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/2p1p3/8/3PpB2/2P1PN2/PP3.comment: An astute positional move, preparing to recapture on d4 with the bishop. It may seem more intuitive to recapture with the pawn, but that would grant Black active prospects for his dark-squared bishop, and subject us to long-term pressure down the d-file. On d4, the bishop lords over the entire position, preventing the active development of Black's DSB and keeping the d-file closed for business. Our next step is to complete our development and get our king to e3, when Black experiences long-term problems with the e4-pawn.

rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/4p3/2p5/3PpB2/2P1PN2/PP2.comment: White will combine kingside and queenside expansion. Next up is g4 followed by h4, and we can expand on the queenside with a4-a5 as well - that is why we left the rook on a1! Finally, after g4 is played, remember that you can transfer your light-squared bishop via f1 to g2, when Black will likely lose the e4-pawn.

rnbqkb1r/pp3pp1/2p1pn1p/3p4/3PNB2/4PN2/P.comment: As tempting as it is, this move meets with an incredible refutation that gives Black attacking chances.
A staggering number of games concluded in this fashion. Black loses the bishop.

rnbqk2r/pp2bpp1/2p1pn1p/3p4/3PNB2/4PN2/P.comment: The weakness of the d4-pawn grants Black sufficient counterplay. Black's attack fizzles out, and White's material advantage will be decisive. Note that the g2-square is controlled by our bishop! As in the 13...Bb4 line, taking the bishop leads to unnecessary complications. Instead, we sidestep the bishop and act with surgical precision. Who cares about the bishop? Black is unable to save the rook and the knight at the same time. The queen trade is inevitable, after which Black loses even more material.

rnbqk2r/pp3ppp/2pBpn2/3p4/1b1P4/2N1PN2/P.comment: An ingenious positional move, opening up the f-file. Our long-term pressure along the f-file will guarantee White a stable advantage. Also, do not forget about c2-c4, which would come at the least convenient moment for Black.

rnb1k2r/pp3ppp/2pqpn2/3p4/1b1P4/2N1PN2/P.comment: Black has no good answer to the straightforward idea of dropping the queen to h3 or g2 and following up with h5, blasting open the h-file. Having induced the dreadfully weakening ...b6, we initiate queenside operations without further delay. It may seem rather brazen to push the c-pawn once we have castled queenside, but Black's pieces are too passive and uncoordinated to present a serious dangerous to our king. Worst comes to worse, the king can always find shelter on b1 or a1. Black's king, on the other hand, has nowhere safe to run. This natural move loses quickly: Black has no obvious continuation: the pawn on d5 is hanging, and his position is on the verge of collapse. Picking up the knight with interest. Even with the queens off the board, we are able to generate a massive initiative in the center with a series of accurate moves:

rnb1k2r/pp3ppp/2pqpn2/3p4/1b1PP3/2N2N2/P.comment: Now, the meek 14.Nxe4 would enable Black to repair his center with 14...d5. Instead, our intentions are far more violent.

rnb1k2r/pp3ppp/2pqpn2/3P4/1b2p3/2N2N2/PP.comment: Black is in trouble: he will lose either d6 or e4, or both. Whichever pawn we capture first, we will bring out the rest of our pieces and surround the other one, likely with Bg2 and Re1 or Rhd1.

rnbqk2r/pp3p2/2p1pp1p/3p4/1b1P4/2N1PN2/P.comment: White has a stable plus in the endgame. We will plant the knight on h5, tying Black down to f6, and follow by preparing c2-c4 or even (after Bg2 and Rhf1) f4-f5, accentuating the weakness of the f6-pawn. Bringing the knight into position. We now threaten to freeze the f6 pawn with g2-g4, when Black will have no good answer to the threat of Nh5. This move is just as powerful here as with the pawn on f6. By opening the h-file, we shift our focus from the f-pawn to the h-pawn. Anatoly Karpov would kill for such a position with White! Our next step is to develop the bishop and stack the rooks. Black's ability to defend h6 is limited by the poor coordination of his pieces and by the fact that the knight on c6 has no access to any central squares.

rnbqk2r/pp3ppp/2p1p3/3p4/1b1PnBP1/2N1PN2.comment: This is also good, and perhaps even more straightforward than 11.Ng3.

It appears that we have blundered a piece, but this is all part of the plan. In return for the minor piece, we will receive two pawns and, most importantly, fantastic chances to checkmate Black on the kingside. From a practical perspective, Black's position is untenable. The h-file is about to open up, and Black will have no answer to the massive amount of material that we will pile up on the h7-pawn, which will include the bishop and the other rook.

rnbqk2r/pp3ppp/2p1p3/3p4/1b1PnBPP/2N1PN2.comment: A scary-looking tactic, but it is easy to parry.

rnb1k2r/pp2qppp/2p1pn2/3pB3/1b1P4/2N1PN2.comment: Using the g-pawn as a "hook" to open the h-file, a typical motif worth remembering!

rnb1k2r/pp2qppp/2p1pn2/2bpB3/3P3P/2N1PN2.comment: Black has a permanent weakness on h7. We will accumulate the pressure with Rdh1, when the pawn's days are likely numbered.

r1bqkb1r/pp1n1ppp/2p1pn2/3p4/N2P1B2/4P3/.comment: In human terms, Black is already in massive trouble.

r1bqkb1r/p2n1ppp/1pp1pn2/3p4/NP1P1B2/4P3.comment: This move signals the key difference between 7.b4 and 6.b4: the knight in d7 is now under fire, and after 8...Bxb4+ 9.c3 we attack two minor pieces at the same time. Amazingly, Black can make this line work using an insane sequence of computer moves, but White still maintains an objective advantage at the end. Most people who stumble into this line will have done so unintentionally!
It transpires that Black has serious compensation for the pawn, in the form of pressure on the c3-pawn and the constant possibility of ...Bxa4. We have to proceed with the utmost precision.

r1bqkb1r/p2n1ppp/1pp1p3/3p4/NP1PnB2/2P1P.comment: Not fearing the check on h4, which is cooly rebuffed by g2-g3. Practically speaking, Black is already in very serious trouble. The engine finds ways to keep Black's initiative going, but it is safe to say that a human will not be able to demonstrate anything resembling sufficient compensation for the piece.

r1bqkb1r/p2n2pp/1pp1pp2/3p4/NP1PnB2/2P1P.comment: Poking and prodding at the b6-pawn. Now, ...b5 yields the c5-square, so Black must defend obediently.

Preventing ...e5, and preparing to develop our knight. We aim to complete our development with Bd3 and 0-0, when Black's compensation will simply evaporate. The engine finds a way to keep the spark of Black's initiative going, but we will bet a silver dollar that this position will never occur in your tournament or online practice :)

rnb1kb1r/pp3ppp/2p1pn2/q2p4/N2P1B2/4P3/P.comment: A rather devious move, threatening to win a piece with ...e5 followed by ...e4. As in most Jobava positions, this knight sally is incredibly effective. In particular, it underscores the extent to which Black misses his dark-squared bishop in these sorts of positions; it is remarkably difficult to kick our minor pieces away from e5; Black can only do so at the cost of seriously compromising the activity of his own minor pieces.

rnb1kb1r/pp3ppp/2p1pn2/q2p4/N2P1B2/2P1P3.comment: Turning up the pressure dial on d5. We have a litany of improving moves that we can follow up with, such as a4-a5 (to grab space on the queenside) and Qd3 (to threaten the h7 pawn and coordinate the rooks). If we can induce ...e5-e4, then we will use the d4-square as an outpost for the queen. Taking this knight permanently damages Black's queenside pawn structure. Taking the sting out of ...e5.

rnb1kb1r/pp3p2/2p1pnp1/q2p3p/N2P1B2/2P1P.comment: We are more than happy to enter an opposite-colored bishop middlegame, where our vise-like grip on the dark squares, coupled with the prospect of opening the center at our leisure with e3-e4, guarantees White a pleasant edge. Black, on the other hand, will have a very hard time deploying his light-squared bishop to a reasonably active square.

rnb1kb1r/p4ppp/2p1pn2/qp1p4/N2P1B2/2P1P3.comment: Using tactics to halt the progress of Black's pawn. Of course, c3 is untouchable due to Rc1. Prying open the queenside, and creating a serious long-term weakness on a6. Note that in response to 13...bxa4, we first have to withdraw the dark-squared bishop to g3 in order to take the sting out of ...e5. Then, we will recapture on a4 and turn up the queenside pressure.

rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/2p1pn2/3p4/3P1B2/2N1P3/P.comment: The beginning of the end. Black loses a ton of material.

rnbqk2r/pp3ppp/2pbpn2/3p4/3P1B2/2N1P3/PP.comment: Transitioning to a furious kingside attack! Even without a knight on e5 to guide them forward, the kingside pawns constitute a formidable force. As a result of Black's compromised queenside pawn structure, the Black king has no safe place to hide.

rnbqk2r/pp3ppp/2pbpn2/3p4/3P1BP1/2N1P3/P.comment: Black's king has nowhere to run! This move halts the progress of White's pawns on the kingside...or so it seems. We take the opportunity before Black has castled to smash open the e-file, giving us a dangerous and enduring initiative.

rnbqk2r/pp3pp1/2pbpn1p/3p4/3P1BP1/2N1P3/.comment: Forcing the queen away from c5 and preparing to entrench the knight on b6. It may seem that the knight is anything but stable here, but we will use some fascinating tactics to justify its placement!
The attack is already quite devastating.

rnbqk2r/pp3pp1/2pbpn1p/3p4/N2P1BP1/4P3/P.comment: The point is revealed: the knight is untouchable due to the fork on e3! Just when it seems that our attack has fizzled out, a lovely tactical shot comes to the rescue. Gorgeous! The queen is taboo due to Nxd7+, and Black is forced to part ways with his extra pawn. We have recovered our material investment, and stand clearly better. Our pawn structure is superior, and we can continue stoking the coals of attack by bringing our bishop out to h3. Of course, ...Qb7 is not dangerous on account of b3, and Black's "attack" comes to an end.

rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/2p1pn2/3p4/3P1B2/P1N1P3/.comment: I have faced this move several times in blitz (DN), and it makes a good deal of sense: 7.b4 is now quite a bit less desirable, since the bishop on g7 will exert rather nasty pressure on our knight. Instead, we defend the pawn in an altogether different way:

rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/2p2n2/3pp3/3P1B2/P1N1P3/.comment: This removes the knight from the line of fire of Black's bishop, and threatens Nb6. Note that ...Qa5+ is never dangerous in such positions due to c3 (followed by b4, chasing the queen right back to its initial square). Refraining from the greedy Qxd5, which causes unnecessary complications. With the knight on a safe square, there is nothing to fear from the deployment of Black's bishop to the long diagonal. An astute positional move. The rook will support the c2-c4 breakthrough.
Here, and only here! The lackluster 7.Bg3 enables Black to recover the pawn without consequences.

rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/2p2n2/3pp3/N2P1B2/P3P3/1.comment: Black has no compensation for the pawn. Moreover, he can barely move, since ...Nde5 will always run into Nb6. We will follow up by completing our kingside development, when our extra pawn and superior piece placement gives us a near-decisive advantage.

rnbqkb1r/p4ppp/2p2n2/1p1pp3/N2P1B2/P3P3/.comment: This is why we put the rook on c1!

rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/2p2n2/3pp1B1/3P4/P1N1P3/.comment: This combative move does not solve Black's problems, but it leads to a good deal of tactical complexity, so it is worth looking over the following moves very carefully.

rn1qkb1r/pp3ppp/2p1bn2/3pp1B1/3P4/P1N1P3.comment: We refrain from capturing on d4, which enables Black to entrench his knight on a powerful central square.
Of course, this is the point of deploying the bishop to g5. Black loses the d5-pawn without compensation.

rn1qkb1r/pp3ppp/2p1bn2/3pp1B1/N2P4/P3P3/.comment: As always, this move is innocuous and merely hastens Black's demise.
This nondescript developing move accomplishes nothing, and enables us to attain an ideal setup on the queenside.

rn2kb1r/pp3ppp/2p1b3/q2pp1B1/N2Pn3/P1P1P.comment: A crucial detail that justifies the entire line! We shut down Black's queenside counterplay, and prepare to recapture the pawn on c3 with a dominant position. The piece sac on b4 leads nowhere:
First, the knight is placed on b6 to slice off the queen's only evacuation route. We now threaten b2-b4, which will trap Black's queen.

rn2kb1r/pp3ppp/2p1b3/3pp1B1/Nq1Pn3/P1P1P.comment: Simple and cold-blooded, preventing Black's only idea. The c3-pawn is not going anywhere! First, we will complete our kingside development, and then capture the pawn at our leisure. Black's position is resignable.

rn2kb1r/pp3ppp/1Np1b3/q2pp1B1/3P4/P1n1P3.comment: The pawn phalanx is totally overwhelming. We can continue by smoking out Black's knight with Ne2, and we can respond to ...Be7 with d5-d6.

rn2kb1r/pp3pp1/1Np2q1p/3ppb2/3P4/P3PN2/1.comment: Shutting down Black's counterplay on the d-file.

rn2kb1r/pp3pp1/1Np2q1p/3p1b2/3Pp3/P3PN2/.comment: Black is borderline lost due to our immense control over key light squares, including e4 and c4. Black also struggles with a total lack of coordination and an inability to find a suitable square for the dark-squared bishop.

rn3rk1/pp2bpp1/2p2q1p/3p1b2/2NPp3/P2BPN2.comment: f3-f4 is coming sooner rather than later.

rn2kb1r/pp3ppp/2p1bq2/3pp3/3P4/P1N1P3/1P.comment: Withdrawing the queen from the center and offering a queen trade. Black has absolutely nothing in return for the pawn.

rn1qk2r/pp2bp1p/2p1bp2/3pp3/1P1P4/P1N1P3.comment: Standard fare, deploying the knight to the beautiful b6-square.

rn2k2r/ppq1bp1p/2p1bp2/3pp3/NP1P4/P3P3/2.comment: Halting the progress of Black's d-pawn. Despite the somewhat chaotic apperance of the position, Black has no active plan and no compensation for the pawn.

rn2k2r/ppq1bp1p/1Np1b3/3ppp2/1P1P4/P2BP3.comment: Taking the sting out of ...e4, which will no longer come with tempo.

rn2k2r/ppq1bp1p/1Np1b3/3pp3/1P1P1p2/P2BP.comment: Keeping things tight in the center!

rn2k2r/ppq1bp1p/1Np1b3/3p4/1P1Ppp2/P2BP1.comment: A devastating final resource, underscoring the potency of the knight. Trading on e5 hands over a decisive pawn phalanx in the center, while 19...Qc8 enables us to recapture the c3-pawn with the other knight, when its colleague on d5 will be unassailable. Black is objectively lost.

rn1q1rk1/pp2bppp/2p1bn2/3pp1B1/1P1P4/P1N.comment: White is now up a pawn for no compensation, but there is one more detail worth mentioning.

A devious resource that was employed against DN in a recent speedrun game. Now, 11.0-0 (as played in the game) runs into 11...Ne4, and Black wins material. As usual, our top priority is to lead our c3-knight to the promised land.

rn2qrk1/pp2bppp/2p1bn2/3pp1B1/1P1P4/P1N1.comment: Cold-blooded and powerful. Black is out of active ideas, and we can improve our position in a litany of ways, ranging from Nb6 to c2-c3 to Rf1-d1.

r1bqk2r/pp1n1ppp/2pbpn2/3p4/3P1B2/P1NBP3.comment: This rare move presents a serious challenge to White's setup. There is no question that Black equalizes, but we can definitely pose some serious problems with accurate play. An inventive way to prevent Qf3, but this enables us to change the pawn structure in our favor.

A classic maneuver: the queen is ferried over to h3, where it exerts long-term pressure against the h7-pawn. Without the possibility of ...c7-c5, Black is consigned to total passivity and must defend very precisely merely to avoid getting checkmated in the next few moves.

r1bqk2r/pp1n1ppp/2pbpn2/8/3PpB2/P2BP3/1P.comment: Asking Black a rather nasty question. Castling fails tactically, while ...g6 creates long-term weaknesses on the kingside. Black can maintain objective equality with a host of computer moves, but no one in their right mind would prefer Black's position here! Trying to force pieces off the board fails tactically.

r1bq1rk1/pp1n1ppp/2pbpn2/8/3PpBQ1/P2BP3/.comment: Black loses the exchange, since 12...Qf6 drops the knight (and then the rook).

r1bq1k1r/pp1n1ppp/2pbpn2/8/3PpBQ1/P2BP3/.comment: A great example of a position where the computer evaluation is utterly useless. The computer gives 0.00, but we strongly believe that White's position is incomparably preferable. We will expand on the kingside with h4-h5, and can follow up by dropping the queen to h3 and advancing the g-pawn. Black has no active plan.

r1bqk2r/pp3ppp/1npbpn2/3p4/3P1B2/P1NBPQ2.comment: The ideal setup is now complete. We are exerting massive pressure on h7, and intend to follow up with the prosaic g4-g5. Amazingly, we have transposed to a position that arises in the 4...b5 line! White's attack is virtually unstoppable.

r1bqk2r/pp3ppp/1npbpn2/3p4/3P1B2/P1NBP2Q.comment: This creates massive holes on the kingside, which we can exploit by repositioning our bishop to a more active square.

r1bqk2r/pp3ppp/1npbp3/3p4/3PnBP1/P1NBP2Q.comment: Ignoring the hanging knight on c3, which is non-essential to our attack. Unsurprisingly, given the superiority of our pieces, the tactics work out perfectly for White. It is important to appreciate the value of these types of moves. Even though White is down a piece, we are in no big hurry, and it is worth bringing in the big boys to ensure that the attack is decisive.

r1bqk2r/pp3p1p/1npbp3/3p2p1/3PNBP1/P2BP2.comment: Smashing through Black's pitiful pawn shell.

r1bqk2r/pp3p1p/1npbp3/6p1/3PpBP1/P2BP2Q/.comment: Another important quiet move, setting up the threat of a discovered check. The simplest threat is Nxf8+ followed by h8=Q. Black's king is forced back into the ring of fire. And now the coup d'grace, skewering the queen! Nominally, Black has a lot of material for the queen, but the minor pieces can only spectate as we get our rook to g1 and follow up with Qg4/g5/g6, setting up unstoppable threats along the g-file.

r1b1k2r/pp3p1p/1npbp3/3p2q1/3Pn1P1/P1NBP.comment: Forcing the queen off of the g-file and lending further support to the knight, taking the sting out of ...Bxe5.

r1b1k2r/pp2qp1p/1npbp3/3p4/3PnPP1/P1NBP2.comment: The point of this move is not to shuttle the king to safety; it was perfectly safe in the center. Rather, by connecting the rooks, we are setting up the unstoppable threat of a sacrifice on g7!
Now, a beautiful sequence decides the game:

r1b1k2r/1p2qp1p/1npbp3/p2p4/3PnPP1/P1NBP.comment: This line demonstrates the incredibly potency of White's construction.

r1bqk2r/pp2bp1p/1np1pnpQ/3p2B1/3P4/P1NBP.comment: The rook lift to h3 will lead to immediate checkmate. The extent of Black's queenside paralysis is rather picturesque.

rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/4pn2/2pp4/3P1B2/P1N1P3/1.comment: This very likely transposes to 4...b5 5.a3 Bb7 6.b4 e6. Of course, Black can also play this line without fianchettoing the light-squared bishop, but that hardly changes the general tenor of the game. White's plan will remain the same: to entrench a knight on e5, develop the light-squared bishop to d3, and light the kingside on fire by maneuvering the queen to h3.
For now, we keep the tension, awaiting a more opportune moment to trade on c5.

r1bq1rk1/pp2bp1p/1n2p1pB/2ppP3/1P6/P1NBP.comment: In these types of positions, you almost never want to capture the rook on f8 because the bishop is such a valuable attacker. White is dominating on the kingside, but we do not even have to rush with h4-h5: an even more powerful continuation in response to 14...Kh8 would be to shuttle the knight around to d4 via e2.

rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/4pn2/2pp4/3P1B2/P1N1PN2/.comment: Black continues to expand on the queenside.

rnbqkb1r/p4ppp/4pn2/1ppp4/3P1B2/P1N1PN2/.comment: It is important to throw this move in to discourage ...Nh5.

rnbqk2r/p4ppp/3bpn2/1ppp4/3P1B2/P1N1PN1P.comment: We cannot hold off on this move any longer, since Black was ready to play ...c4 or ...b4. We now proceed to quickly prepare the e4 pawn break. This forces Black to make another move with his dark-squared bishop, thereby losing a tempo.

rnbqk2r/p4ppp/3bpn2/1pPp4/5B2/P1N1PN1P/1.comment: This is a very common response, but Black will be unable to easily recover the pawn.

rnbqk2r/p4ppp/4pn2/1pbp4/5B2/P1N1PN1P/1P.comment: Importantly, the knight on c6 hinders the development of Black's bishop, and makes it impossible for him to stop e4.
There is no way to win the c5-pawn, which can be supported with b2-b4 as necessary. Our queen can also park itself on e3.

rn1qk2r/pb3ppp/4pn2/1pbp4/5B2/P1NBPN1P/1.comment: Before pushing the e-pawn, we complete our deverlopment.

rn1q1rk1/pb3ppp/4pn2/1pbp4/5B2/P1NBPN1P/.comment: The time has come! Our pieces are perfectly placed to deal with the consequences of this breakthrough.

rn1q1rk1/pb3ppp/4pn2/1pbp4/4PB2/P1NB1N1P.comment: The most common response, resolving the central tension straightaway.

rn1q1rk1/pb3ppp/4pn2/1pb5/4pB2/P1NB1N1P/.comment: A very important idea; this is almost always the desirable response to ...d4. The knight is re-routed to d2, and it can later find a home on b3.
Moving the rook to a better spot and setting up the positional threat of Be4, which will dislodge Black's queen from its active post. This move looks scary, but it simply loses a piece:

rn1q1rk1/pb3ppp/4pn2/1pb5/4pB2/P2B1N1P/1.comment: Staking a claim in the center and popping open the b1-h7 diagonal.

rn1q1rk1/pb3pp1/4pn1p/1pb5/4pB2/P2B1N1P/.comment: White is better for several reasons: 1) The pawn on d4 is a long-term weakness that cannot be easily eradicated; 2) We will proceed with Qe2-e4, a nasty idea that will induce a serious kingside weakness; 3) We have many auxiliary ways to improve our position, such as Rfd1 (after Qe2), Nb3-d2-e4-d6, and a timely a3-a4 can also be employed to underscore the hidden vulnerability of Black's queenside structure. In contrast, Black has no clear way to improve his position or cause problems on either side of the board.

rn1q1rk1/pb3ppp/4pn2/1pb5/4pB2/P1NB1N1P/.comment: This position occurred in Bortnyk-Baryshpolets, Nabokov Memorial 2015. This is best, leading to a small edge. White controls the crucial d4-square.

rn1qr1k1/pb3ppp/4pn2/1pb5/4p3/P1NBBN1P/1.comment: Our dark-square control, coupled with the nasty threat of Qb6, secures a very pleasant game for White. Black's queen on h5 is also somewhat out of commission.

rnbq1rk1/p4ppp/4pn2/1pbp4/5B2/P1NBPN1P/1.comment: We see a virtually identical position in the 7...b5 line; the placement of the pawn on b7 does not change the nature of the position. We are ready to push e3-e4, posing Black with serious positional problems.

rnbq1rk1/p4ppp/3b1n2/1p2p3/3pP3/P2B1N1P/.comment: An innovative alternative, although this is quite unnecessary, since 13.Ne2 transposes into a line that leads to a very dangerous position for Black.

rn1q1rk1/p4pp1/3bbn1p/1p2p3/3pP3/P2B1NNP.comment: This position epitomizes the power of the Jobava London, especially with respect to its ability to puzzle even the strongest engines. Stockfish 15, upon reflection, gives equality with a very small preference to Black. But if you look at White's online results, they are staggering (I myself have won almost all my games, including a crushing win over Nepomniatchtchi - O.B.). This is because White has a very clear plan: to maneuver the f3-knight to h4 (and later to f5) and to blast open the f-file with f2-f4. Black, on the other hand, does not have any clear plan of action on the queenside, since the b4-square is guarded and the c2-pawn is well-defended. If this explanation doesn't convince you, perhaps the subsequent analysis will!

rnb2rk1/p3qpp1/4p2p/1pbnP3/3p1B2/P2B1N1P.comment: Black is in a vise-like grip. The bishop can be maneuvered to h4, and White can follow up by amputating the d5-knight with Qd2 and Nf4.

r1bq1rk1/p4ppp/2nbpn2/1ppp4/3P4/P1NBPN2/.comment: White has a small but stable advantage, much akin to the Exchange Caro where Black has closed in his bishop with a premature ...e6. We will inevitably ensconce on our knight on e5 and follow up by building up the kingside pressure.

rnbqkb1r/p4ppp/4pn2/1ppp2B1/3P4/P1N1PN2/.comment: With the dark-squared bishop gone, it is a perfect opportunity to resolve the tension in the center and launch a furious kingside offensive.

rnbqk2r/p2nbppp/4p3/1pPp2B1/8/P1N1PN2/1P.comment: Blasting open the center, after which our knight will sink its teeth into the juicy d6-square!

rnbqk2r/p4ppp/4pn2/1pbp4/5B2/P1N1PN2/1PP.comment: We follow up with the typical developing move to d3, preparing e3-e4.

rnbqk2r/p4ppp/4pn2/1pbp4/5B2/P1NBPN2/1PP.comment: Without question, Black's setup constitues one of the more problematic lines of play against the Jobava London. Black makes it very difficult for us to open up the center with e3-e4 (in contrast to lines with an early ...Nc6, when it is quite a bit easier to carry out this break) while developing his minor pieces to very active posts. In order to avoid getting squeezed, we must insist on pushing e4 as quickly as possible.

rn1qk2r/pb3ppp/4pn2/1pbp4/5B2/P1NBPN2/1P.comment: This move somewhat contradicts the purpose of Black's overall setup, which is to discourage e3-e4. Still, it is a natural developing move and must be taken seriously.

r2qk2r/pb1n1ppp/4pn2/1pbp4/5B2/P1NBPN2/1.comment: Now, the top computer move is 10...e5, which we refuse to take seriously because no one in their right mind would ever chance upon such a move. Barring that, the position is equal objectively, but definitely easier to play for White.

Despite Black's best efforts, we have succeeded in pushing e4, leading virtually by force to a series of piece exchanges in the center. The resulting position may appear rather lifeless, but upon closer inspection, it turns out that White certainly has the easier practical game.

r2q1rk1/pb1n1ppp/4pn2/1pb5/3pPB2/P2B1N2/.comment: This is tempting, and it works on certain occasions (usually with the queen on d1), but here it fails due to the unfortunate placement of White's queen:

r2q1rk1/pb1n2pp/4pp2/1pb3Bn/3pP3/P2B1N2/.comment: It appears that our pieces are all moving backwards, but we have in fact provoked serious, potentially decisive, weaknesses on both sides of the board. We currently threaten to trap the knight with g2-g4, forcing Black to overextend himself even further.

r2q1rk1/pb1n2pp/5p2/1pb1p2n/3pP3/P2B1N2/.comment: Poking at the weak b5-pawn, and opening up the c4-square for our bishop.

r2q1rk1/pb1n2pp/8/2b1p1pQ/Pp1pP3/3B4/1PP.comment: It turns out that this ultra-natural move is a mistake, but find us a human player who will refrain from this move!

r2qk2r/pb1n1ppp/4pn2/1pb5/3p1B2/P1NBPN2/.comment: Now, 12.0-0 transposes into a position that we reach via 9...Nc6 10.0-0 0-0 11.e4 d4 12.Nb1, but we have a superior move:
