This move now comes with tempo, enabling us to recapture Black's bishop while keeping our queenside pawn structure fully intact. Black's knight sally to h5 has been an abject failure: we are ready to recapture the bishop on a5, and Black has no way to recover the pawn.
Had the bishop been on d2, Black could have captured it with their knight! As it stands, White is simply winning, since we will recapture the bishop and chase away or even trap the knight with f2-f3.

r1bqkb1r/1p2pppp/1np2n2/1p1p4/1P1P4/4P3/.comment: This is the best square for White's queen. On b1, it is far away from the predations of Black's knights, and will link up with bishop (after Bd3) to exert nagging pressure on the e4-knight. Note that ...Nc3 is nothing but an empty threat, in response to which we can simply bring our queen up to b3.

r2qkb1r/1p1bpppp/1np2n2/1p1p4/1P1P4/4P3/.comment: We have successfully completed our kingsid development and kept Black's queenside counterplay at bay. We will follow up by castling and deploying the rook to c1. White's total control over all of the key queenside squares renders Black's compensation for the exchange virtually nonexistant.

r1bqkb1r/1p1npppp/2p5/1p1pP3/1P3B2/3BP3/.comment: The threat of f2-f3 renders Black's knight an utterly ineffective defender. Picking up the pawn with interest.

r1bqkb1r/1p1npppp/2p5/1p1pP2Q/1P3B2/3BP3.comment: Black is dominated on the dark squares, and cannot defend e6 and c7 simultaneously.

rnbqkb1r/4pppp/1pp2n2/1p1p4/1P1P1B2/4P3/.comment: Forming a queen-bishop battery, and preparing to meet 12...c6 with the devastating 13.b6.

rnbqkb1r/4pppp/1pp5/1p1p4/1P1PnB1P/4P1P1.comment: It appears that Black has trapped our bishop, since opening the f-file is unthinkable. But we have one more trick up our sleeve.

rnbqkb1r/4p1pp/1pp2p2/1p1p4/1P1PnB1P/4P1.comment: Counterattacking Black's knight, and forcing Black to relinquish his control over the c3-bishop. The tactics work out in White's favor.

rnbqkb1r/4p1pp/1pp2p2/1p1p4/1P1P1B1P/4PP.comment: Another counterblow, this time hitting the bishop! If the bishop retreats to a5, we can finally save our bishop by taking twice on e5.

Gorgeous tactics. The threat of Ne6+ forces Black to leave the knight on f3. Our king will journey back to the promised land to pick it up! This time, under the able protection of the knight, it will be quite a bit safer on that square. Note that 23...Qe7 should be met with 24.Qxd5, covering the e4-square. The smoke has cleared, and Black falls apart completely.

rnb1kb1r/pp2pppp/2p2n2/qN1p4/3P1B2/2P5/P.comment: Recovering the pawn and preventing Black from castling. Things are already quite bad for Black:

rnb1kb1r/pp2ppp1/2p2n1p/qN1p4/3P1B2/2P5/.comment: It is quite important to throw this move in in response to ...h6, since Nf3 allows Black to pick up the bishop with ...Nh5.

rn2kb1r/pp1bppp1/2p4p/qN1p4/3Pn3/2P4P/PP.comment: (Niemann) After the trade, Black will have a very hard time keeping d6 protected.

rnb1kb1r/pp2pppp/2p2n2/1N1p4/3P1B2/2P5/q.comment: A strange-looking move, but it prevents the queen from escaping via a5 and - much like Nb5 (see typical idea #7) - lures Black's knight to an incredible passive square.

r1b1kb1r/pp2pp1p/n1p2n2/1N1p2p1/3P4/2P3B.comment: Preparing to meet ...h4 with Be5 f6 Bxe4, when Black can only take one bishop at a time! White's advantage is not up for debate.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/2p5/1N1p4/3PnB2/8/PPP1P.comment: Making luft for the bishop. Transposes to 6...Nc6 7.Nf3 0-0 8.c3 Re8 9.h3. This move recurs constantly in the 4...Bd6 line. In this case, we take the sting out of ...g7-g5. Tucking the bishop away and ensuring its permanent safety.
Black drops the d-pawn. This is not particularly scary. It is rather painful to part with our dark-squared bishop, but almost all of Black's problems will remain in the resulting position.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/2p5/1N1p4/3PnB2/7P/PPP1.comment: This move is the opposite of scary. The x-ray against White's king my appear concerning, but with the d4-pawn as secured as it is, Black has absolutely no way to convert his temporary development advantage into anything tangible. After we complete our kingside development, Black will experience long-lasting problems with his center.
This move succumbs to a lovely tactical refutation that underscores how nicely our pieces are coordinated. Picking up the bishop on d7 and emerging a pawn ahead.

rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/2p5/1N1pp3/3Pn3/7P/PPP1P.comment: Recovering the knight and leading to a miserable endgame for Black. His pawn structure says it all! Hitting where it hurts! The only (tactical) way to defend both pawns is ...Qb6, but the queen trade further damages Black's pawn structure and makes it harder for them to defend d5.

rn1qkb1r/pp3ppp/2p5/1N1ppb2/3Pn3/7P/PPP1.comment: The pawn advances to g5, where it will either trap the knight or force the horsey to lose contact with the crucial d5-pawn.

rn1qkb1r/pp3ppp/2p5/1N1ppb2/P2Pn3/7P/1PP.comment: We can continue to improve with Rad1 and Qa2, paving the way for a potential pawn storm on the kingside. Black is saddled with tons of weaknesses in the center, and has no easy way to improve.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/2p5/1N1p4/3PnB2/8/PPPQP.comment: We have a nice space advantage and excellent prospects on the queenside.

rn1qkb1r/pp1bpppp/2p5/1N1p4/3PnB2/5P1P/P.comment: More excellent maneuvering. The bishop politely steps away to make room for the knight. Preparing ...e5. The bishop has its moment in the sun! On a4, it hits the knight on c6, threatening to win a pawn and forcing Black to create serious dark-square weaknesses by advancing the pawn to e4.

rn1qkb1r/pp1bpppp/2p2n2/1N6/3PpB2/5P1P/P.comment: The queen is ferried over to g3. We have the bishop pair, the superior pawn structure, and excellent prospects on the f-file. An incredibly deep move, keeping contact with the f5-pawn so that Black's bishop cannot retreat to f7. White's control over the dark squares ensures total domination.

It may seem that Black has fully rectified his pawn structure and has solved his positional problems, but they are in fact only beginning! Note that we have complete and permanent dominance over the dark-squares: the bishop on h2 is the hidden engine of our position. We can assert our advantage by activating our queen and knight, creating a situation in which Black is devoid of pawn breaks and of any active opportunities on either side of the board. Jobava London-3...e6  2023 The knight trade opens up the d4-square, which we can use as an outpost for our queen. Our bishop controls b8 and prevents Black from engineering the ...f4 pawn break. After we reposition our queen to b4, we can accumulate the queenside pressure with b2-b4 and a2-a4 (preparing b5), or blast open the center by preparing c3-c4. Even after an endless series of accurate moves, there is no end in sight to Black's suffering.

rnbqkb1r/pp2ppp1/2p2n2/3p3p/3P1B2/2N1P3/.comment: Proceeding with development. See 4...Bg7 5.h4 c6 6.Be2 h5 7.Nf3. Our approach is identical to the one we adopt in the main line (5...h5), quickly entrenching our knight on e5 and preparing to ferry our king to safety at a moment's notice.

Rome was not built in a day! Before launching our kingside attack, we must do the bare minimum to complete our queenside development and shuttle our king to relative safety. With this move, we also take the sting out of ...cxd4, which will greatly increase the potency of the bishop sortie to h6. The typical exchange sac works to perfection here, since the d5-pawn is undefended and the newly-castled king will get absolutely terrorized.
It transpires that the pawn on h5 is untouchable due to g2-g4, trapping the bishop! Black has no choice but to retreat in shame.

This is the best possible version of the exchange sac, since Black's king has found itself on the worst possible square. Our next step is to complete our development while leveling threat after threat against Black's hapless king.

Now, h5 obviously becomes a serious threat. Black's response is virtually forced. This is an interesting move that both of us have played, and it offers decent practical compensation for the exchange. However, objectively, there is no question that Black is significantly better with only a few accurate moves. The exchange sacrifice is far less effective here, since Black does not need to spend an additional tempo guarding the c6-pawn (compared to the same position in the 4...a6 line). Black uses this tempo to maneuver the knight to f6, dousing the flames of White's initiative. There is no question that White has good practical chances here, but we decided against reccommending this line, since White's compensation is objectively insufficient.

rnbqkb1r/pp2ppp1/2p2n2/3p3p/3P1B2/2N1PN2.comment: The early bishop sortie to g4 is very common, but the bishop will be tossed around by our pawns. We respond by unpinning our queen and reinforcing the idea of Ne5.
Our response to this move is one and the same!

rn1qkb1r/pp2ppp1/2p2n2/3p3p/3P1Bb1/2N1PN.comment: A nifty little resource, shuttling the knight to b3 and prying the queen away from the d5-pawn.
This exchange is squarely in White's favor: the resulting pawn structure offers White fantastic play in the center and on the kingside, as well as the bishop pair.
This is the only way to "justify" the bishop's development to g4, but the resulting pawn structure works squarely in our favor.

r2qkb1r/pp1nppp1/2p2n2/3p3p/3P1Bb1/2N1PN.comment: Striking at the center without delay.

This creative night sally underscores the awkwardness of the bishop on g4, which will provide fuel for a furious pawn storm in the center. f2-f3 and e3-e4 is coming, and Black can do absolutely nothing about it.

r2qkb1r/pp1n1pp1/2p1pn2/3p3p/3PPBb1/2N2N.comment: It is almost always worth investing a tempo to improve the safety of our king.

r2qkb1r/1p1n1pp1/p1p1pn2/3p3p/3PPBb1/2N2.comment: Deploying the rook, and applying pressure on g6.
An ingenious move, opening up a line of fire to the h4-pawn. Since our lead in development is quite vast, we can afford to leave the h-pawn en prise!

r2qkbnr/1p1n1pp1/p1p1p3/3p3p/3PPBb1/2N2N.comment: This pin is quite nasty, since Black cannot afford to play ...f6 for obvious reasons.

A cold-blooded response, sending the queen back where it belongs! It is now time to smash open the center at all costs! At this point in your Jobava journey, moves like these should not elicit any surprise.

r2qkbnr/1p1n1pp1/p1p1p3/3p2Bp/3PP1b1/2N2.comment: Black is paying a steep price for advancing his h-pawn and opening the g-file: we threaten the devastating Nxh5 gxh5 Bf6, while Black's "attack" hasn't even gotten off the ground. The knight is hanging, and Nxh5-Bf6 is imminent.

r2qkb1r/1p1nnpp1/p1p1p3/3p3p/3PPBb1/2N2N.comment: Another blow, removing the final defender from the e-file. Obviously, taking with the queen loses to Re1, so Black's king has no choice but to go on a walk. A surgical follow-up check, preventing ...Kf8.

r2qkb1r/pp1nppp1/2p2n2/3p1bNp/3P1B2/2N1P.comment: In order to generate a suitable escape square for the bishop, Black must cede total control of the center.

r1bqkb1r/pp1nppp1/2p2n2/3p3p/3P1B2/2N1PN.comment: Black's position is cramped and unpleasant, and is powerless against the ensuing series of kingside pawn breaks. Softening up Black's position.

r1bqkb1r/pp1nppp1/2p2n2/3p3p/3P1B2/2NBPN.comment: This is the strongest move, but it is very infrequently played. Objectively, the position is dynamically equal, but there is no question that it is quite a bit easier to play White.
and White will send away the bishop on the next move.
Continuing to batter away at Black's kingside!

r1b1kb1r/pp1nppp1/1qp2n2/3p3p/3P1B2/2NBP.comment: An important resource, indirectly defending the b2-pawn.

r1b1kb1r/pp1nppp1/2p2n2/q2p3p/3P1B2/P1NB.comment: Lovely tactics! Black is posed with an ultimatum: take the knight and run the risk of losing their queen, or transition into a rather unpleasant endgame in which White's space advantage and better-placed pieces offers the better practical chances.

r1b1kb1r/pp1nppp1/1qp5/3p3p/3P1B2/P1NBPN.comment: Do not be afraid to castle kingside even with the pawn on h4, since Black lacks the machinery and activity to exploit this cosmetic damage. The pawn on e5 is incredibly nasty, since it controls important squares and severs the coordination between Black's pieces.

r1b1kb1r/ppqnppp1/2p5/3p3p/3P1B2/P1NBPN2.comment: Sacrificing the e5-pawn for a furious initiative on both sides of the board.

r1bqkb1r/pp1nppp1/2p5/3p3p/3P1Bn1/2NBPN2.comment: Our knight is ferried to f4, when the pressure against g6 will become seriously alarming. Black has nothing going on the other side of the board. The tactical battle has subsided, and it is time to switch gears to methodical positional play. The first step is to optimize our queenside pawn structure.

r1bqkb1r/1p1nppp1/2p4n/p2p3p/P2P1B2/1PNB.comment: Step one has been achieved, and now it is time for step two: maneuvering the knight to f4, and opening up the queenside with c2-c4. White has a small but stable edge in the endgame. Following that, we will place our rook on b1 and exert nasty pressure on Black's b7-pawn. There is no question that White stands better, and we are playing essentially for two results.

rnbqkb1r/1p2pppp/p1p2n2/3p4/3P1B1P/2N1P3.comment: Here, the exchange sacrifice is fully justified, since the d5-pawn will be undefended in the resulting position, costing Black a crucial tempo.

rnbqkb1r/1p2ppp1/p1p2n2/3p3p/3P1B1P/2N1P.comment: Straightforward and powerful: we threaten to smash open the kingside with g2-g4, which will likely lead to the summary execution of Black's monarch.

Highlighting the ineffectiveness of Black's fourth move. Black must now waste another tempo to defend the d5-pawn, giving us the window of opportunity that we need to develop long-lasting kingside pressure.
Now, 9.g4 is hasty due to ...Nxe5 and ...Nxg4, so one more patient preparatory move is required.

r1bqkb1r/1p1nppp1/p1p2n2/3p3p/3P1B1P/2N1.comment: 11.g4 was possible, but there is no hurry: we are in charge in the center, and Black is too passive and poorly coordinated to generate serious prospects on the queenside.

r1bqkb1r/3nppp1/p1p2n2/1p1p3p/3P1B1P/2N1.comment: Our next move will Rdg1, when everything will finally be ready for g2-g4! Of course, 12...b4 merely exacerbates the issue due to 13.Na4, when Black will be saddled with additional queenside weaknesses.

rnbqkb1r/1p2ppp1/p1p2n2/3p3Q/3P1B1P/2N1P.comment: A crucial resource, aiming our queen-bishop battery at the c7 pawn. Black has no way to defend it without decisively compromising his king safety.

rnbqkb1r/5pp1/ppp1pn2/3p3Q/N2P1B1P/4P3/P.comment: An old friend comes knocking! We are more familiar with the c2-c4 idea in a positional context, but it is just as powerful here. Opening up the c-file enables us to deploy our rook, when the pressure against c7 quickly becomes decisive.

rnbqkb1r/5pp1/ppp1pn2/7Q/N1pP1B1P/4P3/PP.comment: Now, ...b5 runs into the deadly Nc5+, so Black must part ways with the c4-pawn.

rn1qkb1r/1b3pp1/ppp1pn2/7Q/N1pP1B1P/4P3/.comment: It should be clear even to an untrained eye that White's attack is utterly crushing.

rn1qkb1r/1p1b1pp1/p1p1pn1Q/3p4/3P1B1P/2N.comment: The knight on h5 is unassailable, and it controls the key f6 and g7-squares, restricting Black's already ultra-cramped position even further. We can continue by castling queenside, completing our development with Be2, and even finding appropriate digs for the other knight with Na4-b6.

rn1qkb1r/pp3pp1/2p1bn2/3pp2p/3P1B2/1NN1P.comment: We will follow up by castling queenside, landing the d5 pawn in serious trouble. Obviously, Black cannot even dream of any compensation for the pawn!

rn2kb1r/pp2ppp1/1qp2n2/3p3p/3P1Bb1/2N1P3.comment: This leads to the same position as after 11...Qb6, with the pawn on a3 clearly favoring White.

rn2kb1r/pp2ppp1/1qp2n2/3N3p/3P1Bb1/4P3/P.comment: Black has recovered the pawn, and the ensuing check on c3 may appear rather disconcerting, but Black's position remains virtually untenable due to the semi-open h-file, the lack of active prospects for the LSB, and the permanent weakness of the e6-pawn.

rn2kb1r/pp2ppp1/1qp5/3n3p/3P1Bb1/3BP3/PP.comment: Unpinning the knight and preparing to trade on our own terms.

rn2kb1r/pp2ppp1/2p5/3n3p/1q1P1Bb1/3BP3/P.comment: The bishop pair and our incredibly active rook guarantee us excellent winning chances in the endgame.

rnb1kb1r/pp2ppp1/2p2n2/q2p3p/3P1B2/2N1P3.comment: The standard response to Black's last move, underscoring the awkwardness of Black's bishop and preparing g2-g4, which will pave the way for our queen to land on the h-file. Beating Black to the punch!

One more bit of prophylaxis, taking the defensive burden off of our knight. Depending on Black's response, we can finally initiate kingside operations with Bh6 or casually finish our development with Nf3. Simply put, Black has very little to brag about on the queenside, and we have a lot more time on our hands than it may seem! An old friend comes knocking: we bring the knight over to e5, which will likely tip Black's already poorly-coordinated army over the edge.

rnb1kb1r/pp2ppp1/2p2n2/q2p3p/3P1B2/2N1PP.comment: Once the queen lands on h2, Black is totally doomed.

rn2kb1r/pp2ppp1/2p1bn2/q2p3p/3P1B2/2N1PP.comment: This patient move highlights the extent of our dominance. There is no need at all to hurry with Bh6; Black has absolutely nothing going on the queenside. Now, we are ready to thrust the bishop into h6 and follow up with Nf4, with utterly decisive consequences.

rn2kb1r/pp2ppp1/1qp1bn1B/3p3p/3P4/2N1PP2.comment: This position occurred in "Boknoy2019" - "Mustang6000", Lichess (blitz) 2021. White committed a small inaccuracy with Rg7, enabling Black to prolong the game with ...Ke8. Believe it or not, Black actually went on to win the game! Instead, immediate victory is yielded by a move on the other side of the board:

rn2kbnr/pp2ppp1/1qp1b2B/3p3p/N2P4/4PP2/P.comment: The point of getting the knight to c5 was not to win a pawn, but to close off the king's only escape hatch!

rnb1kb1r/pp2ppp1/2p2n2/q2p3p/3P1B2/P1N1P.comment: Gorgeous maneuvering. We prepare f2-f3 and Qh4, when the attack will finally begin in earnest!

rnb1kb1r/p3ppp1/2p2n2/qp1p3p/3P1B2/P1N1P.comment: Black's queen is but a paper tiger, since 14...Qb1+ is cooly met with 15.Kd2 (followed by f2-f3, to eliminate the possibility of ...Ne4+). Cold-blooded and ridiculously powerful. Black's queenside activity has come to a shuddering halt, and now it is our time to shine!  Removing the final obstacle. Without its last faithful defender, the Black king will be left entirely to its own devices. To use a phrase that both of us promised not to use in this course, the position plays itself!

rnb1kb1r/p3ppp1/2p2n2/qp1p3p/1P1P1B2/P1N.comment: A simple but lovely tactic to top it all off. Rh1 is unstoppable, and mate follows in a few moves.

rnbqkb1r/pp3pp1/2p1pn2/3p3Q/3P1B2/2N1P3/.comment: Surgically precise. We saw this exact idea in the 4...a6 5.h4 Bg7 variation. The pawn on c7 represents Black's last hope to generate counterplay; without it, Black will be left without even an iota of play.

r1bqkb1r/p4pp1/p1p1pn2/3p3Q/3P1B2/2N1P3/.comment: Having mangled Black's queenside, it turns out that we do not even need to waste any time capturing the pawn on c7! Instead, we can turn directly to the most important task at hand: getting the rook to h1 as quickly as possible.

r1bqkb1r/p4pp1/p3pn2/2pp3Q/3P1B2/2N1P3/P.comment: Rh1 is coming, and Black's king is doomed.

rnbqkb1r/pp2ppp1/5n2/2pp3Q/3P1B2/2N1P3/P.comment: The point of this move is not so much to snag a pawn (we will give it right back) but to prevent ...c4, ensuring that our bishop remains singularly trained on the h7-pawn.

rnb1kb1r/1p2ppp1/p4n2/2qp3Q/5B2/2N1P3/PP.comment: Black will lose the h-pawn, and with it, any hopes of not getting checkmated before move 20!

r1bqkb1r/pp1npp2/2p2n2/3p2pp/3P1B2/2NBPN.comment: Screwing in the pawn, leaving Black's bishop with no active prospects and the g4-pawn without a key defender.

r1bqkb1r/p2npp2/2p2P2/3p2pp/3P1BP1/2pB1N.comment: Black's position is riddled with holes. We can follow up with Rdf1 and Rh4, picking up the g4-pawn and proceeding to destroy Black on the kingside.

rnbqkb1r/pp2ppp1/2p2n2/3p3p/3P1B2/2N1P3/.comment: Obviously, we are only willing to trade on our own terms. It is almost always worth throwing in this prophylactic move, which ensures that ...Ne4 will never cause us headaches. The fate that awaits Black after this careless move shows that Black cannot keep his king in the center forever.

rn1qkb1r/pp2ppp1/2p2n2/3p3p/3P1Bb1/2N1P3.comment: The Black monarch's days of restful solitude are over. The moment he escapes to the kingside, we will pry open that side of the board with g2-g4. Threatening exd5, and virtually forcing Black to permanently weaken the dark squares in the center. White is more active and better coordinated. Our likeliest follow-up is g4, which is rather problematic for Black even though the king is on the other side of the board. Without any support, the pawn storm is anything but scary.
You should not bat an eye at this move by now, which simultaneously prepares g2-g4 and e2-e4.

rn1qkb1r/pp2ppp1/2p2n2/3p3p/3PPBb1/2N5/P.comment: Having induced these weaknesses, we now switch gears and force the queens off the board.

rn1qkb1r/pp3pp1/2p1pn2/3P3p/3P1Bb1/2N5/P.comment: It transpires that Black is facing a rather problematic double-attack: there is no way to guard d6 and a7 at the same time! Black has no choice but to part ways with the corner pawn.

rn1qkb1r/pp3pp1/4pn2/3p3p/3P1Bb1/2N5/PPP.comment: Black's drawing chances are significant, but we are obviously playing for two results. Note that Black has no way to cut off the knight's evacuation route, since ...Rb4 will always run into a3.

rn2kb1r/pp2ppp1/2p2n2/q2p3p/3P1Bb1/2N1PP.comment: Taking the sting out of ...b4, which will now create a complex of weak squares on the queenside that we are in perfect position to exploit.

rn2kb1r/pp2ppp1/2p2n2/q2p3p/3P1Bb1/P1N1P.comment: An instructive move, showing that our play is not only limited to the center and kingside in this line. We use the attack on c6 to force Black's queen back to his side of the board, which in turn allows our queen to find an ideal perch on a3. Black's "attack" has fizzled out before it began.

rn2kb1r/pp2ppp1/q1p2n2/3p3p/N2P1Bb1/P3PP.comment: As is so customary in the Jobava London, we combine play on both sides of the board. Having taken the c5-square under firm control, we now turn our attention to the kingside, carrying out a typical sacrifical operation aimed at opening the h-file. The queen joins the party, hitting Black where it hurts. Who needs the queen anyway?

r1bqkb1r/pp2ppp1/n1p2n2/1N1p3p/3P1B2/4P3.comment: Developing the bishop and preparing h5.

r1b1kb1r/pp2ppp1/nqp2n2/1N1p3p/P2P1B2/2P.comment: Black's queenside counterplay has ground to a halt, while we are just getting started on the other flank. We will follow up by trading on g6 and maneuvering the knight to e5.

rnbqkb1r/pp2ppp1/5n2/2pp3p/3P1B2/2N1PN2/.comment: This centralizing move is far more accurate than the immediate 8.0-0-0, which would enable Black to generate troublesome queenside counterplay with ...Qa5.

r1bqkb1r/pp2ppp1/n4n2/1Npp3p/3P1B2/4PN2/.comment: In contrast to 5...h5, we will have a harder time engineering a kingside attack, but from a strategic perspective, our advantage is indisputable.

r2qkb1r/pp2ppp1/n4n2/1Npp3p/3P1Bb1/2P1PN.comment: Supporting the knight and taking the sting out of ...Bxf3. Black can barely move a muscle, e.g.

rn1qkb1r/pp2ppp1/2p2n2/3p3p/3P1B2/2N1Pb2.comment: White's pawn structure may be visually unappealing, but the pawn on f3 will help prepare e4, and the semi-open g-file works in our favor as well.

rn1qkb1r/pp2ppp1/2p2n2/3p3p/3P1B2/2N1PP2.comment: The only reasonable attempt to muddy the waters, though it falls woefully short.

rn1qkb1r/pp2ppp1/5n2/2pp3p/3P1B2/2N1PP2/.comment: With the light-squared bishop gone, Black is unable to sustain his center without creating additional weaknesses.

rn1qkb1r/pp3pp1/4pn2/2pp3p/3PPB2/2N2P2/P.comment: Our last two moves underscore the strategic error inherent in the trade on f3.

r2qkb1r/pp1n1ppn/4p3/2ppP2p/3P1B2/2N2P2/.comment: Everything is now in place for the decisive breakthrough. White's knight joins in from the other side. Once it reaches d6, Black will be unable to deal with the countless threats coming from every side. Calm, cool, and collected! It is important to shoo Black's queen away from the kingside before reopening the g-file.

r2qkb1r/pp1n1ppn/4p3/2ppP2p/3P1B2/2NB1P2.comment: Imprisoning Black's rook and reopening the g-file.

rn1qkb1r/pp3pp1/4pn2/2Pp3p/5B2/2N1PP2/PP.comment: Intrepid and powerful! This move is almost never as scary as it looks; we disarm it by vacating an escape route for our king. The check on a1 is innocuous, and we can always bring our bishop to d3 to clog up the d-file.
Hitting Black where it hurts! In the words of my coach, White has compensation for his extra pawn :)

rnbqkb1r/pp2ppp1/5n2/2ppN2p/3P1B2/2N1P3/.comment: This position has occurred countless times in high-level tournament practice. Our first step is to control the e4-square and restrict the mobility of the f6-knight.

r1bqkb1r/pp2ppp1/2n2n2/2ppN2p/3P1B2/2N1P.comment: A crucial follow-up, controlling the e4-square and preparing g2-g4.

r1bqkb1r/pp2ppp1/2n2n2/3pN2p/3P1B2/2N2P2.comment: This tempting move plays right into our hands. Shepherding the king to safety and protecting b2 and d4. Black has no good answer to the typical plan of g2-g4 and h4-h5, which will tear open the kingside and quickly lead to a decisive attack.

r2qkb1r/pp2ppp1/2n2n2/3pNb1p/3P1B2/2N2P2.comment: It is also possible for White to play it slow.

A very interesting and unusual idea that poses serious practical problems. As is the custom all throughout the 3...g6 variation, White combines positional and tactical play on the two flanks: on the queenside, we wish to trade on c6 and control the c5-square with Na4. On the kingside, we are awaiting the perfect opportunity to blast open the landscape with g2-g4 and h4-h5. Black can maintain the balance with perfect computer play, but from a practical standpoint, the position is virtually unplayable. See 9...cxd4 10.exd4 Bf5 11.Bb5.

r2qkb1r/pp2ppp1/2n2n2/3pNb1p/3P1BP1/2N2P.comment: Asserting dominance over the c5-square. Note that Black has absolutely no potential to develop a queenside attack, since the b8-square is permanently under our control and our last move renders ...c6-c5 impossible.
While the engine finds a way to prolong the game, all human moves lead to Black's rapid demise.

r2qkb1r/pp2ppp1/2n2n2/3pNb2/3P1Bp1/2N2P2.comment: Pow! In contrast to the other lines within the 10...Qb6 sub-variation, the decisive invasion will occur along the g-file.

r2qkb1r/pp2ppp1/2n2n2/3pNb2/3P1BP1/2N5/P.comment: Clinical precision! Trading off the light-squared bishop decisively loosens Black's control over h7.

r2qkb1r/pp2ppp1/2n2n2/3pN3/3P1BP1/2Nb4/P.comment: This recapture makes a lot of sense when you keep in mind that the queen's optimal square is on h2.

r2qkb1r/pp2ppp1/2n2n2/3pN3/3P1BP1/2NB4/P.comment: We will follow up with Rdg1 and Nxg4. Black's days are numbered!

r2qkb1r/pp2pp2/2n2n2/3NNbp1/3P1Bp1/5P2/P.comment: Just as in the 13...gxh5 line, this move is an integral part of White's attacking strategy. Eliminating the final defender of the h7-square spells immediate doom.

r2qkb1r/pp2ppp1/2n2nb1/3NN3/3P1Bp1/5P2/P.comment: It may seem that White's attack has ground to a halt, but we are actually just one short step away from setting up a mating net. Calm developing moves like this one should no longer come as a surprise to you. This sets up the virtually unstoppable threat of Nf5+, when ...Kg8 is met with Qxg6+ (that is why we need the services of the bishop!).

r3kb1r/pp2Npp1/2n2nb1/4N3/3q1Bp1/5P2/PPP.comment: The computer's top suggestion here is 22...Qg1+, which tells us all that we need to know about the position!

r2qkb1r/pp2pp2/5n2/3p1Pp1/3P1B2/2N2Q2/PP.comment: Black has succeeded in staving off checkmate for the time being, but his position remains untenable from a practical standpoint. The following line demonstrates the truth of this statement:
Given the total lack of counterplay on the queenside, we are well within our rights to optimize the safety of our king before rolling up our sleeves on the other side of the board.

2rqkb1r/pp2pp2/5n2/3p1Pp1/3P1B2/2N2Q2/PP.comment: It may seem counterintuitive to trade off the queens, but we have plenty of pieces with which to finish Black off on the kingside.

2rqkb1r/pp2pp2/5n2/3p1PR1/3P1B2/2N2Q2/PP.comment: Black loses the h5-knight, and with it, the game.

r2qkb1r/pp2ppp1/2n2n2/1B1pNb1p/3P1B2/2N2.comment: This move is no better than it was on the previous move. In fact, it merely encourages us to do what we wanted to do anyway: assert our dominance over the c5-square.
It may seem brazen to give up the e5-pawn, but our development is our top priority. Furthermore, once Black takes a bite of the forbidden apple, we swiftly transition our initiative to the center.

r3kb1r/p3ppp1/2p2n2/1q1pNb1p/N2P1B2/5P2/.comment: A familiar situation: Black has run out of active ideas on the queenside, and the stage is set for decisive kingside action.

r3kb1r/p2bppp1/2p5/1qNp3p/3P1B2/1P3P2/P1.comment: The tempting 17.g4 is possible, but we have at our disposal a far more powerful - and much more beautiful - idea.

r3kb1r/p3ppp1/2p5/1qNp1b1p/3P1B2/1P3P2/P.comment: A picturesque position that is worth examining for more than a few seconds! Yes, your suspicion is correct - Black's queen is trapped in the middle of the queenside, and he has absolutely no good answer to the threat of a2-a4.

r3kb1r/2B1ppp1/2p5/p1Np1b1p/Pq1P4/1P3P2/.comment: It is rather amazing that we win the game without making a single attacking move on the kingside. Such is the unique power of the Jobava London!

2rqkb1r/p3ppp1/2p2n2/3pNb1p/3P1B2/2N2P2/.comment: At this point, you should be ready to execute the last two moves automatically. With the c5-square under complete control, the stage is set for decisive action on the kingside.

r2qkb1r/pp1nppp1/2n5/1B1pNb1p/3P1B2/2N2P.comment: Here, do not walk into 16.Nc7?? Qxa2 17.Qxd7 Rad8 and White loses instantly!

A critical position has been reached. The natural move is, of course, 15.Nxd5, but that allows Black to force the queens off the board with 15...e6. Instead, we seize the opportunity to force the dark-squared bishops off the board, rendering Black's monarch even more susceptible to all sorts of shenanigans.

r2qkb1r/pp1nppp1/2N5/1B1p1b1p/3P1B2/2N2P.comment: This fails to a lovely tactical sequence that is worth memorizing:

r2qkb1r/pp1n1pp1/2N1p3/1B1p1b1p/3P1B2/2N.comment: Boom shaka-laka! The point of this move, believe it or not, is not to follow up with h5, but rather to open up the knight's access to e4 and g5.

r2qkb1r/pp1n1pp1/2N1p3/1B1p1b2/3P1Bp1/2N.comment: The point of White's entire strategy is on full display in the event of 19...Bxg4, which runs into 20.Qd4+ - that is why it was so important to trade the bishops. Black has no choice but to accept a miserable endgame.

r2qkb1r/pp1n1pp1/2N1p3/1B6/3PpBP1/8/PPP4.comment: Clamping down on the kingside and forcing the queen trade on our terms. We will recover the e4-pawn on the next move, when Black's deficient queenside pawn structure, coupled with the superior activity of our rooks, will grant us excellent winning chances.

r2qkb1r/pp1n1pp1/2N1p3/1B1p4/3P1Bb1/2N5/.comment: The point! The threat of Ng5 is absolutely devastating.

rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/2p2n2/1N1pP3/5B2/8/PPP1P.comment: This merely exacerbates an already critical situation.

rnbqkb1r/1p3ppp/p1p5/1N1pP3/4nB2/4P3/PPP.comment: Black has absolutely no compensation for the pawn.

rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/2p5/1N1QP3/4nB2/8/PPP1PP.comment: Jobava London-Rare 3rd Moves  2023 The rest is clear without further analysis :)

rnbqk2r/pp3ppp/2pbpn2/1N1p4/3P1B2/4PN2/P.comment: In contrast to the 3...e6 line, there is no other way to parry the threat of Nc7+.

rnbqk2r/pp3ppp/2p1pn2/1N1p4/3P1b2/4PN2/P.comment: We have a nice space advantage, control over the light squares, and a massive clamp on the e5-square.

r1bqkb1r/pp1n1ppp/2p1pn2/3p4/3P1B2/2N1PN.comment: This is still very strong, even though we are no longer trying to trap the bishop. Instead, we are storming the kingside with our pawns. Black has a very hard time stopping g4-g5, which has the potential to be devastating. This leads directly to a scintillating tactical confrontation. It is important to combine space-grabbing pawn moves on the kingside with simple developing moves. Once the knight leaves f6, g4-g5 no longer comes with tempo, so we hold off on that move for now. Do not be fooled by the symmetrical appearance of a position like this. White has a massive kingside space advantage, as well as better-placed pieces. It is not easy for Black to find a suitable home for their bishop, and must constantly reckon with a well-timed g4-g5. See 4...c6 5.Nf3 e6 6.Ne5 Nbd7 7.g4.

r1b1k2r/pp1nbppp/1qp1pn2/3p4/3PPB2/2NB1N.comment: The pawn on h5 is a huge weakness which essentially precludes kingside castling. We can push e4-e5 at our leisure.

r1bqkb1r/pp1n1ppp/2p1p3/3p4/3PnBP1/2N1PN.comment: Here, we recapture on d3 with the queen to preserve the integrity of the queenside. On the next move, we will castle queenside and our minor pieces will dominate in the center and on the kingside. White has a small, but very stable, advantage.

rnbqk2r/pp3ppp/2pbpn2/3p4/3P1B2/2NBPN2/P.comment: Rushing the bishop to a5. This idea constitutes one of Black's main responses to 3...e6 4.Nb5. In this version, the placement of Black's knight on d7 granmts us the ability to engineer nasty queenside pressure.

This is simply bad, as it enables us to ruin Black's pawn structure. Additionally, the bishop on f5 will end up totally out of commission. An inexperienced Jobava player would now be tempted to snap off the knight, but we are seldom willing to give up our light-squared bishop for the knight. Given Black's last move, trading the bishop makes very little sense. After recapturing the bishop, Qb3 will come with tempo, leading to a nasty queenside attack and a clear advantage.
This leads to immediate material loss:
Do not be fooled by the symmetrical appearance of the position. Our knight on c3 is superior to its counterpart on d7, and we are able to strike first on the queenside.

rnbqk2r/pp3ppp/2p1pn2/3p4/1b1P1B2/2NBPN2.comment: This is actually the most common move, since ...Bb4-a5 is not the easiest maneuver to find for someone who is not experienced in this type of position.
This is an improved version of the position we reach after 5...Bb4. The inclusion of the moves ...Nbd7 and 0-0 clearly favors White, since ...Ne4 is no longer a palatable option.

White's advantage is indisputable. After buttressing our bishop with h2-h4 and castling short, we will turn our attention toward the center, expanding with e3-e4 and solidifying our center with R(a)d1.

rnbqk2r/pp3ppp/2pBpn2/3p4/1b1P4/2NBPN2/P.comment: Now, it is crucial to refrain from 11.Nb5, which enables Black to seize the initiative with a check on a5 followed by ...Ne4. Instead, we help ourselves to another pawn!

rnbqk2r/pp3ppp/2pbpn2/3p4/3P4/2NBPN2/PPP.comment: We can follow up with Rb1-b7 or Qd4. Black is in serious trouble.

Black has no compensation for the pawn. We will follow up by castling kingside; there is nothing to fear along the h-file, since the h2-pawn is very safely protected by the knight. Black will have a hard time finding shelter for their king. As a case in point, 15...Qc4 is met with the powerful 16.Ne5, angling for c6.

rnbqk2r/pp3ppp/2pbp3/3p4/3PnB2/2NBPN2/PP.comment: We do not back down! It transpires that accepting the pawn sacrifice is unwise, owing to Black's lack of queenside development and the vulnerability of whichever minor piece lands on c3.

rnbqk2r/pp3ppp/2p1p3/8/1b1PpB2/2N1P3/PPP.comment: Yet again, the knight sally to b5 is very effective.

rnbqk2r/pp3ppp/2p1p3/bN6/3PpB2/4P3/PPPN1.comment: This is a lot better than 10.c4, which would justify the placement of Black's bishop on a5. Now, the bishop is taken out of the game and we follow up with a furious queenside pawn storm.

rnbq1rk1/pp3ppp/1bp1p3/1N6/1P1PpB2/2P1P3.comment: Black is under massive pressure due to the threat of c5 as well as Nc3, when the e4-pawn, in the immortal words of GM Robert Hess, will not be long for this board. Note that ...Nf6 can be savagely met with Bg5.

rnbq1rk1/pp3ppp/2p1pn2/3p4/1b1P1B2/2NBPN.comment: Standard Sam! We prepare the typical plan of queenside expansion with b3 and c4, and make the bishop on b4 look rather dumb.

rnbq1rk1/pp3ppp/2p1pn2/b2p4/3PNB2/3BPN2/.comment: Let the queenside pawn storm begin!

rnbq1rk1/pp3ppp/2p1pn2/b2p4/1P1PNB2/3BPN.comment: Eliminating the knight grants our b5-knight a nice retreating square on c3.

rnbq1rk1/1p3ppp/1bp1pn2/p2p4/PP1P1B2/2NB.comment: We have built up a massive clamp on the queenside, and things will go from bad to worse once we stick the knight on c5.

rnbq1rk1/p4ppp/1pp1pn2/3p4/1b1P1B2/2NBPN.comment: The power of doubled pawns on full display. The first c4 break served to soften up Black's queenside, and the second instantiation of this pawn advance will cause even more problems.
Transitioning to tactics! It transpires that the rook runs out of squares!

rn1q1rk1/p4ppp/bpp1pn2/3p4/1b1P1B2/2NBPN.comment: The rook has breathed its last breath.

rnbq1rk1/pp2bppp/2p1p3/3p4/3PnB2/2PBPN2/.comment: It is always worth including this move to take the sting out of ...g5, which is now duly met with Bh2. We are ready to push c4, and we can follow up by smoking the knight out of e4 with Nd2.

rnbqk2r/pp3ppp/3bpn2/2pp4/3P1B2/2NBPN2/P.comment: Keeping the tension. Of course, the impulsive 8.Nb5 would have run into 8...Qa5+, sending the knight right back to c3. Now, it appears that Black can cripple our pawn structure by capturing on d4, since Nxd4 runs into a fork. It turns out that Black is in for quite a surprise!

The most sensible option, preparing to castle kingside. Still, by resolving the central tension, we will attain a stable and long-lasting edge. This prevents Nb5, but costs Black another tempo. We pile up on the queenside without any further delay.

rnbqk2r/pp2bppp/4pn2/2pp4/3P1B2/2NBPN2/P.comment: Tabasco! This knight sally is particularly problematic in ...Nbd7 lines. With our king safely tucked away on the kingside, Black doesn't even have the option of hurrying the bishop around to c7. Before invading down the c-file, it makes sense to snap off a pawn and return to b5. Now, we get down to business. The devastating threat of Nc7+ is unstoppable.

This appears to call White's previous move into question: why provoke a move that grabs space and builds a rather imposing wall of pawns? In reality, the dutiful student of this course will know that ...b7-b5 is almost always a dreadfully weakening move, leaving behind massive holes on the light squares (particularly c6) and handing White the keys to a ravaging queenside initiative.

rnbqk2r/p3bppp/4pn2/1ppp4/3P1B2/2NBPN2/P.comment: It may appear that Black is out of the woods after recapturing on c5, but his troubles are only beginning. Note that the rook on c8 lacks a defender - this tactical deficiency is about to become very important, regardless of which piece Black decides to recapture with. Cold-blooded and ridiculously powerful. As in the 10...Qb6 line, Black suffers primarily because the rook on c8 is not sufficiently defended, so the tension down the c-file is always going to favor White. We now combine the threat of b2-b4 with sharp positional play, maneuvering our knight to the optimal d4-square.

rnbqk2r/p3bppp/4pn2/1pPp4/5B2/2NBPN2/PPP.comment: Sending the bishop back, and paving the way for a straightforward and devastating tactical blow. This is a lot better than 16.Nxf7+, which only wins a pawn.

Not fearing ghosts on the c-file: there is absolutely no risk of a discovered attack, since any move by the Black knight can be shut down with Nc6, followed by Nxe7+ and Qxe7 (not to mention that our queen can also simply retreat).

rnbqk2r/p4ppp/4pn2/1pbp4/5B2/2NBPN2/PPP2.comment: Even better than Nxf6+. The threat of Rc8, which will pick off Black's rook, forces instant resignation. A thematic tactical blow, dealing Black the ultimate punishment for failing to castle in timely fashion. We must remain careful until the end: the sloppy 15.Rxc1 would drop a piece after ...Nxd5, when the check on c8 is parried by ...Bd8 (in contrast to 13...Bb4). Black is a pawn down, and cannot cover both infiltration squares (c7 and c8) at the same time.
We can basically premove Rc7, after which Black will not be able to move a single muscle. Of course, 16...Bxb4 is impossible on account of 17.Rc8+.

rnbqk2r/p4ppp/4pn2/1pbpN3/5B2/2NBP3/PPP2.comment: The rightful culmination of our lightning queenside attack. White wins the bishop.

rnbq1rk1/pp2bppp/4pn2/2Pp4/5B2/2NBPN2/PP.comment: We saw a similar position to this one (with the pawns on d4 and b2) in the 9...Bxc5 10.d4 Bb6 line - this cosmetic difference does not change all that much. Black is still in big trouble due to the threat of Nd6 and the pressure down the c-file.

rnbqk2r/pp3ppp/2p1pn2/bN1p4/3P1B2/3BPN2/.comment: 10.Rc1 is also good, but this is even better, since it essentially leads to a forced queen trade.

rnbq1rk1/pp3ppp/2pbpn2/3p4/3P1B2/2NBPN2/.comment: Classic stuff, controlling the center. Black has a very hard time finding useful moves, because we have complete control over the center as well as more active pieces.

Trading on our own terms! This clever positional move has a lot more meat on the bone than the meek 8.Bg3. White prepares c2-c4, which underscores the awkwardness of the knight on c6. White's extra tempo means that playing copycat with 8...Ne7 will not end well.

rnbqnrk1/pp3ppp/3bp3/2NpP3/3P1B2/3B1N2/P.comment: The doubled d-pawns serve us well, since we can reinforce the center on demand with d4.

rnb1k2r/pp3ppp/1qpbpn2/3p4/3P1B2/2NBPN2/.comment: White has a small but very stable advantage in the endgame.

rnbqk2r/pp3ppp/2pbp3/3p4/3PnB2/2NBPN2/PP.comment: There is no big hurry to play Qb3; it makes sense to shuttle our king to safety first. Even with the bishop on b4 defended, this move is quite powerful.
Capturing with the bishop leads to much the same consequences as 7...Nxc3, further exacerbated by the fact that Black will have insufficient control over key dark squares in the center.

rnbq1rk1/pp3ppp/2pbp3/3p4/3PnB2/2NBPN2/P.comment: A thematic follow-up, forcibly removing the knights and leaving both of Black's minor pieces hanging. Much better than the greedy 13.Qxb7. The knight on h5 is entirely out of commission, and Black has no good answer to the twin threats of Qxb7 and Qd1,which induces a near-fatal weakening of the dark squares around Black's king.
This does not substantively change the nature of the position, since Black is forced to capture on c3 anyway.
Simple and strong: we threaten to accentuate the queenside pressure with a5, thereby creating even more holes on the queenside.

rnbq1rk1/pp3ppp/2pbp3/3pN3/3PnB2/2NBP3/P.comment: Note that the tempting 14.g4 fails tactically to 14...h6 15.Bh4 g5, when Black retains material equality.

rnbqk2r/pp3ppp/2pbp3/3p4/3P1B2/2nBPN2/PP.comment: This is the ideal square for the queen, where it attacks b7 and prevents castling. Black has no choice but to spend a tempo defending b7, enabling us to bring our knight into the fold. It has already become apparent that the pawn sacrifice is more than justified. Black is saddled with the twin threats of Rxb7 and Bxf5 followed by Qd3, recovering the pawn in both cases. More importantly, the incredible vulnerable placement of Black's bishop grants White a virtually decisive initiative.

rnbqk2r/pp3ppp/2pbp3/3p4/3P1B2/2PBPN2/P1.comment: Taking the b7-pawn with the queen is quite a bit more problematic for Black than 11.Rxb7, which would enable Black to ferry their king to safety.

rnbqk2r/p4ppp/1ppbp3/3p4/3P1B2/2PBPN2/P1.comment: It is crucial to induce ...b6, which further weakens the c6-square and makes it even harder for Black to properly develop his knight.

We now threaten the deadly Bb5+, forcing Black to enter full retreat mode. The most resilient defensive move, preparing to castle kingside by slicing off our control over the f8-square. In order to keep the initiative aflame, we must immediately find greener pastures for the lady.
Opening up the c-file is almost always a good idea in the Jobava London, and this position is no exception.

Just when it seems like Black has gotten his king to relative safety, we gang up on the monarch with our queen and minor pieces. The following sequence - 15 moves long - is hardly forced, but it clearly illuminates the extent of White's dominance, and culminates with one of the most beautiful mating combinations that we have ever come across!

rnbqk2r/p4ppp/1p1bp3/2Pp4/5B2/2PBPN2/P1P.comment: An important tactical detail. White wins a piece.

rnbqk2r/p4ppp/1ppbp3/3pN3/3P1B2/2PBP3/P1.comment: Black's desire to prepare castling is understandable, but the queen saunters on over to the adjacent square, and Black's problems are multiplied hundredfold!

r1bqk2r/p2n1ppp/1ppbp3/3pN3/3P1B2/2PBP3/.comment: A picturesque final position! Black drops the queen due to the threat of checkmate on e7.

rnbqk2r/p4ppp/1p1bp3/2ppN3/3P1B2/2PBP3/P.comment: Black is tied hand and foot!

rnbq1k1r/p4ppp/1ppbp3/3pN3/3P1B2/2PBP3/P.comment: A magnificent prophylactic move, taking away the c8-square from Black's queen (once again, Black pays a very steep price for weakening the light squares on the queenside). The point of this becomes clear if Black plays 13...f6: The queen is trapped!
It is obviously not enough to force Black's king onto a compromised square. We now turn our attention back to the queenside, prying open the c-file and adding fuel to the fire.

rnbq1k1r/p4ppp/1ppbp3/3pN3/2PP1B2/3BP3/P.comment: The attempt to generate kingside counterplay (which resembles our own g4-h4 idea) falls short on account of a lovely counterblow.

rnbq1k1r/p4ppp/1ppbp3/4N3/2pP1B2/3BP3/P1.comment: Counter-attacking the knight and summarily halting Black's kingside pawn play. Needless to say, we are more than willing to part ways with the g4-pawn in order to win an additional tempo. An important insertion, using the weakness of the e6-pawn to open up the c-file. The bishop is poisoned, since Black will get massacred on the e6-square and in the center.

rnbq1k1r/p4ppp/1ppbp3/4N3/2pP1BP1/3BP3/P.comment: We are happy to trade queens, but only on our terms! Taking on d7 enables Black to develop the knight and open up escape squares for the a8-rook.

rnb2k1r/p2q1ppp/1ppbp3/4N3/2pP1BP1/3BP3/.comment: White's central pawn phalanx is totally decisive. We will follow up by infiltrating down the c-file with Rac1, doubling rooks if necessary. It is instructive to observe how Black's knights are utterly dominated by our pawns - in particular, the d4 and g4-pawns take away the crucial e5 and f5 squares, condeming the horsies to a passive existence.

rnbqk2r/p4ppp/1ppbp3/8/2pP1B2/3BPN2/P1P2.comment: An important nuance, forcing the bishop away from its protection of the c3-pawn. In order to keep the bishop on a5, Black must seriously weaken seventh rank. Only now, after Black has opened up a direct line of fire to the knight, do we infiltrate with the rook! Black is under assault from all sides.

rnbqk2r/p4ppp/1ppbp3/8/2pP1B2/2PBPN2/P4P.comment: The two pieces are incomparably more powerful than the rook, and the c3-pawn is condemned. Victory is a matter of rather straightforward technique.

rnbqk2r/p4p1p/1ppbp1p1/3p2N1/3P1B2/2PBP3.comment: A thematic attacking idea, shattering Black's kingside.

rnbqk2r/p4p1p/1ppbp1p1/3p2N1/3P1BP1/2PBP.comment: Transforming our advantage. With the g-file wide open, White's attack will not stop with the queens off the board; the rooks are more than happy to pick up the slack!

rnb1k2r/p2q1p1p/1ppbp1p1/3p2N1/3P1BP1/2P.comment: Much stronger than the penny-pinching 18.Bxc7. We have far greater fish to fry! Setting up the threat of Ne6+, and driving Black's king further into the abyss. Clearing g5 for a more deserving piece. Black's king has been rudely shuttled all the way from the kingside to the queenside. Now, 25.Rxd5 obviously keeps a decisive advantage, but we came across a far more beautiful crusher that we cannot help but include: Simply divine! The rook is sacrificed in order to establish control of the b-file. Note that the rook on b1, which thus far has patiently awaited its turn, finally has its moment in the sun! Together with the knight and bishop, it is the architect of the mating construction. A crucial detail!

r1bqk2r/pp3ppp/n1pbpn2/1N1p4/3P1B2/2P1PN.comment: An important and profound positional idea (typical idea #6). Trading away our pawn on d4 seems anti-positional at first blush, but concrete considerations always transcend general reasoning! The point of this move is, of course, to clear the d4-square for our knight. Once it moves back to d4, Black will suddenly be confronted with a host of incredibly nasty positional threats, and his poor coordination will not permit him to address all of them at once. This is obviously forced, since the knight must remain on a6 to guard c7. The point! White has no less than three serious positional threats: 1) Nxf5, gaining the bishop pair (although temporarily) and leaving the d-pawn isolated and weak; 2) Bxa6, crippling the queenside pawn structure; 3) Qa4+, forcing the king to f8. This is unquestionably the lesser evil, but it leaves Black with a pawn structure that is worse than George Washington's teeth!

r1bqk2r/pp1nbppp/n1p1p3/1N1p4/Q2P1B2/2P1.comment: White has a raging initiative, and Black has no way to relieve the pressure whatsoever. The knight from e5 cannot be kicked out (...f6 runs into Nxe6 and ...Bd6 drops a minor piece to Nxg6), and we can add even more heat with h2-h4 and/or c2-c4. In the worst case scenario, White can always snatch the pawn on a6 and castle kingside, when Black will have no compensation whatsoever. But there will likely be no need to cash in your chips in this way.

rnbqk2r/pp3ppp/2pbpn2/3pN3/3P1B2/2N1P3/P.comment: This is probably Black's best move from an objective standpoint, but it leads to a familiar type of position in which White is definitely having all the fun. Most knowledgeable players make this move automatically. By opening up an escape square on h7, Black removes the danger from the advance of the g-pawn. As in the case of 6...Nbd7, this is a sign that we should switch our approach to methodical positional play. As usual, ignoring the brewing storm on the kingside leads to trouble.
A masochistic move! Now, White's kingside pawn storm will be even more devastating.

rnbqk2r/pp3pp1/2pbpn1p/3pN3/3P1B2/2N1P3/.comment: As always, we recapture with the pawn to increase our central control, open the c-file, and carve out a path to b3 for our queen. This position is quite similar to the one that arises after 5...Bd6 6.Ne5 h6 7.Bd3 Bxd3 8.cxd3; the addition of the move ...h6 does not substantively alter the nature of the ensuing struggle. If anything, ...Bd6 is a significantly more useful move, so we would argue that this is a somewhat improved version of an already-pleasant position. As usual, we recapture with the pawn, leading to the classical central pawn formation. Our powerful knight on e5, coupled with our total control over key central squares, promises White a very pleasant game.

r1bqk2r/pp1n1pp1/2pbpn1p/3pN3/3P1B2/2NBP.comment: This is the only way for Black to justify delaying the development of their DSB; remember that this move is not possible when the bishop is on d6 due to dxe5, winning a piece. Now, recapturing with the pawn makes little positional sense.

r1bqk2r/pp3pp1/2pbpn1p/3pn3/3P1B2/2NBP3/.comment: Black has gotten rid of the knight, but the other pieces are more than happy to pick up the slack. Given the relatively docile nature of the position, we have the luxury to spend a tempo creating luft for our king and preventing a knight sortie on g4, which will become important once our queen leaves its initial square.

r1bq1rk1/pp3pp1/2pbpn1p/3pB3/3P4/2NBP3/P.comment: Black has no good answer to the threat of f4-f5, with tremendous play on the kingside. As usual, the impulsive 12...b5 would be met with 13.Ne2 followed by Rac1, accentuating the weakness of the c6-square.
There is no question that Black can keep the balance with computer-like precision, but our vast experience in such positions convinces us that Black has a very unenviable task ahead of him.

r1bq1rk1/pp1n1pp1/2pbp2p/3pB3/3P4/2NBP3/.comment: Preparing to double rooks and assert our dominance on the queenside.

r1bq1rk1/pp1n1pp1/2pBp2p/3p4/3P4/2NBP3/P.comment: Obviously, the queen trade would play right into Black's hands. Our next step is to involve the pawns with b2-b4, increasing our control over key squares on the queenside. Furthermore, Black has quite a few tactical minefields to sidestep; the most natural move walks right into a vicious tactical shot.

r1b2rk1/pp1n1pp1/1qpBp2p/3p4/3P4/2NBP3/P.comment: Bang! This is why we went through the trouble of doubling rooks! Capturing the queen is a lot less clear after ...Rxc1+. Black is down a pawn, and his kingside is in shambles. We will follow up with Qc7, when our opponent's position will collapse like a house of cards.

r1bqk2r/pp1n1ppp/2pbpn2/3pN3/3P1B2/2N1P3.comment: See 4...c6 5.Nf3 e6 6.Ne5 Nbd7 7.g4. At this point in your Jobava journey, this move should be second nature (with the exception of those who have decided to start with this line). Black is already in deep yogurt.

r1bqk2r/pp1n1ppp/2pbpn2/3pN3/3P1BP1/2N1P.comment: As usual, this is clearly superior to 7...Bg6, although it occurs quite a bit more rarely in online play.

r1bqk2r/pp3ppp/2pbpn2/3pn3/3P1BP1/2N1P3/.comment: A situation that you should be intimately familiar with by now! To prevent the loss of a minor piece, Black has to accept a decisive weakening of his kingside.

r1bqk2r/pp3pp1/2pbp3/4n1Pp/3PpB1P/4P3/PP.comment: Bortnyk-Ajay, Chess.com (blitz) 2021. This position hardly needs elaboration!

rnbqk2r/pp3ppp/2p1pn2/3pb3/3P1B2/2N1P3/P.comment: An important position that has occurred frequently in the blitz practice of the authors of this course. It is vital to avoid the tempting 9.Rg1, due to 9...g5. We have both lost countless games in precisely this fashion, especially to Minh Le and Firouzja. Instead, we must target the knight on g4 straightaway. Chasing the knight away. We saw a very similar idea (and position) in the 5...Bd6 6.Ne5 0-0 line; here, Black's king is still in the center, but that does not change any of White's ideas. As always, ...Qh4+ is coolly rebuffed by Bg3. Incredibly tempting, but wrong!

rnbqk2r/pp3pp1/2p1pn2/3pb2p/3P1B1P/2N1P3.comment: As is the custom, we immediately drag Black's king into the open. There is no good answer to the devastating threat of Qg6+, since 12...Ng4 runs into 13.Bg5 followed by either f2-f3 or Bh3.

rnbqk2r/pp3ppp/2p1pn2/3pP3/5B2/2N1P3/PPP.comment: A very difficult move to find, since this involves a minor piece sacrifice (note that this is Black's best move in the 5...Bd6 6.Ne5 0-0 version as well). The alternative, however, leads to a position that can only be described as hellish.

rnbqk2r/pp3p1p/2p1pn2/3pP1p1/5B2/2N1P3/P.comment: White loses the e5-pawn and the game.
In contrast to the ...0-0 line, here this move is incredibly effective, since the capture on e4 enables us to favorably trade queens and draw Black's king onto a vulnerable square.
Delaying the capture of the bishop to take away the h4-square from Black's queen. The immediate 11.gxf5 leads to a total mess after 11...Qh4+.

rnbqk2r/pp3p1p/2p1pn2/4P1p1/4pB2/2N5/PPP.comment: Ignoring the forbidden fruit! Capturing on h3 would have led nowhere good after ...Qh4+. Surgical chess. With this intermediate move, we put a permanent stop to ...Qh4-related shenanigans and exert our complete dominance over the kingside.
Black is in deep trouble, since 12...exd5 loses immediately to 13.Bg5 Qd7 14.Bh3, with total devastation to follow.

rnb1k2r/pp1q1p1p/2p1pn2/4P1p1/4pB2/8/PPP.comment: Black has no good way to defend against the twin threats of Nxg7+ and Bxh6 followed by Nf6.

rnbk3r/pp3p1p/2p1pn2/4P1p1/4pB2/2N5/PPP2.comment: The customary move, threatening h4-h5 and forcing Black's bishop to leave the g-file. In turn, this will enable us to gang up on the tender g7-pawn. Obviously, ...Rg8 would have dropped the knight on h6. Black's objectively best option was to simply abandon the g7 pawn, but we trust that you can handle the resulting position on your own! Quiet and deadly. There is no defense to h5, which will pick up the bishop.

rnbqk2r/pp3p1p/2p1pn2/4P1p1/3p1B1P/2N1P3.comment: Hitting where it hurts! Taking on f5 results in immediate disaster after Nxd5, so Black has no choice but to allow the partial dissolution of his center and the creation of a powerful protected passer on the kingside. The monster pawn on g5 affords us the clearly better game. Note that the pawn on e5, though isolated, is quite easy to defend. More precisely, Black does not have the time to attack it, since we threaten Bxf5 and the trade on d3 enables us to stick our queen on g6. Even if it were to be captured, the open e-file would probably favor us anyway. Needless to say, this is vastly superior to the listless 13.Ne2. The resulting endgame is utterly miserable for Black.

rnbk3r/pp3p1p/2p1pn2/4P1pP/5B2/2p1P3/PPP.comment: Black is under fire from all sides, e.g.

rnbq1rk1/pp3ppp/2pBpn2/3p4/3P4/2NBPN2/PP.comment: Mr. Copycat is in for a rather nasty surprise in this position:
Fighting fire with fire! This forces Black to give up the e-pawn on our terms.

rnbq1rk1/pp3ppp/3Bpn2/2pp4/3P4/2NBPN2/PP.comment: Stunning and immediately decisive. Black's queenside collapses faster than the Stock Market in 1929.

rnbq1rk1/pp3ppp/B2Bpn2/2pp4/3P4/2N1PN2/P.comment: This is the only way to avoid losing a minor piece, though it leads to a dead lost endgame nonetheless.

rnbq1rk1/pp3ppp/2pB1n2/3pp3/3P4/2NBPN2/P.comment: Black loses the e-pawn, and with it the game. We have a great position, with prospects on both sides of the board. The stock plan in such positions is Kh1 followed by Rg1, but we shouldn't forget about Russian schoolboy-type moves such as Rad1 and (eventually) e3-e4.

r1bqk2r/pp1n1pp1/2pbpn2/3pN2p/3P1BP1/2N1.comment: Black cannot keep e6 protected and answer the threat of a discovered check at the same time.

r1bqk2r/pp3ppp/2pbp3/3pP3/4nBP1/2N1P3/PP.comment: Black's bishop has run out of squares! An empty check.
Despite the chaotic appearance of the position, Black is in big trouble. Both of his bishops are vulnerable, and f2-f3 is threatened.

r1bqk2r/pp3ppp/2pbp3/3pP3/4nBP1/2N1PP2/P.comment: Black has run out of ways to stave off the inevitable. He will have some compensation for the pawn due to the somewhat flimsy placement of our monarch, but a few careful consolidating moves, such as Bg2 and Rf1, should render this compensation meaningless.

rnbqk2r/pp3ppp/2pbp3/3p3n/3P1B2/2NBPN2/P.comment: We are happy to give up the bishop, but only on our terms!

rnbqk2r/pp3ppp/2pbp3/3pB2n/3P4/2NBPN2/PP.comment: This horrific move loses on the spot.

r1bqk2r/pp1n1ppp/2pbp3/3pB2n/3P4/2NBPN2/.comment: No more analysis is required! Black will drop h5 with check, with further material losses to follow.

r1bqk2r/pp3ppp/2pbp3/1N1pn2n/3P4/3BPN2/P.comment: The threat of g2-g4 forces Black to introduce serious kingside weaknesses with 10...g6. We can follow up by castling and reinforcing our central control with d3-d4. Once the knight drops back to c3, it can prepare further central expansion with e3-e4.

rnbqk2r/p4ppp/1ppBpn2/3p4/3P4/2NBPN2/PPP.comment: Pow! Indirectly defending the knight and hitting d6, which Black can only defend with his king.

rnbqk2r/5ppp/pppBpn2/3p4/3P4/2NBPN2/PPP2.comment: Moving to the open file and shutting down the b8-knight's development prospects. Black is in terrible shape.

rnbqk2r/pp3ppp/2pbpn2/3p4/3PNB2/4PN2/PPP.comment: Interestingly, we have transposed to a known theoretical position that occurs in the Trompowsky Opening (1.d4 Nf6 2.Bg5). There is only one difference: here, it is White to move! We put our extra tempo to immediate use, knocking the bishop off of e4.

rnbqk2r/pp3ppp/2pbp3/3p4/3PnB2/4P3/PPPN1.comment: A classic idea in the Semi-Slav and many other openings. Black has no choice but to acquiesce to the queen trade, opening up the a-file and handing us a queenside attack on a golden platter.

rnbqk2r/pp3pp1/2pbp2p/3p4/3PnB2/4P3/PPPN.comment: We are playing squarely for two results. We will follow up either with b4-b5, shattering Black's pawn chain and opening up avenues of infiltration, or with Nb3-a5, when Black will have a very hard time defending the b7-pawn, since we (permanently) control the b8-square.

rnbqk2r/pp3pp1/2pbpn1p/3pN3/3P1BP1/2N1P3.comment: This is unquestionably the lesser evil, but Black's position will remain utterly miserable.

rnbqk2r/pp3pp1/2p1pn1p/3pb3/3P1BPP/2N1P3.comment: The normal response is to capture the bishop on g6, crippling Black's pawn structure. However, since Black has already castled, it is worth starting with gxh5, in order to pop open the g-file and facilitate the ensuing attack.
This is far more effective than the stereotypical Nxg6.

rnbqk2r/pp3pp1/2p1p3/3pb2n/3P1B1P/2N1P3/.comment: Black is utterly screwed on the kingside: we will castle queenside, stick a rook on g1, and rush the h-pawn up the board. The smoke has cleared, and the next step is to target Black's incredibly weak kingside pawns.

rnb1k2r/pp3pp1/2p1pq2/3pb2n/3P1BQP/2N1P3.comment: Cold-blooded and powerful, taking the sting out of ...Qxf2 (which will now be met by Qxe6+). Turning up the pressure dial on the e6-pawn. A vital positional resource, ending Black's counterplay along the f-file.
Black's defenses are stretched to the limit, and a gorgeous maneuver seals the deal.

rnbqk2r/pp3pp1/2p1p3/3pb2n/3P1BQP/2N1P3/.comment: The pressure on g6, coupled with the deadly threat of Qxh5+, is decisive.

rnbqk2r/pp3p2/2p1pn1p/3pb1p1/3P1BPP/2N1P.comment: Attacking g6 and paving the way for a timely queenside castle. Further analysis is hardly needed! Black's position is in shambles. We can follow up by castling queenside, or by taking direct action on the kingside with gxh6, Bxh5, and Qh7+. In either case, Black's position is virtually resignable.

rnbqk2r/pp3pp1/2p1p2p/3pP3/5Bn1/2N1P3/PP.comment: Not fearing the check on h4, which is parried with Bg3. Black's knight is sent into exile on h6, when our kingside attack, coupled with our superior piece placement and the total safety of our own king (after we castle), ensures overwhelming compensation for the pawn.

rnbqk2r/pp3pp1/2p1p2p/3pP3/5Bn1/2N1PP2/P.comment: An ingenious defensive move, attempting to pry the bishop away from its protection of the e3-pawn.
Setting up the devastating threat of e3-e4.

rnbqk2r/pp3p2/2p1p2p/3pP1p1/5BP1/2N1P3/P.comment: This check appears intimidating, but White's king calmly sidesteps the trouble by remaining in the center.

rnbqk2r/pp3p2/2p1p2p/3pP3/6P1/2N1p3/PPP1.comment: Protecting the f2-square. We are obviously in no rush to capture the e3 pawn. An important nuance: the immediate 14.Kxe3 runs into ...d4+, so we have to wait for Black's queen to leave the fourth rank to capture the pawn.

To our knowledge, this is the only position in the entire course in which White's king sits on d4 - and the queens are still on the board! Upon closer inspection, it becomes clear that the king is unassailable: it will quickly evacuate back to e3, and Black's initiative fizzles out within a few moves. Phew! Our king has finally reached a safe square, where it is surrounded by friendly forces. Black has nothing better than to acquiesce to the queen trade, when victory will be a matter of straightforward technique.

rnbqk2r/pp3pp1/2p1p2p/3pP3/5B2/2N1nP2/PP.comment: Black threatens ...d4. A superb defensive move that nips Black's initiative in the bud. We prepare to meet ...d4 with Rd1, when Black's play in the center will be instantly disarmed.

rnbqk2r/pp3pp1/2p1p2p/4P3/3p4/2N1BP2/PPP.comment: It may seem more intuitive to castle queenside, but 12.0-0-0 would be a grave error on account of 12...Qh4, when White has no way to save both minor pieces. The issue is that 13.Bf2 runs into Qf4+. In this version, after 12...Qh4+ 13.Bf2 Black's queen is unable to move away with check. One of the few situations in which remaining in the center is more desirable!
Black's compensation for the piece is virtually nonexistant.

rnbqk2r/pp4p1/2p1pp1p/3pP3/5Bn1/2N1PP2/P.comment: Meeting fire with fire! Opening up the center will enable us to more effectively take advantage of Black's incredibly weak pawns.

rnbqk2r/pp4p1/2p1pp1p/4P3/4pBn1/2N2P2/PP.comment: Just because the queens are off the board doesn't mean that White's attack is over! Au contraire, we are just getting started!

rnbqk2r/pp6/2p1pp1p/3pP3/6n1/2N1PP2/PPP4.comment: Black's center has been fully shattered, and we now turn our attention to the kingside. Among other things, White threatens h4-h5 and Qxh6, as well as the prosaic Nb6.

rnbq1rk1/1p3pp1/p1pbpn1p/3pN3/3P1B2/2NBP.comment: Now that our queen has left d1, it is important to take the sting out of the move ...Nh5, which can now be met by the prosaic Bh2. In fact, our next step is to drop the bishop down to h2 (or g3) on our volition, in order to reinforce the knight with f2-f4. The computer assigns White a very modest plus, but our experience leads us to believe that Black's cramped position and lack of a clear plan affords White excellent prospects in the middlegame. A thematic blunder, leaving the bishop on d6 undefended. Bringing our rook into position.
This is somewhat better than 9...c6, but succumbs to a similar tactic: Amazingly, this lovely tactical shot is even more effective than 10.Nxf7.

rnbq1rk1/5pp1/p1pbpn1p/3p4/3P1B2/2NBP3/P.comment: Amazingly, this position has occurred once over the board - in a game played by none other than Shakhriyar Mamedyarov, in the year 2000! Black suffers decisive material losses.

rnb2rk1/1p2qpp1/p1pbpn1p/3pN3/3P1B2/2NBP.comment: Black's last move was a terrible positional mistake, and we exploit it immediately by reinforcing our control over the newly-weakened c6-square. Before planting our knight on c6, it is worth piling up on the c-file with Qc2.

A typical positional move, aiming to situate the knight on c5 when the moment is right. Notice, once again, the indispensable role played by White's central pawn mass: all of the crucial squares in the center, particularly e5 and e4, are under White's control. It is incredibly difficult for Black to find helpful improving moves. White's campaign is one of slow, but steady, queenside expansion. The queen will make way for the other rook, and once we are doubled on the c-file, the queenside pressure will reach a peak. We continue to improve our position in countless ways. The knight will hop into c5, and Black will ultimately be forced into a nasty positional concession.

r1bqk2r/pp1n1pp1/2pbpn1p/3pN3/3P1B2/2NBP.comment: In contrast to the position that arises after 6...Nbd7, the presence of the pawn on h6 affords us an exciting additional possibility.

r1bq1rk1/pp1n1pp1/2pbpn1p/3pN3/3P1B2/2NB.comment: The experienced Jobava player will not bat an eye at this move, which sets up the potentially devastating advance of the g-pawn to g5. Black is best advised to immediately remove the knight from the pawn's line of fire.

r1bqnrk1/pp1n1pp1/2pbp2p/3pN3/3P1B1P/2NB.comment: The threat of g4-g5 is instantly crushing, e.g.

An important positional detail, buttressing the bishop on f4 and taking the venom out of ...f7-f6. Black's incredibly passive situation means that we are in absolutely no hurry to make any committal moves. Defending the b4-square is always a good idea.

r1bqnrk1/pp1n1pp1/3bp2p/2ppN3/3P1BPP/2NB.comment: Obviously, opening up the h-file with ...hxg5 merely hastens Black's defeat!

r1bqnrk1/pp1n1p2/3bp1pp/2ppN1P1/3P1B1P/2.comment: White has opened up a raging attack on Black's king. We threaten both the prosaic h4-h5 and the lovely Nxg6, and Black's impotent army is powerless to stop the avalanche.

r1bqn1k1/pp1n1rp1/2pbppNp/3p4/3P1B1P/3BP.comment: Jobava London-3...Bf5  2023 We will follow up by gradually intensifying the kingside pressure with f3 and g4, while the king can be tucked away to safety on d2. White's robust central pawn phalanx means that our king will almost always remain completely safe in the center.

r3nrk1/pp2bppp/4p3/1q1pP3/5B1P/3P1N2/PP1.comment: This is the most concrete and combative response to the Jobava London. Black immediately tries to underscore the awkwardness of the knight on c3. In contrast to the (regular) London System, we do not have the possibility of supporting the pawn with c2-c3. In the dark ages, White automatically responded with 4.e3, and after 4...cxd4 5.exd4, we reach a position that resembles an inferior version of an exchange Caro-Kann. However, the presence of the knight on c3 affords us another exciting possibility that has completely revitalized this variation! This scintillating counterstrike, which gained notoriety a few short years ago, is incomparably more exciting and challenging than the meek 4.e3. Our idea is straightforward: we aim to exploit our lead in development by blasting open the center. In a way, this move can be thought of as a massively improved Albin Countergambit (1.d4 d5 2.c4 e5). Black is now at a crossroads: three different captures are possible, and all of them must be considered carefully. The resulting positions are complex and full of exciting tactical possibilities. By far the most popular recapture at the highest levels. Black captures the pawn and forces a knight trade, opening up an annoying queen check on a5 and eliminating the future possibility of Nc3-b5. Incidentally, it is the least popular of the three captures online, but due to its objective potency, we have decided to promote it as the main line. Along with 4...cxd4, this is the most popular capture online (with approximately 5,000+ games on Lichess at the time of analysis). We recapture the pawn on c5, posing Black with an unenviable dilemma. Trading queens hands over control of the d-file, while refraining from the trade with 5...Qa5 gives White a dangerous middlegame initiative. It is only move 5, yet we are already asking Black a serious question!

r3nrk1/pp2bppp/4p3/1q2P3/3p1B1P/3P1N2/PP.comment: This is by far the most popular move online (with 2,000 or so games), but it gives us full control over the d-file and leads to a rather dubious endgame. It is important to realize that the trade of queens hardly diminishes White's attacking potential; our initiative does not vanish simply because the ladies are off the board! A few general pointers to help you understand this position better: 1) The pawn on e4 can be either attacked with Nge2-g3, or traded off directly with f2-f3. Both options are on the table depending on Black's setup. 2) After the recapture, White has the immediate threat of situating a knight on b5, forcing Black to contort themselves with the immensely awkward ...Na6. 3) The pawn on c5 is a strength rather than a weakness: it significantly restricts the mobility of Black's dark-squared bishop, and it can be easily supported both with pawns (b4) and with pieces (Be3). The most reasonable move, reinforcing the threat of ...c5. Once again, we do not fear this move, but rather encourage it! Things go from bad to worse, since Black's knight has nowhere good to go! Increasing the blockade on the c5-square. An important resource, covering the check with the knight. Note that 10...e5 is ineffective, since the square is defended twice and only attacked once. In contrast to the endgame arising after 4...dxe5 5.dxc5 Qxd1+ 6.Rxd1, this is an improved version for Black since Nb5 is no longer a threat. However, Black still faces a host of positional problems: the c5-pawn still majorly restricts Black's development and coordination, and White's control over the d-file gives us great play in the center. Objectively, the position is equal, but we have unearthed several ways to confront Black with serious practical problems. We will see this prophylactic move again in the main line (7...Nc6).
