This series of moves should be automatic by now! With Black's pawn not yet on e6, the power of the knight on e5 is increased even further. This move should be automatic as well! Initiating kingside pressure. It is rather painful to part ways with the bishop pair, but there was nothing we could have done: 9.Bg5 would be futile on account of 9...h6 followed by ...g5. Commencing the attack without delay. This is also good, and perhaps even more straightforward than 11.Ng3. A scary-looking tactic, but it is easy to parry. See 8...Bd6 9.g4. Here, the only difference is in the placement of the knight; we believe that it is even better on e2, since ...Bxf4 will always be met with Nxf4. An ingenious positional move, opening up the f-file. Our long-term pressure along the f-file will guarantee White a stable advantage. Also, do not forget about c2-c4, which would come at the least convenient moment for Black. This sacrifice deserves serious merit, although it leads to a rather chaotic tactical battle that requires intense study.  Black's king is driven out and massacred. Visually, Black's position appears more than tenable, but the incredibly weak pawn on g5 tells a different story. We will use that pawn in order to develop enduring pressure down the h-file. Black, on the other hand, has very little going on the other side of the board: our king is perfectly safe on c1. Using the g-pawn as a "hook" to open the h-file, a typical motif worth remembering!

The rook on c1 and pawn on a3 change nothing: this shot is as strong as ever.  Here, it is important not to capture on d5, as that enables Black to develop quickly and dangerously with 8...e6. Shattering Black's center and carving out a dominant outpost on e5. We see the exact same idea in the 3...c5 line.  Capitalizing on our development advantage and applying immediate pressure on the d5-pawn. Indirectly defending the d5-pawn. Securing the bishop pair and reopening the possibility of e3-e4. We now transition to a plan of kingside expansion, preparing to underscore the vulnerability of the f5-bishop with f2-f3 followed by g2-g4. Even without the pawn on d4, our knight is perfectly safe on e5, and the bishop that will take its place in the event of ...Nxe5 will pose the serious threat of Bxf6, crippling Black's kingside pawn structure. Preparing to reinforce the pawn with b4, and essentially forcing Black's hand. Preventing the further progress of Black's b-pawn, and setting up the main idea of the line. This is a rare, but extremely dangerous idea. We freeze Black's queenside play entirely, preventing ...c7-c5. Without this idea, Black is essentially stalemated. We, on the other, have clear ways to improve our position: the knight will be centralized on e5, the bishop developed to d3, and once Black castles kingside, our queen is immediately transported to h3, creating long-lasting and potentially fatal threats on the kingside. Do not be fooled by the engine's assessment: our practice and analysis reveals that Black's position is very hard to play due to the conspicuous absence of a clear active plan. An important inclusion. By preventing ...Bb4, we are making it difficult for Black to find active prospects for the dark-squared bishop. More importantly, we are preparing to take control of the queenside with a well-timed b2-b4, which will make it exceedingly difficult for Black to attain much-needed activity on the queenside.
Grabbing space and inducing even more kingside weaknesses.

An astute positional move, preparing to recapture on d4 with the bishop. It may seem more intuitive to recapture with the pawn, but that would grant Black active prospects for his dark-squared bishop, and subject us to long-term pressure down the d-file. On d4, the bishop lords over the entire position, preventing the active development of Black's DSB and keeping the d-file closed for business. Our next step is to complete our development and get our king to e3, when Black experiences long-term problems with the e4-pawn. The beginning of the end. Black loses a ton of material.

An annoying little move, aiming to fully destroy Black's kingside pawn structure with Bxf6. The bishop pair is meant to be given away! White has a stable plus in the endgame. We will plant the knight on h5, tying Black down to f6, and follow by preparing c2-c4 or even (after Bg2 and Rhf1) f4-f5, accentuating the weakness of the f6-pawn.

Black has a permanent weakness on h7. We will accumulate the pressure with Rdh1, when the pawn's days are likely numbered. Typically, Black does not have any difficulty winning back the pawn, but this position is a notable exception. If Black plays ...e7-e5 (after 5...Nc6), the d5-pawn becomes very soft, and we maintain our material advantage. If, on the other hand, Black goes after the c-pawn immediately with 5...e6, we cling to it with 6.Na4, forcing Black to give up the valuable dark-squared bishop in order to recover the pawn. In either case, White has a long-lasting advantage, but the lines in the 5...Nc6 line are very sharp and it is worth spending an hour or two to understand the zen of the position. We ain't gonna give that pawn up easy! It turns out that Black has no way to win back the pawn without yielding the bishop pair, which turns out to be incredibly valuable in this particular structure. This has been the choice of many strong GMs; in particular, Belarussian GM Sergei Zhigalko has played this line regularly against the authors of this course. Black aims to rapidly deploy the bishop to b7, making it virtually impossible for White to break in the center with e3-e4. We spent a long time on this move, and are proud to recommend a rare idea that confronts Black with serious practical problems.

It is essential to avoid this move, after which our queenside will collapse like a house of cards. In human terms, Black is already in massive trouble. Using tactics to halt the progress of Black's pawn. Of course, c3 is untouchable due to Rc1. Prying open the queenside, and creating a serious long-term weakness on a6. Note that in response to 13...bxa4, we first have to withdraw the dark-squared bishop to g3 in order to take the sting out of ...e5. Then, we will recapture on a4 and turn up the queenside pressure. A sensible way to recapture the c5-pawn, but it comes at the steep cost of Black's development.

3rnr2/1p2bNpk/p3p3/q3P2p/3p1BPP/3P4/PP3P.comment: This move prevents the easy development of the bishop. Black's king has nowhere safe to go, and his structure is in shambles. Hitting where it hurts! Note that 10...Qe7 drops the c7-pawn, so Black has no choice but to part ways with e6.
As tempting as it is, this move meets with an incredible refutation that gives Black attacking chances. The weakness of the d4-pawn grants Black sufficient counterplay.
Here, it is important to preserve the bishop pair rather than to greedily capture on e6, which leads to the complete dissolution of White's center after the trade on f4.

An important intermediate move, to prevent castling. Black loses a decisive amount of material. There is one more detail to keep in mind, though: As in the 13...Bb4 line, taking the bishop leads to unnecessary complications. Instead, we sidestep the bishop and act with surgical precision. Who cares about the bishop? Black is unable to save the rook and the knight at the same time.
The queen trade is inevitable, after which Black loses even more material. Black's position is in ruins. Note that ...Nb4 is not scary, as our queen simply drops down to e2.

Even with the queens off the board, we are able to generate a massive initiative in the center with a series of accurate moves: Breaking through in the center. Now, the meek 14.Nxe4 would enable Black to repair his center with 14...d5. Instead, our intentions are far more violent. Black is in trouble: he will lose either d6 or e4, or both. Whichever pawn we capture first, we will bring out the rest of our pieces and surround the other one, likely with Bg2 and Re1 or Rhd1. It appears that we have blundered a piece, but this is all part of the plan. In return for the minor piece, we will receive two pawns and, most importantly, fantastic chances to checkmate Black on the kingside. From a practical perspective, Black's position is untenable. The h-file is about to open up, and Black will have no answer to the massive amount of material that we will pile up on the h7-pawn, which will include the bishop and the other rook.

3rnr2/1p3Npk/p2bp3/q3P2p/3p1BPP/3P4/PP3P.comment: White has the bishop pair (for now) and a pleasant bishop. Next, we will castle queenside and can play either in the center (e3-e4) or expand on the kingside with f2-f4.

This is the best practical try. The computer gives equality (as usual), but Black's position is remarkably hard to play and traps exist by the basinful. Only 14...Kb8 preserves a double-edged position; the natural moves all fail to the same trap, which wins immediately:

3rnr2/1p2bNpk/p3p3/4P2p/3p1B1P/3P1P2/PP1.comment: Total domination in the center and an unstoppable attack on the queenside. Our next move is to b2-b4, and after the pawn appears on b5, Black will probably be best advised to resign in order to avoid a total massacre. Also do not forget about the possibility of a rook lift to c3, particularly if Black's queen appears on c6.

3rnr2/1p2bNpk/p3p3/q3P2p/3p3P/3PB3/PP3PP.comment: White will combine kingside and queenside expansion. Next up is g4 followed by h4, and we can expand on the queenside with a4-a5 as well - that is why we left the rook on a1! Finally, after g4 is played, remember that you can transfer your light-squared bishop via f1 to g2, when Black will likely lose the e4-pawn.

3rnr2/4bNpk/pp2p3/q3P2p/1P1p1B1P/3P4/P4P.comment: This move signals the key difference between 7.b4 and 6.b4: the knight in d7 is now under fire, and after 8...Bxb4+ 9.c3 we attack two minor pieces at the same time. Amazingly, Black can make this line work using an insane sequence of computer moves, but White still maintains an objective advantage at the end. Most people who stumble into this line will have done so unintentionally! It transpires that Black has serious compensation for the pawn, in the form of pressure on the c3-pawn and the constant possibility of ...Bxa4. We have to proceed with the utmost precision.

Not fearing the check on h4, which is cooly rebuffed by g2-g3. Practically speaking, Black is already in very serious trouble. The engine finds ways to keep Black's initiative going, but it is safe to say that a human will not be able to demonstrate anything resembling sufficient compensation for the piece.

3r1r2/4bNpk/pp1np3/q3P2p/1P1p1B1P/3P1P2/.comment: Poking and prodding at the b6-pawn. Now, ...b5 yields the c5-square, so Black must defend obediently.

Preventing ...e5, and preparing to develop our knight. We aim to complete our development with Bd3 and 0-0, when Black's compensation will simply evaporate. The engine finds a way to keep the spark of Black's initiative going, but we will bet a silver dollar that this position will never occur in your tournament or online practice :)

3rnr2/1p2bNpk/p3p3/q3P2p/3p3P/3P2B1/PP3P.comment: Turning up the pressure dial on d5. We have a litany of improving moves that we can follow up with, such as a4-a5 (to grab space on the queenside) and Qd3 (to threaten the h7 pawn and coordinate the rooks). If we can induce ...e5-e4, then we will use the d4-square as an outpost for the queen.

3rnr2/1p3Npk/p2bp3/q3P2p/3p1B1P/3P1P2/PP.comment: Transitioning to a furious kingside attack! Even without a knight on e5 to guide them forward, the kingside pawns constitute a formidable force. As a result of Black's compromised queenside pawn structure, the Black king has no safe place to hide. This move halts the progress of White's pawns on the kingside...or so it seems. We take the opportunity before Black has castled to smash open the e-file, giving us a dangerous and enduring initiative. Forcing the queen away from c5 and preparing to entrench the knight on b6. It may seem that the knight is anything but stable here, but we will use some fascinating tactics to justify its placement!

3rnr2/1p3Npk/p2bp3/q3P2p/3p1BPP/3P1P2/PP.comment: Black's king has nowhere to run!
The attack is already quite devastating.

1r2nr2/1p3Npk/p2bp3/q3P2p/3p1BPP/3P1P2/P.comment: The point is revealed: the knight is untouchable due to the fork on e3! Just when it seems that our attack has fizzled out, a lovely tactical shot comes to the rescue. Gorgeous! The queen is taboo due to Nxd7+, and Black is forced to part ways with his extra pawn. We have recovered our material investment, and stand clearly better. Our pawn structure is superior, and we can continue stoking the coals of attack by bringing our bishop out to h3. Of course, ...Qb7 is not dangerous on account of b3, and Black's "attack" comes to an end.

3rnr2/1p2bNpk/p3p3/q3P2p/3p1B1P/P2P4/1P3.comment: I have faced this move several times in blitz (DN), and it makes a good deal of sense: 7.b4 is now quite a bit less desirable, since the bishop on g7 will exert rather nasty pressure on our knight. Instead, we defend the pawn in an altogether different way: This removes the knight from the line of fire of Black's bishop, and threatens Nb6. Note that ...Qa5+ is never dangerous in such positions due to c3 (followed by b4, chasing the queen right back to its initial square). For now, we keep the tension, awaiting a more opportune moment to trade on c5.

Here, and only here! The lackluster 7.Bg3 enables Black to recover the pawn without consequences. This combative move does not solve Black's problems, but it leads to a good deal of tactical complexity, so it is worth looking over the following moves very carefully. We refrain from capturing on d4, which enables Black to entrench his knight on a powerful central square. As always, this move is innocuous and merely hastens Black's demise.

See 7...Nbd7 8.Ne5 0-0 9.Bd3 Bd6. This rare move presents a serious challenge to White's setup. There is no question that Black equalizes, but we can definitely pose some serious problems with accurate play.

Black continues to expand on the queenside. It is important to throw this move in to discourage ...Nh5. We cannot hold off on this move any longer, since Black was ready to play ...c4 or ...b4. We now proceed to quickly prepare the e4 pawn break. Importantly, the knight on c6 hinders the development of Black's bishop, and makes it impossible for him to stop e4. Before pushing the e-pawn, we complete our deverlopment. The time has come! Our pieces are perfectly placed to deal with the consequences of this breakthrough. The most common response, resolving the central tension straightaway. A very important idea; this is almost always the desirable response to ...d4. The knight is re-routed to d2, and it can later find a home on b3.

3rnr2/1p2bN1k/p3p1p1/q3P2p/3p1B1P/P2P4/1.comment: Refraining from the greedy Qxd5, which causes unnecessary complications. With the knight on a safe square, there is nothing to fear from the deployment of Black's bishop to the long diagonal. An astute positional move. The rook will support the c2-c4 breakthrough.

3rnr2/1p2bN1k/p3p1p1/q3P2p/1P1p1B1P/P2P4.comment: This is why we put the rook on c1! Forcing Black to get rid of the d4-pawn. Black has no compensation for the pawn. Moreover, he can barely move, since ...Nde5 will always run into Nb6. We will follow up by completing our kingside development, when our extra pawn and superior piece placement gives us a near-decisive advantage.

3rnr2/1p3Npk/p3p3/q3P1bp/3p1B1P/P2P4/1P3.comment: A crucial detail that justifies the entire line! We shut down Black's queenside counterplay, and prepare to recapture the pawn on c3 with a dominant position. The piece sac on b4 leads nowhere: Shutting down Black's counterplay on the d-file. Black is borderline lost due to our immense control over key light squares, including e4 and c4. Black also struggles with a total lack of coordination and an inability to find a suitable square for the dark-squared bishop.

First, the knight is placed on b6 to slice off the queen's only evacuation route. We now threaten b2-b4, which will trap Black's queen. This nondescript developing move accomplishes nothing, and enables us to attain an ideal setup on the queenside.

Of course, this is the point of deploying the bishop to g5. Black loses the d5-pawn without compensation. Withdrawing the queen from the center and offering a queen trade. Black has absolutely nothing in return for the pawn.

3rnr2/1p3Npk/p3p3/q3P1bp/1P1p1B1P/P2P4/5.comment: Simple and cold-blooded, preventing Black's only idea. The c3-pawn is not going anywhere! First, we will complete our kingside development, and then capture the pawn at our leisure. Black's position is resignable.

f3-f4 is coming sooner rather than later. Standard fare, deploying the knight to the beautiful b6-square. Halting the progress of Black's d-pawn. Despite the somewhat chaotic apperance of the position, Black has no active plan and no compensation for the pawn. is futile on account of

3rnr2/1p2bNpk/p3p3/q3P2p/1P1p1B1P/P2P4/5.comment: Calmly defending g2. Keeping things tight in the center! A devastating final resource, underscoring the potency of the knight. Trading on e5 hands over a decisive pawn phalanx in the center, while 19...Qc8 enables us to recapture the c3-pawn with the other knight, when its colleague on d5 will be unassailable. Black is objectively lost. White is now up a pawn for no compensation, but there is one more detail worth mentioning. A devious resource that was employed against DN in a recent speedrun game. Now, 11.0-0 (as played in the game) runs into 11...Ne4, and Black wins material. As usual, our top priority is to lead our c3-knight to the promised land. Cold-blooded and powerful. Black is out of active ideas, and we can improve our position in a litany of ways, ranging from Nb6 to c2-c3 to Rf1-d1.

3rnr2/1p3Npk/p2bp3/q3P2p/3p1B1P/P2P4/1P3.comment: The knight on e5 is completely unassailable: to get rid of it, Black must either part ways with a minor piece or must hand over the bishop pair to White. We see this exact type of setup in many lines. Note the power of the pawn on b4: without the possibility of ...c7-c5, Black has no good way to assail our dominance in the center. An inventive way to prevent Qf3, but this enables us to change the pawn structure in our favor. Asking Black a rather nasty question. Castling fails tactically, while ...g6 creates long-term weaknesses on the kingside. Black can maintain objective equality with a host of computer moves, but no one in their right mind would prefer Black's position here! Trying to force pieces off the board fails tactically.

Black loses the exchange, since 12...Qf6 drops the knight (and then the rook). A great example of a position where the computer evaluation is utterly useless. The computer gives 0.00, but we strongly believe that White's position is incomparably preferable. We will expand on the kingside with h4-h5, and can follow up by dropping the queen to h3 and advancing the g-pawn. Black has no active plan.

A crucial resource, supporting the knight and keeping our extra pawn. Just when it appears that Black is out of the woods, we open a second front. Perfect timing; this move works to perfection with the rook on a8 now undefended. Defending the d4-pawn with tempo. We will capture on a6 on the next move, when the connected passers should swiftly decide the outcome of the game. A classic maneuver: the queen is ferried over to h3, where it exerts long-term pressure against the h7-pawn. Without the possibility of ...c7-c5, Black is consigned to total passivity and must defend very precisely merely to avoid getting checkmated in the next few moves. The ideal setup is now complete. We are exerting massive pressure on h7, and intend to follow up with the prosaic g4-g5. This creates massive holes on the kingside, which we can exploit by repositioning our bishop to a more active square. Get out!

3rnr2/1p3Npk/p2bp3/q3P2p/3p1BPP/P2P4/1P3.comment: Ignoring the hanging knight on c3, which is non-essential to our attack. Unsurprisingly, given the superiority of our pieces, the tactics work out perfectly for White.

3rnr2/1p3N1k/p2bp3/q3P1pp/3p1BPP/P2P4/1P.comment: It is important to appreciate the value of these types of moves. Even though White is down a piece, we are in no big hurry, and it is worth bringing in the big boys to ensure that the attack is decisive. Eliminating Black's only active defender.

3rnr2/1p5k/p2bp3/q3P1Np/3p1BPP/P2P4/1P3P.comment: Smashing through Black's pitiful pawn shell. Another important quiet move, setting up the threat of a discovered check. The simplest threat is Nxf8+ followed by h8=Q. Black's king is forced back into the ring of fire. And now the coup d'grace, skewering the queen! Nominally, Black has a lot of material for the queen, but the minor pieces can only spectate as we get our rook to g1 and follow up with Qg4/g5/g6, setting up unstoppable threats along the g-file. Forcing the queen off of the g-file and lending further support to the knight, taking the sting out of ...Bxe5. The point of this move is not to shuttle the king to safety; it was perfectly safe in the center. Rather, by connecting the rooks, we are setting up the unstoppable threat of a sacrifice on g7! Now, a beautiful sequence decides the game:

3r1r2/1p3N1k/p2bpnp1/q3P1Bp/3p3P/P2P1P2/.comment: The rook lift to h3 will lead to immediate checkmate. The extent of Black's queenside paralysis is rather picturesque.

3rnr2/4bNpk/p3p3/qp2P2p/3p1B1P/P2P4/1P3P.comment: This very likely transposes to 4...b5 5.a3 Bb7 6.b4 e6. Of course, Black can also play this line without fianchettoing the light-squared bishop, but that hardly changes the general tenor of the game. White's plan will remain the same: to entrench a knight on e5, develop the light-squared bishop to d3, and light the kingside on fire by maneuvering the queen to h3. There is no way to win the c5-pawn, which can be supported with b2-b4 as necessary. Our queen can also park itself on e3. An innovative alternative, although this is quite unnecessary, since 13.Ne2 transposes into a line that leads to a very dangerous position for Black. Transposes to 10...Bd6 11.Bxd6 Qxd6 12.e4 etc. We see a virtually identical position in the 7...b5 line; the placement of the pawn on b7 does not change the nature of the position. We are ready to push e3-e4, posing Black with serious positional problems. Now, the top computer move is 10...e5, which we refuse to take seriously because no one in their right mind would ever chance upon such a move. Barring that, the position is equal objectively, but definitely easier to play for White. Now, 12.0-0 transposes into a position that we reach via 9...Nc6 10.0-0 0-0 11.e4 d4 12.Nb1, but we have a superior move:

Staking a claim in the center and popping open the b1-h7 diagonal. White is better for several reasons: 1) The pawn on d4 is a long-term weakness that cannot be easily eradicated; 2) We will proceed with Qe2-e4, a nasty idea that will induce a serious kingside weakness; 3) We have many auxiliary ways to improve our position, such as Rfd1 (after Qe2), Nb3-d2-e4-d6, and a timely a3-a4 can also be employed to underscore the hidden vulnerability of Black's queenside structure. In contrast, Black has no clear way to improve his position or cause problems on either side of the board. This is quite a bit better than the tempting 12.e5, when Black drops the knight back to d7 and reopens the kingside with the nasty ...f7-f6. Moving the rook to a better spot and setting up the positional threat of Be4, which will dislodge Black's queen from its active post. This move looks scary, but it simply loses a piece:

White has definite chances for an advantage: the idea is to expand on the queenside with b2-b4 and c2-c4, ultimately creating an outside passer. Of course, we do not fear ...Bxf3, which hands over the bishop pair and creates a long-term weakness on the light squares. This position occurred in Bortnyk-Baryshpolets, Nabokov Memorial 2015. This is best, leading to a small edge. White controls the crucial d4-square.

Our dark-square control, coupled with the nasty threat of Qb6, secures a very pleasant game for White. Black's queen on h5 is also somewhat out of commission. The position resembles a favorable version of an exchange Caro, with Black's light-squared bishop locked behind his pawns. This forces Black to make another move with his dark-squared bishop, thereby losing a tempo. This is a very common response, but Black will be unable to easily recover the pawn.

Transposes to 9...Nbd7 10.e4, etc. Despite Black's best efforts, we have succeeded in pushing e4, leading virtually by force to a series of piece exchanges in the center. The resulting position may appear rather lifeless, but upon closer inspection, it turns out that White certainly has the easier practical game. The position has simplified considerably, and the symmetrical material may lead you to believe that the position is devoid of serious winning chances. That could not be further from the truth! Black's queenside is rather weak, and the pawn on b5 is more of a liability than an asset. White's play is ultra straightforward: we will castle and quickly position our rooks on d1 and e1, when White's superior pieces grant us easy practical play.
White has an indisputable initiative, with control over the center and a better-placed bishop. Black must continue to make precise moves to keep equality.

Black is in a vise-like grip. The bishop can be maneuvered to h4, and White can follow up by amputating the d5-knight with Qd2 and Nf4. White has a small but stable advantage, much akin to the Exchange Caro where Black has closed in his bishop with a premature ...e6. We will inevitably ensconce on our knight on e5 and follow up by building up the kingside pressure. This is somewhat premature, since the bishop has a suitable escape square on g5.

With the dark-squared bishop gone, it is a perfect opportunity to resolve the tension in the center and launch a furious kingside offensive. White's queen trap falls apart. It appears that our pieces are all moving backwards, but we have in fact provoked serious, potentially decisive, weaknesses on both sides of the board. We currently threaten to trap the knight with g2-g4, forcing Black to overextend himself even further. Poking at the weak b5-pawn, and opening up the c4-square for our bishop.
with excellent kingside prospects connected to the idea of opening the h-file with h2-h4. Black doesn't recover the pawn easily, and must continue to make computer moves.

3rnr2/5Npk/p2bp2B/qp2P2p/1P1p3P/P2P4/5PP.comment: In these types of positions, you almost never want to capture the rook on f8 because the bishop is such a valuable attacker. White is dominating on the kingside, but we do not even have to rush with h4-h5: an even more powerful continuation in response to 14...Kh8 would be to shuttle the knight around to d4 via e2.

3rnr2/4bNpk/p3p3/qp2P1Bp/3p3P/P2P4/1P3PP.comment: Blasting open the center, after which our knight will sink its teeth into the juicy d6-square!

3rnr2/4bNpk/p3p3/qp2P2p/3p1B1P/P2P4/1P3P.comment: This is the most popular move on Lichess, and it is the one you are likely to face at least half the time. Black opens up the dark-squared bishop and establishes a firmer presence in the center. This is a very important move that forces Black to make a positional concession. Black must either give away the bishop pair and damage his pawn structure with 4...Bd6, or permanently misplace his knight with 4...Na6. In the latter case, Black will push away the knight with ...c6, but the knight from a6 will still have a very hard time rejoining the game. There is no question that this is the worst of Black's three main lines, but it is the most popular by a country mile. This is the most straightforward response. Black defends the c7-pawn without giving away the bishop pair. In this line, the strategic potency of Nb5 is on full display: the knight on a6 will have a very difficult time rejoining society: the shortest path involves ferrying the knight around to d6 via c7 and e8, which already takes a staggering number of moves. Our general approach is to quickly complete our kingside development. After we do that...okay, how about we cross that bridge when we get there! Black is at a further crossroads. He can chase the knight away immediately with 5...c6, focus on kingside development with 5...Be7, or strike at the center straightaway with 5...c5. All of these eventualities must be carefully considered - each leads to a fundamentally different type of battle. The main move at a high level. Black retains maximum flexibility, developing his kingside and reserving the possibility to chase away White's knight at a more convenient moment. It is quite clear that our journey to b5 has been anything but a waste of time. Not only is Black's knight awkwardly placed, but it is outright vulnerable: Black must now reckon with the positional threat of Bxa6, permanently ruining Black's queenside structure and creating a massive hole on c5 that we can easily access with our knight. We certainly don't miss the opportunity to create massive, long-term weaknesses on the queenside. Calmly continuing our development. It is important to remember that the combination of ...Bb4 and ...Ne4 is almost never scary in the Jobava: we almost always respond by castling, giving up the c3-pawn but attaining a massive initiative in return. In this case, we will also attain total positional domination on the queenside. As with 8...Ne4, we are more than happy to give up a pawn in exchange for full control over the dark squares.

3r1r2/4bNpk/p3pn2/qp2P2p/3p1B1P/P2P4/1P3.comment: Seizing the b-file and preventing Black from deploying the bishop to b7. In contrast to the 8...Qa5 line, here Black keeps the dark-squared bishop, but it is unable to move back to the a3-f8 diagonal. As such, White still holds complete domination over the dark squares, and the imminent prospect of Ne5 will push Black over the edge. Preventing Ne5 does more harm than good: A familiar idea, establishing a very nasty pin against Black's knight. White's compensation is absolutely massive: Black has no good way to end the pin, since ...g5 creates fatal weaknesses on the kingside and ...Qc7 allows us to capture on f6. We can follow up by intensifying the pressure with Ne5 and f2-f4, followed by a rook or queen lift to the kingside. On the queenside, Black has no active prospects and no good way to activate the light-squared bishop. This knight transfer is incredibly inefficient. Black will eventually re-route the knight to a relatively active square, but the tempi that he burns in the process will grant us an excellent game. We dominate on both sides of the board, and can follow up with Ne5. g4-g5 will be utterly crushing. It is quite important to throw this move in in response to ...h6, since Nf3 allows Black to pick up the bishop with ...Nh5.

It is always a good idea to reinforce the knight, taking the sting out of ...Bd7. Now, rather than the meek 11.g3, we can exploit the vulnerability of Black's knight with a lovely tactic: This is not played to reinforce the knight, so much as to establish contact between the rook and the a3-square, rendering ...Bxa3 ineffective once the knight retreats. Right back to home base! We have achieved our ideal minor piece setup, and can improve our position in a litany of ways. As always, this kind of position favors White, since the knight on b5 cannot be easily driven away. A clever, dastardly resource! Rather than putting our cards on the table with the immediate 6.b4, we set up the threat of b2-b4 and a4-a5, which will trap the bishop on b6. Black must respond by attempting to chase away our knight. A critical position. It may appear that White's queenside play has ground to a complete halt, but the party is only beginning. This is a more desirable way to chase away the knight from a strategic point of view, but it contains a fatal tactical flaw: Black grants us access to the d6-square!
As usual, this move makes very little sense, since it enables the knight to remain on b5 forever.
We pick up the bishop on the next move, with a decisive material advantage.

An important idea, that re-occurs several times throughout this course. While this pin may appear empty, it in fact causes Black very serious headaches. We threaten to capture the knight on f6 and follow up with a fork on d7, an idea that is often overlooked even by extremely strong grandmasters. If Black drops the bishop back to e7, then the c3-knight is liberated, and we can establish our control over the c5-square with Na4. A sad necessity, but this creates long-term weaknesses on the kingside.

We saw a very similar idea in the 8...a5 variation, with the minor difference that Black's rook was on a8 and the pawn was still on c6. These cosmetic differences change very little: White still threatens Bxf6 followed by Nd7, and White is still very much incapable of dealing with the problems that await him on both sides of the board. A pretty in-betweener, driving the queen away from d8 and setting up Bxf6. Black has spent endless tempi to get the knight to an active square, only to be sent back to a6! Winning material. Typical idea #4: we do not miss an opportunity to cripple Black's queenside pawn structure and create a massive hole on c5. A nice desperado move to pick up a pawn. Pushing the pawn may eradicate the weakness on c6, but it does not rid us of the outpost on c5. We are almost always happy to achieve the d4-f4 pawn bind, which resembles a Maroczy Bind shifted one file to the right. The knight on e4 appears imposing, but it can be kicked away at our convenience with f2-f3. The knight has been ferried over to an ideal square. Now, both knights control c5, and we threaten to win the knight with f2-f3. The position plays itself: Nac5 can be followed by Re1, when Black is sinking under the weight of his endless weaknesses. Attacking b2 does not change our plans in the slightest, since we were planning to play Na4 anyway. Dark-square domination! Black is utterly paralyzed.

The knight on e5 no longer requires the support of the d4-pawn, since the bishop does the job perfectly well. Now, it is time for typical idea #5: the queen is ferried over to h3 before initiating a furious kingside storm. Black often starts with this move, but it will almost always transpose to the main line (6...Nc6) after Black develops the knight. Transposes to 6...Nc6 7.Nf3 0-0 8.c3 Re8 9.h3. Transposes to 6...Nc6 7.Nf3 0-0 8.c3. This is surprisingly common, but it simply drops a pawn for no compensation. It is always a good idea to buttress the d4-pawn, rendering ...e6-e5 even less effective. Activating the knight and reinforcing the d6-pawn. Making luft for the bishop. This move is the opposite of scary. The x-ray against White's king my appear concerning, but with the d4-pawn as secured as it is, Black has absolutely no way to convert his temporary development advantage into anything tangible. After we complete our kingside development, Black will experience long-lasting problems with his center.

Having induced serious weaknesses on the kingside, we move on to the pawn storm phase. Our next step is to shift the queen to g3 in order to leave open the path for the h-pawn. Driving the pawn down to h5 and creating the rather nasty threat of h5-h6, which will provoke long-term weaknesses on the kingside. Time to rip open the g-file! White's attack proceeds at a furious pace, while Black has very little going on the other side of the board.

Tucking the bishop away and ensuring its permanent safety. This move succumbs to a lovely tactical refutation that underscores how nicely our pieces are coordinated. Picking up the bishop on d7 and emerging a pawn ahead.

Striking while the iron is hot! The queen has been forced onto a more vulnerable square, enabling our knight to jump into the action. Now, another pawn is temporarily sacrificed in order to tear open the queenside and increase the power of our initiative. Black is absolutely screwed: he can barely move, his queenside is collapsing, and our pieces are on optimal squares. This line really showcases the multi-faceted nature of the Jobava London: it is an opening that promises its adherents not just tactical victories, but strategic masterpieces as well!

Preventing Black from castling, and reinforcing our control over key dark squares along the a3-f8 diagonal. We saw a similar move in the 8...Qa5 line (see White's 15th move). If the pawn is captured, Black's entire queenside will be in tatters; if it isn't, the pawn will deliver a further blow to Black's defensive capacity once it reaches c5. And now, we entrench the bishop on the sexiest outpost on the board! A lovely positional sacrifice, giving up the center pawn in order to carve out a devastating path for our knight. It took us a while, but we finally got our knight on a perfect square! c6 is hanging, and Black has no choice but to allow the infiltration of our rook. This line is worth reviewing several times. Note that White sacrifices three pawns, and all three sacrifices are entirely positional in nature. First, the c3-pawn is sacrificed to spark the flames of the initiative. Then, after the queen is ferried to a3, we open up the queenside with c2-c4. Once Black declines the pawn, it is driven to c5, and we finish with a sacrifice that enables us to carve out a devastating pathway for our knight. A certified Jobava Classic! Defending the pawn with the queen prevents Rb7, but opens Black up to a devastating attack on the kingside. It is worth flicking in this move, which forces Black's bishop on an even more awkward square. Suddenly, we transition from the queenside to the kingside! It turns out that our previous move had a hidden aim: White now intends the gorgeous e3-e4, opening up a pathway from the queenside to the kingside for our rook! In addition, we threaten the banal Bh6, forcing Black to burn a crucial tempo. There it is! We saw this same move in the 11...f6 sub-variation, although it was played for an entirely different reason (to get the knight to e5). Here, the knight is already on e5, and this move is played in order to lift the rook over to the kingside. Note that total dominance of our knight over Black's entire army!
The king is now boxed in, and a beautiful mating pattern seals the deal:
with endless threats against Black's king, all of them unstoppable. We could keep going, but we think you'll be able to take it from here! White dominates on both sides of the board.
A strange-looking move, but it prevents the queen from escaping via a5 and - much like Nb5 (see typical idea #7) - lures Black's knight to an incredible passive square.

3r1r2/4bNpk/p3pn2/qp2P2p/P2p1B1P/3P4/1P3.comment: Now, 12...Kxh7 leads to rapid checkmate after 13.Qxh5, so Black must part ways with a lot of material and give up the final pawn which provides shelter to the king. with three pawns and a rook for two pieces, as well as domination on tthe queenside and the straightforward idea of pushing the h-pawn all the way to h6.

Gorgeous. By covering the e1-a5 diagonal, we ensure that ...Qxc3 does not come with check, so 11...Bxb5 no longer works. After the trade on b3 (which is forced, since we threaten to take on c4), the queen will be driven back to b6 and we will finally be able to deploy our light-squared bishop to d3.
Counterattacking the bishop! This is the first of many fantastic tactical moves that pose serious problems for Black on the queenside. The most popular move.

3r1r2/4bNpk/p3pn2/qp2P1Bp/3p3P/P2P4/1P3P.comment: White is better on both sides of the board! Instead of the regular 14.Na4, here we have a tactic that leads to immediate victory:

3r1r2/4bNpk/p3pn2/qp2P2p/3p1BPP/P2P4/1P3.comment: It is always important to be patient in the Jobava London, and this line is no exception. Before rolling up our sleeves on the kingside, we ensure the safety of our king (and threaten Nb5). While the computer will likely hold off the attack, we believe that the position is totally untenable from a human perspective. We will either open the h-file with hxg6 or, in the event of ...g5, smash open the kingside with f2-f4.

3r1r2/4bNpk/pq2pn2/1p2P2p/P2p1B1P/3P4/1P.comment: It appears that Black has gotten the better of us tactically, but yet another scintillating retreating knight move proves otherwise. Simply divine! The knight moves back to its initial square, establishing contact between the queen and bishop, and facing Black with two threats at the same time. Black has nothing better than to give up the exchange, when his compensation will be woefully insufficient.

3r1r2/4bNpk/pq2pn2/1P2P2p/3p1B1P/3P4/1P3.comment: Our king has been ferried to safety, and Black has nothing going on on the queenside.

3r1r2/4bNpk/p3pn2/1q2P2p/3p1B1P/3P4/1P3P.comment: Typical idea #3: we rush the h-pawn up the board, and Black has too many weaknesses and not enough defenders on the kingside to do anything about it. Obviously, we do not even think about trading queens! A thematic piece sacrifice, smashing open the kingside. With the queen entirely out of commission on b3, Black cannot lend nearly enough reinforcement to the kingside and the attack will end the game in a matter of a few moves.

3r1r2/4b1pk/p3pn2/1q2P1Np/3p1B1P/3P4/1P3.comment: Rebuilding the battery! This time, Black has no pawn to put on g6, and the bishop blocks the f-pawn. Checkmate is coming on the next move.

3r1r2/4b1pk/p3pn2/qp2P1Np/3p1B1P/P2P4/1P.comment: A classic concept, removing the pawn from f7 before returning to h5 and delivering check on h7. Black is mated by force.
Black's king is caught in the crossfire of a lovely attack that quickly results in mate.

3r1rk1/4b1p1/p3p3/qp2P2p/3p1BnP/P2P1N2/1.comment: It appears that our queen is trapped, but we have a nice way to trade it off for its counterpart. We have two pawns for the exchange, and Black's incredibly weak kingside pawns will give us plenty of targets. Furthermore, the h4-pawn - once an attacker - has now become a fearsome passed pawn which will keep Black's rooks at bay.

3r1r2/4bNpk/p3pn2/q3P2p/Pp1p1B1P/3P4/1P3.comment: White's position is preferrable:we have quite a bit more space, long-term pressure down the h-file, as well as total domination over key queenside squares and the eventual possibility of pressure down the c-file.
An ultra-rare and not particularly threatening move. We are more than happy to withdraw our bishop from f4.

This ingenious (though rare) move must be taken seriously. Black aims to recapture on a5 with the knight after the smoke clears on the queenside. The first step is always to open the diagonal for our bishop and buttress the b-pawn.

An inventive alternative to the more conventional 11.Nf3, pinning the knight on f6 and inducing a major kingside weakening with ...h6-g5. If Black does not chase the bishop away, White will maintain lasting pressure on the kingside. Now that Black has castled kingside, ...g7-g5 comes with a far steeper price tag. In the finest traditions of the Jobava London! With the dark squared bishop gone, Black will have a very hard time insulating the kingside against the litany of threats that our bloodthirsty queen-bishop tandem will pose. The queen is terribly overextended, paralyzing the knight on a5. Setting up the vicious threat of Bxf6+ and Qh4+, picking off Black's queen.

Using the compromised position of Black's knight to stake a claim in the center. Clearly, Black has insufficient compensation for the exchange. Our next step is to calmly develop our kingside and ferry the king to safety.
Picking up the pawn with interest.

Forming a queen-bishop battery, and preparing to meet 12...c6 with the devastating 13.b6. Transposes to 8..c6 9.e3 Bd7. Intrepid play is a prerequisite if you want to consider yourself a real Jobava player! As scary as this appears, Black simply does not have the firepower to exploit the king's compromised position. He has no choice but to spend time on castling and on activating his knight with ...Ne4; we will use this time to carve out shelter for our king on g2. Before building shelter for our king, we induce a queenside weakness and make it difficult for Black to untangle on the queenside. The best defense is attack! Despite appearances, White's king on f3 is perfectly safe, and we can hide it on g2 at our convenience.

3r1r2/4bNpk/p3pn2/q3P1Bp/Pp1p3P/3P4/1P3P.comment: Quiet and powerful. By completing our development, we ensure that our kingside attack will never fizzle out. Black has nothing better than to give back the material with 19...Ne4. We readily sacrifice the pawn on b5 in order to complete our development. The idea is to properly time the trade on a8 and to follow up with Bxf6, permanently ruining Black's kingside pawn structure and offering White a lasting initiative. Putting the bishop on g5 to work! Black instantly pays the price for the sloppy capture on a1. The queen must babysit the a8-square, forcing Black to recapture with the pawn. White has fantastic compensation for the pawn, as defined by several factors: 1) The bishop on b5 has no active prospects, while the knight has countless ways to join the game, ranging from Nf4-Nh5 to the more creative d5 followed by Nd4. 2) Black's pawn structure on both sides of the board, but particularly the kingside, is horrific. 3) We control the center and the only open file on the board; 4) There is no shelter anywhere on the board for Black's king. The subsequent lines are obviously not forced, but they nicely illustrate the way in which these factors translate to a monster initiative. Incredible geometry. After provoking ...Kh7 (which may seem counterproductive), the queen returns to b1, attacking the bishop and creating an x-ray against the King. But White does not follow up with e5+, which would be futile. The correct continuation is far more explosive! There is the rub! The bishop is forced away from c6, leading to the destruction of Black's entire queenside. What a variation! The zigzag pattern adopted by our queen leaves quite the lasting impression. Smashing open the d-file, and carving out the d4-square for the knight. From a practical perspective, White's compensation for the two pawns is absolutely overwhelming. Black is facing a litany of threats in the center and on the kingside, the most immediate being Nf5.

The queen shuttles back to b1, forcing Black's king to relinquish its control over the h6-pawn. Back to c1 we go! The pressure has reached a zenith, and in order to emerge unscathed, Black must uncork a series of jaw-dropping computer moves. A lovely deflection sacrifice that would be decisive if not for an even crazier counter-combination. Luring the king to g2, upon which Black can intercept the c1-h6 diagonal with ...e3+ and pick up the rook on d8. Of course, we refuse to cooperate!

3r1r2/4bNpk/p3p3/q3P1Bp/Pp1pn2P/3P4/1P3P.comment: A typical prophylactic move, dealing a blow to the knight's prospects. Wonderfully inventive chess! The king embraces its new role as an integral part of the kingside mosaic. Its role on f2 will be revealed on the next move. This weakens the e5 square and enables us to maintain the bishop pair. Despite our outward lack of piece coordination, we are able to hold Black's knight at bay on the strenghth of some badass tactics.

3r1r2/4bNpk/p3p3/q3P1Bp/Pp1pn2P/3P1P2/1P.comment: The knights are pinned, and Black loses a minor piece:

3r1r2/4bNpk/p3pn2/q3P2p/Pp1p3P/3P4/1P1B1.comment: It turns out that Black's bishop is most certainly not out of the woods! The smoke has finally cleared, and it is obvious that we are the one calling the shots. We can follow up by solidifying our central control with f2-f4. Black suffers from a lack of space and the permanent weakness of the b5-pawn. Underscoring the counterproductive nature of Black's seventh move. This move now comes with tempo, enabling us to recapture Black's bishop while keeping our queenside pawn structure fully intact. Black's knight sally to h5 has been an abject failure: we are ready to recapture the bishop on a5, and Black has no way to recover the pawn. An important moment. It is very tempting to agree to the queen trade, but the resulting position offers Black satisfactory compensation for the exchange due to his more active pieces and the long-term weakness of the b5-pawn. This is the best square for White's queen. On b1, it is far away from the predations of Black's knights, and will link up with bishop (after Bd3) to exert nagging pressure on the e4-knight. Note that ...Nc3 is nothing but an empty threat, in response to which we can simply bring our queen up to b3. We have successfully completed our kingsid development and kept Black's queenside counterplay at bay. We will follow up by castling and deploying the rook to c1. White's total control over all of the key queenside squares renders Black's compensation for the exchange virtually nonexistant.

3r1r2/4bNpk/p3pP2/q6p/Pp1p1B1P/3P4/1P3PP.comment: Black is dominated on the dark squares, and cannot defend e6 and c7 simultaneously.

3r1r2/4bNpk/p3p3/q3P2p/Pp1pnB1P/3P2P1/1P.comment: It appears that Black has trapped our bishop, since opening the f-file is unthinkable. But we have one more trick up our sleeve. Counterattacking Black's knight, and forcing Black to relinquish his control over the c3-bishop. The tactics work out in White's favor.

Another counterblow, this time hitting the bishop! If the bishop retreats to a5, we can finally save our bishop by taking twice on e5. Gorgeous tactics. The threat of Ne6+ forces Black to leave the knight on f3. Our king will journey back to the promised land to pick it up! This time, under the able protection of the knight, it will be quite a bit safer on that square. Note that 23...Qe7 should be met with 24.Qxd5, covering the e4-square.

3r1r2/4bNpk/p3p3/qp2P2p/3pnB1P/P2P4/1P3P.comment: (Niemann) After the trade, Black will have a very hard time keeping d6 protected.
Preparing to meet ...h4 with Be5 f6 Bxe4, when Black can only take one bishop at a time! White's advantage is not up for debate.

3r1r2/4bNpk/p3pn2/qp2P2p/3p3P/P2P4/1P3PP.comment: Recovering the knight and leading to a miserable endgame for Black. His pawn structure says it all! Under different circumstances, this type of pawn structure can favor Black, but with no dark-squared bishop, it makes a lot less sense. We have active ideas on both sides of the board. The pawn advances to g5, where it will either trap the knight or force the horsey to lose contact with the crucial d5-pawn.
The knight is trapped! Since ...e4 is never scary, we simply continue our development.

This is a great square for the queen, from where it pressures two pawns and stays out of the way of the rest of our pieces. Continuing to improve our position by reinforcing the bishop, which will prove useful in the event that Black takes on d4.
Hitting where it hurts! The only (tactical) way to defend both pawns is ...Qb6, but the queen trade further damages Black's pawn structure and makes it harder for them to defend d5.

The queen is ferried over to g3. We have the bishop pair, the superior pawn structure, and excellent prospects on the f-file. An incredibly deep move, keeping contact with the f5-pawn so that Black's bishop cannot retreat to f7. White's control over the dark squares ensures total domination. It may seem that Black has fully rectified his pawn structure and has solved his positional problems, but they are in fact only beginning! Note that we have complete and permanent dominance over the dark-squares: the bishop on h2 is the hidden engine of our position. We can assert our advantage by activating our queen and knight, creating a situation in which Black is devoid of pawn breaks and of any active opportunities on either side of the board.

The knight trade opens up the d4-square, which we can use as an outpost for our queen. Our bishop controls b8 and prevents Black from engineering the ...f4 pawn break. After we reposition our queen to b4, we can accumulate the queenside pressure with b2-b4 and a2-a4 (preparing b5), or blast open the center by preparing c3-c4. Even after an endless series of accurate moves, there is no end in sight to Black's suffering.  This is an ultra-rare continuation, yet it is the choice of several very strong Grandmasters. It is somewhat outside the scope of this course, yet we have decided to dedicate a small file to it in order to point you in the right direction. By delaying ...Nf6, Black aims to nip White's central counterplay in the bud.

2r2r2/4bNpk/p3pn2/qp2P2p/3p3P/P2P4/1P3PP.comment: We can continue to improve with Rad1 and Qa2, paving the way for a potential pawn storm on the kingside. Black is saddled with tons of weaknesses in the center, and has no easy way to improve. This sacrifice is the opposite of scary.

It is also possible to take with the e-pawn, but we prefer this recapture, which opens up the queenside. This may seem to favor Black, but his control of the c-file is temporary - Black must burn a tempo to prevent Bb5, which we will use to contest the c-file with Rac1.

3r1r2/4bNpk/p3pn2/1p2P2p/q2p3P/P2P4/1P3P.comment: It is crucial to get right down to business! White prepares e2-e4, aiming to provoke Black to develop the knight to f6.

3r1r2/4bNpk/p3pn2/1p2P2p/q2p3P/P2P1P2/1P.comment: White's central control and prospects along the f-file guarantee us a long-lasting initiative.

3r1r2/4bN1k/p3pn2/1p2P1pp/q2p3P/P2P1P2/1.comment: Markoja-Richter, corr. 2015. White overwhelmingly dominates in the center, and the b2-pawn is clearly untouchable:
An incredible idea! White simultaneously threatens f4-f5 and Be2. In order to keep the minor piece alive and preserve the balance, Black must reproduce several impossible computer moves.

3r1r2/4bN1k/p3pn2/1p2P1pp/q2p1P1P/P2P4/1.comment: The endgame is miserable for Black, who suffers from a total lack of coordination and a permanently weak pawn on d4.

3r1r2/5Npk/p2bpn2/1p2P2p/q2p3P/P2P1P2/1P.comment: Boeven-Mueller, German Senior Championship 2015. White opted for the rather odd Nce2, but simple improving moves yield an excellent position, e.g.

3r1r2/5Npk/p2bpn2/1p2P2p/q2p2PP/P2P1P2/1.comment: White's aim is to regroup with Bc1, Nhf4, followed by Qd2 and Nd3, controlling key squares in the center. Black is dreadfully cramped.

3r1r2/5Npk/p3pn2/1p2P2p/qb1p1B1P/P2P1P2/.comment: Most Grunfeld and King's Indian players choose this system. The resulting positions are quite complex, and markedly different from those that arise after 3...Bf5, 3...e6, and 3...a6. We begin by solidifying our center and initiating a furious kingside assault. Black is at an early crossroads: the most popular move by a country mile is 4...Bg7, but Black has a few serious alternatives that must be studied carefully. By far the most common response, completing the fianchetto. Although much less popular than 4...Bg7, this alternative must be taken seriously. Black solidifies his center and prepares an eventual queen sally to b6. As usual, we initiate kingside operations and pose Black with an early dilemma. Analogously to the position after 4...Bg7 5.h4, Black has two main ways to meet Harry's march: Black can continue developing with 5...Bg7 (transposing to a position that we analyze via the 4...Bg7 5.h4 c6 move order), or meet White at the top with 5...h5. Proceeding with development. The early bishop sortie to g4 is very common, but the bishop will be tossed around by our pawns. We respond by unpinning our queen and reinforcing the idea of Ne5. This exchange is squarely in White's favor: the resulting pawn structure offers White fantastic play in the center and on the kingside, as well as the bishop pair. Striking at the center without delay. It is almost always worth investing a tempo to improve the safety of our king. Deploying the rook, and applying pressure on g6. An ingenious move, opening up a line of fire to the h4-pawn. Since our lead in development is quite vast, we can afford to leave the h-pawn en prise!

3r1r2/5N1k/p3pnp1/1p2P2p/qb1p1B1P/P2P1P2.comment: This pin is quite nasty, since Black cannot afford to play ...f6 for obvious reasons. Black is paying a steep price for advancing his h-pawn and opening the g-file: we threaten the devastating Nxh5 gxh5 Bf6, while Black's "attack" hasn't even gotten off the ground. The knight is hanging, and Nxh5-Bf6 is imminent. A cold-blooded response, sending the queen back where it belongs! It is now time to smash open the center at all costs! At this point in your Jobava journey, moves like these should not elicit any surprise. Another blow, removing the final defender from the e-file. Obviously, taking with the queen loses to Re1, so Black's king has no choice but to go on a walk. A surgical follow-up check, preventing ...Kf8. We will follow up by castling queenside, landing the d5 pawn in serious trouble. Obviously, Black cannot even dream of any compensation for the pawn! This leads to the same position as after 11...Qb6, with the pawn on a3 clearly favoring White. Black has recovered the pawn, and the ensuing check on c3 may appear rather disconcerting, but Black's position remains virtually untenable due to the semi-open h-file, the lack of active prospects for the LSB, and the permanent weakness of the e6-pawn. Unpinning the knight and preparing to trade on our own terms.

This creative night sally underscores the awkwardness of the bishop on g4, which will provide fuel for a furious pawn storm in the center. f2-f3 and e3-e4 is coming, and Black can do absolutely nothing about it. In order to generate a suitable escape square for the bishop, Black must cede total control of the center. This is the strongest move, but it is very infrequently played. Objectively, the position is dynamically equal, but there is no question that it is quite a bit easier to play White. An important resource, indirectly defending the b2-pawn. Lovely tactics! Black is posed with an ultimatum: take the knight and run the risk of losing their queen, or transition into a rather unpleasant endgame in which White's space advantage and better-placed pieces offers the better practical chances.  This and the next moves truly emphasize how deadly the queen + knight tandem can be in the right circumstances.  Game, set, match! Transposes to 4...Bg7 5.h4 c5 6.Nb5 Na6 7.c3. However, since Black has already castled, it is worth starting with gxh5, in order to pop open the g-file and facilitate the ensuing attack.

Bortnyk-Ajay, Chess.com (blitz) 2021. This position hardly needs elaboration! Amazingly, we have transposed to 3...a6 4.e3 Nc6 5.Nf3 Bf5 6.Ne5 e6 7.g4 Nxe5 8.gxf5, so we advise you to head on over to the 3...a6 file and refresh your memory on the subsequent moves. Black cannot keep e6 protected and answer the threat of a discovered check at the same time. Black has run out of ways to stave off the inevitable. He will have some compensation for the pawn due to the somewhat flimsy placement of our monarch, but a few careful consolidating moves, such as Bg2 and Rf1, should render this compensation meaningless. Obviously, opening up the h-file with ...hxg5 merely hastens Black's defeat! White has opened up a raging attack on Black's king. We threaten both the prosaic h4-h5 and the lovely Nxg6, and Black's impotent army is powerless to stop the avalanche.
Despite the chaotic appearance of the position, Black is in big trouble. Both of his bishops are vulnerable, and f2-f3 is threatened. Black's bishop has run out of squares! An empty check.

3r1r1k/8/p2bp1pB/1p2P2p/q2p3P/P1NP1P2/1P.comment: The queen has done its job on a4, and we now reposition it to the optimal square.

3r1r1k/8/p2bp1pB/1p2P2p/3p3P/PqNP1P2/1P4.comment: White's advantage is indisputable. After buttressing our bishop with h2-h4 and castling short, we will turn our attention toward the center, expanding with e3-e4 and solidifying our center with R(a)d1.

3r1r1k/8/p2bp1pB/1p2P2p/q2p3P/P2P1P2/1P1.comment: Yet again, the knight sally to b5 is very effective. This is a lot better than 10.c4, which would justify the placement of Black's bishop on a5. Now, the bishop is taken out of the game and we follow up with a furious queenside pawn storm. Black is under massive pressure due to the threat of c5 as well as Nc3, when the e4-pawn, in the immortal words of GM Robert Hess, will not be long for this board. Note that ...Nf6 can be savagely met with Bg5.

with a pleasant edge. It is worth flicking in this move to grab some space on the kingside and soften up the bishop on g6. A classic idea in the Semi-Slav and many other openings. Black has no choice but to acquiesce to the queen trade, opening up the a-file and handing us a queenside attack on a golden platter. We are playing squarely for two results. We will follow up either with b4-b5, shattering Black's pawn chain and opening up avenues of infiltration, or with Nb3-a5, when Black will have a very hard time defending the b7-pawn, since we (permanently) control the b8-square.

3r1r1k/8/p2bp1pB/1p2P2p/qP1pN2P/P2P1P2/6.comment: We have built up a massive clamp on the queenside, and things will go from bad to worse once we stick the knight on c5.

We saw a similar position to this one (with the pawns on d4 and b2) in the 9...Bxc5 10.d4 Bb6 line - this cosmetic difference does not change all that much. Black is still in big trouble due to the threat of Nd6 and the pressure down the c-file.

2Rr1r1k/8/p2bp1pB/1p2P2p/q2pN2P/P2P1P2/1.comment: This appears to call White's previous move into question: why provoke a move that grabs space and builds a rather imposing wall of pawns? In reality, the dutiful student of this course will know that ...b7-b5 is almost always a dreadfully weakening move, leaving behind massive holes on the light squares (particularly c6) and handing White the keys to a ravaging queenside initiative. It may appear that Black is out of the woods after recapturing on c5, but his troubles are only beginning. Note that the rook on c8 lacks a defender - this tactical deficiency is about to become very important, regardless of which piece Black decides to recapture with. Sending the bishop back, and paving the way for a straightforward and devastating tactical blow. Even better than Nxf6+. The threat of Rc8, which will pick off Black's rook, forces instant resignation.
10.Rc1 is also good, but this is even better, since it essentially leads to a forced queen trade.

2Rr1r1k/8/p2bp1pB/1p2P2p/3pN2P/Pq1P1P2/1.comment: Hitting f7. Black is woefully overextended. This is a lot better than 16.Nxf7+, which only wins a pawn.

3r1r1k/8/p1Rbp1pB/1p2P2p/3pN2P/Pq1P1P2/1.comment: We can basically premove Rc7, after which Black will not be able to move a single muscle. Of course, 16...Bxb4 is impossible on account of 17.Rc8+.
The rightful culmination of our lightning queenside attack. White wins the bishop.

2r2r1k/8/p2bp1pB/1p2P2p/q2pN2P/P2P1P2/1P.comment: Now, we get down to business. The devastating threat of Nc7+ is unstoppable.

3r1r1k/8/p2bp1p1/1p2P1Bp/q2pN2P/P2P1P2/1.comment: Note that the tempting 14.g4 fails tactically to 14...h6 15.Bh4 g5, when Black retains material equality.

3r1r1k/8/p2Np1pB/1p2P2p/q2p3P/P2P1P2/1P4.comment: The attempt to generate kingside counterplay (which resembles our own g4-h4 idea) falls short on account of a lovely counterblow.

3r1r1k/8/p2Np2B/1p2P1pp/q2p3P/P2P1P2/1P4.comment: Counter-attacking the knight and summarily halting Black's kingside pawn play. Needless to say, we are more than willing to part ways with the g4-pawn in order to win an additional tempo. An important insertion, using the weakness of the e6-pawn to open up the c-file. The bishop is poisoned, since Black will get massacred on the e6-square and in the center.

3r1r1k/8/p2Np2B/1p2P1pp/q2p2PP/P2P1P2/1P.comment: We are happy to trade queens, but only on our terms! Taking on d7 enables Black to develop the knight and open up escape squares for the a8-rook. The pawn cannot be defended, and our bloodthirsty heavy pieces will tear Black's pitiful army to shreds.

3r1r2/7k/p2bp1pB/1p2P2p/q2pN2P/P2P1P2/1P.comment: Setting up the threat of Ne6+, and driving Black's king further into the abyss. Clearing g5 for a more deserving piece. Black's king has been rudely shuttled all the way from the kingside to the queenside. Now, 25.Rxd5 obviously keeps a decisive advantage, but we came across a far more beautiful crusher that we cannot help but include: Simply divine! The rook is sacrificed in order to establish control of the b-file. Note that the rook on b1, which thus far has patiently awaited its turn, finally has its moment in the sun! Together with the knight and bishop, it is the architect of the mating construction. A crucial detail!

3r1r1k/8/p2bp1pB/1p2P2p/q2pN2P/P2P1P2/1P.comment: Black is down a pawn, and his kingside is in shambles. We will follow up with Qc7, when our opponent's position will collapse like a house of cards.
We continue to improve our position in countless ways. The knight will hop into c5, and Black will ultimately be forced into a nasty positional concession.

3r1r1k/8/p3p1pB/1p2b2p/q2pN1PP/P2P1P2/1P.comment: An important position that has occurred frequently in the blitz practice of the authors of this course. It is vital to avoid the tempting 9.Rg1, due to 9...g5. We have both lost countless games in precisely this fashion, especially to Minh Le and Firouzja. Instead, we must target the knight on g4 straightaway. Chasing the knight away. We saw a very similar idea (and position) in the 5...Bd6 6.Ne5 0-0 line; here, Black's king is still in the center, but that does not change any of White's ideas. As always, ...Qh4+ is coolly rebuffed by Bg3. Incredibly tempting, but wrong! Black is utterly screwed on the kingside: we will castle queenside, stick a rook on g1, and rush the h-pawn up the board.

A very difficult move to find, since this involves a minor piece sacrifice (note that this is Black's best move in the 5...Bd6 6.Ne5 0-0 version as well). The alternative, however, leads to a position that can only be described as hellish. This is far more effective than the stereotypical Nxg6. Attacking g6 and paving the way for a timely queenside castle. Further analysis is hardly needed! Black's position is in shambles. We can follow up by castling queenside, or by taking direct action on the kingside with gxh6, Bxh5, and Qh7+. In either case, Black's position is virtually resignable. As usual, this move changes nothing, since the bishop is quickly sent back to g6. Not fearing the check on h4, which is parried with Bg3. Black's knight is sent into exile on h6, when our kingside attack, coupled with our superior piece placement and the total safety of our own king (after we castle), ensures overwhelming compensation for the pawn. An ingenious defensive move, attempting to pry the bishop away from its protection of the e3-pawn. This check appears intimidating, but White's king calmly sidesteps the trouble by remaining in the center. Protecting the f2-square. We are obviously in no rush to capture the e3 pawn. An important nuance: the immediate 14.Kxe3 runs into ...d4+, so we have to wait for Black's queen to leave the fourth rank to capture the pawn. Black threatens ...d4. A superb defensive move that nips Black's initiative in the bud. We prepare to meet ...d4 with Rd1, when Black's play in the center will be instantly disarmed. It may seem more intuitive to castle queenside, but 12.0-0-0 would be a grave error on account of 12...Qh4, when White has no way to save both minor pieces. The issue is that 13.Bf2 runs into Qf4+. In this version, after 12...Qh4+ 13.Bf2 Black's queen is unable to move away with check. One of the few situations in which remaining in the center is more desirable! Black's compensation for the piece is virtually nonexistant. Grabbing space and preventing the check on h4 once and for all. Note that it is important for us to complete our queenside development and shuttle our king to safety before initiating the kingside attack in earnest. Meeting fire with fire! Opening up the center will enable us to more effectively take advantage of Black's incredibly weak pawns. Just because the queens are off the board doesn't mean that White's attack is over! Au contraire, we are just getting started!

The twin threats of exf6 and Bxh6 spell immediate doom. The queen is better placed on e2 than on d2, since ...d4 can now be met with 0-0-0. Furthermore, after we castle, e3-e4 will come with far greater effect due to the x-ray that our rook will exert against Black's queen. Setting up the devastating threat of e3-e4. Black's center has been fully shattered, and we now turn our attention to the kingside. Among other things, White threatens h4-h5 and Qxh6, as well as the prosaic Nb6.

3r1r1k/8/p3p1pB/1p2b2P/q2pN2P/P2P1P2/1P6.comment: There is no good answer to the devastating threat of Qg6+, since 12...Ng4 runs into 13.Bg5 followed by either f2-f3 or Bh3. The smoke has cleared, and the next step is to target Black's incredibly weak kingside pawns. Cold-blooded and powerful, taking the sting out of ...Qxf2 (which will now be met by Qxe6+). Turning up the pressure dial on the e6-pawn. A vital positional resource, ending Black's counterplay along the f-file.
Black's defenses are stretched to the limit, and a gorgeous maneuver seals the deal. The pressure on g6, coupled with the deadly threat of Qxh5+, is decisive.

3r1r1k/8/p3p1pB/1p2b1Pp/q2pN2P/P2P1P2/1P.comment: White loses the e5-pawn and the game. In contrast to the ...0-0 line, here this move is incredibly effective, since the capture on e4 enables us to favorably trade queens and draw Black's king onto a vulnerable square. Ignoring the forbidden fruit! Capturing on h3 would have led nowhere good after ...Qh4+. Surgical chess. With this intermediate move, we put a permanent stop to ...Qh4-related shenanigans and exert our complete dominance over the kingside. Black has no good way to defend against the twin threats of Nxg7+ and Bxh6 followed by Nf6.  Black is in deep trouble, since 12...exd5 loses immediately to 13.Bg5 Qd7 14.Bh3, with total devastation to follow. The customary move, threatening h4-h5 and forcing Black's bishop to leave the g-file. In turn, this will enable us to gang up on the tender g7-pawn. Obviously, ...Rg8 would have dropped the knight on h6. Black's objectively best option was to simply abandon the g7 pawn, but we trust that you can handle the resulting position on your own! Quiet and deadly. There is no defense to h5, which will pick up the bishop. Delaying the capture of the bishop to take away the h4-square from Black's queen. The immediate 11.gxf5 leads to a total mess after 11...Qh4+. We decide to refrain from going after the bishop altogether (12.h5 is certainly possible, but we concluded that the position after 12...fxe3 13.hxg6 fxg6 is extremely messy and hard to handle). Instead, we reestablish material equality and prepare for a devastating kingside pawn storm. Hitting where it hurts! Taking on f5 results in immediate disaster after Nxd5, so Black has no choice but to allow the partial dissolution of his center and the creation of a powerful protected passer on the kingside. The monster pawn on g5 affords us the clearly better game. Note that the pawn on e5, though isolated, is quite easy to defend. More precisely, Black does not have the time to attack it, since we threaten Bxf5 and the trade on d3 enables us to stick our queen on g6. Even if it were to be captured, the open e-file would probably favor us anyway. Needless to say, this is vastly superior to the listless 13.Ne2. The resulting endgame is utterly miserable for Black. Black is under fire from all sides, e.g.

3r1r1k/4b3/p3p1pB/1p2P2p/q2pNP1P/P2P4/1P.comment: Black loses the e-pawn, and with it the game.

3r1B1k/8/p2bp1p1/1p2P2p/q2pN2P/P2P1P2/1P.comment: Black does not even manage to gain a pawn for the exchange.

3r1r1k/8/p2bpNpB/1p2P2p/q2p3P/P2P1P2/1P4.comment: This stops g2-g4, but creates more holes on the kingside. We now transition to straightforward development, and follow up with pawn play on the queenside. The knight has nowhere good to go, since d7 is taken up by the other knight! Step 1 has been achieved. Time for phase 2, expanding in the center and preparing to shove the pawn down to e5, cramping Black even further.

3r1r1k/4b3/p3pNpB/1p2P2p/q2p3P/P2P1P2/1P.comment: A versatile move, with two main ideas. The knight can be repurposed to d3 (via f4, once the bishop moves), and by un-blocking the c-pawn, we are preparing rapid queenside expansion with an eventual c2-c4. Everything is ready for the queenside attack! Anyway! In order to un-trap the queen, Black has to give up f5: Note that we avoided 18.Rxb7 because of Nc5! White's massive queenside pressure, coupled with our pawn superiority in the center, grants us a decisive advantage.
Ignoring the possibility of ...Ne4, which doesn't bother us!
Note the power of the rook on b1, which shines through in the event that Black trades on c3. The awkwardness of Black's queen is on full display here. Driving the pawn down and gaining more space.

A sexy move indeed! We lift the rook up to g3, creating massive threats against Black's king, which has just lost its last loyal defender. White's pawn structure is visually unappealing, but our central pawn mass does a fantastic job of holding Black's counterplay at bay. For a more thorough explanation, see the note to Black's 11th move in the main line (6...Bxd3 7.cxd3). Now, it is important to avoid 15.d4, which grants Black the e4-square. Instead, we use our other pawn to push Black's knight back.
A worthwhile alternative, initiating immediate queenside play along typical lines. Of course, the pawn is untouchable due to a3.

It is worth pausing and appreciating the unique potency of White's central pawn structure. The d4-e5/e6-d5 pawn chains resemble an Advanced French, with the chief difference being the additional presence of White's pawn on d3. Visually, White's pawn mass appears rather ugly, but the pawn on d3 is actually a great asset. Any time Black pushes the c-pawn - and this is Black's only active idea - White can capture on c5 and rebuild the pawn chain with d3-d4, highlighting the hidden value inherent in having doubled pawns! Expanding on the kingside. Just because we are castled kingside certainly does not mean that we can't attack on that side of the board! Note that this move does not commit us to anything in particular: the pawn on h4 is not a serious weakness, and we are not obliged to follow up with h4-h5. We are in charge on all three sides of the board: on ther queenside, we are ready to act with b2-b4. In the center, Black has nothing going and 12...c5 fails to break up our center (see main line). On the kingside, we can expand gradually with h5, g2-g3, Kg2, Rh1, etc. Black aims to generate a semblance of activity. White aims to regroup the minor pieces by retreating the bishop to e3 (this also discourages ...c5), and repositioning the knight on f4, from where it can jump to h5.

3r1r1k/4b3/p3p1pB/1p2P2p/q2pN2P/P2P1P2/1.comment: An attempt to jump-start a kingside attack, but it falls rather short. Pushing away the knight.

Simple and powerful. We threaten to blast open the queenside with b4-b5, and the pawn is untouchable due to the pin against the queen. White is having all the fun: apart from the imminent threat of b4-b5, there are many ways to improve the position and accentuate the pressure, such as Qb3 and Be5. If Black is forced to take on c4, the e4-pawn will become a long-term weakness. Also note the awkwardness of the h5-pawn: anytime Black castles, Be5 will carry the additional threat of Bxf6 and Qxh5.

3r1r1k/4b3/p3p2B/1p2P1pp/q2pN2P/P2P1P2/1.comment: Attacking f5 and inducing yet another weakness. White's next step is to blast open the center with e3-e4. Time for the queenside pawn storm! This positional sacrifice shatters Black's central pawn chain. The knight is coming to f4, and Black is forced to capture on c4 anyway. See 14..dxc4 15.Be5 0-0. First, we centralize the bishop. The ability to take on f6 will serve us well in the long run, especially if our knight moves on to c3 or g3.
Prying open the b-file. White's compensation for the pawn is overwhelming: we are already threatening to win the pawn back with Nxh5 and Bxf6-Nxe4, but the prospect of Nf5 is even scarier.

Calmly withdrawing the king to a safer spot, underscoring the ineffectiveness of Black's pawn invasion. Black's monarch, on the other hand, has no safe haven. Our next move is c2-c4, prying open the queenside and leading to the collapse of Black's pawn structure. A sample line: The same idea that we saw in the 12...Ndf6 13.Nxe4 fxe4 14.c4 line, forcing open the b-file and leading to a long-lasting attack against Black's king.

3r1r1k/4b3/p3p2B/1p2P1pp/q2pN1PP/P2P1P2/.comment: Targeting f5 and x-raying Black's king. Rfb1 is coming next.

3r1r1k/4b3/p3p1pB/1p2P3/q2pN1pP/P2P1P2/1.comment: White's queenside attack is virtually unstoppable.

3r1r1k/3Nb3/p3p1pB/4P2p/qp1p3P/P2P1P2/1P.comment: A little prophylaxis before launching the kingside attack. We've taken the sting out of ...Bxb4, since the knight will no longer hang with check.

3r1r2/3Nb2k/p3p1pB/4P2p/qp1p3P/P2P1P2/1P.comment: The attack commences! Black has nothing going on the Q-side, while we are fully ready to tear Black apart on the other side of the board.

3rNr1k/4b3/p3p1pB/1p2P2p/q2p3P/P2P1P2/1P.comment: Using tactics to force the knight out of c5. Once again, it is important to refrain from 16.d4, which would grant Black a powerful post on e4.

2RrNr1k/4b3/p3p1pB/4P2p/qp1p3P/P2P1P2/1P.comment: Black is pushed to the edge of the board, and we will wrest the c-file from his control with Rfc1 on the next move.

3rNr1k/8/p3p1pB/1p2P2p/q2p3b/P2P1P2/1P4P.comment: Ignoring the situation on the kingside! In reality, we are preparing a devious maneuver that will force Black to lose contact with the e6-pawn.

3rN2k/4br2/p1R1p1pB/1p2P2p/q2p3P/P2P1P2/.comment: Gaining back the piece, with a clearly overwhelming position.

r1bqkb1r/ppp1pppp/2n2n2/3p4/3P1B2/2N5/PP.comment: Black has no way to defend c7 without giving up additional material. You will undoubtedly win more than a handful of games in this way!

r1bqkb1r/ppp2ppp/2n2n2/1N1pP3/5B2/8/PPP1.comment: This merely exacerbates an already critical situation.

r1bqkb1r/ppp2ppp/2n1pn2/3p4/3P1B2/2N1P3/.comment: Securing the bishop pair, or forcing the knight to a6.

r1bqk2r/ppp2ppp/2n1pn2/1N1p4/3P1b2/4PN2/.comment: We have a nice space advantage, control over the light squares, and a massive clamp on the e5-square.

r1bqkb1r/1pp2ppp/p1n5/1N1pP3/4nB2/4P3/PP.comment: Black has absolutely no compensation for the pawn.

r1bk1b1r/ppN2ppp/2n5/3qP3/4nB2/8/PPP1PPP.comment: The rest is clear without further analysis :)
